16025-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
For September 30, 1897, the children's newspaper The Great Round World led with news from the Ottoman Empire. The Sultan of Turkey, it reported, had at last ordered a commission to visit Armenian villages hurt by massacres, noting destroyed schools, churches, and monasteries. Two Muslims, three Armenians, and one Greek sat on the commission, which was also to plan orphan asylums.

The paper's promise was news made readable for children, without long speeches or hard words. Each number mixed foreign affairs with home news and short features, so a school reader could follow the world week by week. This issue captures a moment of late Victorian concern for Armenia and for the victims of mass violence.
23572-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, number three hundred seventy nine for May eighteen forty seven, opens with a long essay on M. de Tocqueville, hailed as one of the greatest political thinkers of the day, fit to stand beside Machiavelli and Bacon. Less caustic than Tacitus and less eloquent than Burke, Tocqueville earns praise for calm judgment, a keen eye, and just reflection.

Born amid French party strife, placed between feudal ruins and modern rebuilding, he surveyed both worlds with rare balance, the essay argues. Other pieces in the number keep Blackwood's mix of politics, literature, and review. Readers of Victorian journals will enjoy the essay as a contemporary verdict on Democracy in America, written while its author still lived and Europe still argued over his ideas.
23690-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine for April 1847 opens with a long review essay on Cromwell, taking Thomas Carlyle's edition of Cromwell's letters and speeches as its text. The reviewer praises Carlyle as an editor while sharply disputing him as a commentator, calling his hero-worship of the Puritan leader extravagant and his view of English Puritanism paradoxical.

As a monthly miscellany, the issue goes on to other articles, tales, and reviews in Blackwood's Tory voice. The Cromwell essay sets its tone: learned, combative, and sure of its judgments. For modern readers it is a window onto how Victorian Britain argued about its revolutionary past, in the very pages where such arguments were fought.
25633-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, number 384 for October 1847, volume sixty-two, gathers essays, tales, and reviews in the monthly's usual mix. Transcribers note that vowels with macron and breve marks are rendered with special signs in this text.

Contents list Hans Christian Andersen and the Emperor's New Clothes, the Vision of Cagliostro, pieces on Tiberius, Agrippa, Milton, Mirabeau, and Beethoven, Maga in America, and the times of George II. Art in early Christian ages, the Portrait, hounds and horses at Rome, and a song follow, with a note on Andersen's Improvisatore opening the reading.
26484-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine for June 1847 leads with an essay on North America, Siberia, and Russia, following Sir George Simpson's overland circuit of the globe. The Hudson's Bay governor galloped from the Atlantic to the Pacific, then on to the British Channel, glancing at the Wall of China and the Arctic Circle. He pressed through polar regions, past tribes whose names alone survive, to the Russian court.

The essay wonders at the journey's purpose, which a governor dedicating his volumes to his company's directors does not reveal. Elsewhere the number turns classical, tracing a passage of Catullus to a freer rendering of Euripides' Hippolytus, where a garland is offered to Artemis from an untouched meadow. Travel, empire, and letters share the issue.
27020-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine for August 1847, number 382, opens with a long review of Grote's History of Greece, praised as equal to the demands of a critical age. The reviewer sets Grote above earlier historians like Mitford for his judgment of evidence and his feel for past times.

The rest of the number ranges widely: Ben Nevis and Ben Muich Dhui, a letter on truths in popular superstitions, and a history of Napoleon's captivity at St. Helena. Fiction and essay follow, with Juancho the bull-fighter, The Emerald Studs, and a piece on Reid and the philosophy of common sense.
31859-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, number 377, March 1847, volume sixty-one, opens with an essay on pauperism and its treatment. It is introduced by Wordsworth's lines on turning elsewhere to see ill sights of maddening passions mutually inflamed. Its argument insists that to deal with pauperism, one must know the causes that impoverish individuals and masses.

The essay follows displaced workers, coachmen, guards, ostlers, horse-keepers, harness-makers, and farriers, into the back streets and alleys of London, the records of benevolent institutions, and conversations with administrators of parochial relief. Readers get a Victorian magazine issue that treats poverty as a practical problem, not a natural law.
32539-eight-days-in-new-orleans-in-febru:
Albert J. Pickett's Eight Days in New-Orleans in February, 1847 gathers sketches first printed in the Alabama Journal of Montgomery. Written from a few days' sojourn in the Crescent City, the book opens with De Soto's discovery of the Mississippi and the fate of his expedition.

Pickett describes New Orleans as a magnificent emporium of commerce, setting its present trade against its early history. He warns readers that his time for collecting facts was short and that he was trying descriptive and historic writing for the first time, asking charitable friends to forgive imperfections.
58888-graham-s-magazine-vol-xxxi-no-4-oc:
Graham's Magazine for October 1847 forms this number, the fourth of its thirty-first year. The list of parts splits the sheet in two halves, as the sheet splits its fare. The first half is prose: tales, lore, and prose pieces. A tale of a town's sawbones stands at the head. A court of old days and a tale of a firkin of butter, a tale of a flirt, and a tale of the red men come in its train.

More prose runs on: the isles of the gulf in a long tale cut in parts, a ruse, a man with a big box, and the hunt. A look at new books closes that half. The next half gives verse, tune, and dress. Names like Le Follet, Brain Work and Hand Work, and Midnight and Daybreak show its spread.
andersen-improvisatore-howitt-1847:
Hans Christian Andersen published The Improvisatore in Denmark in 1835, and Mary Howitt Englished it in 1847. The novel made Andersen famous across Europe a decade before his fairy tales ruled nurseries. Antonio, a poor Roman boy with a gift for improvised song, tells his own story from childhood onward.

Antonio rises from street singer to admired performer, through love, loss, and patronage. Rome, Naples, and Venice glow in the background of his fortunes. Andersen drew on his own Italian travels and his hunger for recognition. Howitt, a tireless carrier of Scandinavian writing into English, gave the book its English life. It stands apart from the tales, as his great novel of the artist.
arxiv-2412-08547:
Véronique Bruyère, Jean-François Raskin, Alexis Reynouard, and Marie Van Den Bogaard wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-four. It studies how to build a system that holds its own when rational foes reply with subgame perfect play.

In these graph games one player, the system, states its plan first. The rest, the environment, then answer with strategies in subgame perfect equilibrium. Goals are ω-regular, given as parity conditions. The authors encode the task as a three-player game with hidden facts, which puts the cost in double-exponential time. With the foe count fixed, the cost drops a class, though the task stays hard both ways. For reach goals with fixed players, a fast method exists.
arxiv-2412-09847:
Keiko Nagao studies how to detect dark matter that has been sped up by other dark matter in a 2024 particle physics study. The model holds two dark matter components, one heavy and one light, linked by a hidden force. Heavy particles annihilating near the center of the Galaxy can kick light ones to high speeds, making them easier to spot in a detector.

Directional detectors, which record which way a recoil points, suit this search because the boosted particles stream from the Galactic center. Nagao estimates event rates reaching the order of ten per year in a modest mass of detector material. Such rates put the scenario within reach of planned experiments.
arxiv-2412-10247:
Basilio, Kupriyanov, and Kurkov study a charged particle in a noncommutative electrodynamics in twenty twenty-four. The theory is the semi classical limit of a noncommutative gauge theory. Space coordinates in it fail to commute in a Lie algebra pattern. The authors focus on one charged point particle in a fixed gauge background.

They derive explicit formulas for gauge invariant variables that give the particle position. They then write the classical action and the equations of motion in full. In the limit where noncommutativity vanishes, standard relativistic dynamics return. As an example, they solve the Kepler problem under angular noncommutativity exactly. Other examples illustrate the framework. The work clarifies how noncommutative effects alter particle motion.
arxiv-2412-11347:
Dial and ten co-authors report a detailed study of a single fast radio burst caught by an Australian array in two thousand twenty-three. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. Fast radio bursts are millisecond flashes from deep space whose sources stay unknown. A few show a near-regular pulse pattern inside the flash, which can hint at what made them.

This burst stood out for its rich shape in both time and polarization. The team fit its profile to test for rhythm, scattering, and twinkling. They found a possible beat of a few milliseconds, but the signal was weak. Its strong circular polarization did not come from a known conversion effect. Most traits fit a magnetar whose beamed emission carries fine structure. Other sources, the authors note, are not yet ruled out.
arxiv-2412-12147:
Seongwoong Cho, Donggyun Kim, Jinwoo Lee, and Seunghoon Hong present Meta-Controller, a framework for robot imitation learning, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-four. A useful robot policy should transfer to new robot bodies and new tasks. Modular methods adapt to bodies but not tasks, while imitation methods usually assume one body.

Their few-shot behavior cloning needs only a handful of reward-free demonstrations. A joint-level representation unifies state and action spaces across different robots. A structure-motion encoder captures both shared knowledge and body-specific knowledge. A matching-based policy network then predicts actions for the new setting. Tests in the DeepMind Control suite showed the adaptive policy resisted overfitting while generalizing broadly.
arxiv-2412-13847:
Yuchong Geng and Ao Tang propose a concept-centric framework for learning across modalities, in a two thousand twenty-four machine learning paper. Humans learn once and reuse knowledge across senses through a shared understanding of the world.

The framework centers on a modality-agnostic concept space holding structured, abstract knowledge. Separate projection models map each kind of raw input into that space and are trained independently, so new modalities plug in without retraining the core. Experiments show faster convergence than baseline models. On two downstream tasks the framework matches standard results with a smaller training footprint, no task-specific fine-tuning, and the interpretability of reasoning inside a shared concept space.
arxiv-2412-18047:
Lo Pang-Yun Ting and five colleagues design a control system, in a 2024 preprint, for charging electric cars at workplaces. New chargers can also discharge cars back into the building, which adds options and risk. Prices change through the day, and drivers leave at uncertain times. The goal is to cut the building's power bill while giving each car the charge it needs. A single controller would face too many shifting parts at once.

Their design splits the job into two levels. A top agent watches prices and decides which cars charge or discharge. Lower agents set the exact power for each car. A special critic tweak helps the lower agents judge choices when departure times are unsure. Tests on real power data showed clear savings. The system still met charging needs under both fixed and uncertain leaving times. A case study shows it shifting energy in real time.
arxiv-2412-20047:
Phi Vu Tran presented a simple recipe in 2024 for finding rare objects in images. Real datasets are long-tailed: a few common classes have many examples, while most classes have barely any, and detectors starve on the rare ones. Earlier fixes leaned on huge labeled databases from outside, which many real projects cannot use, or added complex meta-learning machinery.

SimLTD works in three plain steps: train on the abundant classes, transfer to the scarce ones, then fine-tune on a balanced sample of both. Optional unlabeled images, cheap to gather, can join through semi-supervised learning. On the hard LVIS benchmark the framework set new records in both modes. Simplicity is the point: no outside labels, no distillation tricks.
arxiv-2501-00647:
Abdesselam Ferdi, writing solo, builds a lean detector for broken bones in children's wrist X-rays. The paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five, with a late two thousand twenty-four posting. Computer-aided diagnosis helps doctors read images faster. Existing fracture detectors are heavy and hungry for compute. Clinics with modest hardware cannot run them well. A lighter design is the goal.

His G-YOLOv11 builds on the newest YOLO detector family. Ghost convolutions cut the arithmetic while keeping feature counts. Fewer operations mean cheaper, faster scans. Tests use a public dataset of pediatric wrist images. Detection quality stays respectable at the smaller size. Point-of-care tools for children's injuries gain a candidate.
arxiv-2501-01147:
Gopi Chand Ananthu and Riadul Islam wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It designs a bridge chip block that lets a fast system bus talk to slow add-on gear, built and tested on an FPGA with a Raspberry Pi in the loop.

The high-speed AHB bus links cores and memory, while the lean APB bus serves slow parts. The bridge turns burst AHB trades into single APB steps, and handles clock gaps and flow pace so the two sides stay in step. Written in Verilog and run in Xilinx Vivado, the design is checked by test benches across many cases. The project shows a sound way to mix fast and slow parts on one chip.
arxiv-2501-05447: Piotr Pokora studied plane curves in twenty twenty-five through two polynomial invariants that encode their topology. The Betti and Poincare polynomials summarize a curve's homology in compact algebraic form. Computing them for complex curves is often done in bits. Small parts are added one at a time. Pokora uses this addition technique in a set way. The work gives polynomial identities. They link the invariants of reduced plane curves to those of their parts. Such formulas let researchers build global topological facts from local pieces.
arxiv-2501-06547:
Three authors, Chazottes, Gallo, and Takahashi, built a way to guess time series values path by path. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with category and count series whose symbol set has no bound. The task: from a finite sample, learn a rule that guesses a held out chunk from the rest with near best odds. Old stats paths first guess the chance laws in full. Their path skips that step and learns the guess rule direct.

Its learn speed does not rest on the size of the symbol set. The proof spans a wide class: finite Markov chains, some hidden ones, count models, and Gibbs forms. A margin term sets the pace. Readers in time series get a guess tool for wild symbol worlds.
arxiv-2501-07047:
Jianming Tong and ten co-authors run homomorphic encryption on AI chips to close the efficiency gap with custom hardware. Their paper from twenty twenty-five tackles encryption that lets clouds compute on sealed data. The privacy is strong; the cost is brutal. Graphics cards help but trail bespoke chips on energy by a wide factor. AI accelerators like TPUs promise ASIC-grade thrift at commodity scale.

Two mismatches block the port. Encryption math wants wide integers, while the chip's fast engine eats small ones. Its coarse memory also hates fine data shuffles. Their CROSS compiler fixes both. One transform recasts wide modular math as dense small-integer matrix work. Another bakes reordering into the kernels ahead of time. On a current TPU, throughput per watt beats the listed GPU and ASIC rivals.
arxiv-2501-08947:
Leen Lambers, Lucas Sakizloglou, Taisiya Khakharova, and Fernando Orejas present the first systematic taint analysis for graph APIs, aimed at broken access control. Their paper from twenty twenty-five taints any graph node holding data that needs privileges to touch. Source and sink calls are modeled as graph transformation rules. Critical pair analysis then hunts dependencies that betray a tainted flow.

Direct and indirect flows get separate treatment, with conditions for when the static pass catches each. Flagged flows guide the design of dynamic security tests that confirm real risks. A slice of GitHub's GraphQL API serves as the testbed. Both failure directions surface: users wrongly locked out, and users wrongly let in. API security gains a systematic audit method.
arxiv-2501-09547:
Mathieu Perron-Cormier and Nathan Deg lead a large team on this paper from two thousand twenty-five. It compares how lopsided the hydrogen gas in real galaxies looks, in the WALLABY pilot survey, against the same trait in the SIMBA simulation of galaxy growth.

The team built a scanline method to make fake survey data cubes with less noise than older particle-based ways. They then measured one- and three-dimensional lopsidedness for the real finds. The most lopsided cases were merging systems or ones with bridges and tails. Fake survey draws from SIMBA showed fewer high cases, but the gap was not firm. Bigger survey and simulation runs should sharpen the test.
arxiv-2501-10147:
Mayu Hiraishi, Kensuke Tanioka, and Hiroshi Yadohisa propose a clustering method in a twenty twenty-five paper. Clustering groups data points so that alike points sit together. Their base method uses a scoring matrix from discriminant analysis, kept sparse so the groups stay readable.

The new version adds a penalty drawn from convex clustering. The penalty pulls points in one cluster closer and pushes apart points from distinct clusters, which sharpens the picture when plotted. The scoring matrix must stay orthogonal while it learns this shape, a hard pair of demands. The team builds an update rule with a majorizing function and tests it on simulations and real data.
arxiv-2501-13347:
Qingyue Long, Can Rong, Huandong Wang, and Yong Li build one model for many mobility trajectory tasks. Their twenty twenty-five paper proposes the GenMove framework. Trajectory data support network planning and city services alike. Past models were trained for single tasks like prediction or recovery.

Different tasks share common movement patterns, the authors argue. Masks unify the varied input and output formats. Past trajectories supply context about place, time, and user habits. A conditional diffusion model then handles generation, recovery, or prediction. One system replaces several separate task-specific models. The design aims to transfer learning across tasks instead of starting over each time.
arxiv-2501-18347:
Dennis Perepelitsa describes di-hadron saturation signals with a universal nuclear parton approach in two thousand twenty-five. Paired hadron yields drop in proton nucleus hits at forward angles. That drop is often read as a sign of QCD saturation. The width of their angle spread stays put, which clashes with that tale.

Modern nuclear parton sets may explain the whole pattern instead. Shadowing of low momentum gluons does the work in his checks. Sets tuned by fresh precision data fit most of the drop. No extra dynamics that warp event links are needed. The width puzzle gets a natural answer that way.
arxiv-2502-00847:
Jiawen Zhang, Kejia Chen, and five colleagues pursue privacy and robustness for language model services at the same time, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. The two goals are usually chased separately: encryption schemes guard user data, while prompt ensembling blurs attacks by averaging several prompted answers.

Their system, SecPE, fuses the two lines of work. Private inference encrypts the data sent to and processed by the model. Prompt ensembling asks the model several rephrased versions of a request and aggregates the replies, which dilutes adversarial tricks. Simply bolting the two together is inefficient, the authors show, so they design the combination from scratch. The result aims at inference that is both confidential and hard to fool. Services facing the public need both traits at once. The paper is among the first attempts to deliver them jointly.
arxiv-2502-05447:
Xinke Xie, Yang Lu, and Zhiguo Ding design wireless transmitters whose antennas can slide along a guide in a 2025 study. Pinching antennas place small dielectric pieces on a waveguide so signals radiate close to users, cutting the loss that grows with distance. Placing those pieces well, and setting their power, is a joint design problem.

The authors model the link between antennas and users as a bipartite graph. A graph neural network then learns placement and power choices together. Learning replaces repeated hard optimization for each new layout. Flexible antennas that follow users could raise data rates in crowded indoor and urban networks.
arxiv-2502-06147:
Eri Onami, Taiki Miyanishi, Koki Maeda, and Shuhei Kurita built LegalViz in twenty twenty-five, a data set pairing legal documents with diagrams that explain them. Judgments and court orders demand expert knowledge; a simple diagram of parties, transactions, and legal sources can open them to lay readers. Their collection spans twenty-three languages and over seven thousand cases, with diagrams written in the DOT graph language.

The authors add evaluation metrics that judge a generated diagram by its graph structure, text similarity, and legal content. Few-shot and fine-tuned language models were tested across the languages. Models trained on LegalViz beat existing systems, including GPT-class models. The work treats legal visualization as a translation problem with its own quality measures.
arxiv-2502-07647:
Simon Grad and Sandi Klavžar count matched edge sets in graphs built by gluing. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, studies matchings, sets of edges that share no endpoints. A k-matching holds exactly k such edges. Counts of these sets matter in chemistry, where graphs stand for molecules.

Their method uses a transfer matrix built on a matching vector. It works for any graph assembled by joins over two-point sets. That reach goes far past past methods for chains of rings found in fuels and dyes. Two worked cases show the steps, one of them a full chemical example. The tool turns a hard count into routine matrix work.
arxiv-2502-08547:
Doudou Zhou leads a large team from the United States and France on a data problem in hospital research. Their two thousand twenty-five paper deals with electronic health records. Records are rich, but each hospital codes facts in its own way. Privacy rules also block sharing patient-level data across sites. Joint studies stall when the same idea wears many codes.

The team treats harmonizing the codes as a learning task on a graph. Their framework learns shared forms for clinical ideas across sites. It does so without moving raw patient data. The goal is studies that span many hospitals in both countries. Cleaner shared forms should make such joint work faster and more sound. The paper aims at research that no single site could run alone.
arxiv-2502-12147:
Xiang Fu and colleagues judged atomistic AI models by whether their simulations conserve energy in a 2025 paper. Machine learning potentials mimic quantum calculations at a sliver of the cost, yet low test error often fails to predict success on real properties like stability or heat flow. The authors propose a practical gate: run molecular dynamics and check that total energy stays constant, as physics demands.

Models that fail the gate show telltale design choices, which the team used to fix a highly expressive architecture. The resulting model, eSEN, topped benchmarks across materials stability, thermal conductivity, and lattice vibration tasks. A physics sanity check, they argue, predicts downstream usefulness better than leaderboard error alone.
arxiv-2502-12847:
Marjieh, Anglada-Tort, Griffiths, and Jacoby wrote in twenty twenty-five about how songs change as people pass them along in groups. Culture can shift through what is on offer, what people pick, and how well they copy it. Past work rarely tested all three forces at once. The team placed two thousand four hundred four people in networks. Each person chose a tune from neighbors and sang it back.

Tunes in these networks grew more complex and more pleasant than in simple chains. The shape of the network mattered for what emerged. When the team removed choice bias or copying bias, those network gaps shrank. That pattern shows the forces work together, not alone. The study gives a clear test bed for how shared culture forms.
arxiv-2502-14847:
Pengfei He, Yupin Lin, Shen Dong, Han Xu, Yue Xing, and Hui Liu expose a security hole, in a 2025 preprint, in systems where several AI agents work as a team. Such teams solve hard problems by passing messages between agents. That message channel is also a weak point no one had tested. The authors act as attackers and ask whether the whole team can be corrupted without touching any single agent. They may only intercept and rewrite messages in transit.

Their attack, called Agent-in-the-Middle, uses an AI-powered adversary to edit those messages. A reflection step helps it craft edits that fit the flow and each agent's role. Tests across frameworks, team shapes, and real applications showed the attack works. Teams followed the poisoned messages and failed or misbehaved. The authors warn these systems need defenses built around their communication layer, not just each agent.
arxiv-2502-15547: Hsueh and Hsu present a paper from twenty twenty-five on a scoring method for a dice board game. Their method builds the board score from data, with no hand tuning. It records how far each piece sits from the target corner, a list they say captures the core of the game. Their scorer beat many classic hand-made scorers and won first place in a twenty twenty-three contest for the game.
arxiv-2502-19047:
Truong and Le built this two-way tool in twenty twenty-five for guarding image generators. Diffusion models can be backdoored: a hidden trigger makes them output a set harmful image. Owners need to spot such traps, yet the search method itself is powerful. Their framework, PureDiffusion, works on both sides of that line.

Two new loss functions guide a search that reconstructs the hidden trigger. One uses shifts the trigger causes across the model's time steps. The other uses a consistency quirk that fires when the backdoor wakes. Recovered triggers then flag attacks with near-perfect accuracy in tests. Turned around, the same search can sharpen a planted trigger. The authors report far faster, stronger attacks that way.
arxiv-2502-20347:
Ozkan, Chrstos, Canova, and Stockar modeled driver behavior in speed advisory systems in twenty twenty-five. Such systems show drivers a suggested speed, and the car works better when it can predict how the human will respond. Driver responses are nonlinear and change over time, which makes them hard to model.

Their approach uses the Koopman operator, a tool that recasts nonlinear dynamics into a linear form suited to fast prediction. A recursive least squares update keeps the model adapting as a driver's behavior drifts. They validated it on data from a human-in-the-loop driving simulator covering varied driver styles. The offline model already predicted behavior closely, and online updates improved accuracy further.
arxiv-2503-05547:
Hati and nine co-authors describe a way to make a very steady radio signal from light signals. Their paper, from two thousand twenty-five, reaches doubt levels below one part in a huge count.

Two chains each start with a laser held steady by a cold or glass space. Comb tools turn the light first to a fast wave signal, then down to a slower radio one. The team built a new, low-noise digital tool to check each step. They match its results with a known check method. The work aids clocks and tests that need radio tones of the utmost steadiness.
arxiv-2503-07047:
Yongle Zhang and co-authors tackled image repair in 2025 for objects that are only partly damaged. Text-guided diffusion editors can repaint a masked region from a written prompt. But a prompt cannot say exactly where surviving edges and textures should continue, so repairs often clash with the intact part of the object. Sketch guidance helps, yet earlier sketch methods let information flow only one way, from the sketch into the hole.

Their method, built on a pre-taught diffusion model, makes the contact run in both directions. Context from the uncorrupted area first informs the sketch traits, and the enriched sketch then guides the inpainting, a pairing the authors call context-to-sketch and sketch-to-inpainting contact. The two-way exchange keeps the filled region steady with the surviving form, reducing the mismatches that betray a repair.
arxiv-2503-09347:
Hongyu Chen and Seraphina Goldfarb-Tarrant show that language models judging content safety can be swayed by surface tricks, not substance. Their paper from twenty twenty-five tests eleven judge models across key safety domains. Three checks structure the study: consistency across repeat judgments, agreement with humans, and sensitivity to artifacts like apologetic or wordy phrasing. Verdicts wobble on all three.

Apologetic language alone can swing preferences by up to ninety-eight percent. Bigger models are not reliably tougher; some small ones resist specific artifacts better. Jury voting across models helps both robustness and human alignment, yet artifact sensitivity survives the best juries. The authors warn that comparative safety claims built on such judges rest on sand until artifact-proof methods arrive.
arxiv-2503-10147:
Wenrui Yu and three co-authors secure distributed consensus in twenty twenty-five. Multi-agent systems often agree on a median value, which resists outliers and bad sensors. The data behind that median can be sensitive. Privacy-preserving median consensus had barely been studied.

The authors give the first rigorous analysis of privacy for this problem. Working in an L1-norm minimization frame, they find exact conditions for a double win. Consensus can be exact while privacy is perfect, meaning zero information leakage. Guarantees hold against passive and eavesdropping adversaries. Numerical experiments confirm the theory's practical feasibility. Readers in distributed systems get a rare case where accuracy and secrecy need not trade off.
arxiv-2503-10247:
Zhijie Zhu, Lei Fan, Maurice Pagnucco, and Yang Song wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It classifies images by object parts the model can point to, so each call comes with a reason a person can check.

Part prototype networks mimic how people judge: this looks like that beak, that wing. Past builds lean on dull, repeated parts, which thin the story they tell. Here the parts are learned by clustering deep traits from foundation vision models, with no set shape imposed. The parts come out distinct and varied for each class. Two new scores grade how distinct and how full the account is. On bird, car, and dog sets the method matches past scores while reading far better.
arxiv-2503-14347:
Zishun Liu, Sam Power, and Yongxin Chen give a new proof of a core concentration inequality for sub-Gaussian random variables. The inequality bounds how sharply the norm of a random vector, or the operator norm of a random matrix, concentrates around its expectation. Standard proofs use epsilon-nets and union bounds.

Their method instead works with an averaged version of the moment generating function. Avoiding the union bound promises tighter concentration estimates. The argument covers both the vector and matrix cases in a unified way. Such inequalities underpin high-dimensional statistics and random matrix theory, so a cleaner proof with better constants has broad technical value.
arxiv-2503-14647:
Hanchen Li, Yuhan Liu, Yihua Cheng, and two colleagues ask a money question about language model caches, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Many apps now reuse stored key-value caches. The model can then skip re-reading repeated input, cutting the wait for a first reply.

The open question is cost. Keeping those caches on cloud services means paying for storage, network transfer, and compute. The savings depend on how often text repeats, how long replies run, and how big the model is. The authors build a tested analytical model of those cloud costs. Their early results map when reuse pays for itself and when it quietly loses money. The work gives developers a way to price a popular speed trick before adopting it. It treats the cache not as free memory but as rented shelf space.
arxiv-2503-15747:
Sylwia Cichacz and Claire Hilaire lead a team characterizing graphs where some path passes near every vertex, and exactly which forbidden patterns force that to happen. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Path eccentricity measures the worst distance from a chosen spine path. A classic result guarantees a fully spanning path when two small patterns are excluded.

Generalizing, they show that excluding two specific graphs caps eccentricity below any chosen bound. Conversely, a single excluded pattern works exactly when it hides inside two named families. Their proof leans on structural domination theory from earlier work. A polynomial-time algorithm finds the witnessing path robustly. The result also closes an open question from a recent paper. Such characterizations turn vague intuition about graph shape into checkable conditions. Algorithmic payoffs ride along with the theory.
arxiv-2503-16047:
Bisola Faith Kayode and a team of co-authors set out a new network defense model, called TSAN, to spot denial-of-service attacks in network traffic. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Such attacks flood a service to knock it out, and they cost firms a great deal. Old rule-based and count-based tools adapt poorly as attack forms change. The new model watches both when traffic moves and how it spreads, so it can catch odd shapes that old tools miss. It joins a transformer-style encoder for time with a shaped filter for space. The aim is a guard that keeps pace with fast-changing attacks.
arxiv-2503-17547:
Bart Bussmann, Noa Nabeshima, Adam Karvonen, and Neel Nanda redesign sparse autoencoders, a tool for reading the concepts inside a neural network, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. These tools learn a dictionary of features from a network's activity, but the dictionary's size forces an awkward trade-off.

Make the dictionary bigger and the pressure for sparsity splits broad features into narrow ones, warping or erasing the high-level ideas. The team's Matryoshka variant trains several nested dictionaries at once, from small to large. Each smaller dictionary must rebuild the input on its own, without leaning on the bigger ones. That pressure sorts features into levels: small dictionaries hold general concepts, larger ones add specifics. High-level features survive instead of being absorbed. The design borrows its name from nesting dolls, and it aims to give interpreters a cleaner map of what a network knows.
arxiv-2503-24147:
Charles St-Arnault and a large team report a record optical link for data center reaches, moving three point two trillion bits per second down two kilometers of fiber. The system uses intensity modulation with direct detection in the O-band, carrying eight lanes of two hundred twenty-five gigabaud four-level signals. Thin-film lithium niobate modulators do the encoding, driven by a three-nanometer chip. Two standard configurations, for longer and shorter reaches, are both demonstrated.

A faster variant reaches four point two trillion bits per second with eight-level signaling. Error rates stayed under the hard-decision forward error correction threshold. The authors claim the first demonstration at these rates with this component pairing. Data centers hungry for bandwidth between buildings are the audience. The result presses commodity-style optics toward rates once reserved for coherent systems.
arxiv-2504-00147:
Collin Zhang, John X. Morris, and Vitaly Shmatikov study how much text can be recovered from a numeric summary of that text, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Such summaries, called embeddings, power search tools and data stores. If text can be rebuilt from them, private content may leak.

Older recovery methods need a fresh trained model for each kind of embedding, plus many queries. The new method needs no such training and works on any embedding. It builds guesses by steering a text generator against the target summary. Tests on several embeddings show it recovers the key meaning of the source texts. The work gives a cheaper way to audit this leak risk.
arxiv-2504-01147:
Dana Avramescu and four co-authors studied in twenty twenty-five how the glasma — the dense color fields filling a heavy-ion collision's first instants — pushes heavy quarks around. Heavy quarks are born early and witness the whole collision; whether the pre-equilibrium glasma stage leaves fingerprints on them was unclear. The team evolved the fields with classical Yang-Mills equations and the quarks with Wong's equations.

They computed the momentum-broadening coefficient, finding it anisotropic and initially very large. The standard suppression observable for heavy quarks, R-AA, shifted only moderately under glasma effects, less than nuclear parton distribution effects. The striking impact was on pairs: charm and anticharm quarks created back-to-back had their azimuthal correlation strongly smeared by the glasma fields — a potential early-stage signature.
arxiv-2504-01647:
Tobias Fischer and a large team teach a generative model to imagine the extra viewpoints that a sparse three-dimensional scan is missing. Gaussian splatting renders scenes beautifully in real time, but quality collapses away from the photographed angles, and dense photo shoots are slow and costly. Earlier fixes distilled two-dimensional generators or hallucinated extra views from a few references, producing inconsistent inventions that corrupted the reconstruction. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team's flow matching model instead learns the direct path from a sparse reconstruction's renderings to the renderings a dense capture would give.

Trained on millions of paired images, the model processes dozens of views in one pass on a single high-end graphics card. Pipelines using it beat earlier works on standard view-synthesis benchmarks in both sparse and dense regimes, the authors report. Virtual reality capture is the motivating customer.
arxiv-2504-02547:
Patricia Puchhammer, Ines Wilms, and Peter Filzmoser checked whether official data groups match statistical clusters in a 2025 paper. Experts often pre-label observations into groups, by diagnosis or design, yet the data themselves may cluster differently, and single bad cells in a spreadsheet can wreck the comparison. Their multi-group Gaussian mixture model is the first built to ask that question directly, using prior groups as a starting point while letting the data reassign members to better-fitting groups.

Each group's observations are modeled as a mixture over all group profiles, so evidence can pull a case across the border. A penalized estimation method flags outlying cells and keeps them from distorting the fit, with proven breakdown resistance and an efficient algorithm.
arxiv-2504-04147:
Zhibin Li, Danning Li, and Mei Huang looked for fingerprints of a critical point in quark matter in a 2025 paper. Holographic models borrow gravity calculations to mimic the strong force at high heat and density, where a critical end point may mark where smooth change turns into a sharp phase transition. Jets of quarks plowing through the hot matter lose energy, and how much they lose could betray the nearby critical point.

Across systems with two or more quark flavors, the team tracked the jet quenching measure and the energy loss of light and heavy quarks near the transition. All rose rapidly close to the critical temperature. Heavy quark loss also scaled with speed differently than familiar charged-particle loss in electric matter, hinting at collisional drag.
arxiv-2504-07647:
Ignacio Santamaria, Jesús Gutiérrez, Mohammad Soleymani, and Eduard Jorswieck study rates in beyond diagonal RIS systems in two thousand twenty-five. A reconfigurable intelligent surface shapes radio waves to aid a link. Beyond diagonal forms couple the surface elements in richer ways. Their case has line of sight paths to and from the surface.

The direct link lacks a line of sight path in their setup. They derive a closed form for the rate that can be reached. From it they get the best surface matrix in closed form too. Tests show the fix stays strong under a more standard fading model. Gains hold when the direct link is weak.
arxiv-2504-07947:
Grant Brodnik and colleagues show how to build tiny optical devices that convert laser light to new colors at high power without extra noise. Inside a ring-shaped resonator, a pump laser can split into two new waves, but rival processes usually compete and spoil the output. Earlier designs used a patterned ring to open a band gap that allows only chosen interactions. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team adds careful shaping of the mode spacing so unwanted interactions are suppressed, while the band gap switches on just one desired conversion.

Their devices produced strong output waves with clean spectra and weak side modes. By changing only the patterning numbers, they built four oscillators that each selected different output colors, showing the design can be tuned on demand. The authors present patterned resonators as a flexible and nearly lossless toolkit for compact light sources.
arxiv-2504-08547:
Vassili Korotkine, Mitchell Cohen, and James Richard Forbes locate a robot that cannot tell its landmarks apart. Their paper came out in two thousand twenty-five. The robot measures relative positions to known landmarks. It does not know which landmark each reading came from. Guessing wrong can wreck the position estimate. Local solvers often settle into that wrong guess.

Their method casts the problem as a semidefinite relaxation. It solves for robot states and landmark matches together. The answer is globally optimal, not just a local best. For moderate noise, the relaxation is tight in most cases. Tests in simulation and experiment beat Gauss-Newton baselines started from dead reckoning. The team also shares software for the method. Certifiable localization gains a practical tool.
arxiv-2504-10847:
Saikat Das, Bing Zhang, Soebur Razzaque, and Siyao Xu test what a single ultra-high-energy neutrino says about cosmic rays. Their paper from twenty twenty-five studies an event caught by the KM3NeT telescope. The neutrino's huge energy points to a parent cosmic ray of even greater force. A light-based birth path for it needs extreme cosmic-ray power per particle.

Three source stories are weighed: a brief flare, a steady diffuse glow, and a line-of-sight hit. Fits draw on KM3NeT alone and on joint data with IceCube and Auger. A flare source would need a new, common, gamma-dark class of events. The diffuse story strains the KM3-only fit at far distances. The joint fit holds for sources not too far away. A point-source birth near bright galaxy cores also stays in line with known limits.
arxiv-2504-13747: Parisel presents a paper from twenty twenty-five on scoring privilege risk in Microsoft Azure cloud accounts. Two scores cover the control side and the data side of the cloud. The control score orders accounts by their power to change settings. It weights write, action, and read rights in rising order. The data score gauges the widest reach of data theft or forgery. It leans on the tree shape of Azure tenant grouping. Together the scores form one frame for permission analysis.
arxiv-2504-14447:
Jeonghwa Lee, writing alone in two thousand twenty-five, finds the large-scale limit of a walk whose steps rest on a fresh kind of linked chance chain. The chain can hold long-range links between its terms.

The limit is a new class of spread paths with no fixed step memory. In it are paths whose links fade at a set rate, as a power, or as a power damped by a set rate. Their spread rules take a split-order form, in some cases damped in time. Two known laws come out as set cases. Lee also treats time-changed forms of the paths, and sets out their rules and link build.
arxiv-2504-15347:
Miguel Prado Reynoso and five co-authors study sharp state changes in Kerr parametric oscillators, small quantum systems driven from outside. These systems serve in quantum computing, sensing, and basic research, and are built in circuits and light based setups. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The team looks at how spin like symmetry in the system's phase space shapes its state changes. They study drive rates at one, two, three, and four times the natural rate. With the classic form of the system math, they find the key points where states shift. They also track true and near crossings of energy levels and how those crossings affect tunneling between states.
arxiv-2504-18147:
Rob Romijnders, Stefanos Laskaridis, and colleagues transfer knowledge between model modules without leaking private data in a 2025 study. Big models are often trained on mixed sources, and even modular designs, where experts specialize, can leak information about those sources. Training each module in isolation protects privacy but blocks the generalization that shared learning brings.

Their framework joins differential privacy with a two-stage, parameter-efficient fine-tuning scheme. Knowledge moves between modules under a privacy budget that bounds what any output can reveal. Modular adaptation with guarantees suits hospitals and firms that must pool skill without pooling records.
arxiv-2504-18947:
Sainik Karak, Akshay Kumar, and Tanmoy Paul study when extending a linear measurement is forced to be unique in a 2025 mathematics study. The Hahn-Banach theorem guarantees that a functional defined on a subspace can be extended to the whole space, but extensions need not be unique. In locally convex spaces, broader than Banach spaces, they ask which subspaces enjoy a uniqueness property modeled on a classical one.

Characterizations follow for the new property, along with a description of spaces where every subspace has it. A bridge result ties the classical property to the weak topology version, letting old theorems do new work.
arxiv-2504-19047:
David Almog wrote this economics paper, published in 2025. It uses an online experiment to show why people ignore good advice from AI: they worry about how taking the advice makes them look, even when looking bad costs them nothing.

Hopes for human and AI teamwork rest on each side playing to its strengths. In practice, people often underuse AI tips. Almog shows that image concerns, cares about others' perceptions with no money attached, push participants to set AI recommendations aside. Performance on the task drops as a result. The finding names a quiet social force behind a common puzzle in workplaces and products. It suggests that making AI use look normal, rather than just making AI better, may be needed for people to accept its help.
arxiv-2504-19747:
Sora Kobayashi and Kei-Ichi Kondo settle which three-qubit entangled states can serve as the channel for perfect quantum teleportation. Teleporting an unknown qubit state perfectly is well known to work with a GHZ state shared between sender and receiver. Whether the other famous three-qubit class, the W state, can do the same was the open question.

The authors give an impossibility proof: the W state cannot be used to realize perfect teleportation of an arbitrary qubit state. The contrast with the GHZ state is sharp. They then show how to modify the shared state into what they call a W-like state. With that state, and under a prescribed measurement basis, they give a procedure achieving perfect teleportation. The result maps the boundary between two fundamental entanglement classes by what they can actually do, a distinction that matters for designing quantum networks.
arxiv-2504-21347:
Seonghee Lee and six co-authors introduce the IRL Ditto in this two thousand twenty-five paper. The Ditto is an embodied AI agent that stands in for a remote colleague in a shared office. People who are present in the room can meet this digital stand-in as they walk by. It can start greetings, share updates, or make small talk, much like the real person might.

The team ran a four-day study in an office. They asked how the Ditto shapes contact and ties among colleagues. They found that gains in social ties rested on how well people already knew the person the Ditto stood for. Strong prior ties helped; weak ones did less. The study shows that a fake presence can support office ties, but it cannot build them from nothing.
arxiv-2505-02047:
Gómez-Bueno, Castro Díaz, and Parés presented this numerical methods paper in twenty twenty-five. It deals with balance laws, equations that track flows with sources, such as water depth or gas motion. Good numerical schemes should keep steady states exact rather than letting errors creep in. Earlier schemes did this by solving a hard problem in each grid cell at each step.

Those cell problems worked only when steady states were known in closed form. The authors recast each problem as a control task on a related equation system. A gradient from a companion problem then drives a Newton solver. They test the method on systems from a simple wave equation to shallow water and gas flow with gravity. Results confirm accuracy and exact steady states.
arxiv-2505-04147:
Lixing Niu and eight co-authors build a video data set that tests whether AI models can read a room the way people do. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Reading a room means guessing what others believe, want, and feel from faint social cues. Past data sets used scenes too simple to match real social life.

Their set holds rich clips of tangled social scenes, marked in fine detail. Notes cover events plus beliefs, intents, desires, and feelings, and the causal chains that link them. Questions come from both human writers and models. Tasks span grasping events, gauging minds, and tracing social causes. Top vision-language models fell well short of human-level steadiness. A prompting trick based on theory of mind helped them do better. The set gives the field a harder, fairer yardstick.
arxiv-2505-10347:
Gabriel Gama and Valdir Grassi compare training schemes for multi-task learning in this two thousand twenty-five paper. When one model learns several tasks at once, the tasks can fight each other. Their gradients may clash or differ in size. Specialized optimizers were built to balance this fight. Recent critics claim plain equal weighting does just as well, if tuned with care. The authors set out to settle the dispute with broad tests.

They ran the latest specialized methods on harder multi-task problems than past studies used. The specialists did perform well against plain uniform loss. Yet fixed well-chosen weights also stayed competitive. The paper explains when uniform loss keeps pace and when it falls behind. Code is shared for others to check the claims.
arxiv-2505-14047:
Jihye Hwang and a large team of co-authors map magnetic fields where stars form in twenty twenty-five. The target is a massive clump called P2 inside a dark filamentary cloud. Magnetic fields shape star formation from core to clump scales. The team measured field orientations and strengths across parsec and sub-parsec scales.

Observations came from a polarization camera on the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope. The survey is BISTRO-3, the third round of a long-running program. Dust grains align with the local field, so their polarized light traces field direction. Comparing orientations across scales shows how the field twists as gas gathers. Readers get a field map of a region where massive stars are being born.
arxiv-2505-14547:
Krever and three co-authors built a framework for making realistic games to test game theory algorithms in twenty twenty-five. Algorithms for equilibria are usually tested on toy games, economic classics, or random matrices. Security games model patrols and protection. They are realistic, but their underlying data, most of all target values, are rarely public.

Their framework, GUARD, builds matrix and security games from open datasets. Animal movement data model anti-poaching patrols. Demographic and infrastructure data model facility protection. Users can tune payoffs and parameters. Ready-made instances are included. The authors prove limits of random-game benchmarking. They also compare their generated games with random ones across standard equilibrium solvers. These include linear programming and no-regret self-play. They argue realistic instances expose weaknesses that random benchmarks hide.
arxiv-2505-15447:
Ziqiang Xu and seven co-authors present ViaRL, a frame that teaches video models to pick the frames that matter. Their paper from twenty twenty-five notes that human viewing is goal-led: we scan for what our task needs. Video chain-of-thought systems lack a direct signal for that pick. Heuristic rules and fake labels fill the gap at high cost and low reach.

ViaRL trains a frame picker by rule-based reinforcement learning. The reward is the final answer's accuracy from a partner model. No hand labels are needed. An iterated loop refines picker and answerer in turns. Tests on VideoMME, LVBench, and MLVU show steady gains in time grounding. One needle-in-haystack task jumped by a wide margin. The method scales across tasks with no costly annotation.
arxiv-2505-16947:
Dékány and four co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on training chat models to resist trick prompts. Attackers can still force top models to produce harmful text. Training against attacks helps, but real attack prompts are costly to build at scale. Faster training uses smooth fake attacks, yet those miss some real weak spots. Their method mixes strong real attacks with fast smooth ones in one training run. They also coin a score for worst-case weakness across attacks.

Their mixed training cut worst-case attack success to under one in five. Prior defenses left success above one in two in their tests. Run time stayed close to the fast smooth methods. They also probe how chat formats and size cuts shift the results. The authors offer a safer path for model builders.
arxiv-2505-18347:
Mohamed Mohamed and colleagues turn a browser game about growing cells into a testbed for agents that must keep learning forever. Continual reinforcement learning studies agents whose world keeps changing, so no fixed policy stays good. Existing setups mostly fake the change by swapping tasks between episodes, or offer worlds too small to be interesting. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team adapts the game Agar.io, where a cell eats, grows, and risks being eaten in an endless, partly hidden, ever-shifting arena. Their platform supports both one long open-ended challenge and smaller tasks that isolate single skills.

Standard algorithms were benchmarked on the main challenge and the side tasks, and three continual learning methods were evaluated as well. The suite separates which ingredients of the game, such as partial sight or sudden threats, break which learners. The platform is offered as shared infrastructure for the field.
arxiv-2505-19347:
Yongmin Yoo, Qiongkai Xu, and Longbing Cao build PatentMind, a frame that judges how alike two patents are, by a graph of thought across many sides. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Patent likeness is key to work on who owns what. Past ways miss the rich build of a patent, which joins tech traits, legal bounds, and use fields. PatentMind splits each patent into those three sides and scores each side on its graph. The scores are then weighed by a step that reads the case's cues, in the way an expert would. The team built a test set of five hundred pairs, marked by people. Their scores tracked expert marks with high accord.
arxiv-2505-19747:
Ligong Bian and a large team of colleagues reviewed gravitational wave cosmology in a 2025 paper, surveying their research program's recent advances. Ripples from the early universe carry direct news about primordial physics, the nature of gravity, and cosmic expansion, unfiltered by the electromagnetic fog that limits telescopes. The review organizes that promise around the stochastic backgrounds, the faint hums left by ancient processes.

Inflation, phase transitions, and topological defects each leave a characteristic background, and the authors summarize what pulsar timing arrays and planned space detectors can already say, and may soon say, about each. Primordial black holes as wave sources and possible dark matter follow, then the imprint of large-scale structure on passing waves.
arxiv-2505-20047:
Ganguly and co-authors ask when to trust chat tools in proof-based task work. Chat tools can draft proof specs and open such work to more hands. Yet tools run on odds, while proof needs firm vows of truth. That clash is the core strain the work probes in full. Five top chat tools took a set test of proof drafts. SMT-based drafts swayed truth by field in the test runs.

Logic tasks gained 34.8 percent, while fact tasks lost 44.5 percent. Stock doubt marks, like word odds spread, missed those flaws. A chance grammar frame, PCFG, models tool outs in the work. That frame gives a more fine doubt sort for the outs. Doubt marks prove task-tied: grammar spread fits logic best. A light fuse of marks lets pick checks cut flaws a lot.
arxiv-2505-22047:
Claus Metzner, Achim Schilling, Andreas Maier, and Patrick Krauss ask how biology-style wiring changes artificial neural networks in this two thousand twenty-five paper. A recurrent network can oscillate, run chaotic, or settle to fixed points, known to rest on the stats of its link weights. Brains have weights with order, though how such order steers dynamics was not clear. The team built weight matrices where three orders can be dialed up gradually.

The kinds are Dale's principle, where each neuron's outputs share one sign, and reciprocal symmetry, as in Hopfield networks. A third is modular structure: blocks with strong links in a weak background. Tuning each while they watched dynamical signs and reservoir marks gave verdicts. Dale monopolarity and modularity made marks better. Hopfield reciprocity hurt, driving early saturation and capping how the reservoir can bend. The upshots hint which biology design rules are to copy.
arxiv-2505-23047:
John Ball leads a team measuring fusion output from a spinning mirror plasma device for the first time. Their paper came out in two thousand twenty-five. The Centrifugal Mirror Fusion Experiment sits at the University of Maryland. A central cathode sets up a radial electric field. Plasma then shears in a fast circular flow. That shear should improve confinement and calm instability.

Fusion yield is read from neutron emission. Two liquid scintillator detectors give the total count, calibrated by simulation. A larger detector tracks how the fusion rate changes over time. A helium gas tube detector, fixed in place, adds an independent check. Runs under varied conditions show how yield responds. The measurements ground hopes for this compact fusion concept.
arxiv-2505-23847:
Ronny Ko and colleagues map the security agenda for language model agents that cooperate across organizational borders. Joint disaster response and supply chains tempt firms to link their agents without surrendering data ownership. Cross-domain teamwork shatters the single trust zone that alignment techniques assume. A well-behaved agent can leak secrets or break policy purely from an untrusted peer's messages.

The position paper names seven categories of novel security challenge. Each comes with plausible attacks, candidate evaluation metrics, and research guidelines. The risks spring from emergent multi-agent dynamics, not classic software bugs. Containment built for one model in one house does not transfer. The authors aim to set the field's agenda before deployment outruns defense. Their taxonomy gives security teams a shared map of where cross-domain agents can be turned.
arxiv-2505-23947:
Müller and four co-authors argue in twenty twenty-five that a new kind of pre-trained net is the future of forecast work. These nets learn by training on huge sets of fake data made from a prior hunch. Once trained, they can act like a full Bayes model on fresh, small data sets.

The authors say this fits a world where compute power grows fast but fresh real data grows slow. Work that once fit tiny tasks now fits larger and harder ones. They map where the method could go and what holds it back now. They urge more work on these nets and kin tools.
arxiv-2506-00047:
Jan Göpfert, Jann Weinand, Patrick Kuckertz, Noah Pflugradt, and Jochen Linßen wrote this perspective piece in two thousand twenty-five. It warns of the risks that come as AI agents take over more of product development, and sketches ways to blunt them.

Machine-made design promises faster, better goods, but trust in non-human hands brings fresh hazards. The authors set out principles for safer work, stressing human oversight, clear accountability, and designs that can be explained. They sort risks into technical ones, which hurt the product, and social ones, which hurt the wider world. The field is young, they note, so the time to set norms and rules is now, without stalling the gains.
arxiv-2506-02147:
Joshua Rozner, Leonie Weissweiler, and Cory Shain test if small language models trained on child-scale data learn grammatical constructions. Construction grammar holds that learners gain form-meaning pairs from the stats of their world. Past work showed trained models are sensitive to constructions. But those models used amounts of data no child could meet. That cast doubt on their link to human learning.

The team uses causal probing on masked language models from the 2024 BabyLM Challenge. That challenge limits training data to amounts a child might meet. Even so, the models learn varied constructions. They include hard cases that look much alike on the surface. The team also finds linked proof that knowledge of constructions matters in use. Models that depict constructions better score better on the BabyLM benchmarks.
arxiv-2506-02647:
Niklas Baumgarten and David Schneiderhan wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It finds the best control for systems ruled by partial differential equations when the inputs are not known for sure, with a multilevel gradient method.

The twist is the gradient source: a parallel multilevel Monte Carlo scheme stands in for the true gradient. That gives tight rein over both the bias from coarse grids and the noise from sampling. Resources go where they pay most. The method homes in at a linear rate, yet never pays for the full gradient at top fidelity. On a two-dimensional case of flow through soil with wild coefficients, it beats plain batched descent on speed and accuracy both. Step rules and budget plans are weighed too.
arxiv-2506-03947:
Tabeart, Gürol, Pearson, and Weaver wrote a numerical methods paper in twenty twenty-five on faster ways to solve the huge linear systems inside weather data assimilation. Those systems lean on covariance matrices, which describe how errors in one place relate to errors elsewhere.

A newer all-at-once layout spreads the work across many processors, but it needs a strong preconditioner, a helper that makes the solver converge in fewer steps. The best-known helper only works when a key matrix can be split by a Fourier transform, which often fails in practice. The authors give two workarounds. One uses a classic polynomial iteration with new error bounds; the other rewrites the problem in a real-valued saddle point form. Tests show both can match the best case when computing power is ample. A tuned version also holds up on a tight budget.
arxiv-2506-04747:
Hedge and colleagues wrote in twenty twenty-five about finding a young galaxy cluster around a powerful radio galaxy. Radio galaxies can mark dense regions in the early universe. The team scanned a bright radio source with a large telescope array in Chile. Gas line signals fixed its distance at a redshift near three point nine. That places it when the universe was quite young. Its host galaxy is very faint in near-infrared light.

Gas around the host fell in two moving parts, hinting at a recent merger. Nearby sources with matching gas signals revealed five more cluster members. Photometry uncovered a rare, optically dark and very massive galaxy nearby. Simulations suggest the cluster will grow into a giant present-day cluster. The find shows radio beacons can locate hidden early clusters.
arxiv-2506-04847:
Mandar Thatte, Shreya Banerjee, and Prasanta Panigrahi design a two-way quantum communication protocol that reads a shared entangled state without destroying it. Quantum dialogue lets both parties send messages over one quantum channel. Reusing the state, rather than consuming it, saves scarce entanglement.

Their scheme discriminates a five-qubit cluster state non-destructively using ancilla measurements, so the entanglement survives for further rounds. The chosen form of the state needs only four components instead of thirty-two, and Pauli operations encode the messages while preserving its stabilizer structure. Security against common quantum attacks is argued, and scaling to longer messages is outlined. A run on IBM's Torino backend served as proof of concept, with a built-in error correction bonus.
arxiv-2506-08747:
Boyang Sun and six co-authors proposed a sample-efficient conditional independence test in twenty twenty-five for data that arrive discretized. Many real variables are recorded in bins because of measurement limits, and running standard independence tests on the bins can mislead. Earlier fixes binarize the data to reason about the latent continuous variables, but binarization throws away information and weakens the test.

The new test skips binarization. The authors show the latent independence question can be recast as an over-identifying restrictions problem solvable by the generalized method of moments. They derive a test statistic with the correct asymptotic distribution using nodewise regression. Theory and experiments across data sets show the test beats binarization-based competitors, especially when samples are scarce.
arxiv-2506-11347:
Wenqian Ye, Guangtao Zheng, and Aidong Zhang present Evidential Alignment, in a 2025 preprint, a way to stop networks from leaning on spurious clues. A camel classifier that keys on desert sand fails in a zoo. Most fixes need group labels marking which examples carry the fake clue. Such labels are costly, and helper models may miss the full bias. This method needs neither. It measures how much evidence backs each prediction, using uncertainty math. Second-order risk training plus a calibration step expose where the model leans on the shortcut.

Once exposed, those leanings are suppressed while the core features stay. The authors back the method with theory: it can learn a biased model's patterns and debias it blind. Across architectures and data types, group robustness rose markedly in tests. The authors offer the method as a scalable, principled answer to shortcut learning.
arxiv-2506-13447:
Ning Li and Qizhou Wang share first credit on this paper from two thousand twenty-five, with He, Burguete-Lopez, Xiang, and Fratalocchi. It reports a camera-based sensor that spots dopamine at trace levels, in real time, with no added chemicals.

Catching brain chemicals this faint is a long goal for the study of brain disease. The platform uses crafted light-scattering films and optical boosters built into trade vision cameras. It reads dopamine live at video rates, even with uric and ascorbic acid in the mix, at levels far below past best tools. The setup swaps a bulky bench station for a small camera box. The booster can be retrained for other targets, the team notes.
arxiv-2506-14347:
Yoav Ravid and six co-authors study how curved parts in a cell's skin steer the shape of the whole sac. Their work, from two thousand twenty-five, is a theory study.

The parts come in two forms: bow-shaped and saddle-shaped. They sense curve, line up like a liquid crystal, and meet at flaw points, all under a fixed bulk. For sacs fully clad in bow parts, the shape shifts from a string of beads to a tube as the lined-up acts grow strong. For part-clad sacs, saddle parts hold the necks between bare, round zones. The team maps the calm shapes and finds flaw points sit at set spots.
arxiv-2506-17347:
Jennifer Wang, Andrew Selbst, Solon Barocas, and Suresh Venkatasubramanian argued in twenty twenty-five that AI regulation must split task-specific systems from general-purpose ones. Over the past decade, policy tools were built for narrow AI that does one job. General-purpose AI, which adapts to many jobs, breaks several assumptions baked into those tools.

The authors name four gaps. General systems make a poor single target for rules; their evals are hard to design; they raise fresh legal questions with new stakeholders; and their supply chain is spread across many firms. They urge policymakers to sort which older tools still fit and where new ones are needed. Three recommendations close the paper, on picking targets and using pressure points across the wider ecosystem.
arxiv-2506-20147:
Xi Geng, Sheng Wang, and Weijun Xu find the exact long-time growth of a random heat equation on curved space in a 2025 probability study. The parabolic Anderson model describes a quantity spreading while multiplied by a frozen random landscape, a picture used for populations in patchy environments and for disordered materials. Their space is hyperbolic, where volume grows far faster than in flat space.

With a steady Gaussian random potential, the solution starting from constant data grows, with probability one, at a precise exponential rate in time. Both the power of time in the exponent and the constant differ from the flat-space values. An explicit optimization produces the constant.
arxiv-2506-21047:
Tianyu Wang and seven co-authors show that fast electron diffraction can film electrons and hydrogen atoms moving together. Their paper from twenty twenty-five tackles a core wish of ultrafast science. Watching coupled electron and nucleus motion in real space and time has been out of reach. Their test case is ammonia breaking apart under light.

Mega-electron-volt electron pulses scatter off the excited molecule. A charge-pair distribution function is drawn from the scatter. Fine time resolution lets that map split the intertwined paths of valence electrons and hydrogens. The linked dance during the split becomes visible. The authors stress method reach over the single molecule. Many quantum dynamics studies could adopt the charge-pair lens. It opens a route to movies of charge and matter in joint motion.
arxiv-2506-21647:
Guha Majumdar sets a working threshold for when spatial entanglement survives ionizing hits in twenty twenty-five. Entanglement is fragile when one partner sheds energy through ionization or scattering. A full quantum electrodynamics model tracks the decay here. The fall off proves exponential, driven by recoil spreading the momentum.

A sharp line splits the quantum coherent side from the classical side. Cross it when total recoil blur tops the state's own momentum width. The rule reaches past weak coupling and Gaussian toy models. It gives numbers to design hardier quantum sensors and imagers. Radiation rich settings are the target use.
arxiv-2506-23147:
Jonathan Schuster and Fabian Transchel release a Python package that sorts driving maneuvers from vehicle sensor streams. Their paper from twenty twenty-five works in vehicle telematics. Naming maneuvers helps score driving for insurance, safety, and fuel use. The task needs steady time series classification on data that is awkward to move, clean, and store.

Past work dwelt on data gathering and model craft. A ready toolkit was the gap. Their package covers preprocessing, modeling, and scoring in one place. A built-in LSTM network can be reshaped to fit new tasks. The demo uses phone sensor data from three drivers on real roads. The authors pitch the package as a fast on-ramp for telematics teams. It turns raw streams into maneuver labels with set tooling.
arxiv-2507-00747:
Diemen Delgado-Cano, Erick Kracht, and colleagues learn simple equations for systems with fast and slow parts in a 2025 study. A popular data-driven method finds sparse, readable dynamics, but high-dimensional slow-fast systems make its regression huge and ill-conditioned. Restricting attention to the slow manifold, where long-term behavior lives, should shrink the problem.

The catch is that dropped fast variables must be repaid with higher-order terms, which explode the candidate list again. The authors develop ways to manage that growth while staying on the manifold. Compact learned models help engineers predict systems from turbines to climate components without simulating every fast detail.
arxiv-2507-02247:
Jinlu Li, Xing Wu, and Yanghai Yu prove negative results for fluid equations in twenty twenty-five. They study the basic equations of fluid dynamics on a torus. The Euler equations describe inviscid flow, while Navier-Stokes adds viscosity. Solutions are sought in Besov spaces, a scale of function spaces used for rough data.

The authors construct new initial data and give a simple proof of ill-posedness. That means solutions in the chosen space fail to depend well on their starting values. Their result covers earlier work on both Euler and surface quasi-geostrophic equations. They also prove that the inviscid limit fails to converge in the same space. Both Navier-Stokes and quasi-geostrophic flows are covered. Readers get sharper limits on where fluid theory can hold.
arxiv-2507-02347: Marco Mackaay, Vanessa Miemietz, and Pedro Vaz took early steps in 2025 toward categorifying the Zelevinsky tensor product for extended affine type A Hecke algebras. They worked with Soergel bimodules induced from a maximal parabolic subalgebra. Categorification lifts algebra-based forms into richer categorical ones, and the Zelevinsky product is a key construction on representations of these algebras. The paper begins that program for the extended affine setting.
arxiv-2507-03247:
Ruining Zhao and six co-authors report spectra of the comet 12P/Pons-Brooks in two thousand twenty-five. The comet is of Halley type and prone to outbursts. Spectra were taken in visible and near infrared light during two outbursts. Big telescopes on the ground did the work.

The infrared spectra show dips that match water ice. Fine crystals of ice at cold heat fit the bands well. Tiny hard grains, like amorphous carbon, add the red dust glow. Visible light shows gas bands from carbon and nitrogen groups. Gas ratios mark the comet as typical in one trait and low in another. Ice change likely drove the outburst.
arxiv-2507-04747:
Aliev, Guliyev, and Jabiyev solve a best approximation problem for functions of three variables in twenty twenty-five. The question asks how well such a function can be matched by a sum of three single variable functions. Each term depends on just one coordinate. The error is measured by the largest gap over the unit cube.

They prove a formula that computes this smallest possible error. The formula holds under certain conditions on the function. The infimum runs over all triples of continuous one variable functions. Results of this kind are rare in multivariable approximation theory. Exact error formulas help judge when separable approximations suffice. The work is a theoretical contribution to approximation theory.
arxiv-2507-08947:
Lorenzo Miretti, Slawomir Stańczak, and Giuseppe Caire prove that two jobs radio staff now do apart can stay apart at no cost. The jobs are to gauge the channel and to form beams. In nets with lots of users and antennas, send-side beam work and read-side blends could tangle with the gauge work. Their split rule says no. MMSE gauge first, then MMSE beams, is as good as any joint plan.

Two stock net types fall in the rule's reach. One is cell-based and leans on the two-way trait of air paths. The next is cell-free and huge. Hub-based and spread-out builds are in scope. Plain cases and test runs show the uses. Build the gauge block and the beam block apart. Each can be best at its own task.
arxiv-2507-10747:
Kaustubh Tangsali and colleagues set out a test frame for AI models that predict airflow for cars. The frame sits inside the open-source NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo-CFD toolkit. It is meant to check accuracy, speed, scale, and how well models cope with new cases. It does so in a set, shared way.

The frame supports a wide set of scores that matter for car design work. Users can add more models and more data sets. To show it in use, the team tests surface and volume flow results from three AI models. The models are DoMINO, X-MeshGraphNet, and FIGConvNet, and the data set is DrivAerML. They also give rules for adding scores that fit the physics. Clear tests should help teams pick and improve AI tools for car design.
arxiv-2507-16147:
Jian-Qi Liu, Yan-Hong Yao, Yan Su, and Jia-Wei Wu test a cosmos where dark matter flows like a fluid with pressure. Cold, pressureless dark matter rules the standard model but strains at small scales. Their variant gives dark matter one fixed pressure trait. Dark energy, meanwhile, emerges from the cosmos itself rather than sitting as a constant.

The team checked the model against four major data sets. Sky maps of the early universe, galaxy distance markers, and exploding stars all fed the test. The combined data hint that the dark matter trait sits above zero. Its sound speed shares the same value in their setup. Yet when models were scored head to head, the standard model won by a wide margin. The authors report both the hint and the verdict plainly.
arxiv-2507-16547:
Edoardo Ballico and Changho Keem study Hilbert schemes of smooth curves of low degree in five-dimensional projective space. A Hilbert scheme parametrizes all curves of a given degree and genus in that space.
