The authors focus on the Hilbert function of a general member of each component, especially for degrees up to fifteen.

They determine the irreducibility of these Hilbert schemes for degrees up to fourteen. They also study in detail the natural map from the Hilbert scheme to the moduli space of curves. For a general curve, they describe the fiber of that map over the curve's moduli point, and they determine when the curve is projectively normal or arithmetically Cohen-Macaulay. The results map out how low-degree curves sit inside projective space and how their equations behave. Such classification work underpins algebraic geometers' understanding of curves and the spaces that collect them.
arxiv-2507-18647:
Rayyan Ridwan made a pneumonia sensor for children's chest X-rays that explains itself in a 2025 paper. Pneumonia kills many children worldwide, and fast, trustworthy reading of scans could help clinics with few specialists. Deep models can be exact yet opaque, which slows adoption where a wrong call is dangerous. The study pairs a residual network with an explainability method that also reports its own doubt.

The network reached high accuracy and discrimination scores on a large pediatric data set. Its visual explanations highlighted regions health staff found meaningful for the diagnosis. Pairing a strong score with an honest map of evidence, plus doubt where the map is unsure, is the combination health rollout demands.
arxiv-2507-19447:
Daniil Klyuev and Joseph Vulakh wrote this math paper in two thousand twenty-five. It sorts the positive traces on two families of algebras known as Coulomb branches, which arise from gauge theories in three and four dimensions.

A positive trace is a map on the algebra with a sign-like trait tied to a flip of the algebra. In the first case the algebra is a quantized Kleinian singularity of type D, with a bound on the parameter. In the second it is a larger algebra built from a loop group, holding the branches for two related gauge groups. Sorting these traces can sharpen what is known about the theories at hand. The paper is a work of pure theory.
arxiv-2507-21447:
Zachariah Sollenberger, Rahul Patel, Saieda Ali Zada, and Sunita Chandrasekaran test whether large language models can write and grade compiler tests, in a two thousand twenty-five software engineering paper. The target is directive-based parallel programming models such as OpenMP.

Their dual system pairs a generative model that makes tests with a discriminative model that judges them, aiming at fully autonomous verification. Hallucination and unverifiable thinking are the central worries. Several models of varied sizes are compared across ten carefully defined metrics. The findings suggest language models can indeed generate quality compiler tests and check them automatically, a hopeful route to cheaper test development for high-performance computing.
arxiv-2507-22647:
Lorenzo Volpi, Alejandro Moreo, and Fabrizio Sebastiani wrote this machine learning paper, published in 2025. It deals with transductive learning, where the unlabeled data a model must label are known ahead of time, during training.

The paper tackles model selection, the step of tuning a model's settings, when the class balance in the data has shifted. Standard tuning relies on cross-checks within the labeled training data, which can mislead under such a shift. The authors propose tuning the settings directly on the unlabeled target data instead. Tests show this targeted approach beats the standard route. The work matters for tasks like sorting documents or screening cases, where the mix of classes in new data rarely matches the training mix.
arxiv-2508-05747:
Wahid and five colleagues propose using Composer packages to speed student Laravel projects in twenty twenty-five. Laravel is a web framework widely taught at universities. Students often struggle to finish projects within tight academic timelines. Composer is the standard dependency manager for the PHP language.

The paper curates packages that cut development effort for typical student systems. It frames their use in both practical and pedagogical terms. Good packages also teach professional workflows and code quality habits. Risks include package conflicts and over reliance on ready made tools. The authors give best practices to mitigate those risks. They stress that teachers must explain when and why to use a package, not just how.
arxiv-2508-06847:
Lam Ngo, Huong Ha, Jeffrey Chan, and Hongyu Zhang widen a search tool for hard design tasks. The work came out in 2025. The tool is Bayesian search, used to tune costly black-box systems. Most forms of it need smooth knobs that turn by small steps. Many real tasks do not fit that mold at all.

Some picks come from a fixed list, like which stuff to use or which build to pick. High counts of knobs make the search worse. Their tool, MOCA-HESP, cuts the space into curved zones. It tries more than one way to turn list picks into numbers. A bandit rule learns on the fly which code works best. The frame is a meta tool, so other search tools can plug in. The team built three such tools on top of it.
arxiv-2508-08447:
Grant Moles and Talha Khan study when orders in real quadratic number fields are locally associated, a notion introduced in twenty twenty-five to tackle factorization problems. An order is a subring of a number field, and properties like being associated, ideal-preserving, or locally associated govern how elements factor inside it. The paper restricts to fields obtained by adjoining the square root of a prime.

The authors develop strategies and results that make determining whether a given order in such a field is locally associated much easier. They also highlight the relatively few cases that defy simple characterization. Those stubborn cases lead to a conjecture about solutions of Pell-type equations. Factorization in non-maximal orders is famously unruly, with non-unique factorization the norm. Classifying which orders enjoy tamer local behavior gives number theorists a map of where the pathology lives. The work is pure number theory.
arxiv-2508-08647:
Nobu Kishimoto and Kiyeon Lee analyze a nonlinear Schrödinger equation from plasma physics, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. The kinetic derivative version adds derivative nonlinearities and a nonlocal term from the Hilbert transform. Such features make long-term behavior hard to prove.

The authors establish global existence for small initial data in a weighted Sobolev space. They also prove optimal time decay for the solutions. Energy methods and a frequency-localized gauge transformation handle the nonlocal difficulties. Beyond decay, the solutions show modified scattering. A precise asymptotic profile, with a suitable phase correction, describes them at large times. The results give a rigorous picture of how these plasma waves settle down.
arxiv-2508-09247:
Francesca Acanfora and Felix Kahlhoefer study a hard-to-see dark sector process, in a 2025 preprint, and how the Belle II experiment could catch it. Dark photons are proposed particles that could link dark matter to normal matter. Most searches look for dark photons that decay fully into visible matter or fully out of sight. The authors focus on a middle case, where a dark Higgs boson is also produced.

In their setup, the dark Higgs lives a long time before decaying into normal particles. That gives a decay point away from the collision point, plus missing energy. The process can appear alone or with an extra photon. Both shapes carry clear peaks that help cut background noise. The authors argue Belle II could cover ground that past searches missed. Pairing the two shapes could also reveal facts about the dark sector itself.
arxiv-2508-12647:
Hengnian Gu and colleagues set out Cognitive Structure Generation, a frame to build a student's cognitive structure on its own. A cognitive structure is how a student sorts a body of knowledge. It holds concepts and the links between them, as the student has built them. To gauge such a structure has long been a hard task in student modeling.

The frame first trains a diffusion model to build such structures from prior facts about schooling. It then tunes the build steps as a policy. It uses reinforcement learning with layered reward signals. The aim is to match real growth levels in how students think. Tests on four real data sets from schools show the built structures depict students more fully. Scores rose a lot on knowledge tracing and on diagnosis tasks.
arxiv-2508-14247:
Saswata Jana, Subhajit Pramanick, Adri Bhattacharya, and Partha Sarathi Mandal send short-sighted robots onto a graph to occupy a vertex cover. The robots enter one by one through special door vertices and see only a limited distance. Working asynchronously with purely local knowledge, they must settle so every edge touches an occupied vertex, using as few vertices as possible.

The authors set lower bounds on the visibility range needed and on the running time. For trees they give two algorithms: a single-door version optimal in both time and memory, and a multi-door version optimal in memory. Their technique even finds the minimum cover on trees with one door, despite that problem being hard in general.
arxiv-2508-16447:
Álvaro Guglielmin Becker and Gabriel Bauer de Oliveira tested in 2025 whether large language models can write working board game software from written rules. Coding a board game by hand is slow, and language models have shown skill at code generation for narrow tasks. A framework that turns plain-language rules into playable games would speed up prototyping considerably.

The authors asked three leading models to implement a dozen popular and obscure games, both freely and inside Boardwalk, their proposed general game playing framework. Game names and parts were disguised so models could not lean on memorized knowledge. Programs were scored for playability and rule compliance. The approach proved viable: the best model produced over half the games with no errors at all, and the study catalogs success rates and the common mistakes each model made.
arxiv-2508-17347:
Shaban and Habash proposed a new score for Arabic dialects in twenty twenty-five. Arabic varies widely by region, yet computer models often treat each dialect as a fixed box. A recent measure grades how dialectal a text is, but it squeezes rich variation into one number.

Their Arabic Generality Score instead grades how widely a word is used across dialects. They built a pipeline that aligns words across texts, measures spelling distance with respect for word origins, and smooths the results. A model then learns to predict the score for words in context. It beat strong existing systems on a multi-dialect test set. The authors offer the score as a grounded way to enrich how models represent Arabic.
arxiv-2508-18047:
Shruti Dubey, Nilanjana Kumar, Tanumoy Mandal, Subhadip Mitra, and Rachit Sharma probe a paired new-physics case in this two thousand twenty-five particle physics paper. Collider hunts have long sought leptoquarks and vectorlike leptons, each on its own. In views with enhanced gauge symmetries, both could be there at once. Acts through leptoquarks would then boost how many vectorlike tau leptons the Large Hadron Collider makes.

The team studies odd leptoquark acts. These make new marks in how the heavy tau partners are made and how they break down. They weigh the odds of a find in the high-luminosity phase of the collider. The end states hold one lepton or two. More paths that could count are also talked through. The work shows a risk in one-at-a-time thinking. Marks can show up just when two guessed kinds of particle act on each other.
arxiv-2508-19247:
Lin Li and colleagues present VoxHammer, a method with no training to edit three-dimensional objects with care in their native 3D space. Local 3D editing matters for games and for robot work. Past methods edit rendered multi-view images and then rebuild the model. But they fail to keep unedited regions exact. They also fail to keep the whole object coherent.

VoxHammer first predicts a model's inversion path. It captures its inverted latents and key-value tokens at each step. In denoising and editing, it swaps the traits of regions meant to stay untouched with those cached values. Kept areas are thus rebuilt in a steady way, while edited parts fit in well. To gauge this well, the team built Edit3D-Bench, a data set marked by humans. Tests show VoxHammer beats past methods by a lot.
arxiv-2508-19847:
Erdi Kara and Panos Stinis build a fast solver for flow through porous rock or soil. Their paper from twenty twenty-five treats two linked tasks. One is steady flow, set by the Darcy rule. The other is the spread of a dissolved substance over time. The substance starts from sharp, narrow sources, which make steep fronts that are hard to compute.

Their method pairs two tools. A finite element solver finds the flow field with high care. A neural operator network, trained with the physics built in, then learns how sources map to spread patterns. A smart choice of test points helps it track steep fronts. Tests match trusted solutions well. The method runs far faster than classic solvers, which suits real field use. Code is shared in public.
arxiv-2508-21647:
Rupert Yu studies orbit structure inside Lie algebras in this two thousand twenty-five math paper. His setting is a Borel subalgebra of a complex semisimple Lie algebra, a standard scaffold in the theory. Inside it sit nilpotent ideals, sets closed under the algebra's operations. The author looks at a special subset of nilpotent elements tied to one such ideal. This set stays fixed as a whole under the action of the matching Borel subgroup.

He proves the set contains exactly one closed orbit under that action. That orbit belongs to a nilpotent element whose support is the set of smallest roots for the ideal. Pinning down a unique closed orbit anchors the whole orbit picture. The result serves specialists in representation theory and algebraic groups.
arxiv-2509-00047:
Jina Kim, working alone, studies brain-inspired replay as a cure for forgetting in neural networks in 2025. When a network learns new tasks in sequence, it tends to lose old skills, a flaw called catastrophic forgetting. Brains ease this loss by reactivating past traces during rest, a process tied to memory consolidation, which firms up new memories.

Internal replay revives hidden codes for past cases while new learning proceeds. Kim tests it on the CIFAR-100 image set in a class-by-class setup, alone and with Synaptic Intelligence, a method that guards key weights. Replay cuts forgetting a lot, most when paired with that guard, but it lowers early accuracy on new tasks. The trade-off frames how brain tricks might steady lifelong learning.
arxiv-2509-00247:
Yong Zhao, working alone, reviews fresh steps in 2025 that sharpen how the inner traits of the proton are computed from lattice QCD. Partons are the quarks and gluons inside a proton. Their maps show how the proton's momentum is shared among them. Large Momentum Effective Theory, called LaMET, gets those maps from lattice sims of the strong force.

LaMET matches lattice values, called quasi-distributions, taken at large proton momentum to the true maps. New gains include a hybrid scheme that tames a known runaway term, plus matching terms worked out to more loops. A gauge-fixed route also eases the work and sharpens maps of side-wise momentum. Tighter error bars bring lattice results closer to what lab tests can check.
arxiv-2509-00447:
Rupendra Yadav and Aparna Mehra present a robust portfolio optimization framework in 2025 built around mixed conditional value at risk. Portfolio choice balances return against risk. Mixed conditional value at risk blends several tail-risk gauges into one objective, while a chance constraint guards expected returns and a cardinality limit caps how many assets are held.

The robust model assumes ellipsoidal support for random returns, with no fixed distribution. An uncertainty set built in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space handles the chance constraint, and the problem reduces to a second-order cone program, a tractable convex form. Tests on six financial markets show higher expected returns and better reward-risk ratios than nominal, market, and equal-weight portfolios.
arxiv-2509-00747:
Francesco Caravelli leads a team of six authors on physical learning systems. Their topic is self-organising memristive networks. Learning with physical systems uses a material's own dynamics to learn. It avoids running neural software on standard transistor hardware. These networks are built from nanoscale resistive memory parts. Their electrical circuitry reconfigures itself as they run.

The authors review experiments on such networks. They cover mean-field theory and graph theory as analysis tools. They also discuss links to criticality in disordered systems. Parallels with plasticity in biological neurons are drawn. Such networks could give brain-like continual learning at low energy cost. Uses include edge intelligence, sensing, and personal healthcare devices.
arxiv-2509-01647:
Interstellar comets carry material from around other stars, and 3I/ATLAS is a newly found visitor of that kind. Luis E. Salazar Manzano, with eight co-authors, reports a ten-night campaign of spectroscopy and photometry in August 2025, using two telescopes at the MDM Observatory. The comet was inbound, between about three point two and two point nine times Earth's distance from the Sun.

Nightly spectra caught the onset of gas activity: a weak CN emission feature, absent at first, grew steadily in the coma. The measured CN production rate sits toward the low end seen in solar system comets. Photometry also showed the coma's profile and dust measure rising slightly. The team derives a gas-to-dust production ratio and reads the pattern as evidence of strong carbon-chain depletion, a chemical trait that sets this visitor apart.
arxiv-2509-01947:
Mahdi Farzandway and Fatemeh Ghassemi automate repair of C programs by pairing fault localization with large language models. Their loop first flags suspect code regions from test pass and fail patterns. Runtime feedback and a chain of thought prompt, where the model reasons step by step, guide each patch try. Past patch outcomes feed the next round of reasoning.

That memory cuts repeated errors and clarifies why some bugs resist fixes. The loop edits code, reruns tests, and refines its plan each cycle. On a benchmark of thousands of bugs, their method fixes a higher share than strong baselines. The gain over a top model with the same prompting style is a few points. The work shows a practical route for AI assisted debugging.
arxiv-2509-02247:
Rasika Vijithasena leads three co-authors in a calm aware joint talk and steer plan for wireless control webs. Such webs close steer loops by air links with thin stores of power and range. Non straight, control non affine acts, where steer acts in tangled ways, make calm hard to vouch. Next gen nets are set to back these live self led loops at scale.

A deep Koopman model lifts non straight acts to a straight space where reads and plans come easy. A Lyapunov based plan deals talk slots by calm need and stock on hand. Steer acts come from a straight type rule in that lifted space. Tests in mixed terms beat base lines that take affine steer or same acts in both spaces. Calm holds with fewer sends than the base lines need.
arxiv-2509-02347:
Alessio Lapolla wrote a 2025 solo mathematics paper deriving recursive formulas for survival chances and first passage times in systems with many moving parts. The focus is the nth component of a jump-and-diffusion process that faces a killing barrier, an absorbing limit that ends the process.

Lapolla starts with two components, then extends the formulas to three or more. He admits the results are general but hard to implement. Two examples show their use. One is single file diffusion, where particles cannot pass each other. The other is financial: pricing an nth-to-default credit default swap, a contract that pays when the nth firm in a group defaults.
arxiv-2509-02447:
Xinrui Zhong and eight co-authors present a 2025 systems paper on finding watermarks hidden in generated images across huge collections. Accuracy under edits and attacks gets much attention, but raw detection speed at scale is often ignored.

Their QRMark system borrows error correction ideas from QR codes and splits images into tiles. A Reed-Solomon code repairs accuracy lost through tiling. On the system side, a resource-aware fusion policy gives more processing streams to heavy stages. Tile workloads are interleaved so data loading overlaps with computation, and kernels are scheduled across stages. End-to-end tests show detection running more than twice as fast as a sequential baseline, while keeping accuracy and robustness.
arxiv-2509-02547:
Guibin Zhang and twenty-four co-authors wrote a 2025 survey of agentic reinforcement learning for large language models, where models act as autonomous agents in changing environments rather than answering in one step. The survey draws on more than five hundred recent works.

Older language model training fits a single-step decision model, while agentic settings stretch over time with partial information. The authors organise the field two ways: by core abilities such as planning, tool use, memory, reasoning, self-improvement, and perception; and by application domains. Their central claim is that reinforcement learning turns fixed heuristic modules into adaptive behaviour. A compendium of open environments, benchmarks, and frameworks supports future work. Open challenges for building general-purpose agents close the survey.
arxiv-2509-02847:
Arjen van der Wel and Sharon E. Meidt present a 2025 astronomy paper proposing EASE, a mechanism where short-lived spiral arms reshape galaxies early in cosmic history. Between redshifts one and three, many galaxies already show early-type shapes, and their formation needs explaining.

EASE stands for early, accelerated, secular evolution. Torques from stellar spirals, seen by the Webb telescope in young galaxies, slowly heat and compact the galaxy and build its bulge. The process is secular yet fast, because orbital times were much shorter then. A new wave calculation shows transient open spirals influence a wider region than steady spirals do. Using galaxy size as the test, EASE predicts an early-type size distribution matching observations. Spirals are common enough at those epochs to drive the transformation.
arxiv-2509-02947:
Ambuj and 6 co-authors wrote a 2025 paper that brings a classic idea from communication theory into game theory. Claude Shannon's zero-error idea asked when messages can cross a noisy channel with no mistakes at all. Here the players hold private information and must land together on a Nash equilibrium, a stable outcome no one gains by leaving alone.

The authors show some Bayesian games, where players act under uncertainty about each other, allow no sure classical coordination. Links known as Bell nonlocal correlations, a quantum effect tying distant particles, make it possible there. They also build games for three players, where true entanglement is required, and for two players under a stronger demand. The edge survived realistic noise in their checks.
arxiv-2509-03147:
Karl Dilcher and Larry Ericksen wrote a 2025 combinatorics paper sparked by a counting pattern that hides famous numbers. They study colored partitions in base three, ways of splitting a whole number into parts whose labels carry colors and place value. The counting function for one such family contains the even perfect numbers, numbers equal to the sum of their divisors, as a subsequence.

The authors define polynomials in four variables, arranged as a sequence, and explore their properties and counting meanings. Certain subsequences connect to the Chebyshev polynomials, a classic family with two kinds. Later sections turn to single-variable polynomial sequences with their own counting interpretations. Their zero distributions, the patterns of where these polynomials vanish, also get attention.
arxiv-2509-03447:
Aexandre Fernandes, Zbigniew Jelonek, and José Edson Sampaio proved a metric version of Arnold's corank problem in a 2025 mathematics paper. In 1975 Arnold asked whether the corank of a holomorphic function, a measure of its degeneracy, is unchanged by ambient topological changes of the surrounding space. The metric version asks the same for bi-Lipschitz changes, which may stretch distances but only within bounded factors.

The authors obtain a complete positive answer to that metric question. A consequence is that, for complex hypersurfaces, having multiplicity equal to two is also an ambient bi-Lipschitz invariant. They further prove the original Arnold problem for holomorphic functions of three variables. Other topological invariants are presented along the way. The work settles a fifty-year-old question in its metric form.
arxiv-2509-03647:
Self-preference bias in large language models used as judges is examined in a 2025 research paper by Dani Roytburg and five co-authors. When a model grades answers, it tends to favour its own outputs over other models' work. That favouritism threatens fairness in preference tuning and model routing, where judges steer real decisions.

The team asks whether small steering vectors, directions added inside the model's activations at answer time, can curb the bias without retraining. Their curated dataset separates justified self-preference, where the model's answer really is better, from unjustified cases. Two construction methods are tested: contrastive activation addition and an optimisation-based approach. Steering cuts unjustified self-preference by up to almost all of it, beating prompting and preference-training baselines. Yet the same vectors behave unstably on legitimate self-preference and on neutral agreement. Self-preference seems to span several, possibly nonlinear directions, limiting simple fixes.
arxiv-2509-03847: Graphs belonging to the Wp class, a family defined inside graph theory, are what Do Trong Hoang and two co-authors examine in a 2025 mathematics paper. They establish new characterisations of such graphs, meaning equivalent conditions that decide membership in the class. Within the same class, they also characterise locally triangle-free alpha-critical graphs, a special family where small changes alter a key independence property. As a consequence, their results give a partial answer to Plummer's 1993 question, for the case p equals two.
arxiv-2509-04347:
Johanna Brunar and two co-authors prove that certain puzzle-like languages are far less expressive than they appear in a 2025 mathematics paper. The setting is constraint satisfaction, where values must honor a set of rules, extended here to infinite domains. Temporal and phylogeny systems, tied to family trees of species, carry famous complexity classes. Systems failing to build everything turn out to be solvable quickly, a known result the authors deepen.

Such systems can only interpret very limited graphs and hypergraphs through a standard building method. Many algebraic results follow, including special four-ary polymorphisms, symmetry operations that keep solutions valid. Two unlike families share a common proof core. The work supports a major open conjecture in the field.
arxiv-2509-04447:
Bitan Roy, writing alone, extends two classic counting theorems to Dirac systems that leak energy in a 2025 physics paper. Dirac fermions are particles described by the Dirac equation, and textured mass patterns or magnetic fields can trap robust zero-energy states on them. Index theorems by Aharonov-Casher and Jackiw-Rebbi or Jackiw-Rossi count those trapped states exactly. Roy augments the Dirac Hamiltonian with a mass-like anti-Hermitian term, making the operator non-Hermitian, as suits open systems that exchange energy with surroundings.

Across a wide parameter range the energies stay fully real, governed by an effective Fermi velocity. Explicit zero-mode solutions show magnetic fields of any shape still bind such states when flux is finite. Mass textures bind them only when that velocity is real.
arxiv-2509-04547:
Alexandre Champagne-Ruel and two co-authors test whether spatial patterning alone can fake a signature of life in a 2025 research paper. Assembly theory holds that only living systems produce certain complex molecules in bulk, offering a life-detection tool. Controls so far used meteorite samples or well-mixed chemistry. Self-organization research warns that spatial patterns can foster complexity without life, risking false alarms. The team modeled a fake chemistry where molecules spread and react across layouts.

Transport factors like diffusion strongly shifted which species appeared where. Ordered lattices raised the bar for abiotic complexity a bit, though arbitrary complexity never emerged. Diffusion could also hide high-complexity molecules from detection. Life-hunting missions must mind geography, the results warn.
arxiv-2509-04647:
Games where each player's cost depends on the whole population's states and strategies are analysed by P. Jameson Graber, lead author with two co-authors, in a 2025 paper on mean field games of controls. The system uses a fractional Laplacian, an operator that captures long-range effects. Solutions are shown to exist for a range of its orders.

The authors assume the Lasry-Lions monotonicity condition on the coupling. They derive moment estimates, estimates for fractional parabolic equations, and new results on how the population distribution changes in time. Those estimates, with a fixed point theorem, establish existence of solutions.
arxiv-2509-04947:
Critical points in lattice models can be hard to find when systems are small. Anran Jin and one co-author apply an entropy-based strategy to that search in a 2025 note on strange correlators. The strategy uses an entropy function designed to detect criticality even at small system size, combined with transfer matrices built from a topological holographic principle.

The authors find the combination cost-effective for identifying critical boundary conditions. It also estimates central charges and maps entire phase diagrams in a multi-dimensional parameter space. Their note presents the method as an efficient route to critical lattice models.
arxiv-2509-05747:
Two people acting out everyday scenes together, faces and voices included, form a new motion dataset from Leo Ho and seven co-authors in a 2025 computer graphics paper. Earlier capture work covered one person, or two people talking with bodies nearly still, missing how partners move through space over longer interactions.

InterAct holds hundreds of motion sequences, each a minute or longer, where two actors with assigned roles and emotion labels complete a shared task. Audio, body motion, and facial expression are all recorded. The activities are diverse and the interaction patterns longer than in earlier sets. A diffusion-based method that estimates both people's motion and expressions from speech is demonstrated.
arxiv-2509-06447:
Electricity, gas, and heat networks in one mathematical picture is the framework of a 2025 paper by Marwan Mostafa and three co-authors. Sector coupling and decarbonization tangle the three systems together, and separate models miss their interactions. The authors build a multi-layer graph: one layer per energy carrier, with coupling technologies as edges between layers through a dedicated coupling layer.

A block-structured Newton-Raphson solver computes flows and state variables for all carriers jointly at steady state. On a realistic case study from a German distribution network, the solver converges accurately with consistent cross-domain behavior. The team offers the model as a base for system-wide analysis and future optimization of integrated energy systems.
arxiv-2509-06647:
Shining strong light on quasicrystals to probe how their electrons get trapped is proposed by H. K. Avetissian and three co-authors in a 2025 condensed matter paper. Quasicrystals sit between ordered and disordered matter, and they can show Anderson localization and mobility edges without any disorder. Optical probes that work without contact are therefore valuable.

Using general Aubry-André-Harper models and a smooth incommensurate potential, the authors show that high-harmonic output, light emitted at multiples of the driving frequency, tracks those trapping changes. They define a new quantity, dipole mobility, capturing how transitions within a band affect the signal. Harmonic output can differ by orders of magnitude between regimes, and the cutoff frequency shifts with the edge's position. That shift gives experimenters an accessible signature of the trapping in this matter.
arxiv-2509-06747:
Finding known planets in reflected starlight starts with knowing where to point, and Logan A. Pearce and two co-authors build a tool for that in a 2025 astronomy paper. Future telescopes will image cold, mature planets directly. Planets found by radial velocity or astrometry are prime targets, but many orbits are too imprecise to predict a planet's spot on the sky.

Their open-source Python package, projecc, turns published orbit solutions into probability maps for a planet's sky position. Two test cases show the range: one planet's location is well pinned down, while Proxima Centauri b remains highly uncertain. A web app lets observers explore these predictions for the known targets plus many more from the literature. Planned upgrades aim to support observing campaigns with the coming generation of large telescopes.
arxiv-2509-06847:
Escaping air on sixteen giant exoplanets is measured through a helium line by Jaume Orell-Miquel and seven co-authors in a 2025 astronomy paper. The near-infrared helium triplet is a strong tracer of atmospheric escape on close-in planets. Observations came from the Habitable Zone Planet Finder spectrograph on the ten-meter Hobby-Eberly Telescope, at high resolution.

First constraints are reported for five planets, earlier detections are confirmed for five more, and several non-detections are recorded. One earlier narrow-band detection was not confirmed at high resolution. Combining the survey with published studies, patterns emerge: warm Jupiters with helium detections orbit K-type stars. Hot Jupiter detections sit in low-density planets around F-type stars, and no ultra-hot Jupiter shows helium. The compiled sample of irradiated giants still needs growth, the authors note.
arxiv-2509-07247:
Florian Frick and 1 co-author prove broad generalizations in 2025 of the Borsuk-Ulam theorem, a classic result in topology. The theorem says any continuous map from a sphere to lower-dimensional space sends some opposite pair of points to the same place. Their route runs through Fan's combinatorial labeling result for triangulations of spheres, which they extend in several directions.

The extensions do more than bound complexity, the usual use of Borsuk-Ulam: they also reveal the structure of objects that meet the bound. That structure is governed by order types of point sets and by how faces intersect under maps from a simplex. Applications include sphere coverings, Kneser-type colorings, Hall-type matching results, and mass partitions by hyperplanes. A new proof of the topological Hall theorem falls out along the way. The work unifies tools that combinatorial geometers reach for often.
arxiv-2509-07347:
Nuo Xu and 2 co-authors propose the first model in 2025 for time series arranged as matrices of whole numbers. Such data arise in sociology and economics, for instance counts laid out by region and category over time. No earlier work had modeled matrix-valued count series directly, leaving analysts to flatten or approximate them.

The new autoregressive model, where each period depends on earlier ones, uses two thinning operators that act from the left and right of the matrix to keep values whole. The authors study the model's properties and give two estimation methods, projection and iterative least squares, with their large-sample guarantees. A rule for choosing the model's order is also supplied. In simulations and comparisons, the model beats both continuous matrix models and flattened count models on this data type.
arxiv-2509-07447:
Taiying Peng and 3 co-authors benchmark how well AI models read user intent from first-person video in a 2025 paper. Egocentric video, shot from the wearer's viewpoint, records focus, actions, and context together, which could power proactive personal assistants. The team argues that gaze, where the eyes point, is a strong clue to intent that earlier benchmarks ignored.

Their benchmark, EgoGazeVQA, pairs gaze data with video questions generated by multimodal models and refined by human annotators. Existing models struggle to infer intentions accurately on the longer daily-life clips. Prompting methods that feed the model spatial, temporal, and intent cues drawn from gaze improve performance markedly. Further tests cover gaze-based fine-tuning and how errors in gaze estimation affect the gains. The results make a case for gaze as core input for personal AI.
arxiv-2509-07947:
Shao-Hua Hu and 1 co-author extend a trick called circuit knitting to light-based quantum states in a 2025 physics paper. Knitting lets a lab fake a hard quantum step by joining many runs of easy steps. The trick was built for systems with a fixed, finite size. Light modes are not like that. Their states live in an endless space.

The pair build a general frame for making non-Gaussian states from the states a lab has on hand. They also prove a hard limit. Some exact jobs would need an endless number of samples, so no lab could ever run them. The work still covers useful cases, such as photon-number states and grid states used to fix errors in quantum machines.
arxiv-2509-08147:
Self-driving cars plan paths among human-style drivers of many temperaments in a 2025 paper by Zhen Tian and 3 co-authors. Interactive planning must balance safety, efficiency, and scale, while many existing methods cost too much computation or lean on external safety critics to veto bad plans. The authors ground their approach in mean field game theory, where each driver optimises against the crowd's average behaviour.

An interaction-enriched unified potential field fuses style-dependent benefit and risk landscapes through a physics-inspired variational model. Conservative, aggressive, and cooperative behaviours emerge without extra safety modules, and stochastic equations support equilibrium guarantees. Traffic is a game of mutual prediction; a planner that encodes driving styles directly should merge and yield more like a person.
arxiv-2509-08247:
Critical care data from many hospitals could train fairer, more general clinical AI, if the data could be merged cleanly. Xiaolong Luo and Michael Lingzhi Li present CRISP in a 2025 research paper. CRISP is a processing pipeline for the CRITICAL dataset, a multi-institutional collection in a common data model. The dataset holds billions of records from hundreds of thousands of patients at four institutions.

The pipeline manages data quality with full audit trails. It maps varied medical vocabularies onto unified standard codes, deduplicates records, and standardizes units. Its modular design processes the whole dataset in under a day on ordinary hardware. Baseline prediction benchmarks come included, giving future studies a shared starting point. The authors say CRISP saves researchers months of preprocessing. That saved effort can go into the clinical questions instead.
arxiv-2509-08447:
Cosmic rays leaking out of the Cassiopeia A supernova remnant should glow in gamma rays, and P. Blasi calculates that glow alone in a 2025 astroparticle physics paper. How accelerated particles escape remnants is central to the origin of cosmic rays and still poorly understood. New LHAASO observations map gamma rays across a two-degree region around Cas A.

Shock evolution and particle propagation near the source are treated with special care, because both shape the expected emission. The modelling tests whether very high-energy protons were accelerated during Cas A's past activity. A young, nearby remnant is the best laboratory for escape physics: its escaping particles are the cosmic rays that eventually rain on Earth.
arxiv-2509-08747:
Wei Guo and 4 co-authors show a backdoor attack that stays silent until a model is sparsified in a 2025 paper. Semi-structured sparsity prunes two of every four weights in modern hardware. That step speeds inference and cuts memory with little accuracy loss.

Their attack, called SUS, trains two sets of weights in two phases. Kept weights carry the hidden backdoor, while pruned weights hide it in the full model. Formal guarantees say the attack will switch on after pruning. Tests beat older compression aware attacks, bypass common defenses, and survive user fine-tuning. The work warns that pruning itself can be a trigger.
arxiv-2509-09047:
Rahul Dalal and 2 co-authors construct multi-qubit golden gates in a 2025 paper. Golden gates are optimal topological generators for unitary groups, used to build any quantum operation efficiently. Earlier work covered single qubit cases in detail.

A variant of the Sarnak-Xue density hypothesis is proved using the classification of automorphic representations. That yields gate sets for higher dimensions. For two qubits, the new set needs about ten times fewer costly T-type gates than the standard Clifford plus T set at a given accuracy. Bounds for the Clifford plus CS set, friendly to fault tolerant use, are also proved tight.
arxiv-2509-09847: Mateusz Rajs studies linear recurrent sequences in a 2025 paper and asks when they nearly meet the Dold condition. A sequence counts as realizable when it passes both a sign test and the Dold test. Rajs weakens the second demand: a sequence almost passes when multiplying every term by one fixed positive constant makes it pass. He characterises which recursively defined sequences, of any order, have that property, and he bounds how large the needed constant can be.
arxiv-2509-10147:
Nenad Tomasev and 6 co-authors sketch the economy that AI agents are about to build in a 2025 position paper. The agents will trade mostly among themselves. They already transact faster than any human overseer can watch. That speed forms a new economic layer on top of the old one. The authors name that layer the sandbox economy. They sort its futures along two axes. One axis asks if it grows wild or by design. The other asks if its walls leak or hold.

Current momentum points to one version. It is vast and spontaneous. It is also highly open to the human economy. That mix brings rich coordination. It also brings systemic risk and deeper inequality. The authors weigh counterweights in turn. Auctions could split resources fairly. Mission economies could rally agents around shared goals. Trust systems could keep any steered market answerable.
arxiv-2509-10347:
Trapping a handful of atoms in laser tweezers is now routine, but predicting their behavior together is not. Matee ur Rehman and three co-authors test a quantum-chemistry-style method for such confined few-particle systems in this 2025 physics paper, going beyond simpler mean-field treatments that ignore how particles influence each other.

Their approach uses Cartesian Gaussian functions as building blocks and a Morse potential, a realistic curve for atom-atom attraction and repulsion. Making that work required implementing demanding six-dimensional integrals. They check correctness and speed against nearly exact results for two atoms in a round harmonic trap, using full configuration-interaction calculations. The work lays groundwork for arrays of traps arranged however an experiment demands.
arxiv-2509-10447:
Rare charm decays could betray physics beyond the Standard Model. Angelo Di Canto and six co-authors map that chance in this 2025 paper. Their setting is a future flavor facility. It would run at the Z pole with high luminosity, like FCC-ee or CEPC. There, huge numbers of Z bosons decay to charm quarks.

The authors single out clean null-test observables. Such quantities should be nearly zero unless new physics intervenes. One case is a dineutrino decay of the D0 meson. The other is a polarized lambda-c decay, to a proton and two leptons. They sharpen the theory of the first mode. They work out polarization asymmetries in the second, which can reach several percent. Simulations with the IDEA detector concept are hopeful. Branching fractions deep into new-physics territory seem within reach. The program would complement what the LHC can do.
arxiv-2509-10547:
Pascal Helson and Arvind Kumar argue, in a 2025 paper, that the hunt for brain disease biomarkers is stuck on the wrong method. Clinics rarely use brain features to diagnose or forecast illness, despite mountains of data and strong AI tools. The usual approach compares a patient group against healthy controls and looks for a separating feature.

The authors say that route cannot work, because brain features are degenerate: very different brains can produce the same measurement. A thought experiment they call Brain Swap makes the point. Instead, they urge studies that gather several kinds of data at once, including activity, chemistry, and imaging, followed over time, and let that richer record define patient groups before biomarkers are named.
arxiv-2509-11147:
Rahul Sinha, Ankit Gupta, and P. S. Burada wrote this 2025 physics paper on active Brownian particles, tiny self-propelled swimmers, moving through three-dimensional channels whose walls slowly pulse in and out.

Using a generalized Fick-Jacobs method, which collapses the three-dimensional motion into an effective one-dimensional description, the authors compute average speed and spread semi-analytically and check them against simulations. At one best pulsing frequency both speed and diffusion peak, an effect resembling stochastic resonance, and the peak grows with the particles' own swimming speed and the wall motion's size. The results point to better designs for microfluidic devices that steer tiny particles or biomedical tools.
arxiv-2509-11547:
Shanmuka Sadhu and 3 co-authors revisit a classic claim about eye movements in a 2025 study: that an observer's task can be decoded from how their eyes move. A famous hypothesis by Yarbus proposed exactly that, but machine learning results on real eye-tracking data have been mixed.

The authors augment a small in-person study dataset with synthetic eye movement samples from several generative models. Adding synthetic data improved task classification accuracy even for traditional algorithms. One deep sequence model reached far higher accuracy when five times more synthetic data joined the real samples, compared with a random forest baseline. The framework outperformed earlier studies on the same dataset. Results were validated across algorithm and data combinations.
arxiv-2509-11647:
Carsten van de Bruck and four co-authors prove a no-go theorem for a family of gravity theories. This 2025 cosmology paper treats bumblebee models. In them, a vector field settles at a nonzero value. Space-time symmetries break on their own. The literature holds many variants.

The authors build the most general bumblebee action. All allowed marginal terms go in. A general potential goes in too. The aim is to cover every variant studied. A full linear perturbation analysis runs on an expanding universe. For generic couplings, the scalar sector carries extra modes. One mode is expected for a massive vector. Extra ones are not. Forcing the right count fixes the potential fully. The last scalar ends up infinitely strongly coupled. Four listed conditions cannot all hold at once.
arxiv-2509-12347:
Coloring a graph with fewer colors than the obvious guarantee allows is the puzzle. Shyan Akmal and one co-author study it in 2025. Their method packs triples of mutually non-adjacent vertices. Such triples are called co-triangles. The analysis splits in a win-win way. Find many triples, and the answer is quickly yes. Find few, and deleting them leaves a simpler graph.

Building on that split, they match the running time of an earlier randomized algorithm. They use the stronger co-triangle condition to do it. One payoff speeds up dual coloring noticeably. A harder variant also becomes tractable. That variant is parameterized by clique size plus a matching measure. Two natural cousins provably do not become tractable.
arxiv-2509-12847:
Alireza Shooshtari, Antonio Pepiciello, and José Luis Domínguez-García propose grid-aware sharing rules for renewable energy communities in a 2025 paper. In such communities, members produce and consume local energy. When producers and consumers concentrate on varied feeders, the lines that distribute power, community incentives can create local grid congestion.

Their feeder-aware allocation method reflects grid topology in how energy is shared, prioritizing sharing within the same feeder. That choice incentivizes balancing generation and demand locally and boosts grid operation. They test equal, proportional, and rank-based sharing coefficients in static and dynamic forms. Data came from a real energy community whose members were distributed across four feeders. Study considered the whole community, single feeders, and single members.
arxiv-2509-13047:
Nolan Platt and Pragyansmita Nayak train a small sea model from big model output in 2025 at a sliver of the cost. Ship tracking data is huge but hard to teach from. Large models are too dear to run live for sea watch.

Billions of ship pings became tens of thousands of question pairs via two big teachers. Mixed teachers curb overfit and keep logic sound. A tuned small model hit three-quarter scores on sea tasks. Cost fell by more than two hundred fold versus live big use. The frame suits safety, guard, and traffic work at sea.
arxiv-2509-13347:
Zihao Wang and 6 co-authors present OpenHA in a 2025 paper on hierarchical agents in Minecraft. Anyone building agents that learn end to end must choose an action space: the set of moves the agent can pick from. That choice matters a great deal, and nobody has settled it. Working in the open-ended world of Minecraft, the authors first compare the leading options on a large scale.

The comparison gives an awkward answer. No one action space wins everywhere. Which one works best depends heavily on the task. Their way out is called Chain of Action. An abstract action is not handed down as an order to a separate policy. Instead it serves as a middle step in the model's own reasoning, guiding the final action that can actually be carried out.
arxiv-2509-13447:
Macarena Arenas, Kasia Jankiewicz and Daniel Wise show in 2025 that a compact nonpositively curved cube complex that is not a product has a proper quotient keeping both traits. Fundamental groups carry the claim: the group maps onto a strictly smaller group of like origin.

Non-product structure is the key hypothesis throughout the proof. Curvature and cubical form both persist in the quotient complex. The result rules out a minimal dead end for such non-products. Cube complex groups gain a descent step that later rigidity or decomposition work can iterate with care.
arxiv-2509-13547:
Harper Reed, Michael Sugimura, and Angelo Zangari test a simple idea in a 2025 artificial intelligence paper. Give language model agents the social media and journaling tools that human problem solvers use. Then let the agents choose when to use them. Their agents, built on Claude Code, worked through a set of Python programming challenges.

On the hardest problems, the tools cut cost, turns, and completion time by clear margins. On the full set the effects were mixed. Different models adopted different strategies without being told to. One wrote broadly across tools. Another leaned on journal search only when stuck. Agents also wrote far more than they read. Putting thoughts into words, it seems, drives much of the gain.
arxiv-2509-13647:
Trystan S. Lambert and six co-authors release Nessie in a 2025 astronomy software paper, a galaxy group finder written in Rust and packaged for both R and Python. Group finders cluster galaxies that belong together, and the friends-of-friends method links neighbors that lie close enough on the sky and in redshift.

Nessie needs only sky position and redshift, so it works on surveys without a well-defined brightness function. Binary search and tree-based preselection cut the pair checks sharply. Tuned on mock catalogs from the GALFORM model, it earned a strong accuracy score, and runs on the GAMA and SDSS surveys matched published catalogs. It processed about a million galaxies in roughly ten seconds on a standard laptop.
arxiv-2509-14047:
Taiki Nakano and five co-authors design controllers for interconnected systems without models in a 2025 control paper. Networks of coupled subsystems, microgrids being the motivating example, need stabilizing control, but each operator may know only its own local data. Dissipativity, an energy-balance property of a subsystem, is the key that lets local guarantees compose into global ones.

The team first derive a data-driven test for synthesizing a local controller that makes its subsystem dissipative, then give decentralized stability conditions for the whole network built from those local certificates. Both steps reduce to linear matrix inequalities, making one unified algorithm. A special version handles diffusive coupling, and numerical microgrid examples confirm the method works and scales as systems grow.
arxiv-2509-14247:
Phil Attard, writing alone in 2025, offers a heat and energy based account of why superconductors push magnetic fields out. That expulsion is called the Meissner-Ochsenfeld effect. A superconductor is a material that carries current with no resistance when cooled enough.

Attard starts from a rule for superfluid flow, namely that energy is lowest when entropy, a measure of disorder, is held fixed. Applied to currents in a superconductor, the rule yields a changed form of the first London equation, a basic law for such currents. In the new form, fields are not trapped inside the material. The account also names the physical process by which a strong enough field, the critical field, destroys superconductivity.
arxiv-2509-14447:
Sriram V. C. Nallani and Sahil Shah present a learning rule in 2025 for brain machine interfaces that read signals directly from cortex. Decoders must adapt as neural signals drift, yet run within strict memory limits on implanted or nearby hardware.

Their dual timescale Hebbian rule updates a spiking neural network at each time step, with memory fixed no matter how long the sequence runs. Fast and slow eligibility traces, error modulated updates and a simple homeostatic control replace heavy gradient tools and replay buffers. On two primate data sets, decoding accuracy stayed strong while measured memory fell by well over half against backpropagation through time. Constant memory online learning suits interfaces that cannot pause to retrain.
arxiv-2509-14547:
Yi Lin, Lujin Zhao and Yijie Shi propose PriorDynaFlow in 2025, a system that builds multi agent workflows before a task runs, not only from past experience. Carefully designed workflows of language models beat single models on hard tasks. Most builders lean only on historical cases.

History helps, but each new task has unique traits that old workflows miss. Their framework first uses Q-table learning to prune and guide the decision space from experience. Agents then collaborate to construct a workflow tailored to the current task characteristics. The a priori design balances proven patterns with task specific adaptation. Better upfront workflow design could cut the costly trial and error that multi agent systems usually need at run time.
arxiv-2509-14647:
NVJK Kartik and three co-authors present AgentCompass in 2025, a test frame for agentic workflows that are already live in firms. Multi agent systems built on large language models fail in emergent, system wide ways that launch tests miss. Firms need checks and debugging built for agents in use.

AgentCompass copies expert debuggers in stages: find and sort errors, group them by theme, score them with numbers, then sum up a plan. A dual memory, episodic and semantic, carries lessons from case to case. The pipe turns scattered agent failures into ranked, clear findings. Owners of live agents gain a repeat audit loop, not fire drills driven by tales after each mishap.
arxiv-2509-14747:
SanMin Wang, in a solo 2025 number theory paper, builds algorithms for modular parametrizations of elliptic curves over the rational numbers. A modular parametrization maps the curve X0(N) onto an elliptic curve E. Wang constructs a family of modular polynomials that connect a modular function on that curve with the j-invariant of E.

With those polynomials, readers can locate the poles of the parametrization exactly and compute its values at cusps. Wang also gives algorithms for ramification points and for the fibres above any chosen point of E. A detailed example works out a complex multiplication point for conductor 389, tracking a large Galois group action. The paper closes by linking the construction to points of infinite order on the curve.
arxiv-2509-15447:
Caitlin Cisar leads a team of eight that steers fake data made by language models. Many apps use made up personas to guide such data, but plain text personas leave the model to guess which traits matter. That guess work makes the output sound fake and hard to steer. The team wanted a clearer dial for style and mind traits.

Their method, PILOT, first turns a persona sketch into scores across word and mind traits. Those scores then guide the writing along clear axes. Tests on three large models with twenty five personas show the score based path cuts fake sounding repeats. It also lifts how cleanly outputs group by topic. The trade off is shorter, tighter text.
arxiv-2509-15647:
M. Peigné, C. Pham, and T. D. Vo prove a fine grained limit result for a special random walk. Kemperman's walk switches its step rule as it crosses between negative and positive whole numbers. Such walks are called oscillating. The team ask for the exact long term chance that the walk returns to a set point.

Their route tracks a hidden sub process that captures the swings between the two sides. They handle both cases: walks that return for sure and walks that drift away. A widened theorem on renewal operators, acting on a space of functions, joins with a split of the walk's path. Under mild rules on step sizes, they get the exact decay of the return chance.
arxiv-2509-15947:
Katharina Eckstein leads a large team that tests pre-training for finding objects in 3D medical scans. Spotting tumors and organs in volumes is a key part of computer aided diagnosis. Pre-training has helped image cutting a lot, yet its use for 3D detection stayed underexplored. Past attempts leaned on flat scans or photos of the natural world.

Theirs is the first systematic study of how pre-training fits top detection designs, both classic and transformer based. Pre-training lifts detection scores across tasks and data sets in a steady way. Self taught pre-training based on rebuilding inputs beats supervised pre-training. Contrast based pre-training gives no clear gain here. Code is public for reuse.
arxiv-2509-16147:
Terwilliger algebras are matrix structures built from grouping schemes, and a key question is when they come close to being commutative. Nicholas L. Bastian and Stephen P. Humphries add a sixth test for this trait in a broad class of cases. They then sort out which finite groups yield such algebras when the scheme comes from the group's own classes.

Only two kinds of groups qualify: those where all elements commute, and a special class known as Camina groups. The authors also compute the size of each algebra and show how the schemes break into simpler parts. The work tightens the map of these algebraic objects.
arxiv-2509-16547:
Adrian Wurm, in a solo 2025 paper, asks how hard it is to check rules pulled out of neural networks. A rule here states a broad pattern that holds over much of a network's input space. People extract such rules to grasp what a network has learned. Wurm studies that checking task through the lens of complexity theory.

He looks at networks that use a common activation and at simpler Boolean networks. Several kinds of rules are covered. He shows how the checking tasks can be turned into each other. Most of them turn out to be hard in a precise sense. The work sets limits on what rule checking can promise.
arxiv-2509-16847:
Constanza Valdivieso and co-authors refine a profile for cosmic ray showers in a 2025 physics paper. When a gamma ray hits the air, it spawns a cascade of particles. A classic profile, named for Greisen, predicts how many particles appear at each stage. At low energies, that profile drifts from simulations. The team add a fix tied to shower age and angle.

Their modified profile cuts deviations to under a twentieth across heights and angles. The classic profile drifted far more. Tests span high sites and a wide range of incoming angles. Better profiles help mountain observatories count particles with cheap math instead of heavy simulation runs.
arxiv-2509-16947:
Adilson Berlatto and Tulio Santos study self-similarity in nilpotent groups in a 2025 math paper. A self-similar group can act on a tree in a way that copies itself at each branch. The groups here are finitely generated, torsion-free, and nilpotent, a class with tame commutator behavior. The pair link this trait to geometric equivalence, a coarser sameness between groups.

Their result settles a question posed by S. Sidki. It builds on work by other authors on this circle of problems. Connections like this help sort which groups can arise from self-similar actions. That sorting matters for dynamics and for group-based models in computing.
arxiv-2509-17247:
Dongheon Lee, Younghoo Kwon, and Jung-Woo Choi built one model that handles many listening tasks at once. Their 2025 arXiv paper tackles auditory scene analysis, where several sounds overlap, echo, and move through space. A single system must split the sources, clean the echoes, name each event, class the sounds, and say where each one comes from.

Their model, DeepASA, wraps sound features into object-like units, one per source, and refines them step by step through linked inference rounds. A feature extractor, a transformer that merges facts, and a separator that yields per-object features feed task-specific decoders. Working with objects sidesteps the mix-ups that plague track-by-track tools. A matching step guards against early split errors by checking that features stay coherent over time, and tests on recorded scenes back the design.
arxiv-2509-17347:
Yoonjae Park and Adam P. Willard model how electrons hop between a molecule and an electrode in a 2025 arXiv paper. The standard rate estimate samples the energy gap between states and treats the hop as an instant switch of atomic charges. The authors instead give the moving electron an explicit path-integral form, so it spreads over many paths at once.

They join path integral molecular dynamics with Marcus-Hush-Chidsey theory to price a test hop between a gold electrode and a ferrocyanide complex. They vary the hop distance and the applied voltage. Rates and thermodynamics from the explicit method match experiments better than the fixed-charge version does. The team then studies how nearby spectator cations bridge the hop and shift the rate. Again the explicit method gives cation effects closer to what labs observe.
arxiv-2509-17847:
Saghir Alfasly and 4 co-authors make fake tissue images to train medical image tools. Their 2025 paper deals with pathology slides, where tissue types mix in fine detail. Hand-tagged slides are scarce, and plain text prompts miss the true look of each tissue type.

Their diffusion model takes both a map of tissue zones and real crops from those zones. For untagged slide sets, it first groups slides into many tissue types to build maps on its own. Fake images from the plan scored close to real ones on later tasks. Scores for image likeness also rose a lot.
arxiv-2509-18047:
Nicolas Salvade and Tim Hillel let each person's tastes be a learned function of who they are. Their 2025 paper deals with panel choice data, where the same folk choose again and again. Fixed-effect models strain when each person has few choices, while random-effect models rest on strong shape guesses.

Their Functional Effects Model maps traits such as age and income to a person's own taste values, using strong machine learning tools. That lets the model forecast choices for folk never seen before. Tests on fake and real data sets show it can recover true taste values. It also avoids the flaws of both older styles.
arxiv-2509-18347:
Small carbon-rich dust grains called PAHs glow in many galaxies, but they grow scarce where heavy elements are rare. Cory M. Whitcomb and 13 co-authors study that drop with new space telescope images. Their 2025 paper uses JWST camera maps of M101, a nearby spiral galaxy. The maps cover zones from Sun-like makeup down to about two-fifths of it.

The team tracked the shortest PAH glow, which comes from the smallest grains. Its share of all PAH light tripled as the heavy element share fell, rising from about one percent to about three percent. That trend matches a model where grain growth is held back in poor material. Some loss of small grains to harsh light stays possible if the size cutoff stays low. Oddly, the small-grain glow rose against total heat glow even as all PAH output fell. The smallest grains may simply be the toughest.
arxiv-2509-18647:
Heavy quarks are born in the first instants of a heavy-ion collision, so they can probe the fireball's earliest stage. Mayank Singh, Manu Kurian, Björn Schenke, Sangyong Jeon, and Charles Gale study charm quarks in that early window in this 2025 paper. Their test observables are two measures of how D-mesons, particles carrying charm, are suppressed and deflected. The setting is lead-lead collisions at a top collider energy.

The team models the bulk matter with a chained framework of established codes. Charm quarks start from a standard event generator and then diffuse through the medium under Langevin dynamics. Even though the earliest stage broadens charm momentum a lot, the final D-meson measures barely respond. That weak response means the observables mostly reflect later stages. The result tempers hopes of reading the pre-equilibrium phase from charm data alone.
arxiv-2509-19147:
Madeleine I. G. Daepp and eight co-authors, in a working paper, study how generative AI is actually used to sway public opinion. They interviewed defenders such as fact-checkers, journalists, and officials in Taiwan, and creators such as influencers and political consultants in India and Taiwan. Both places see heavy online propaganda. The word deepfakes, they find, dominates defenders' fears and skews which countermeasures get priority.

The authors build a taxonomy that splits uses by whether AI involvement is obvious or hidden, and whether the aim is to promote or to tear down. Deception was rarely the point: Indian creators often flaunted AI use to cut legal risk, seeking persuasion instead. The real gains were efficiency, working across languages and formats, and slipping past human and algorithmic detection. They urge security researchers to widen their threat models beyond deepfakes.
arxiv-2509-19247:
Nikku Madhusudhan and three co-authors survey what the James Webb Space Telescope is revealing about sub-Neptune planets, worlds between Earth and Neptune in size. Such planets dominate the known exoplanet population, yet nothing like them orbits our Sun. They may range from rocky gas dwarfs to water worlds to mini-Neptunes, with wildly different surfaces and interiors. Webb's atmospheric readings are the first real window into that diversity.

Early highlights include carbon-bearing molecules found in K2-18 b, a sub-Neptune in its star's habitable zone. Measured abundances hint at chemical disequilibrium and trace how metal content scales with planet mass. For water-rich worlds, rising steam content with temperature suggests a threshold where cold-trapped atmospheres turn steamy. The authors organize the emerging zoo, from possibly habitable hycean worlds to supercritical water worlds, into a working taxonomy.
arxiv-2509-19347:
Sara Todorovikj and two co-authors argue that scoring language models on knowledge graph tasks by accuracy alone misses what the tasks demand of a thinker. They characterize the tasks inside a public benchmark framework using three frameworks from cognitive psychology, which grade mental work by kind and complexity. The goal is a richer picture of what each task actually asks. Their analysis maps how task demands are distributed across the benchmark.

It also identifies demands that the benchmark barely tests, leaving blind spots in evaluation. Underrepresented kinds of thinking mean a model can score well while staying untested on harder cognition. The authors motivate more diverse task design and richer interpretation of results. Their approach complements correctness scores with a profile of cognitive load, offering benchmark builders a way to see what their tests really measure.
arxiv-2509-19447:
Cosmic rays streaming through a galaxy push on its gas and drive winds, but simulations must model their transport honestly to capture that feedback. Joki Rosdahl and five co-authors implement a two-moment cosmic ray fluid solver inside RAMSES, a widely used astrophysics code. The method tracks both the rays' energy density and its flux in three dimensions, rather than energy alone. Diffusion, streaming, and advection are all handled, and a battery of multidimensional tests, including shocks, checks the solver's robustness.

The team then runs a full simulation of an isolated galactic disc, where supernova explosions launch galaxy-wide outflows. Comparing the new solver with the code's older one-moment version shows what the extra moment buys. The implementation gives modelers a sturdier tool for the feedback physics that shapes galaxies.
arxiv-2509-19847:
Waves born from buoyancy ripple through the Sun's lower atmosphere, hauling energy upward. Oana Vesa and four co-authors watch those gravity waves with two instruments at once: a ground-based spectrometer and a space observatory. They sort the waves by phase and coherence across wavelengths. Magnetic fields, especially their tilt, should steer the waves as they climb.

Propagating waves with the expected traits were detected. The magnetic steering, though, left only faint marks in the standard phase diagrams. After filtering to the wave regime, the team estimates the upward energy flux. Solar atmospheric heating remains an open puzzle, and every carrier of energy counts. Careful wave bookkeeping helps test which mechanisms can supply the heat the corona demands.
arxiv-2509-19947:
Backdoor attacks poison training data so a model obeys a hidden trigger while labels stay clean. Zhixiao Wu and five co-authors note that two attack ingredients are usually tuned apart: which samples to poison, and what trigger to plant. Stacking the best of each gives disappointing results, they find. Sample choice and trigger design interact in both directions.

Their generalized component set co-designs the pair collaboratively. Hard samples carry triggers better; triggers reshape which samples count as hard. Attack success and stealth are graded together. Security research publishes such attacks to force defenses awake. Clean-label poisoning is especially worrying because inspection of labels reveals nothing. A framework that unifies the design space helps defenders model the true threat.
arxiv-2509-20147:
Siddharth Chandak, Ilai Bistritz, and Nicholas Bambos wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on distributed learning. They model a setting where several tug-of-war games run at the same time. In each game, pushing harder helps the pusher but lowers everyone else's reward. Each player joins only one game at a time and may switch.

The authors propose the Meta Tug-of-Peace algorithm for this system. Action updates use a simple stochastic approximation rule. Decisions to switch games rely on rare one-bit messages between players. They prove the algorithm settles at an equilibrium that meets a target quality-of-service reward for every player. Simulations cover power control, task allocation, and sensor network activation. In each case, the algorithm performed as the theory predicts.
arxiv-2509-20547:
Graphene quantum dots could replace toxic semiconductor dots in sensors and devices, argue Kumar Gautam and seven co-authors in a 2025 arXiv review-style paper. Classic dots like cadmium telluride perform well but raise toxicity and stability worries. Graphene dots are tiny honeycomb carbon flakes with tunable electronic and optical behavior. The paper surveys how they are made and where they fit.

Synthesis routes split into top-down cutting and bottom-up building, each with trade-offs. Compared with standard dots, the graphene versions offer better light stability, friendlier biology, and adjustable energy gaps. Those traits suit sensitive biosensing, real-time food safety checks, and smart packaging that could cut grain waste. The authors also discuss biomedical, electronic, and energy storage uses. Integration with quantum technologies is presented as the longer horizon.
arxiv-2509-20847:
Some groups have no lattice inside them, and point patterns in such groups behave differently. Nachi Avraham-Re'em, Michael Bjorklund, and Rickard Cullman study that difference in a 2025 companion paper on point processes in abelian groups without lattices. Examples include p-adic groups and the finite adeles.

For cross sections with evenly spread return times, the authors prove the intersection covolume is at least twice the intensity. That is a strict gap compared with the lattice case, where equality can hold. Cut-and-project systems, they show, are the unique ones reaching the minimum. As an application, the authors characterize generalized Farey fractions in the finite adeles through their Banach density. The paper complements their joint work on cross sections.
arxiv-2509-20947:
When a black hole is struck, it rings with waves whose shape should be stable against small disturbances. Liang-Bi Wu and four co-authors verify that stability in a 2025 paper accepted by the European Physical Journal C. They approximate the Regge-Wheeler potential, which governs the ringing, by a staircase of steps.

Treating the difference between the true potential and its step approximation as an environmental perturbation, the authors compute waveforms with a Green's function method. They derive analytic waveforms for an initial pulse placed near the horizon or far away. The waveforms barely change under tiny potential modifications, confirming stability. A broader initial bump, however, leaves a stronger mark, a nuance the authors highlight for gravitational-wave modeling.
arxiv-2509-21247:
Image networks often cheat, labelling pictures from shallow clues instead of the real object. The paper is the work of Ryan Yang and 2 co-authors. Convolutional networks often cheat by using shallow clues in an image. They may give the right label for the wrong reason. Human sight is more robust because attention focuses on what matters. Past fixes needed costly expert notes on where to look.

The authors use vision language models to make attention maps from text prompts. No manual notes are needed. A loss term aligns the network attention with those maps. Tests used hard sets such as ColoredMNIST and DecoyMNIST, where colour or decoy patches mislead models. The method reached top results on one set and stayed competitive on others.
arxiv-2509-21447:
Speech can be encoded by how the vocal tract moves, not just by sound. Jihwan Lee and 8 co-authors propose a six dimensional encoding in a 2025 paper. Real time MRI data grounds the design. Key regions include the velum, tongue root, and larynx. The framework is called ARTI-6, and it has three linked components.

First, a six dimensional feature set represents the vocal tract regions. Second, an inversion model predicts those features from speech acoustics using speech foundation models. Its prediction correlation was high. Third, a synthesis model rebuilds intelligible speech from the features alone. Even this low dimensional code gave natural sounding speech. The framework is interpretable, efficient, and physiologically grounded.
arxiv-2509-21547:
Learning is choice under uncertainty, Yevgeny Seldin argues in a 2025 book on machine learning theory. Candidate output rules are selected by empirical hit rate estimates on data. Random sampling makes those estimates noisy, so choice can mislead. The book supplies statistical tools for theoretical guarantees on choice outcomes. Concentration of measure inequalities are the main instrument throughout.

Those inequalities control how far an empirical expectation deviates from the true one. A broad range is covered, from Markov and Chebyshev to Hoeffding, Bernstein, and split kl variants. Classic offline learning is studied after the inequalities. The science of choice framing unifies the topics. Students and researchers in statistical learning theory are the meant readers of the book.
arxiv-2509-21647:
Training a machine learned interatomic potential needs high quality data sets and careful checking. Adam Lahouari and 2 co-authors automate that workflow with language model agents in a 2025 paper. Their Automated Machine Learning Workflow unifies dataset creation through model checking. Language model agents assist with electronic form code choice, input preparation, and output conversion. An analysis suite based on the ASE library supports molecular model runs.

The workflow builds on the MACE design for potentials. Acridine polymorphs supply the checking case. Fine tuning a base model gave low errors on energies with a straightforward setup. Near quantum hit rate at much lower cost is the promise of such potentials. Automation aims to make reliable potential building routine rather than artisanal.
arxiv-2509-21747:
Judging the emotion of a whole group in a photo is harder than reading one face. Qing Zhu and 5 co-authors propose a framework using scene context and label semantics in a 2025 paper. Past methods underestimate visual scene context when modelling individual relationships. They also overlook semantic information carried by emotion labels themselves. Both gaps are addressed in the design.

A visual context encoding module uses multi scale scene information to encode relationships diversely. An emotion semantic encoding module prompts a large language model with group level labels. Nuanced emotion lexicons are generated and refined into comprehensive semantic representations. Combining scene and semantics aims for more complete emotion understanding. Group level emotion recognition in complex scenes is the task.
arxiv-2509-21947:
Safety teams attack language models on purpose, hunting for prompts that make them produce harmful content, so the holes can be fixed.
