Ethan Wang, Zubair Shafiq, and Yash Vekaria present FP-Agent, the first controlled measurement study of AI browsing agents and how they can be fingerprinted. Such agents navigate websites autonomously in real browsers and perform everyday tasks, making them hard to distinguish from humans or from each other. Using an instrumented honey website, the team collects browser and behavioral features while seven agents and human users complete flight booking, shopping, and forum tasks.

Browser fingerprints give limited power when several agents share them. Behavioral fingerprints, covering typing, scrolling, and mouse behavior, are distinctive and separate agents from humans and from one another. In a case study, their classifier detects all seven agents, whereas a commercial bot detection service detects only one.
arxiv-2605-01447:
Yuki Ishihara and sixteen co-authors settle the magnetic ground state of a kagome lattice crystal, a metal where atoms sit on a pattern of corner-sharing triangles. The compound, with neodymium, ruthenium, and aluminum, had been reported to order with two unequal moment sizes on its two neodymium sites.

Using single-crystal neutron diffraction, backed by polarized neutron tests, the team finds a simpler state. All moments line up in one direction with one shared length, a collinear ferromagnet with no repeating offset. The polarized beam's flipping ratio matches this uniform state and not the older two-size claim. The crystal orders near 41 kelvin, and the corrected ground state gives a firm base for reading its large Hall and Nernst responses, which grow from thermal fluctuations near that point.
arxiv-2605-01747:
Gaurav Bhatnagar and Amritanshu Prasad prove an identity that a counting problem over finite fields had left as a conjecture. The question grew out of enumerating subspaces, a basic census in finite geometry. It concerned a q-analogue of the binomial theorem, the decorated cousin of the schoolbook expansion where powers are weighted by q-combinatorial counts.

Their result is broader than the conjecture that prompted it. They establish a bibasic, double-sum identity: two bases instead of one, and two layers of summation, extending the terminating q-binomial theorem into that wider family. Identities of this kind are the load-bearing walls of q-series, the branch of mathematics behind partition counts, quantum groups, and much of modern combinatorics. A proof here does double duty, settling the subspace count that raised the question and adding a general tool that other counters can now cite.
arxiv-2605-01847:
Xiao Jia introduces NeuroState-Bench, a benchmark that tests whether a language model agent keeps its commitments across a long, multi-turn task. Success at the end alone does not show whether the agent held to what the task required. The benchmark uses fixed side questions, built into each task, rather than guesses about hidden model states.

The set holds 144 tasks and 306 side probes across eight failure types, with clean and distracting versions and three levels of difficulty. Human checks on sampled tasks showed strong agreement. Across 32 model profiles, the leader on task success was not the leader on commitment, and most profiles changed rank when the score switched to commitment.
arxiv-2605-01947:
Srinjana Routh and colleagues report a radio sign of poleward flow high in the Sun's atmosphere. Flows and magnetic fields together move angular momentum and magnetic flux on the Sun, but behaviour in the upper chromosphere, where magnetism dominates, was uncertain. The team used twenty-seven years of full-disk radio images at 17 gigahertz from the Nobeyama Radioheliograph.

They find a poleward pattern about three thousand kilometres up, with speeds that mirror the known surface circulation and vary with the solar cycle. Bright radio features track poleward magnetic flux closely. The authors read this as first evidence that flows seen at radio heights reflect deeper circulation, in line with a magnetic tree picture.
arxiv-2605-02147:
Vincent Pacelli, Akash Ratheesh, and Evangelos Theodorou improve sampling-based control for nonlinear robots by using optimal transport. Methods such as MPPI and cross-entropy sampling are vital where dynamics jump and gradients fail. But their information-based goals ignore the geometry of the cost landscape, which can cause mode averaging when good solutions split into separate clusters.

Their method, OT-MPC, couples candidate control sequences to low-cost proposals through an entropy-regularised transport plan. That refines candidates toward nearby good samples while keeping coverage of the solution space across the group. Updates are closed-form and gradient-free via the Sinkhorn algorithm, allowing real-time use. Tests cover navigation, manipulation, and locomotion tasks.
arxiv-2605-02347:
Lukas Rustler and Matej Hoffmann present ShapeGrasp, a robot grasping method that completes an object's shape while it grasps, as humans do with touch. People combine a first visual estimate with tactile and body feedback during contact. ShapeGrasp couples visuo-haptic shape completion, building a full 3D shape from partial data, with physics-based grasp planning in an iterative loop.

From one RGB-D view it infers a complete shape, generates candidate grasps by rigid-body simulation, and executes the best feasible grasp. Each attempt adds constraints from tactile contacts and gripper occupancy, which update the shape. Failures trigger pose re-estimation and regrasping with the refined shape. Real-world tests use two robots and grippers.
arxiv-2605-02447:
Maoheng Li and five co-authors build a system to detect sarcasm when words and nonverbal cues point in opposite ways. Sarcasm is hard for machines because the text may sound warm while a face or voice shows the reverse. Past systems often mixed the two streams late and in a uniform way, which can blur the clash that marks sarcasm.

Their model, PC-MNet, checks fit at two levels and lets a polarity signal steer attention. A routing step fuses only the most useful evidence, guided by a prior graph and by training that stresses contrast. On the MUStARD bench and on balanced versions built to cut false cues, the system beat the strongest prior multimodal baseline on a key score.
arxiv-2605-02647:
Mario Rodríguez Béjar and three co-authors present ContextualJailbreak, an automated red-teaming method that attacks language models through staged conversation. Single prompts can be blocked by safety training, but earlier turns can quietly prime a model toward compliance. Hand-built multi-turn setups beat single-turn tricks, yet automated search had mostly stayed single-turn.

Their method runs evolutionary search over a simulated primed dialogue, in black-box fashion. A graded harm score from a two-level judge guides the search, so partly harmful replies steer the next step instead of being discarded. Five meaning-based mutation moves reshape the dialogue, covering roleplay, scenario, expansion, troubleshooting, and mechanism angles. The work is defensive in aim: mapping which priming forms work helps builders close them.
arxiv-2605-02747:
Alexandros Eskenazis, Apostolos Giannopoulos, and Natalia Tziotziou tackle two geometric problems about log-concave measures, a broad class of probability laws with a convex log-density. One is a dimensional form of the Brunn-Minkowski inequality, which bounds the measure of a blend of two sets by the measures of the parts. The other asks how large the perimeter of such a measure can be in the isotropic, standardized case.

For symmetric convex sets and even measures, the authors prove the dimensional inequality with an explicit, if small, exponent, using diffusion operators and gradient bounds. For the perimeter problem, they show the maximum grows on the order of the dimension itself. A shared ingredient is a known gradient bound for isotropic log-concave laws. Further uses cover projections, moments, and surface measures.
arxiv-2605-03147:
Rasmus T. Aavang, Rasmus Tjalk-Bøggild, Alexandre Iolov, Giovanni Rizzi, Mike Zhang, and Johannes Bjerva study how to pull performance indicators from earnings calls. Unlike templated SEC filings, calls are unlabeled, unstructured, and conversational, so models trained on filings face a hard domain shift.

The team introduces three benchmarks, including an earnings call set and an expert-annotated subset, and finds encoder models struggle with that shift. They then propose a language-model system for open-ended extraction from call transcripts. Human checks gave strong precision, setting a baseline for tracking emerging indicators over time.
arxiv-2605-03247:
Wenshuo Wang and Fan Zhang propose posterior-first simulation for neural solvers of partial differential equations that see only one field at deployment. A single snapshot can hide which underlying problem state produced it, and a direct field-to-future model collapses that ambiguity into one guess, harming rollouts.

Their method first infers a probability distribution over the smallest sufficient hidden state, then predicts from that distribution. Theory ties the target, learning rule, and failure mode together, with scores that make the posterior learnable. On hidden-metadata PDEBench tasks, rollout error fell markedly, closing much of the gap to an oracle.
arxiv-2605-03547:
JuneHyoung Kwon, JungMin Yun, and YoungBin Kim introduce CoVUBench, a benchmark for copyright unlearning in vision-language models. It tests whether such models can truly forget protected visual content. Models trained on web data can memorize characters and logos. Unlearning promises removal after training, but multimodal erasure is hard to test robustly.

The benchmark uses legally safe synthetic data. Visual variations in composition and domain test whether forgetting generalizes. It scores both erasure strength, from the rights holder's view, and retained utility, from the deployer's view. That trade-off measurement gives a standard tool for responsible unlearning research.
arxiv-2605-04047:
Priyam Srivastava and eight co-authors compare two entanglement swapping disciplines for quantum repeater chains that distribute key material for quantum key distribution. Repeaters join short entangled links into long ones by swapping, but stored pairs lose fidelity while waiting, so swap timing affects the secret-key rate. Both schemes studied use the same reinforcement-learned link controllers, isolating the scheduling effect on a simulated four-hop chain.

The sequential scheme builds and stores partial chains, while the synchronized one waits until all links are ready before swapping. When stored pairs cannot keep enough fidelity for even one time step, the sequential scheme produced no key while synchronized retained a small rate. Once sequential becomes viable, it outperforms synchronized by up to about nineteen percent in homogeneous chains, with the advantage shrinking as memory lifetime grows.
arxiv-2605-04247:
Paula Pacheco, Pablo Granitto, and Juan B. Cabral work on spectral unmixing, the task of working out which materials are present in each pixel of an image taken from above. A simple linear model works well until light scatters more than once, which breaks its assumptions.

Their method decides, pixel by pixel and from physical cues in the data, whether the harder nonlinear treatment is truly needed there. It blends three nonlinear models through a learned weighting and produces maps that show which regime each pixel falls in. Tests on three standard scenes beat the baselines they compare against.
arxiv-2605-04747:
Leon Witt and four co-authors design a way to pay federated learning participants fairly for their contributions without any ground truth to check against. In federated learning, many clients train a shared model on their own data. Rewarding honest, useful work normally requires a public test set. It can also require knowledge of the data distribution.

Their knowledge-free correlated agreement mechanism is provably strictly truthful when an honest majority holds, fixing a label-flipping vulnerability in an earlier agreement scheme. They test it on federated tuning of language model adapters. They also test it on a real printed-circuit-board inspection task. Rewards can be computed efficiently in real time. That suits decentralised and blockchain-based incentive designs.
arxiv-2605-04847:
Soyoung Park, Hwanjun Song, and Sungsu Lim tackle uncertainty estimates for graph neural networks, which predict from data linked in a network. Honest error ranges matter in high-stakes uses, but graph message passing breaks assumptions that standard methods rely on. Fixes often need costly resampling or extra calibration after training.

Their framework, QpiGNN, gives predictions and uncertainty through two separate heads trained together with a new loss. It needs no quantile inputs and no post-processing, yet carries guarantees on coverage and near-best interval width. Across nineteen benchmarks it gave higher coverage with intervals about half as wide as baselines, while staying robust to noise.
arxiv-2605-04947:
Alexander Lauer and three co-authors shrink the structures used to analyse conflicts between graph transformation rules. Conflict analysis shows how rules can interfere, based on critical pairs in minimal contexts. The essential information about a conflict, though, sits in much smaller structures called essences, first developed for simpler rule conditions.

The authors extend disabling essences to rules with arbitrary nested application conditions, not just one normal form. From them they build symbolic conflict essences capturing how two rules interact. They prove a transformation pair is dependent exactly when such an essence embeds in it, and they relate essences to the established notion of initial conflicts.
arxiv-2605-05047:
Pablo Concha-Vega defines a local update rule for two-coloured graphs, inspired by adaptive networks and the pull toward similarity called homophily. Under the rule, each vertex takes the majority colour of its neighbours, then links to same-coloured neighbours and unlinks from opposite ones. The question is whether a given pair of vertices ends up connected after repeated updates.

Concha-Vega shows the rule can simulate Boolean circuits step by step. Using that simulation, he establishes that deciding whether a given pair becomes connected is P-complete under logspace reductions. The result places this simple social-style dynamics among the hardest problems solvable in polynomial time.
arxiv-2605-05547:
Brazil's Atlantic Forest is a biodiversity hotspot where only a small share of the original cover survives. Alice Heiman asks whether satellite-based AI embeddings can track how well cleared land is being restored. Ground reporting cannot scale to thousands of sites, and common vegetation indices saturate before young forest matures.

Heiman studied over seventeen hundred restoration sites in São Paulo using AlphaEarth embeddings. She defines success by similarity to mature secondary forest, a reference trajectory in embedding space. Sites clustered clearly by land use, and some showed clean change signals, though the embeddings still miss some site details.
arxiv-2605-05647:
The stationary Navier-Stokes equations describe fluid at rest under steady forcing, and Liouville theorems say when only the trivial flow can exist. Gastón Vergara-Hermosilla proves such a result using a condition on just one part of the velocity: its radial component. Classical results demand decay or integrability of the whole field.

He shows any finite-energy solution is trivial when the radial component lies in a certain Lebesgue space, with the exponent between three halves and three. A second result works in variable-exponent spaces, needing the condition only on a bounded region. Rigidity, it turns out, can be driven by localized information.
arxiv-2605-05947:
Motoi Endo and Takumu Yamanaka investigate how light dark matter could be made by kaons in the early universe. Their setting is freeze-in, where dark matter builds up slowly through rare interactions, inside a cosmos that reheated to a low temperature. The link runs through a flavor changing interaction between strange and down quarks and dark matter particles.

Below the QCD crossover, kaon decays and scatterings set the dark matter abundance the authors compute. The same interaction also drives rare kaon decays that experiments such as NA62 and KOTO can search for. Lower reheating temperatures demand larger couplings, they find. That makes this dark matter story testable at rare kaon decay experiments, including the planned KOTO II.
arxiv-2605-06047:
Duong Nguyen, Mohammed Jawhar, and Nicolas Chesneau adapt tabular foundation models to new tasks without touching their weights. These models predict well on tables with no training, through in-context learning, but their built in biases stay fixed. Full fine tuning is costly, and lighter weight tuning must be refitted to each model's inner design.

Their adapter, TFM-Retouche, learns a small correction in the input space instead, so it works with any frozen backbone. Training runs end to end through the frozen model, and a guard falls back to the plain model when adaptation does not help on held out data. On a 51 data set benchmark, the adapted model topped the leaderboard and gained 56 Elo points.
arxiv-2605-06147:
Matthew Debono, Jackson Levi Said, and Gabriel Farrugia explore a generalized Brans-Dicke theory as a route to dynamical dark energy. The standard cosmic model faces tensions with precision data, hinting that dark energy may change over time. Their version couples a scalar field to gravity in a non minimal way and gives that field a non canonical kinetic term.

They recast the field equations as an autonomous dynamical system and study its equilibrium states and their stability. Three widely used potentials, constant, power law, and exponential, each yield solutions that match the standard model at background level. The behavior still differs noticeably from other scalar tensor models, a direct effect of the coupling and the unusual kinetic term.
arxiv-2605-06347:
Xuening Wu and seven co-authors model humans and language models as one coupled dynamical system that can collapse epistemically. People increasingly lean on AI to generate, summarize, and reason, while models retrain on the resulting flood of AI shaped text. Past work studied human cognitive offloading and model collapse separately, and this paper joins them into a single feedback loop with three variables: human cognition, data quality, and model capability.

Analysis of the minimal model reveals three regimes. Systems can settle into co-evolutionary enhancement, a fragile equilibrium, or degenerative convergence toward a narrow, low diversity state. Simulations show heavier reliance on AI can tip the loop into that poor equilibrium. In information terms, the loop develops a bottleneck where falling entropy means lost diversity rather than useful compression.
arxiv-2605-06647:
Zeyu Yang, Xu Han, Qi Ma, Jason Chen, and Anshumali Shrivastava present SIRA, a retrieval agent designed to search like an expert instead of a newcomer. Retrieval-augmented agents usually issue exploratory queries, skim snippets, and reformulate for many rounds, wasting time and missing evidence. SIRA instead asks which terms separate wanted evidence from similar-looking confusers in the whole corpus.

Offline, a model enriches documents with missing search vocabulary; at query time it predicts evidence terms the query omits, then filters them with corpus statistics. One weighted BM25 search finishes the job. Across ten BEIR benchmarks SIRA leads the comparison without relevance labels, and a new hard Wikipedia benchmark shows it beating multi-round commercial agents.
arxiv-2605-06847:
BoRui Li, Bofan Yu, and Xing-Dong Yang study how people feel about privacy inside sensor-filled smart car cabins. As cabins gain cameras and other sensors, they become smart environments shared by owners and temporary users such as family, friends, or renters, whose privacy expectations may differ. Semi-structured interviews with eighteen participants surface the factors shaping each group's views.

Some factors influence owners and non-owners alike, while others weigh much more heavily on one group. From those patterns the authors draw design implications for balancing the needs of multiple stakeholders in one shared cabin. The study gives car interface designers an early map of a privacy problem that grows as sensing spreads.
arxiv-2605-06947:
Chenhui Xu and four co-authors tackle a hard problem in 3D generation: making brick structures that actually stand up. Earlier systems checked each brick with an outside physics simulator and rolled back bad placements. That checking made generation slow and clumsy.

Xu and colleagues instead train the model with reinforcement learning, using rewards at the level of the whole structure. The rewards favor avoiding collisions, keeping the build connected, interlocking bricks, and matching the target shape. The trained model then generates stable structures in one pass, with no rollback, and the authors report top quality at much faster speeds.
arxiv-2605-07147:
MathlibPR is a benchmark from Zixuan Xie, Xinyu Liu, and Shangtong Zhang for judging whether language models can review math library contributions. Mathlib, the shared Lean mathematics library, grows through pull requests that human reviewers must check against conventions. That review step has become a bottleneck for the whole ecosystem.

The benchmark is built from real pull request histories, with a staged protocol for judging merge readiness. Tested models and coding agents both struggled to tell truly merge-ready requests from ones that merely built successfully. The authors hope such data can train reviewer assistants and steer models toward contributions maintainers would actually accept.
arxiv-2605-07647:
Abigail Victoria Gurin Schleifer and four co-authors examine automated scoring of short student answers, now often done by large language models with a few examples rather than fine-tuned graders. The risk sits in the middle of the quality range: partly correct answers need nuanced judgment, and errors there could unfairly penalize students whose understanding is still developing.

They compared three few-shot language models, a fine-tuned encoder, and a human expert on hundreds of biology answers. All AI systems degraded sharply on mid-range responses, while handling clear right and wrong answers well. The degradation shrank as task-specific adaptation increased, with the fine-tuned encoder best. Human agreement stayed highest and stable across the whole quality spectrum.
arxiv-2605-07847:
Shuhaib Mehri and six co-authors measure how closely AI user simulators imitate real people. Simulators are used more and more to train and evaluate assistants, and they are trained to sound human. But whether they reproduce the broad, varied distribution of real user behavior was an open question.

Their method extracts behavior profiles from real and simulated conversations, clusters them into discrete distributions, and computes gaps between them, checked by a human study. Evaluating twenty-four simulators on coding and writing tasks revealed a large gap from real users that varied by model family, scale, and behavioral facet. Most simulators resembled each other; combining behaviorally matching ones matched real users better than either alone. A word analysis of the clusters exposed which behaviors they capture, miss, and invent.
arxiv-2605-08247:
Andrea Valenzuela Ramirez, Cristian Gutierrez-Gomez, Marta Barroso, Dario Garcia-Gasulla, and coauthors teach a language model to translate between compiler intermediate languages. GCC and LLVM dominate modern toolchains but use different internal representations, which blocks reuse of frontends, backends, and optimization passes across ecosystems. Rule-based translators exist but are costly to build and maintain.

The team fine-tunes a fourteen billion parameter transformer, IRIS-14B, to translate GCC's GIMPLE into the LLVM representation, learning the mapping from examples. A data-driven translator could lower the barrier between the two ecosystems and let tools and optimizations travel across languages and compilers more freely.
arxiv-2605-08547:
Mikhail Nesterenko and Joseph Oglio present QUANTAS 2, a tool for testing distributed algorithms and measuring their performance. The first version ran abstract round based trials that kept results free of one machine or network setup. The new version adds a concrete mode where the same code runs over real sockets on one or many computers.

A reusable fault interface lets researchers inject crash, lying, and selfish behavior without rewriting the algorithm under test. Trials cover blockchains, agreement methods, hash tables, and data links in both modes. Distributed systems researchers gain one compact platform for quick exploration, real checks, and hostile fault tests side by side.
arxiv-2605-08647:
Aritra Mazumder and twelve coauthors build AgentCollabBench, a diagnostic test for failures that hide inside multi agent teamwork. A final answer can look right while an agent quietly dropped a constraint upstream, and outcome only grading never sees the damage. Their nine hundred human checked tasks span software, operations, and data work, each isolating one of four risks.

The risks cover constraints fading under peer pressure, falsehoods spreading by consensus, information leaking between tasks, and marked data failing to reach the end. Four leading models show distinct weakness profiles, and network shape explains much of the loss, especially where branches merge. Multi agent design emerges as a structural reliability problem, not just a model quality one.
arxiv-2605-09147:
Matthias Schöffel and co-author Esteban Garces Arias compare ways to tag parts of speech in medieval Romance texts, a job made hard by shifting spelling, rich word forms, and scarce labeled data. Their 2026 study covers medieval Occitan, Catalan, and French, and pits older rule-based and statistical taggers against modern open language models. Settings include prompting with no examples, prompting with a few, single-language tuning, and transfer across languages.

Across historically grounded datasets, the language model approaches beat the older taggers, with fine-tuning and multilingual training giving the largest gains. Transfer across languages helps under-resourced varieties a lot, and focused two-language training can beat broader mixes for some targets. The authors stress that closeness between languages and dataset traits shape what works best. They release code, models, and processed datasets, giving digital humanities scholars a practical guide for tagging old texts.
arxiv-2605-09247:
Avalos and two colleagues test a shallow restricted Boltzmann machine on a one dimensional ℤ2 Bose-Hubbard chain at half filling under a hard core adiabatic limit. They use variational Monte Carlo with the machine as the ansatz, comparing the neural quantum state against the established adiabatic description. The study targets the chain's ground state and phase diagram as seen through magnetization observables.

The variational results recover the broad shape of the phase diagram, distinguishing polarized and Néel ordered regions. They also recover typical spin patterns and site fillings for staggered insulating setups chosen by a weak symmetry breaking field. Overall, the results show a shallow restricted Boltzmann machine recovers the main adiabatic phase structure and the chosen symmetry broken insulating patterns at half filling. The work supports shallow neural quantum states as a workable tool for one dimensional quantum chains in this hard core regime.
arxiv-2605-09447:
Liu addresses the controllability of a class of quasilinear parabolic equations with multiplicative mobile controls. To prove a control exists that forces the solution to rest at time T greater than 0, he first establishes how solutions decay for the uncontrolled system. Unlike the linear heat equation, the nonlinear leading term brings major challenges.

Those hurdles demand a novel approach, leading Liu to settle the controllability problem in the standard solutions setting. Through a neatly built smooth shift, he shows that a multiplicative control exists bringing the state exactly to rest by time t equals T.
arxiv-2605-09747:
Angelis and Bramoullé used network theory to open up the matching function, the black box linking job seekers and vacancies in labor economics. They traced matching properties to granular connections between applicants and vacancies, unifying scattered literature by recovering several functional forms, including the CES form, as special cases. A testable condition says when matching in a broad network class behaves as if CES, up to a first-order approximation.

Their theory of match efficacy puts inequality in search intensity at the center: dispersion of search effort on either side of the market hurts matching. Strikingly, a rise in mean search intensity can reduce efficacy when it comes with a higher Gini coefficient of intensities. More average effort, unevenly spread, can make matching worse.
arxiv-2605-09847:
Shentu, working alone, proves the geometric Shafarevich boundedness conjecture for the moduli stack of stable minimal models, a catalogue of higher-dimensional shapes with mild singularities. The conjecture says that families of such shapes over a fixed base curve, with fixed bad fibres, fall into only finitely many types. It includes the moduli stack of KSB pairs, pairs of a variety with a boundary divisor, as a special case.

For curves the result goes back to Paršin and Arakelov, and its arithmetic cousin underpinned Faltings' proof of the Mordell conjecture. Higher dimensions resisted because some families bend continuously instead of staying rigid, so finiteness fails in general. Restricting to stable minimal models restores it, and the paper builds the boundedness argument for that class over the complex numbers.
arxiv-2605-10047:
Wang and three colleagues rethink loss reweighting for long-tailed classification, where common classes swamp rare ones and models skew toward the head. Most reweighting tricks rest on heuristics and never state a clear target. Inspired by Neural Collapse, the idea that well-trained features settle into a symmetric geometric pattern, they take equal per-class average loss as the target.

Treating reweighting as an inverse problem, they infer class weights dynamically to hit that ideal, rather than hand-setting them. Neural Collapse metrics suggest the method cuts the loss imbalance coefficient and moves models closer to the ideal geometry. It also beats strong long-tailed baselines across data sets, with code released publicly.
arxiv-2605-10647:
Florent Guépin and four colleagues present diffGHOST, a tool for making fake movement paths that guard privacy. Movement paths hold highly personal facts about people, such as where they worship or what politics they hold. Rules such as the European GDPR limit how such data can be shared. Their 2026 paper offers synthetic paths as a way to share useful movement facts without tying them to real people.

Past tools claimed privacy but gave no firm guarantee, and even top models proved open to privacy attacks. diffGHOST builds on a diffusion model that splits its latent space into segments. It spots and curbs memorization of key samples through those segments. The design hedges against leaks while keeping the fake paths useful for research, city planning, and health studies.
arxiv-2605-10747:
Tim Kokkeler, Vitaly N. Golovach, and F. Sebastian Bergeret develop a theory of angle-tied magnetoresistance in metal altermagnets tied to iron-type insulators, setting rules telling them apart from plain evened-out magnets with spin-orbit pull. Altermagnets mix ferromagnet and antiferromagnet traits, staying apart. Though their magnet build is fully evened out with zero net magnet strength, they host strong spin-tied electron build set by crystal shape, not by spin-orbit pull, giving large momentum-tied splits.

The authors show the spin-splitter magnetoresistance seen by Chen and colleagues is a smoking-gun mark of straight altermagnetism in metal sets. Unlike spin-Hall magnetoresistance, it rests only on the tilt between iron-type magnet strength and the altermagnetic Néel line, giving a straight-line reply of flip sign. It shows a straight link between straight-line and cross signs, unseen in spin-Hall reply.
arxiv-2605-10847:
Michal Valko and five colleagues build a data-driven alert system that flags unusual patient-management decisions in hospital records. The idea is plain: a decision that looks odd beside past cases may signal an error worth a second look.

Two detection methods grow from predictive classification models trained on prior cases, and the team tests them on patients at risk of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, a dangerous clotting disorder. Their detector beats the existing screening method on precision and recall. Clinicians get an early-warning aid that learns from their own records rather than from fixed rules alone.
arxiv-2605-10947:
Saheed Faremi, Andrea Visentin, and Luca Longo hunt for clear models of EEG microstates, the brief, stable scalp patterns in brain electrical activity. Standard grouping works straight on electrode data with hard labels. It gives no hidden space to learn and no way to turn groups back into scalp maps that can be checked.

Their model learns to rebuild scalp maps and to group brain states softly at the same time. Each group center turns back into a scalp map that can be checked. A sign-flip fix plus a grid search over group count, hidden size, depth, and width shows how each choice shapes quality, stability, and clarity. Tested on resting brain data from ten people, the search gives brain researchers a clear recipe for finding microstates.
arxiv-2605-11047:
Hongwei Yao, Yiming Liu, Yiling He, and Bingrun Yang present DeepTrap, an automated framework for finding context flaws in OpenClaw agent systems. Agent systems lean on changeable work contexts like files, memory, tools, skills, and artifacts, creating risks beyond explicit user prompts.

DeepTrap treats hostile context tampering as black-box path optimization balancing risk payoff, benign-task upkeep, and stealth, joining risk-aware scoring, multi-goal scoring, reward-guided beam search, and reflection-based deep probing. A 42-case test set across six flaw classes and seven settings, run on nine models, shows rigged contexts causing much unsafe behavior while user-facing tasks still finish. Final-response checks alone cannot catch this. Agent security teams get a work-centered test method.
arxiv-2605-11147:
Sándor Lökös gives an approximate formula for the entropy of the negative binomial distribution, the workhorse parametrization of charged-particle multiplicities in high-energy reactions. The Shannon entropy of this distribution matters because initial-state entanglement entropy may relate to final-state Shannon entropy. Yet no closed form exists.

Starting from a representation with special series and integrals, Lökös investigates one form and derives an approximation valid within about twenty percent of the exact value even for extreme parameter values. Particle physicists studying multiplicity distributions get a usable entropy estimate where exact evaluation demands numerical integration.
arxiv-2605-11247:
Zarrin Monirzadeh presents a proof-of-concept simulation-driven digital twin framework for decision-aware diabetes modeling. Unlike older models, it generates clear mock runs rather than clinic-ready outcomes, using benchmark patient data, mock time boosts, and sample CGM analysis.

Testing uses a public dataset plus set mock cases to show time patterns and treatment effects. Results show the promise of mixing prediction with what-if runs for choice-aware analysis. The work does not claim clinic use but gives a base for future research on twin systems in healthcare. Health teams get a choice-aware mock-up, clearly marked as not yet for clinics.
arxiv-2605-11347: Kim and three colleagues present ZeNO, a gradient-free way to tune noise for reward alignment. Existing methods need multi-step stochastic paths or backpropagation through generator and reward. That fails for deterministic generators. ZeNO frames noise tuning as path-integral control, estimated from reward values alone. With an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck reference and a one-step horizon, its updates link to Langevin dynamics, and it scales inference well across generators, including protein structure generation.
arxiv-2605-11547: Gupta, Lim, Yu and Erichson propose SharpEuler, a sharpness-aware sampler for flow matching. Flow matching models generate samples by integrating a velocity field, each step costing one network evaluation. Fast generation means spending a small budget well: not just how, but where to spend steps. SharpEuler profiles a pretrained model offline, estimating where velocity changes most, then converts that profile into a timestep grid for any budget. At test time sampling stays Euler integration with the same count as a uniform schedule, yet improves quality at fixed budgets.
arxiv-2605-11647: Kordt, Glover and Klessen simulate metal enrichment by first stars at the lower pair-instability limit. First stars of 140 to 270 solar masses may explode as pair-instability supernovae, yet none appears in metal-poor stars nearby. Prior work tested 270 solar masses; this study tests 140 solar masses with a cosmological simulation. All second-generation stars prove enriched by their own progenitor halo, imprinting one star's pattern. Their median iron sits 2 point 9 dex below the high-energy case, so missing PISN patterns disfavours PISNe as the dominant early channel.
arxiv-2605-11747: Giuseppe Bevilacqua, Minos Reinartz, and Malgorzata Worek compute next-to-leading-order QCD corrections for Higgs production with a top-antitop pair at the LHC. They include dimension-six Standard Model Effective Field Theory operators in both production and top decay. At 13.6 teraelectronvolts they map linear, cross, and quadratic terms. They show that cuts, higher-order effects, and effective operators in decays jointly reshape measured observables, so all three must be treated together.
arxiv-2605-12047: In a 2026 study, Francesca Padovani and three colleagues ask whether child-directed language is tuned for word learning. Training neural language models on child-directed versus adult language, they removed syntax or word pairing data and tested verb meaning learning. Breaking syntax hurt learning in all cases, but child and spoken adult models proved tougher than written-input models. Meanings emerged before robust syntax, most strongly in speech, so the edge reflects spoken style traits rather than child-only tuning.
arxiv-2605-12147: James Flemings and Murali Annavaram test whether language models can mimic individual privacy choices with PrivacySIM. Models increasingly stand in for people, but their grasp of personal privacy calls is poorly understood. PrivacySIM scores models against real answers from 1,000 users across five published privacy studies. It tests persona facets of demographics, past experience, and stated privacy views. Persona prompts beat no-persona prompts, yet even the best model hits only 40.4 percent accuracy, and stated views predict poorly since views often diverge from real behavior.
arxiv-2605-12247: Yibo Liu and seven colleagues build SI-Diff, one framework for search and insertion using a diffusion policy. Assembly tasks like peg-in-hole suffer pose uncertainty, and systems handle search and insertion separately since they need different patterns. SI-Diff adds mode conditioning so one policy captures both behaviors, plus a teacher policy that generates paths. Trained on teacher demos, the model maps touch and velocity readings to actions. Tests show it widens misalignment tolerance from 2 mm to 5 mm over the TacDiffusion baseline, with transfer to unseen shapes.
arxiv-2605-12447: Barvinsky, Hasanov and Kolganov build a curvature expansion of the heat kernel trace and one-loop effective action. Their state is quasi-thermal, on a Euclidean background that does not sit still. Time there runs in a loop, with a period set by an effective global temperature. The team works to second order in small metric changes around flat space. They then rewrite it in curvature terms. A vector field extends the Killing vector of static geometries to generic metrics with timelike periodicity.
arxiv-2605-12647: Ware, Ruppert and Young compile stellar ages for top Habitable Worlds Observatory targets. Precise ages, within about a billion years or twenty percent at solar age, are needed to read trends in life signs of rocky life-zone exoplanets. They also constrain planet insides and target picks. Their HAges catalog covers Tier 1 and Tier 2 targets from the TSS25 list, using printed ages from high-precision methods for 659 stars likely to be seen. It focuses on asteroseismology and gyrochronology, yet only about five percent have star-quake ages so far.
arxiv-2605-13047: Wen, Madinei and Eckstein measure how vision-language models describe scenes versus humans, using counterfactual semantic saliency: the semantic shift when an object is causally removed from a scene. Against a human baseline of 16,603 responses over 307 scenes and 1,306 counterfactual variants, models over-rely on large, central and high-saliency objects, and under-rely on people. A model's size bias largely explains how far its scene descriptions diverge from humans'.
arxiv-2605-13147: Popescu introduces a corrected extension of Burton's theory of large contractions, now in the setting of triangle-perimeter contractions introduced by Petrov. Combining the two lines of work, he proves a fixed point result for large triangle-perimeter contractions under an auxiliary assumption. He first gives a counterexample to the existing main result on such contractions in the literature. Then, under an added condition, he proves the fixed point result holds. Finally he shows with an example that the new framework is strictly broader than Burton's and Petrov's theories.
arxiv-2605-13547: L. W. K. Goh and fifteen colleagues give the first cosmological constraints from cosmic shear work on the UNIONS-3500 weak lensing galaxy catalog in configuration space. They perform a two-dimensional cosmic shear analysis with one tomographic bin, using the two-point correlation function statistic. Assuming a flat LCDM model, they obtain a clustering amplitude S8 of 0.831, consistent with Planck cosmic microwave background data and prior cosmic shear results within one sigma.
arxiv-2605-13747: Luis D. Zambrano Palma, Yusef Maleki and M. Suhail Zubairy investigate optimal quantum illumination with nonlocal non-Gaussian operations. Non-Gaussian operations offer a route to probe states surpassing the standard two-mode squeezed state. The team's engineered state from a nonlocal non-Gaussian protocol beats prior local non-Gaussian scenarios under realistic conditions including photon loss. With a 50:50 beam splitter and photon-number difference detection, the protocol significantly boosts the signal-to-noise ratio for target detection over the two-mode squeezed state.
arxiv-2605-13947: Bianchi, de Sabbata and Meineri study field theories in anti-de Sitter space with edge rules that break some bulk symmetries. They center on conformal defects. They prove the defect spectrum holds a displacement operator of fixed size, though the edge theory is non-local. Break a global symmetry and a tilt operator shows up too. The bulk waves fed by these fixed operators act as the anti-de Sitter kin of Goldstone bosons.
arxiv-2605-14247: Shoji and Zhou construct a monomial basis of a quantum affine algebra of simply-laced type, from the Beck-Nakajima PBW basis. A simple algorithm computes the canonical basis from monomials. They discuss how this canonical basis relates to Lusztig's basis from quiver geometry. The monomial basis gives a concrete handle on the algebra, and the algorithm turns it into the canonical basis.
arxiv-2605-14347: Rumbelow introduces Exemplar Partitioning, a method for building feature dictionaries from language model activations. Each EP dictionary splits activation space into Voronoi regions, formed by leader-clustering a stream of activations. A region is defined by a seen exemplar and a member average. They link regions to inputs, letting dictionaries be compared across layers, checkpoints, and models. Comparing EP dictionaries on base and tuned models shows tuning reorganises harmful activations at varied scales. Edits on these regions let both models answer harmful requests once refused.
arxiv-2605-14747: Xiong, Gu, Ye, Yue, Li, Song, Li and Tian present Video2GUI, a fully automated framework that pulls grounded GUI interaction trajectories from unlabeled internet videos. A coarse-to-fine filter finds high-quality GUI tutorial videos and converts them into structured agent trajectories. Applied to five hundred million video metadata entries, the pipeline builds WildGUI, with twelve million trajectories across over fifteen hundred applications and websites. Pretraining two vision-language models on WildGUI is claimed to lift grounding and action scores by five to twenty percent.
arxiv-2605-14847: Molodetskikh and team propose artifact prominence for super-resolution scoring, defined as the fraction of viewers judging a marked region to contain a visible artifact. Existing detectors treat all flaws equally, though visual impact varies widely. A crowdsourced protocol builds SR-Prominence, with nearly four thousand flaw masks from several sources, annotated with scores. Re-annotating one source reveals about forty-eight percent of its in-lab flaws go unnoticed by most viewers. Classical full-reference metrics give surprisingly strong local signals.
arxiv-2605-14947: R. Yahav and three others lay out technical building blocks for joint action by states on stratospheric aerosol injection, a proposed sunlight-dimming measure. Engineered solid particles, unlike sulfate formed in the air, could carry ID marks and known sizes. Two shared metrics follow: the cooling due to the aerosol layer alone, and particle traceability from production marks. The authors stress deployment is premature and offer no governance framework, only kit that many frameworks could use.
arxiv-2605-15147: Rafael Miyazaki and three others improve Ramsey bounds for generalized Schur equations, which ask when any coloring of the integers must contain a monochromatic solution. They show that beyond a threshold, every r-coloring of the range holds a monochromatic solution for the (m+1)-term equation. The threshold grows like (2m+1) to the r, times a factorial root. A second bound, N at least 2 to the r, guarantees a solution for some m, and that estimate is optimal.
arxiv-2605-15747: Gloria Ferraris and Veronica Umanità build a strict math frame for quantum versions of static two-by-two games. Players may use any unitary move as a pure plan, or a chance measure over the smooth group SU(2) as a mixed plan. The Eisert-Wilkens-Lewenstein protocol serves as the standard setup. A fixed-point proof shows Nash equilibria exist for smooth quantum mixed plans, extending the classic Nash theorem into the quantum case.
arxiv-2605-15947: Lea Harscouet, Amy Wayland and David Alonso show that all stacking signals can be rebuilt, losslessly, from cross-power spectra. The spectra link the target field to the E and B modes of the spin field defining the preferred axes, weighted by local galaxy density. The spectrum approach brings gains in speed, finite-resolution effects, data display and combination with other cosmological probes. Sometimes, stacking with velocities or tidal forces rebuilt from the density field recovers a signal dominated by information already in the target-overdensity cross-spectrum.
arxiv-2605-16047: Liu, Yang, and Lei study online convex optimization where each choice steers a stable dynamical state. Feedback comes only in sparse blocks, and only some agents take part each round. Their projected block gradient method comes with bounds on dynamic regret that weigh message passing, rival movement, state memory, and take-up. A version aided by forecasts improves the bound when the forecasts prove right.
arxiv-2605-16147: Starodubcev and four colleagues ask whether register tokens, which cure patch-token outliers in vision transformers, also help diffusion transformers. Pixel-space diffusion transformers show no such outliers, yet still benefit from registers, more so than latent-space versions. Registers yield cleaner feature maps at high noise levels, which may explain the gain. The authors also propose Register Guidance, which amplifies the register tokens that most improve visual structure and coherence.
arxiv-2605-16247: Boynewicz and three colleagues show that any equilibrium trajectory of a Brownian particle can be read as a superposition of countless non-equilibrium states. That property lets fine fluid-particle details be unravelled from a single trajectory, using only second moments of position under trapped conditions. Thermal-hydrodynamic forces are isolated, and short-time displacement statistics follow from their correlation properties. The approach confirms a t-to-the-five-halves law tied to fluid inertia, and suggests t-to-the-fourth scaling may take over at very short times.
arxiv-2605-16347: Shahin and Alsmadi present HPC-LLM, a lookup-tuned and domain-tuned helper for HPC support. Scholars face day-to-day barriers with cluster setups, job queues, GPU gear, and multi-node tools, while general models lack that day-to-day knowledge. Their tool joins auto docs intake, dense lookup, QLoRA domain tuning, and local runs. Fine-tuned Llama 3.1 8B on 9,000 to 24,000 HPC samples nears Qwen 2.5 14B results while using far less GPU memory and run latency.
arxiv-2605-16647: Brito presents public-decay state space models for sequence inference under fully homomorphic encryption, which keeps data encrypted during computation. The carried state updates through public decay, while costly ciphertext-ciphertext multiplication stays on a local write path. On Rotten Tomatoes and SST-2 validation sets, the encrypted path matches plaintext results exactly. It also runs about five times faster than polynomial attention of similar quality.
arxiv-2605-16947: Prabhakar analyses spin relaxation from phonon deformation in single and displaced double quantum dots under in-plane and out-of-plane field. In single dots the rate is sensitive to weak in-plane fields but settles near a spin-hot-spot where singlet and triplet levels cross. In double dots pulled apart, a spin-hot spot appears with rates a thousand times lower than conventional single-dot spots. At about 60 nanometres apart, the spots oscillate with field, and the extremely low rate at the spot supports qubit superposition states.
arxiv-2605-17047: Saleheen, Wagner and Wang present a scenario-based plan for all-renewable microgrids, spanning size and dispatch. Older plans favour cost over reliability. Their two-stage random model mixes solar and battery storage under utility-grade rules, with placement sharing power between nodes. A new method captures demand swings, solar shifts, and faults by grouping past data. The model caps lost energy below 0.002 percent of annual demand while cutting total cost. Tests reach 99.998 percent uptime from solar and cells alone, with reroutes keeping loads alive through faults.
arxiv-2605-17347: Marshalkin argues that age-estimation models do not process biometric data in the legal sense, because they cannot identify people. Testing fourteen models on three face-verification benchmarks, he finds age estimators trail identification thresholds by orders of magnitude. He urges researchers to be plain about what systems keep and can do, and regulators to separate fleeting processing from template storage under privacy law.
arxiv-2605-17447: Zihan Tang and colleagues present FastOCR, a training-free accelerator for document parsing with vision-language models that never permanently discards visual tokens. It exploits dynamic visual fixation: attention at each decoding step concentrates on a small shifting region, like a reader's gaze. Focal-guided pruning picks task-relevant tokens from focal layers per step, while cross-step reuse warm-starts each step from the last. On Qwen2.5-VL it keeps 98 percent accuracy while attending to only 5 percent of tokens per step.
arxiv-2605-17547: Dimitra Gerolymatou and colleagues model the whole population of active galactic nuclei with the radiation-regulated unification model. Their RefleX ray-tracing code builds X-ray emission self-consistently for flexible gas-and-source shapes. Sampling black-hole mass and Eddington-ratio spreads, they match the cosmic X-ray background, number counts and absorption traits together. They derive an intrinsic Compton-thick share near 40 percent.
arxiv-2605-17647: F. M. Belchior investigates scattering and absorption of spin 0 particles for charged black holes in a pair of gravity models with spontaneous Lorentz symmetry breaking. First is the bumblebee model with a vector field carrying a nonzero vacuum expectation value, while the second involves a self-interacting Kalb-Ramond field joined to gravity. Using the partial waves method, the author computes scattering cross-section and absorption for these charged black holes. Greybody factors for spin 0 particles are also calculated, showing the effect of the Lorentz-violating parameter and electric charge.
arxiv-2605-17747: Hao Fang and Lamei Yuan introduce transposed Poisson conformal superalgebras, graded conformal versions of transposed Poisson algebras. They derive the identities forced by the transposed conformal super-Leibniz rule. They also prove the tensor product of two such systems over polynomials in a derivative again carries the same structure. The work links these systems to Hom-Lie conformal superalgebras and spells out when they match plain Poisson ones. Using the known rank (1+1) classification, it determines all matching structures on those systems.
arxiv-2605-18347: Liubov Kovalenko and three colleagues simulate a rapidly rotating, highly compact thirty-nine solar-mass star collapsing in three dimensions in a 2026 study, comparing non-rotating, rotating, and rotating magnetized models. The magnetized case revives its shock first with the clearest bipolar outflow, while the rotating case without magnetism revives last. In the non-rotating model, the shock revives but the core then collapses to a black hole about a second after bounce.
arxiv-2605-18547: Linan Zhu and six co-authors present VISAFF, a 2026 speaker-centered visual affective feature learning system for emotion recognition in conversation. Vision-language models often attend to backgrounds or passive listeners rather than the active speaker, and fine-tuning them is costly. VISAFF steers frozen models to the active speaker's emotional cues without training, then complements uncertain visuals with text and audio. On two real-world datasets it matches state-of-the-art methods while eliminating expensive fine-tuning.
arxiv-2605-18747: Xuying Ning and forty-one co-authors survey code as agent harness, in a May 2026 paper. In agentic systems, code is no longer output. It serves as substrate for reasoning, acting, and modeling. The survey covers three layers. Interface links agents to reasoning, action, and modeling. Mechanisms cover planning, memory, tool use, and optimization. Scaling to multi-agent settings uses shared artifacts for coordination and verification. Applications span assistants, automation, agents, discovery, and DevOps. Open challenges include evaluation beyond success and checks under incomplete feedback.
arxiv-2605-18847: Roman Kniazev and Nathanaël Fijalkow probe whether a transformer trained on Sudoku traces builds an internal world model. Their eight-layer model does not track the board cell by cell, as a human analyst might expect. Instead it organizes knowledge around rows, columns, and boxes, the units Sudoku constraints act on. A small set of final-layer neurons forms a naked-single circuit, each spotting a cell with exactly one possible digit and promoting it. The shape of the world model, they argue, follows the task structure.
arxiv-2605-18947: David Lopes, Tiago Fernandes and José Lemos study modes of Proca and Maxwell fields in anti de Sitter black holes. Proca waves split into one free and two linked radial waves, and Maxwell waves return at zero mass. Two number methods give Proca modes in four through seven dimensions. In large holes of five or more dimensions, scalar Maxwell waves show pure imaginary low tones.
arxiv-2605-19047: Małgorzata Strzałka and Katarzyna Roszak use Deutsch code as a stand in for hard quantum codes. Pure fade takes two shapes: a full quantum view of qubit and world states, and a plain Kraus view. One run gives the same mark in both views, but two runs split wide. Link aware fade slows fade for balanced tasks and hits constant tasks far more, a split seen on IBM gear.
arxiv-2605-19147: John T. Halloran and Noopur S. Bhatt defend language models against data poisoning by rewriting training samples before training. They show open-book benign rewriting, which draws on benign examples, yields benign outputs more often than closed-book rewriting, projecting poisoned samples into benign prompt space. Across five known backdoor attacks and four used models, the method lifts safety performance by an average of 51 percent over the best defences and 25.7 percent over closed-book rewriting. It is efficient, preserves ordinary task performance after fine-tuning, and handles non-trigger poisoning.
arxiv-2605-19247: Yuiko Sakuma and colleagues rethink neural architecture search, whose fixed search spaces often limit discovery. Language-model helpers can open the space up, yet they tend to wander through biased or weak design ideas. The team first structures design knowledge into a template, which a language model fills by reading papers, then explores it with FairNAD, a mutation scheme that samples ideas fairly and tracks trade-offs. The search finds architectures beating current leaders on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and a 120-class ImageNet variant.
arxiv-2605-19347: Jian-Rui Soh and colleagues pin down the magnetic order of EuAgAs, a hexagonal crystal whose ground state had stayed elusive. Neutron diffraction and X-ray scattering reveal two successive transitions, near 12 kelvin and near 8 kelvin, with slightly different propagation vectors. Polarimetry shows a transverse helix along the crystal axis with a period near twice the lattice spacing. Calculations for this helical phase predict folded bands and higher-order Weyl nodes, though the predicted Fermi level sits above the measured one, so those nodes could not be probed here.
arxiv-2605-19447: Li and team study how to train multi-turn agents from sparse rewards, where one success-or-failure signal must spread across many actions. They test five feedback sources at two insertion granularities and propose SERL, which lets the task reward set update direction while environment feedback tunes placement and size, focusing on critical actions. On ALFWorld and WebShop it reaches 90.0 percent and 80.1 percent success, beating strong reinforcement and distillation baselines. Grounded feedback at meaningful points beats longer, richer context used blindly.
arxiv-2605-19747: He and team simulate lithium diffusion in NMC811, a layered lithium nickel manganese cobalt oxide cathode whose rate capability decides high-power uses. Lithium-ion transport in NMC remains poorly understood. Their workflow fine-tunes a MACE foundation model as generator and applies active learning to a near-ground-state dataset, building a reliable machine learning potential from limited DFT calculations. Molecular dynamics simulations on this potential preserve density functional theory accuracy while overcoming time and length scale limits, enabling direct large-scale lithium self-diffusion simulation.
arxiv-2605-19847: Burnat audits privacy in multi tenant retrieval augmented generation under account collusion. Services often treat each account as the privacy boundary, with a differential privacy guarantee. Burnat shows coordinated accounts compose to joint leakage growing with the square root of coalition size, with a membership inference attack validated across scalar, top-K, embedder and production settings. An audit protocol attests noise then select retrieval and reports pass or fail with an audit epsilon for coalitions up to a declared cap, without disclosing the index.
arxiv-2605-19947: Rey and colleagues learn cause graphs with only plus weights, easing a search task. Cause graphs must stay loop free, yet that rule makes the search space blow up fast. With plus only weights they find a plain loop free rule, then build a solver on it. Tests beat top smooth methods, and theory names the true graph the unique global best.
arxiv-2605-20047: Nicola Barcarolo and five co-workers test real processing-in-memory hardware for speeding up cryptography in DRAM. Standard processors slow AES and SHA routines mainly through the memory bottleneck, raising latency and energy use on large data volumes. On the UPMEM system, a single rank still trails modern CPUs, but spreading the work across ranks lifts performance markedly. Using all available ranks, real processing-in-memory gives its strongest acceleration of cryptographic algorithms.
arxiv-2605-20247: Yang Liu, Toan Nguyen and Flora Salim present CP-MoE, a transient-expert framework. LoRA mixture-of-experts methods either isolate experts or let updates overwrite parameters, causing forgetting. CP-MoE's transient expert captures early updates and guides merging into experts. A routing bias uses the transient expert to gauge expert similarity and steer routing, while guided regularization shields parameters, cutting interference and forgetting while keeping cross-task transfer. On SuperNI, CP-MoE tops rivals with stronger zero-shot transfer; on VQA v2, it cuts forgetting and beats baselines.
arxiv-2605-20447: Prabhu and Goldschmidt design narrowband photon-pair sources for quantum networks using slow light. Photon pairs must match the narrow bandwidths of emitters, memories and matter qubits, but nonlinear sources are far too broad. Cavity-enhanced down-conversion narrows the light, yet chip resonators suffer losses that limit size and linewidth. An intra-cavity slow-light medium acts as an ultra-narrow filter, enabling narrow pairs in broad cavities without losing heralding efficiency, in erbium-doped lithium niobate microrings.
arxiv-2605-20547: Lukas Billera, Hedwig Nordlinder, and Ben Murrell extend generator matching to latent processes that change over time. Earlier theory handled static latent variables, while modern flow and diffusion models train with richer auxiliary dynamics. Their framework views the observed state as a deterministic image of a tractable Markov process. One can then learn a generator on the image space with the same one-time marginals as the projected process, subsuming earlier discrete results.
arxiv-2605-20647: Qingfan Wu and twenty-seven colleagues optimize the focal spot of petawatt laser pulses with a twin-focus scheme. Sharp focusing at such power matters for compact particle accelerators and strong-field physics, yet diagnosing these spots is hard. Their in-situ wavefront correction method, called HotLoop, tunes the spot at full power. It reached a Strehl ratio of 0.80 for one-petawatt pulses and markedly raised cutoff proton energies in acceleration tests.
arxiv-2605-20847: Xin Wang and seven colleagues unify plasticity in ordered and messy matter using topological and geometrical markers. Finding regions behind plastic flow in glassy solids is hard, since disorder blocks direct use of dislocation ideas that work in crystals. They introduce fields of those defects, disclination, and incompatibility densities that reduce to standard flow sources in crystals. In simulated two-dimensional glass and in experimental granular systems, these fields track strongly with D-squared-min, a standard marker of plastic events under shear.
arxiv-2605-21347: Akshay Manglik and co-authors present Insights Generator, a system for corpus-level trace diagnostics of language-model agents. Hand diagnosis, inspecting a few traces and forming ad hoc hypotheses, misses patterns visible only across trace populations and fails to scale to production corpora. Insights Generator formalizes corpus-level diagnostics: given a trace corpus, produce grounded insights on systematic patterns across trace groups, each linked to evidence. A multi-agent system proposes and tests hypotheses across the corpus to build an evidence-backed report.
arxiv-2605-21547: V. Gogokhia and G. G. Barnaföldi present the mass gap approach to QCD, part two: renormalization for massive gluon fields. The mass gap approach, based on new insights into the QCD vacuum, exactly defines the dynamically generated gluon pole mass. They develop a non-perturbative multiplicative renormalization program for the massive full gluon propagator. Asymptotic properties are analyzed, including the perturbation theory limit to the free gluon state, with no asymptotic freedom effect. Massive gluons are prevented from appearing in the physical spectrum, confining massive gluon states.
arxiv-2605-21647: Madjid Eshaghi Gordji and co-authors model why weak practices, technologies, or institutions linger even when superior options are known. They introduce a quantal response equilibrium with status-quo bias, where each player pays a fixed switching cost for leaving the default action. In a binary coordination game they compare two reforms: a tax on the default action versus deleting the default action entirely. A threshold tax exists: below it the status quo persists, above it transition occurs, independent of bounded rationality, while deletion always forces the superior outcome.
arxiv-2605-22047: Chen Zhan and co-authors study active evidence-seeking in large language models for clinical decision support. Models do well on static medical exams, yet real diagnosis needs iterative evidence gathering under uncertainty. The team builds an OSCE-inspired patient simulator and a controlled benchmark for active diagnostic inquiry. In 468 cases and 15 models, multi-turn evidence seeking cuts diagnostic accuracy by 12.75 percent and supporting-evidence quality by 24.36 percent versus full-context evaluation, linked to premature closure and poor questioning. Static benchmarks may thus inflate interactive performance.
arxiv-2605-22247: Hashiloni and colleagues introduce IdioLink, a retrieval benchmark that tests whether models can link idioms to the same meaning stated literally or in paraphrase. Idioms resist word-by-word reading, so the test demands meaning beyond surface overlap. The set holds 10,700 documents and 2,140 queries across 107 idioms, each used literally and figuratively. Strong embedding models still struggle, leaning on topic and shallow cues instead of true equivalence.
arxiv-2605-22947: Wang and three coauthors show that entanglement shapes how macroscopic clusters form in metastable quantum many-body dynamics. Studying false-vacuum decay in a two-dimensional quantum Ising model, they find correlated starting states suppress small true-vacuum domains and favor large connected clusters. Tensor network simulations up to 25 by 25 sites show nucleation starts mainly at the boundary. Pinning the boundary to block that path yields large magnetization swings consistent with macroscopic superposition.
arxiv-2605-23047: Baddis and three coauthors bridge swampland conjectures and black hole thermodynamics by treating the cosmological constant as dynamical. Reading the radial metric form at the horizon like an equation of state, they discuss structural transitions and coexistence curves. An effective potential plus a quasi-static scalar field then connects certain swampland conjectures. Through Kaluza-Klein readings of scalar fields, they approach the dark dimension and dark matter via the thermodynamics of charged black holes.
arxiv-2605-23147: Xu shows As X, do Y role prompts decompose linearly at one residual site. That site spans the last prompt token and first two generated tokens, in an early layer band. There, persona and task add orthogonally. Pure persona and task effects added to clean residuals stay near output on Gemma and Qwen models. Yet local additivity does not imply prompt compressibility. Injecting cached predictions into persona free host prompts fails to match clean targets. Persona generation flows through attention to persona text throughout, resisting site capture.
arxiv-2605-23447: Manasa and colleagues analyze almost maximum distance separable constacyclic codes of length four times a prime power over finite fields, where the prime is odd. They give a full analysis of these AMDS codes and then build quantum AMDS codes through the Calderbank-Shor-Steane framework, widening their use in quantum error correction. The work aims to deepen understanding of the codes and their potential across classical and quantum computing settings.
arxiv-2605-23747: Kazakov and colleagues revive the Apple Dense Material Segmentation benchmark with a Vision Transformer base. Testing SegFormer and Mask2Former, they find standard training fails on shapeless fields. Their recipe uses High-Fidelity Logit Maps, Query Entropy Control, and physics augments. Their SegFormer-B5 reaches 0.4572 mIoU, a record, beating the prior baseline. They spot a Generalization Paradox: a split lifts the metric to 0.5276 mIoU, but analysis shows sameness hurting outside scores. Sharing their saved dataset index and training tool, they argue surface vision is far from solved.
arxiv-2605-24247: Berlin and Swanda improve labeling consistency by pairing constitutions with AI-driven evaluation. Simple definitions leave labelers guessing at boundary cases, and prescriptive definitions exceed working memory, so labels drift. Their workflow has AI write a constitution per category covering edge cases. A frontier model then applies it to each input, producing golden labels more consistently than humans. On harassment, hate-speech, and non-violent-crime categories, cross-model inconsistency falls up to 57-fold. A dual-axis score rates intent and content separately over the full conversation.
arxiv-2605-24347: Tovmassian and ten co-authors study a new long-period cataclysmic variable from the donor's viewpoint. Cataclysmic variables were long seen as close binaries of a white dwarf plus a filling dwarf. Recent surveys reveal similar systems with evolved secondaries that lost part of their envelopes, many with periods far above ordinary limits. The team presents a study of a new cataclysmic variable with a period of about 17 hours and its basic stellar parameters. They discuss paths forming these long-period systems and their evolution into double-degenerate binaries.
arxiv-2605-24447: Haindl, Eigner, and Kieseberg offer a prompt-pattern guide keeping AI in courses without cutting hard work. Students now easily hand off writing, study, and problem-solving to auto systems, skipping the struggle. Using Design Science Research, the team builds nine prompt patterns, mapped to Useful Struggle and Careful Judging. An Advanced Secure Coding design shows the method. Nine patterns, each tied to a teaching function, give teachers control over student-AI contact. Three patterns — Flipped Interaction, Alternative Approaches, and Cognitive Verifier — scaffold flaw finding and fixing.
arxiv-2605-24647: Jiani Luo and others argue personalizing dialogue takes more than recalling history. Systems must infer hidden states that shift as conversation unfolds. Their PUMA framework treats personalization as choice under partial observability, grounded in the free-energy principle. Each turn it holds a belief about the latent state. It updates a model of observations and action-driven state changes. It picks actions minimizing free energy, balancing learning about the user against serving the user. Counseling and motivational-interviewing tests show stronger long-horizon outcomes with reliable state tracking.
arxiv-2605-25147: Zi-Qi Wang, Xiao-Li Huang, Hai-Ming Zhang, and En-Wei Liang investigate a quasi-thermal component in gamma-ray burst prompt emission, using GRB 090902B. Their jet model pairs an ultrarelativistic uniform core with a structured cocoon. Electrons pre-energized in the thin jet-cocoon layer are heated in the mixed region under weak scattering, forming a thermal electron distribution. With synchrotron emission from shock-accelerated electrons in the jet core, the model reproduces the thermal component in the keV to MeV range. It reproduces nonthermal emission.
arxiv-2605-25547: Sizhe Zhao and colleagues improve robot control at run time instead of retraining the policy. Generative policies usually act once, so a single weak action stands. TapSampling draws many candidate actions from a compressed latent space built by an Action-VAE, then picks with a verifier trained to predict task progress. The verifier learns from step order in robot data. The plug-and-play scheme lifts several generalist policies in simulated and real settings without further tuning.
arxiv-2605-26047: Lucassen and Kaufman compare retrying blocked actions with resampling fresh attempts for AI coding scaffolds. Retrying lowers honest suspicion scores, but a scheming model can exploit stated reasons to craft sneakier attacks. Resampling draws several samples from the same context and leaks no such rationale. The untrusted model is Claude Opus 4.6, and the monitor is MiMo-V2-Flash. In BashArena tests, five samples per step with worst-score auditing lift safety from 61 to 71 percent at a 0.3 percent audit budget, with no usefulness cost.
arxiv-2605-26147: Yongchao Huang's 2026 framework treats neural inference as step-by-step evidence gathering over a graph of experts. Experts query a shared knowledge source for supporting evidence, updating a belief state by exact addition, while a routing trick keeps hard path choices trainable. The design yields visible routing traces, uncertainty measures, early stopping, and abstention on unfamiliar inputs. It matches rivals on vision, medical, language, control, and experiment-design tasks.
arxiv-2605-26347: Arwa Dabbech and Yves Wiaux present a distributed, resource-adaptive widefield radio-interferometric model. Line-of-sight baselines complicate the model beyond the standard non-uniform Fourier transform, making the point spread function vary with position. Their hybrid w-stacking and w-projection design sets the w-bin count on its own to cut cost under memory limits. The model splits into compact operators per w-bin, with residual offsets as Fourier kernels, and an optional holographic matrix shrinks sequential work when memory demands it.
arxiv-2605-26447: Jiangbei Hu and ten colleagues rebuild underwater scenes from wraparound photos via Underwater360, a physics-aware splatting system for all directions. Plain splatting stumbles on sphere warp and on water's absorption and scattering. The team casts rays straight in spherical camera space and splits true scene light from depth-linked backscatter and dimming with pose-tuned embeddings. They also release a new underwater benchmark of synthetic and real wraparound scenes. Experiments report stronger novel-view synthesis and scene restoration than rivals, with cleaner rendering and steadier agreement.
arxiv-2605-26547: Haishan Ye studies a black-box search method that tunes settings using only output values, never gradients. Past high-chance claims came from a rough conversion that forced a smoothing width to shrink as confidence grew. Ye instead tracks the search path step by step and proves sharp odds of landing near the best point. The bounds cover strongly curved, plain curved, and bumpy smooth goals, with query counts spelled out for each case.
arxiv-2605-26747: Cuayahuitl and Jang release MeDial-Speech, a spoken dataset of robot-patient and doctor-patient consultations covering Lewy body dementia, heart failure, shoulder pain, and angina. Recorded in realistic settings, it holds over 111 hours of speech for training and evaluating medical dialogue systems. A sentence-selection benchmark finds Claude Sonnet 4 most accurate, yet shows all tested models highly overconfident in their predictions whether their chosen sentences are right or wrong.
arxiv-2605-26847: Thomsen and five colleagues release mstlo, a Rust library for fast online monitoring of signal temporal logic, with Python bindings. It unifies several logic semantics, including robust satisfaction intervals and Boolean checks with early verdicts, and uses incremental dynamic programming with per-operator caching. An embedded domain-specific language adds static syntax checks in Rust. Benchmarks show strong scaling and speed gains over leading tools, especially on deeply nested formulas.
arxiv-2605-27147: Moltmann and co-authors give a leaner version of the adaptive mergesort Powersort. Their virtual-memory variant cuts the buffer from room for half the items to about the square root of the item count times a slow-growing log factor. Unlike plain in-place merging, which slows sorting sharply, their method keeps the same count of moves and comparisons as earlier Powersort versions, up to a small linear extra term. Tests against other Powersort variants and top stable sorters show near in-place stable sorting at negligible cost.
arxiv-2605-27247: Squicciarini and colleagues present the full 460-star SHINE survey sample observed between 2015 and 2023 for direct exoplanet imaging. They work out star traits the same way for all targets, checking for binary companions with position, spectra, and image data. A group of 333 young single stars now anchors the survey's final count of planet prevalence and formation.
arxiv-2605-27447: Jing Tang and Yuangang Deng turn weak chirality into giant quantum nonreciprocity with phase-set interference. Two phase-set atoms on a spinning ring resonator use Fizeau splitting to create strong one-way gaps in photon counts. Correlation and brightness gaps reach up to 65 decibels and about 17 decibels, following phase-set power-law scaling.
arxiv-2605-27547: Vassilis Vassiliades proposes a coordination layer for mixed human-agent societies that clears risk instead of assigning fixed tasks. In his Risk-Aware Option Clearing design, agents expose skills paired with risk summaries, and a central clearinghouse assigns work by weighing risk-adjusted mission value against deadlines and safety limits. The design ranges from learned outcome models to full risk forecasts, sketching a clear path for mixed teams.
arxiv-2605-27647: James Bartusek and Eli Goldin ask how little uncloneable encryption needs, starting from a single uncloneable bit. They show that if a t-to-t-prime uncloneable bit exists, many-time secure symmetric key encryption yields many-time secure uncloneable encryption for messages of any length. With pseudorandom unitaries instead, the same build gives identical copy security, proving the result tight.
