Boateng, MacDonald, and Kumar argue that the search grounding of production agents should be a system layer, not a feature rented from the model provider. The work is a 2026 AI systems paper. Such grounding bundles retrieval policy, provider choice, cost, latency, and generation behavior behind one boundary. That makes it hard to inspect, tune, reuse, or port. It can trigger verbose answers that break output contracts.

Their Decoupled Search Grounding moves grounding outside the reasoning model, behind a gateway compatible with the Model Context Protocol. It exposes provider routing, source-aware context rendering, fallback, retrieval-depth control, and caching as controls. Across five frontier models, it nearly matched native accuracy on SimpleQA, at a fraction of the search cost. It held concise answer contracts, and reached warm-cache hit rates with lower latency. In an e-commerce deployment, it matched native accuracy, while cutting search cost by ninety-eight percent.
arxiv-2606-19047:
Fang and colleagues propose RODS in 2026, a method that makes fresh training data while a tool-use agent learns. Multi-turn tool-use training quickly drains the useful samples in a fixed dataset. Gradient signal concentrates on tasks near the agent's skill boundary, where success and failure are near balanced. As training shifts that boundary, the pool of such boundary samples in static data runs dry, and learning stalls.

RODS reuses reward variance from rollouts already computed as a free boundary detector. It spots boundary tasks, then synthesizes new multi-turn variants with matching structure, like API layout and dependency depth. A dynamic replay buffer grows and shifts with the policy. Starting from a few hundred human seeds, RODS keeps a small active pool. It matches a far larger offline pipeline while using many times fewer trajectories. It also beats fixed data synthesis.
arxiv-2606-19347:
Liu and colleagues study how language models fail and generalize in register-transfer level coding for hardware design in 2026. Turning sequential programming habits into the parallel temporal logic of hardware is a key bottleneck for these models. The team introduces an error taxonomy grounded in problem solvability, inspired by cognitive theory. Failures sort into syntactic, semantic, solvable functional, and unsolvable functional types.

Evaluations reveal a strict ceiling on a standard Verilog benchmark. Frontier models plateau at an initial pass rate just above ninety percent. The plateau is defined by unsolvable functional errors, persistent knowledge gaps that more test-time compute does not fix. A surface convergence gap also appears. Optimization readily removes syntax errors but makes deeper functional failures worse at the same time. The findings suggest alignment mainly teaches models to compile. Repeated sampling can patch solvable errors, but capacity stays bounded by pretraining knowledge.
arxiv-2606-19447:
Zimmerman and Narayanan present Phot-Gal in 2026, a machine learning tool that reimagines spectral energy distribution fitting for galaxies. SED fitting is the standard way to recover galaxy properties from observed light data. It rests on many assumptions, collapsing a three-dimensional, spatially varying object into a point. Modern inference is also compute-heavy, a growing problem in the era of huge survey datasets.

Phot-Gal instead trains a model on photometry generated from three-dimensional radiative transfer of simulated galaxies with a wide range of physics. A nearest-neighbors imputation strategy lets it accept arbitrary amounts of input data. The fiducial model predicts redshift, stellar mass, dust mass, and star formation rate, with uncertainties. Against the used Prospector tool, Phot-Gal recovers each property more accurately on the test set. With few band constraints its stated errors can understate the true scatter, a caveat the authors flag.
arxiv-2606-19647:
Vinicius Covas traces a goalkeeper's overnight fame through language in a 2026 pilot study. Vozinha, Cape Verde's 40-year-old keeper, held Spain to a goalless draw at the 2026 World Cup. His follower count leapt from about 50 thousand to over 8 million within a day.

Covas builds a corpus in Portuguese, Spanish, English, and French around the match. A nine-frame taxonomy tags story angles, from underdog heroism to national history and late recognition. Language model suggestions plus human validation drive the annotation pipeline. Each language carried distinct frames: Portuguese mobilised, Spanish framed crisis, English built nationhood. The follower metric itself acted as shared proof of visibility across tongues. Only one scraper count is exact; other figures stand as typed estimates with confidence marks. The pilot releases its schema, taxonomy, and guidelines for later full annotation.
arxiv-2606-19847:
Yanyu Yao and six colleagues give language model agents a long-term memory built from atomic facts in 2026. Fixed context windows stop agents from carrying knowledge across sessions. Existing memory add-ons often store coarse chunks and update them unstably.

AtomMem's Fact Executor pulls high-value atomic facts from long interactions. Those facts serve as compact, value-dense memory units. Hierarchical event structures group them into coherent episodes. Temporal profiles track how user traits evolve over time. At retrieval, an associative memory graph reconnects scattered facts. On the LoCoMo benchmark AtomMem posts leading scores across reasoning tasks. The design stays cheap enough for practical deployment. Personal agents that remember users over months are the target use.
arxiv-2606-19947:
Merijn Moody, Zier Mensch, Miranda Cheng, Peter Bolhuis, and Max Welling introduce QMaxCal in 2026, a way to regularize quantum control using path-space mathematics. Noise from the environment, decoherence, corrupts controlled quantum dynamics, and standard penalties only curb the size or roughness of the control signals. Monitored open systems produce measurement records whose drift reflects the noise, so Girsanov's theorem yields a closed-form estimate of how far two trajectory distributions diverge.

Two regularizers built on that estimate push the system toward states where decoherence bites least. One suits general noise models; the other excels under stated conditions. Across single-qubit, multi-qubit, and an IBM Kingston-calibrated chain benchmarks, the penalties cut infidelity by up to half and grow more valuable as noise assumptions drift. Control design gains a physically grounded objective.
arxiv-2606-20347:
Aryeh Brill and Tom Ingebretsen Carlson propose critical percolation as a principled synthetic data model for testing interpretability methods. Their 2026 paper notes that neural networks learn features reflecting the layered structure of natural data, while synthetic datasets used to grade model-reading tools usually lack that structure. Their datasets are hierarchical functions defined on critical mean-field percolation clusters. The clusters are sparse, fractal, and power-law distributed in size, like real data's long tails.

Latent variables arranged as a taxonomic hierarchy generate each point's target value, and known critical exponents fix the model's properties without tuning. A mapping between percolation clusters, random trees, and additive coalescence yields an almost linear-time sampler that builds a tree and its latent split together, at arbitrary scale. Probing experiments show the ground-truth latents can be linearly decoded from network activations. Such methods can finally be graded against known truth.
arxiv-2606-20847:
Liqiang He and four colleagues use large language models in 2026 to design heuristics for video encoding with the VVenC encoder. Frame-level quantization sets how much detail each frame keeps. Fixed settings ignore content. Classical rate-distortion methods optimize a tradeoff, but their multiplier settings are often inaccurate. Their framework lets a model propose heuristics as ideas with executable code, inside a closed loop.

Each candidate acts as a scoring function. It compares quantization choices using statistics from past frames and current candidates. Candidates are judged by actually encoding video. Across several test sets, the evolved heuristic improves rate-distortion results over fixed settings and the classical baseline. Further analysis examines what the model discovered. Letting a language model search heuristic space, with a real encoder as judge, could automate tuning work that codec engineers now do by trial and intuition.
arxiv-2606-21547:
Kubushishi and Phillips build an effective theory in 2026 for halo nuclei whose core is deformed, extending earlier halo theory that assumed a spherical core. In a halo nucleus, one or two neutrons drift far from a compact core because they are barely bound. When the core also rotates, with a low-lying rotational band, the theory needs halo and rotation degrees of freedom together, recovering the Bohr-Mottelson particle-plus-rotor picture at leading order.

The authors identify the leading operators and the small parameters that organize the theory's power counting. Calculations for beryllium-11 and carbon-17 reproduce the low-lying spectra well at leading order, and Coulomb breakup predictions sit in reasonable agreement with data. Adding one higher-order operator stabilizes the asymptotic normalization coefficients and removes most of the cutoff drift in breakup cross sections.
arxiv-2606-21647:
Jason Lefever, Jiahao Xu, Yuanfang Cai, Rick Kazman, and Ernst Pisch present ConcernBERT in 2026, a model that learns which pieces of code share a responsibility. Good design asks for separation of concerns, high cohesion, and single responsibility, yet spotting cohesive groups of methods and attributes still leans on developer intuition. Their BERT-based model is trained at the entity level with triplet loss, using class membership as context.

A replication dataset spanning over two million Java files from more than six thousand repositories supports the training. The test merges methods from two or more classes into unlabeled groups and asks the model to recover the original classes. ConcernBERT beats existing models by a wide margin, giving tools for architecture recovery, extract-class refactoring, and cohesion measurement a stronger base.
arxiv-2606-21847:
Han and colleagues present UniRank in 2026, a method for shrinking large language models. It decides how much each weight matrix can be compressed. Low-rank decomposition swaps a large matrix for two smaller ones. But the right rank differs by layer. Hand rules travel poorly between models, and learned allocation costs a lot to compute.

UniRank turns the global choice into a sorting-and-truncation pipeline. Each component gets two scores. One score measures its share of energy inside its own matrix. The other measures functional importance, from how alike a module's inputs and outputs are. The authors verify that high input-output similarity tracks low effective rank. They then fine-tune the decomposed weights directly, avoiding losses from re-truncation. In one-shot compression with no fine-tuning, perplexity fell by up to fifty percent against uniform and heuristic baselines. Gains held across decomposition schemes, model sizes, and architectures.
arxiv-2606-21947:
Li and colleagues propose ScalePredictor in 2026, a method for quantizing vision transformers, shrinking their numbers to fewer bits so they can run on small edge devices. Post-training quantization normally applies one fixed scheme to every image, calibrated once on a small dataset. Natural images vary widely, though, so a single static setting is suboptimal for many inputs.

The authors first uncovered a hidden correlation: the distribution range of activations in shallow layers predicts the best scales for deeper layers. ScalePredictor extracts robust range statistics early, then feeds them into a polynomial projection module, motivated by Taylor expansion, that generates all scales at once. This avoids costly per-image calibration while adding negligible computing overhead. On ImageNet experiments, ScalePredictor beat prior post-training quantization methods, achieving a better balance between accuracy and efficiency across the tested models.
arxiv-2606-22147:
Mishra and colleagues show, in 2026, that warm inflation can leave behind a relic inflaton condensate that serves as dark matter. Warm inflation is an early-universe scenario where the inflaton field steadily leaks energy into radiation. The standard expectation is that this drainage empties the condensate completely by the end of inflation.

The authors show the expectation fails in a simple, viable regime. In strong dissipation, the loss rate falls rapidly after inflation ends, choking off further energy transfer to the thermal bath. A leftover condensate survives and evolves as a plain scalar field. For potentials with a stable quadratic minimum, that remnant behaves as cold dark matter. The observed dark matter abundance fixes its mass near 0.02 mega-electronvolts, while larger masses would overclose the universe. The transition happens well before the first elements formed.
arxiv-2606-22247:
Eghbali and colleagues introduce, in 2026, documentation-to-code equivalence: the property that a snippet's docs accurately and completely describe what the code does. Docs are often incomplete, outdated, or wrong, and language models increasingly rely on them for software engineering tasks. Their tool, Documentary, generates equivalent docs for a given snippet by itself.

Documentary produces equivalent docs for 53.4 percent of the tested function-level snippets. The authors then test two downstream tasks, code understanding and code editing. With equivalent docs, a language model predicts a function's output with 12.8 to 24.5 percent higher accuracy than with human-written or baseline-generated docs. Human developers also judge its docs more useful than the originals for understanding and editing code. The results argue for treating doc quality as a checkable equivalence property.
arxiv-2606-22447:
Andreas Maier, Siming Bayer, and Patrick Krauss build a research tool for explainable AI in this 2026 paper. Checking an explanation requires ground truth about how the system works inside. Simple systems offer that truth but test nothing, while complex neural networks hide it entirely. The authors wanted a study object that is genuinely complex yet fully known.

They re-implemented the Atari 2600 console as two independent differentiable emulators, one in Julia and one in JAX. Both match the reference emulator on all sixty-four games, with byte-identical memory and pixel-identical screens. Treating the cartridge as a weight tensor and memory as a soft tape, they prove the gradient-friendly execution matches the original bit-for-bit going forward. That design exposes surrogate gradients where the chip's logic has none. The result is a complete computer architecture that explanation methods can face rigorously.
arxiv-2606-22547:
Yaoxuan Zeng and Malte Jansen model ocean convection on icy moons in this 2026 planetary science paper. Rapid rotation organizes convection there into slantwise columns aligned with the spin axis. Those columns carry heat toward the poles, shaping the ice shell thickness above, a key mission observable.

Global ocean models cannot resolve the convective motions, and standard schemes cannot represent the slanted form. Zeng and Jansen build such a scheme inside a global ocean model. Benchmark tests in a spherical shell compare its fluxes against convection-resolving simulations. The scheme reproduces the poleward heat transport inside the tangent cylinder, where slantwise convection dominates. The resulting surface heat flux varies by about as much as the imposed bottom heating. It captures the bulk interior temperature gradient, though not the full temperature structure near boundaries. The scheme also suits other rapidly rotating oceans, including deep exoplanet oceans.
arxiv-2606-23047:
Illyyne Saffar, Aurelie Boisbunon, and Shruti Bothe weigh the energy cost of adapting models inside future wireless networks in a 2026 paper. Sixth-generation networks will shift constantly as traffic and conditions change. Models trained once will decay as data drifts away from their training world. Unsupervised domain adaptation retunes a model for the new conditions without fresh labels. Such pipelines add modules and extra training steps, so their energy bill may exceed plain retraining. The authors ask when adaptation actually becomes the greener choice.

Saffar and colleagues measure the energy use of adaptation against single-task training. Their comparison also prices in human labeling effort, which retraining needs and adaptation avoids. From those measurements they derive a threshold. It gives the minimum number of target domains beyond which adaptation beats retraining on total cost. The aim is practical guidance for network operators choosing between the two strategies.
arxiv-2606-23647:
Mitra, Manna, and Saha design communication tasks that can certify a genuinely quantum property of measurement devices, in a 2026 paper on quantum information. Quantum instruments are the most general description of quantum dynamics, covering both measurements and channels. Two instruments are incompatible when they cannot run together on one input, a hallmark of nonclassical behavior. Certifying that without trusting the devices is hard.

The authors introduce three party tasks with a sender, a relayer, and a receiver, using only classical inputs and outputs. They derive a tight score bound that every pair of compatible instruments obeys, equal to the best classical performance under the same dimension limits. Beating that bound certifies incompatibility of the relayer's instruments. The certification is genuine: it holds even in the hardest case, where every induced measurement and channel is pairwise compatible.
arxiv-2606-23747:
Babbar, Javed, and Maji classify a mixed family of operators acting on multivariable analytic functions, in a 2026 paper on operator theory. Toeplitz and Hankel operators are structured operators tied to function theory, control, and signal processing. Their sums form a combined class studied for decades on the disc. The polydisc is the multivariable stage, where many one variable results fail.

Working on the vector valued Hardy space over the polydisc, the authors give a complete classification of Toeplitz plus Hankel operators. Equivalent algebraic conditions characterize them, each phrased through how the operator interacts with shifts in every variable. They also characterize paired operators on the matching square integrable space over the torus. For an inner function, they further describe the paired operators tied to its Beurling submodule. The results extend recent disc classifications to arbitrary dimension.
arxiv-2606-23847:
Altoè redesigns a classic laboratory sound so that two faint, unwanted steady tones no longer contaminate hearing experiments, in a 2026 paper on psychoacoustics. Schroeder's harmonic complexes are periodic signals that sound like a tone gliding up or down in frequency. Hearing scientists use them to study frequency dispersion in the ear. The catch is that the components at the edges of the signal's band do not share that glide. They sit at fixed frequencies and are easily audible.

Those edge tones can quietly distort behavioral results, since listeners might respond to them rather than to the glide. Altoè presents a variation that largely suppresses the steady components while keeping the time varying frequency character. The signal stays periodic and band limited, so existing experiments can adopt it directly.
arxiv-2606-24047:
Choudhury and colleagues build a tool to flag depression risk among female sex workers, a group facing violence, stigma, and money hardship that raise mental health risks. Published in 2026, their study combines two selection methods, analysis of variance and mutual information, to pick the most useful survey features. A Harris Hawks optimisation routine, inspired by hunting hawks, then tunes a logistic regression model for prediction.

Applied to records from 3,005 women, the combined model beats standard classifiers on accuracy and related scores, reaching an area under the curve near the top of the scale. Explainable AI techniques, which reveal why a model flags someone, point to post-traumatic stress, violence from clients, and job-related factors as the strongest contributors. The authors argue such a tool could guide earlier support and better targeted psychosocial care for a marginalised population.
arxiv-2606-24147:
Lee, Mimura, and Moriya help speech recognition models learn the alignment between sound and text gradually instead of all at once. Aligner-Encoder models predict each output token directly from a matching encoder position, so the encoder must internalise the alignment with no cross-attention to help. In practice that alignment snaps into place abruptly in the upper layers, making training touchy and long utterances brittle, a weakness their 2026 method, InterAligner, targets.

An intermediate aligner objective lets alignment form progressively through the network's depth, while an intermediate CTC loss steadies optimisation along the way. On LibriSpeech with a seventeen-layer Conformer, a final-only aligner trails badly, the intermediate CTC variant improves matters, and InterAligner improves further still, with the largest gains on long utterances. Lee's team, based at NTT in Japan, argues staged alignment objectives should be standard practice for this model family.
arxiv-2606-24247:
Yin and colleagues squeeze more sensitivity from a microwave receiver built on excited atoms, by letting the atoms move. Rydberg atoms, boosted to huge, fragile orbits, make exquisite electric-field sensors. Their receiver uses a two-photon ladder scheme inside a vapour cell. In 2026 the team sends probe and coupling lasers travelling together, co-propagating, amplifying the Doppler effect from atomic motion instead of cancelling it.

Microwave dressing shifts the resonance condition differently for atoms at different speeds. Fast atoms are thus recruited into the signal, strengthening the transparency response. The heterodyne receiver reaches a sensitivity better than the counter-propagating version by a solid factor. The local oscillator field needed drops by a far larger factor, easing power and radiation concerns. Co-propagation also simplifies hardware. Several laser fields can arrive through one optical fibre. Yin's result turns Doppler broadening, usually unwanted, into the mechanism of improvement.
arxiv-2606-24547:
Iyer, Goh, and Gompper survey how intelligent active particles organise themselves. Such particles propel themselves, sense their surroundings by direction, process data, decide, and steer toward goals. Their interactions are thus non reciprocal: a predator reacts to prey differently than prey to predator. Examples span biology, from cells and bacteria to insects, birds, fish, and walkers. Built microbots and nanobots join them.

Because many agents move through water, hydrodynamic forces strongly shape group dynamics. Emergent behaviour includes swarming and flocking, predator prey pursuit and evasion, and steering through complex settings. All arise without any central controller. Signal spread through the group is as key as physical forces. The 2026 overview maps this young field for physicists and engineers. It covers what intelligence at the particle level means, which collective effects it produces, and why self ordering is the lens that unifies systems from microbe colonies to robot swarms.
arxiv-2606-24747:
Lavinia Ghita, Dhruv Desai, and Ioana Boier derive scaling laws for shrinking large language models for one task area. Big models perform well but cost too much where speed and price matter. Distillation trains a small model to copy a large one. The authors ask how quality scales with pruning schedule, supervision format, compression ratio, and dataset size. Their test domain is quantitative finance, with headline classification as the concrete task.

Two distillation styles are compared under repeated structural pruning: logit based and LoRA based. A blended chain of thought loss steadies training over reasoning traces. In domain quality falls predictably as compression deepens. General knowledge benchmarks, by contrast, collapse much earlier. Supervision format drives the trade off, Ghita and colleagues find. Chain of thought supervision actively recovers general knowledge that pruning erases. The team releases its FinHeadlineMix dataset, the scaling results, and practical guidance for compression choices.
arxiv-2606-25147:
Industrial recommender systems usually model users as dense embedding vectors, whose fixed size constrains what they can express. Qingyun Liu and seventeen colleagues present TokenMinds, a system that gives users discrete tokens as well, extending the PLUM framework from item retrieval to user modelling.

An encoder decoder built from pretrained language models produces both semantic ID based user tokens and dense user embeddings. The dual output keeps the grounded, readable benefits of discrete tokens while staying compatible with downstream models that expect vectors. Because items and users now share one semantic ID vocabulary, long form and short form video behaviour can be modelled in a single system, cutting training and serving costs. TokenMinds is validated through extensive offline experiments and live launches.
arxiv-2606-25247:
Swipe typing decoders usually learn one keyboard layout and break when the layout changes. David Lee Miller and Aleksandras Kostarevas describe FUTO Swipe in 2026, a neural decoder that receives the layout only at the moment of use. Along each swipe, the model predicts whether the finger is signalling a character and where that character sits in space. The active layout then maps those spatial predictions onto its own keys, so nothing about the layout is baked into training.

To gather training data, the team released a corpus of over one million donated swipes from more than twelve thousand sessions, openly licensed. Geometric tricks that warp both swipe paths and layouts during training forced the model to rely on gesture shape. It then handled layouts never seen in training, sometimes beating its accuracy on the familiar one.
arxiv-2606-25447:
An agent's success depends not only on its model but on the harness around it: which tools it sees, how they are described, and what extra information rides with each observation. Kyungmin Kim and colleagues make that scaffolding an experimental variable in 2026, extending a standard text world testbed so harness designs can be swapped and environments shifted after training. They then post train agents under different harness choices and measure what carries over.

Training with the harness in mind improved performance both on familiar tasks and under changed task and tool conditions. Under a minimally designed harness, by contrast, post training gains collapsed when the tool environment shifted strongly. The study argues the harness deserves the same design care as the training algorithm, since the two interact rather than merely adding up.
arxiv-2606-25947:
Alberto González-Sanz, Marcel Nutz, and Austin Stromme sharpen the statistics of regularized optimal transport. Optimal transport compares probability distributions by the cheapest way to morph one into the other. Real data give only samples, so the empirical cost wobbles around the truth. Regularization smooths the problem, at the price of bias. The team bounds both bias and variance for finite samples.

General convex penalties fall under the results. Kullback-Leibler divergence and power penalties are both covered. Bounds show explicit dependence on the smoothing strength and the data's intrinsic dimension. Entropic transport gets improved state-of-the-art bounds. Power penalties get their first fully quantitative treatment. For quadratic cost, the quadratically regularized estimator hits the fastest known rate. It estimates the true transport cost faster than any rival based on regularized transport. The unified approach replaces a patchwork of case-by-case results.
arxiv-2606-26247:
John Campbell, Stefan Höche, and Max Knobbe build a subtraction scheme for precision collider calculations. Next-to-next-to-leading order predictions in quantum chromodynamics drown in infinities that must cancel between real and virtual emission terms. Subtraction tames them locally, point by point in phase space. Their counterterms borrow the shape of a parton shower: scalar radiators and pure splitting functions carry the singular behaviour.

Overlapping singularities get untangled by partial fractioning. The kinematics map follows an iterated next-to-leading order pattern. For electron-positron annihilation into a quark pair, the double-real remainder stays finite in both single and double unresolved limits. Monte Carlo convergence checks out numerically. Scalar counterterm integrals are computed in the back-to-back configuration, by analysis and by sector decomposition. Colour-singlet decays, like those of the Higgs and Z bosons, are the scheme's home ground.
arxiv-2606-26347:
Clement Wong and colleagues mine health clues from grid battery faults that already happened. Lithium battery modules on the grid need watching, because cell faults can turn catastrophic. Parallel-connected cells hide their individual states from sparse sensors, and shifting operating conditions muddy every signal. Their framework extracts health features from field data and calibrates them against conditions, so faulty groups can be separated from healthy ones inside the same module.

Twenty-five commercial modules supply the evidence. Each held fourteen series groups of parallel cells, and exactly one group per module was confirmed faulty after teardown. Calibrated capacity, capacity fade rate, and voltage-curve peak heights separate the faulty groups with statistical significance. Internal resistance does not, a pointed surprise. Resistance-only fault watching, the industry habit, would have missed these failures. The feature signatures also hint at the mechanisms behind the faults.
arxiv-2606-26447:
M. C. Babiuc Hamilton, A. P. Gross, and O. T. Odney examine gamma rays from neutron star mergers. Gamma rays are the most energetic form of light. Merging neutron stars forge heavy elements through rapid neutron capture. The decay of those new nuclei powers a fading glow called a kilonova. It also emits gamma rays that telescopes could detect directly. Such rays would probe the nuclei created.

Standard models track only each nucleus's ground state, its lowest-energy form. They assume excited states relax instantly. The authors instead follow nuclear isomers as separate network entries. Isomers are long-lived excited states of a nucleus. Their transition rates depend on temperature. Two predicted emission lines stood out. Planned observatories might detect them at distances within our galaxy. Only a small set of isomeric nuclei was included. The authors therefore urge fuller treatment in future merger models.
arxiv-2606-26547:
Xavier Routh and six colleagues present ApproxHDC, a compiler framework for hyperdimensional computing. That approach represents data as very long vectors and computes with simple operations on them. It tolerates noise well and maps naturally onto varied hardware. Small losses in answer quality can buy large speed gains. Finding the best places to approximate, though, is a huge search problem.

ApproxHDC extends an existing compiler so one program can target many back ends. Targets include ordinary processors, graphics processors, and simulated memory-based accelerators. The space of software and hardware approximations grows exponentially, so exhaustive search is impossible. The framework uses efficient search and analysis to find high-impact approximations instead. The authors report substantial performance gains with minimal quality loss. The work aims to make approximation tuning automatic rather than a hand craft.
arxiv-2606-26847:
Shinsuke Koyama and Ryota Kobayashi infer the hidden dynamics of rhythmic systems directly from noisy recordings. Oscillations run through brains, hearts, and daily biological cycles. The Hopf normal form is the universal low-dimensional description near the onset of oscillation. The authors embed that form in a probabilistic model of the data. Latent states and system parameters are estimated together.

The method recovers natural frequency, growth rate, and phase robustly, even far from the onset point and under strong noise. Combined with Gaussian process regression, it also rebuilds how phase and amplitude respond to nudges. Tests on the van der Pol oscillator, a classic self-sustaining rhythm, beat existing phase-based and regression methods clearly. The work links normal-form theory with statistical inference for messy real signals.
arxiv-2606-26947:
Wenwang Huang, Yusen Fu, and seven colleagues scale image generation that follows several reference images at once. Personalised generation from one reference works well. Mixing many references of mixed types is much harder. Existing benchmarks barely test those complex cases. Their new OmniRef-Bench covers rich combinations and large reference counts.

Mainstream open models struggled on the new benchmark. Performance fell sharply as mixed-type references multiplied. Their training framework, DyRef, attacks the problem in two stages. Supervised fine-tuning first teaches the basic multi-reference skill. A second stage reweights learning by difficulty and stretches reward differences within groups. Hard cases with many references thus get more training pressure. The authors report clear gains on complex generation tasks.
arxiv-2606-27147:
Xue and colleagues ask how safe images from autoregressive generators really are. Such models build pictures token by token, picking each small visual piece from a learned codebook. That language-like design reads text prompts well, but harmful pictures can slip through. Their fix repairs the codebook itself, the dictionary that maps codes to visual patterns. The model judges its own outputs, so no human labelling is needed to spot unsafe generations in this method from 2026.

Flagged outputs form harmful and safe image-text pairs. Those pairs map a harmful space inside the codebook, guiding edits that erase harmful mappings. Adaptive fine-tuning inside the safe space then restores picture quality. Rounds repeat until gains stop. Safety improves using only the model's own judgement, with no outside feedback loop. Harmful outputs fall while ordinary generation quality is preserved.
arxiv-2606-27447:
Alves leads the report of a community survey on the future of scientific publishing, commissioned in 2026 by the journal Astronomy and Astrophysics. Publishing is being reshaped by open access, artificial intelligence, and demands for transparency and equity, while article volume strains editors and reviewers. The survey went to nearly twenty-nine thousand of the journal's authors and drew close to three thousand responses from sixty-nine countries. Questions covered journal choice, peer review, open access, research evaluation, and AI's role.

Quality and reputation dominate where researchers choose to publish, with cost second. The top peer review worry is reviewer expertise and fairness, not speed. Citation counts still matter, but many want broader, more qualitative impact measures. Most prefer public or institutional funding for open access. Views on AI split sharply: help with administration and language is welcome, autonomous decisions or generated content are firmly rejected.
arxiv-2606-27547:
Yan, He, and Tai argue that human motion generators are starved not by their architectures but by their data. Motion capture datasets over-represent common, repetitive actions and miss the long tail of complex movement, so learned motion vocabularies stay small. Their framework generates large-scale synthetic human motion that is diverse and plausible, well beyond the captured range. In the 2026 computer vision paper, a redesigned quantised tokenizer trains on the expanded corpus, jointly scaling the training data and the discrete codebook.

Training with synthetic motion improves the coverage of the learned motion vocabulary in the reported experiments. Gains follow across generation tasks such as text-to-motion and motion continuation. The tokenizer remains fully compatible with existing tools, including a leading motion language model. The bottleneck, the authors conclude, is the support of the learned representation, not model design.
arxiv-2606-27647:
Dekui Peng studies the shadowing property in 2026. Shadowing means a rough orbit of a system is followed by a true orbit that stays close to it. The systems here are endomorphisms of locally compact groups. An endomorphism is a map of a group into itself that respects the group rule.

For Lie groups, Peng gives a complete test based on the map's differential, its best linear approximation. Shadowing holds if and only if that differential is hyperbolic. Two results follow. Maps that spread points apart must also expand the space in the topological sense. For reversible maps, spreading, shadowing, two-sided shadowing, and the Anosov property all coincide. Connected semisimple Lie groups are sharper still: the maps with the property are exactly the nilpotent ones. Totally disconnected groups flip the story. There, every continuous endomorphism has the property automatically, shown with Willis's tidy decomposition.
arxiv-2606-27847:
Distributed algorithms on graphs often rely on shattering. After a randomised pre-phase, the leftover unresolved pieces should be small and scattered. Mohsen Ghaffari and three colleagues show in 2026 that standard versions of this argument have a gap. The analyses treat distant nodes as independent. That fails when the pre-phase runs for more than a constant number of rounds, since effects build up over time.

Several literature results are therefore incomplete as written. Maximal independent set, graph colouring, and the distributed Lovász Local Lemma are affected. The authors repair the analyses. Their main contribution is a corrected analysis of the Fischer–Ghaffari local lemma algorithm. General tools capture patterns common in modern algorithms, yielding the needed decay bounds without any independence assumption. The paper also gives explicit cases where popular lemmas fail. It aims to give the technique a robust reusable foundation.
arxiv-2606-28047:
The nerve theorem ties a space's homology to the pattern of a cover. Its classical form uses spectral sequences and cannot always compute it effectively. Sucharita Barik and four colleagues develop an effective version in 2026. Discrete Morse theory supplies the machinery. The homology of a simplicial complex is computed explicitly from its parts and their non-trivial overlaps. Gradient vector fields on each piece are the input.

The approach is purely combinatorial. No geometry or continuity notions are involved. Given gradient fields on the pieces and on their overlaps, the main theorem assembles the answer for the whole. The construction mirrors the classical nerve picture while staying computable. Complexes covered by finitely many subcomplexes are the setting. The work turns an existence theorem into a procedure.
arxiv-2606-28147:
Victor Reis and Thomas Rothvoss prove a sharper result about sparsifiers, small stand-ins that mimic a large matrix while keeping only a few rows. Their 2026 theorem concerns the version where row lengths are measured by adding absolute values, a measure mathematicians call the l1 norm.

Reis and Rothvoss show that any matrix has such a stand-in. Its kept rows grow only slightly faster than the number of columns, with a mild penalty tied to the allowed error. The same result restated geometrically says a many-sided shape called a zonotope can be closely mimicked by one built from far fewer segments. Their bound improves the best known one, due to Talagrand in 1990, by trimming a wasteful factor.
arxiv-2606-28347:
Charles L. Wang, Keir Dorchen, and Peter Jin argue that the safety of advanced artificial intelligence agents is being certified the wrong way. Today's methods, from training-time alignment to monitoring and red-teaming, mostly snapshot how a system behaves now, even as systems grow more capable, self-improving, and free to modify themselves over time.

Wang and colleagues propose teachability as the property that matters: a system's capacity to stay correctable under bounded human, institutional, or environmental intervention. A system can look competent while quietly eroding the internal conditions that future correction would need, in its representations, its algorithms, or its meta-decisions. Safety, on their account, is a matter of what can be known about the evolving learner, not just behavior of the current policy. Safe systems must remain teachable later.
arxiv-2606-28747:
Kazuki Ota, Takayuki Osa, and Tatsuya Harada ask whether an agent can stock its own mathematics library. Successful proof systems lean on human-curated theorem collections, leaving open whether useful theorems can emerge from the axioms alone. Their agent starts with nothing but axioms and inference rules in a formal system.

The self-supervised algorithm alternates between proof search and harvesting: theorems proved along the way are extracted, judged useful, and shelved as lemmas that make later searches cheaper. The loop discovers tens of thousands of theorems and proves human-written benchmark problems, evidence the discoveries are not formal junk. Handed to a language model as prompt lemmas, the discovered theorems improve its proof performance, suggesting a route toward self-evolving mathematics systems whose every discovery remains formally verifiable.
arxiv-2606-28947:
Elser and Lal define what it means for a large set of patterns to be machine-learnable, in a precise formal sense. Informally, a learnable set has three traits: its members are easy to recognise, easy to generate, and both tasks are easy to learn from examples. Their formalism uses binary strings, and learnability means a bounded-complexity Boolean autoencoder exists that leaves every member of the set unchanged.

An autoencoder here compresses and rebuilds its input. Fixing the set's members means it rebuilds them perfectly. The authors implement these autoencoders as nets of Boolean threshold functions, simple units that fire when weighted inputs pass a limit. Experiments show learnability for Rorschach patterns, symmetric inkblot-like designs that may flip contrast in the mirrored half. Wilder sets, whose members are only roughly fixed, are also studied. A simple iteration evolves them until they become properly machine-learnable.
arxiv-2606-29047:
Ahnert and colleagues present weak dominant balance, a way to read physical mechanisms straight out of messy flow data. Finding which terms of an equation dominate in each region reveals local mechanisms, but the method needs accurate derivatives of the data. Taking derivatives numerically amplifies noise, fails for higher-order equations, and struggles on irregular shapes. Past work thus stayed with clean simulations of simple systems.

Their framework avoids differentiating the data at all. It projects the equations into a weak, integral form, shifting the differentiation onto smooth test functions the analyst chooses. The data itself stays untouched. The method kept identifying regimes accurately under severe noise where existing approaches failed outright. It produced the first data-driven split of a third-order equation, applied to turbulent duct flow. Matching splits across simulation and lab measurements of a wavy channel flow uncovered a previously unknown flow regime.
arxiv-2606-29147:
Singh analyses a neural network method for solving convection-diffusion equations, which model transport plus spreading, on curved domains. Physics-informed neural networks train a network to satisfy the equation at sampled points. The standard squared-error loss fails when convection dominates. The solution forms a thin boundary layer where the residual explodes. The few points inside the layer then dominate training, and the smooth bulk is left unresolved.

His variant penalises the interior residual in a weaker norm, its exponent tuned to the point count. Boundary conditions enter through a trace norm that treats flat and curved shapes uniformly. Under stated assumptions he proves one error bound across the exponent range. Its optimal rate is set by a cut-cell floor specific to curved geometry. Experiments on a rectangle and a disk confirm this. As layers sharpen, the standard loss turns fragile, while his version trains reliably.
arxiv-2606-30447:
Juan M. Gimenez, Fehmi Cirak, and Michael Ortiz design a quantum algorithm for a classic slow-flow problem. The steady Stokes equations govern incompressible viscous flow. Their setting is a two-dimensional periodic domain. The method leans on the Quantum Fourier Transform. Fourier space gives the Stokes operator a friendly structure there.

In spectral form the Laplacian becomes diagonal and easy to invert. A Helmholtz projection enforces incompressibility mode by mode. A mode-dependent rotation splits velocity into longitudinal and transverse parts. Component-conditioned scaling then applies the inverse Laplacian correctly. Velocity and pressure live as quantum states over Fourier modes. Polynomial amplitude blocks implement the spectral factors. Tests include a steady vortex and a force-dipole benchmark. A multiscale fluctuation benchmark recovers averaged energy without full fields. Circuit size grows very slowly with grid resolution. Standard assumptions on state preparation underlie that scaling claim.
arxiv-2606-30547:
Keith Tran, Samiha Marwan, and Thomas Price test whether a short lesson can teach students to prompt AI programming helpers. Prompt-based programming states goals in plain language instead of code. It lowers barriers for non-specialists. Vague prompts still produce poor results, beginners find. The authors built a forty-five-minute lesson with guided practice. A randomized study pits it against ordinary lab work.

Fifty-five engineering students took part. The control group spent the same time on code tracing. Prompting students improved more on average. The gap was ten points against one point. It did not reach statistical significance, though. Gains in prompting self-efficacy were significantly larger for the lesson group. Those gains were thirty-five points against twenty-two. The authors judge a brief lesson helpful. Prompting skill needs more practice to grow further. The lesson needs no prior computing background to use.
arxiv-2606-30747:
Marcelo Rezende Barbosa reviews the super TTbar deformation of two-dimensional field theories. The plain TTbar deformation reshapes a theory through its stress-energy tensor. It is exactly solvable: the new energy spectrum follows from the old one by a closed formula. The super version extends the trick to theories with supersymmetry, a symmetry linking particles and their partners.

Barbosa works in superspace, a formalism that handles space and superpartners together. He also draws on super-Riemann surfaces, the geometric stage for superstring worldsheets. He shows the deformations can be read as a noncritical RNS superstring theory. That is string theory below the critical dimension, in the Ramond-Neveu-Schwarz formalism. Through field redefinitions, he also proposes reading them as two-dimensional supergravity in superspace. The review ties deformation theory to string constructions that might otherwise seem unrelated.
arxiv-2606-30847:
Simon Spoorendonk releases bucket-graph-spprc, an open-source C++ library for the shortest path problem with resource constraints. That problem, finding the cheapest route that respects limits on resources like time or load, is the pricing subproblem inside branch-cut-and-price solvers for vehicle routing. The library implements a bucket-graph labelling algorithm with two-way search, bucket fixing and arc elimination, storing labels in a layout built for fast vectorised dominance checks.

Its key design choice is a compile-time resource concept, through which a new variant is added via a fixed seven-function interface, and resources combine into the label state with no run-time dispatch. Five resources ship built in. On the shared public benchmark instances, at an identical bound, the library beat the main open-source rival, PathWyse, by factors of 1.3 to 2.35 in shifted geometric mean.
arxiv-2606-31247:
Li and eleven colleagues introduce FlexiSLM, a spoken language model whose speech frame rate can change on demand. Spoken language models turn speech into tokens at a fixed rate, usually 25 or 12.5 frames per second. Speech carries uneven information over time, though, so a fixed rate wastes effort on quiet stretches.

FlexiSLM uses dynamic frame rate coding for both speech input and output. At its high-quality settings it beats fixed-rate seven-billion-parameter models such as Qwen2.5-Omni and Kimi-Audio. The rate can be steered down to 4 frames per second, and at 6.25 frames it roughly halves inference time against the 12.5 rate while keeping strong speech-to-speech quality. Users gain a direct trade-off between speed and fidelity.
arxiv-2606-31547:
Blumer, Feuerpfeil, Lopes and Quadrelli recast a field invariant called the Kaplansky radical in the language of group cohomology. So it can be defined for any profinite group and any prime p. The radical collects field elements represented by every norm quadratic form in two variables. Their version takes the orthogonal of a first cohomology group under the cup product pairing.

For absolute Galois groups the new cup radical recovers the classical radical at p equal to two and the p-radical of Dario and Engler in general. The authors also state a group version of the H-conjecture, a norm relation first posed by Kijima and Nishi. They prove it matches the field property while depending only on the maximal pro-2 quotient. They verify it for local and global fields, function fields, and several new families of pro-p groups.
arxiv-2606-31947:
Hosseini-Kivanani and Dowerah present LuxEmo, an expressive speech corpus for Luxembourgish, a low-resource language largely missing from speech technology. Speech data sets concentrate on major languages, and expressive text-to-speech is usually trained on acted studio recordings. Real broadcast speech is messier: noisy, with voices over each other, and full of code-switching.

LuxEmo holds 21 hours of expressive, chat-style speech drawn from RTL youth broadcasts, spanning four emotion groups and four speakers who recur across 7,562 short segments. A partly automatic workflow joins voice activity detection, denoising, language ID, splitting, emotion cues and focused human review. Five expressive synthesis systems are benchmarked on the corpus, covering cross-lingual transfer from German, multilingual support, Luxembourgish adaptation and prosody transfer.
arxiv-2608-00047:
Rengel and Krumstroh revisit a suspected impact site in the Venezuelan Guiana Shield. Aerial views in the 1980s raised the impact idea. A round landform seemed to fit a crater shape. Radar images were shared, but the reading stayed unresolved. Newly found letters and images allowed a fresh look.

Modern SRTM elevation data drove the re-evaluation. The higher-resolution maps show no diagnostic crater forms. The shape fits the Nuria ring dike intrusive complex instead. Similar round intrusive complexes, like the Kondyor massif, make the same point. Round shape alone cannot prove an impact. The study shows how better maps and context settle old landform puzzles.
arxiv-2608-00147:
Drexel and co-authors present RadPRISM for radiology image representations with built-in concept structure. Vision-language pretraining learns rich codes from radiology reports. Past variants share one embedding space for all concepts. Concept structure then had to be recovered after the fact. That post hoc route limits transparency and clinical use.

RadPRISM makes a clinician-defined schema its stratification axis. A local language model pulls per-concept text spans from free-text reports. Each clinical concept aligns in its own visual subspace. On 203,602 chest examinations with a 19-concept schema, zero-shot macro AUROC rose by about fifteen points, to 0.868. External tests matched a purpose-built reference model. Visual grounding beat that reference by up to 4.3-fold. A radiologist study confirmed concept-stratified retrieval skill.
arxiv-2608-00347:
Calderon studies a rectangular form of Gaussian binomial coefficients. The object is a 2D factorial ratio over the Gaussian integers. It follows Kalinin's Gaussian take on Wolstenholme's theorem. For a prime p equal to 3 mod 4, these coefficients are first shown p-integral. The main result is a supercongruence of Ljunggren-Jacobsthal type.

Scaling all four parameters by p^k shifts the coefficient by a multiple of p^{3k}. That proves the inert-prime case of a Kalinin conjecture. A Bailey-type congruence mod p also holds for this rectangular form. Its shape echoes Bailey's refinements of Lucas's theorem, with two extra binomial factors. Proofs mix power-sum bounds with block factorizations.
baron-trigault-s-vengeance-pg547:
Emile Gaboriau wrote Baron Trigault's Vengeance as a sequel to The Count's Millions, continuing his French crime saga of ruined fortunes and patient revenge. The opening pages dwell on vengeance itself: a man whose honor and fortune were wrecked by conspiracy dreams of repaying his persecutors a hundredfold. Cool calculation soon replaces the first heat of hatred.

Gaboriau follows the conspirators, their victims, and the working people caught between them, including women worn old by hard work and weeping. Parisian shops, money, and marriage bargains all serve the plot. Readers of his Lecoq detective novels will recognize the method: secrets buried in respectable life, uncovered piece by piece until revenge or justice arrives.
boole-mathematical-analysis-logic-1847:
George Boole published The Mathematical Analysis of Logic as a pamphlet in 1847. In those few pages he founded symbolic logic. Boole treated reasoning as a calculus, with symbols that could be joined and split by rule. Deduction became something like algebra, open to exact handling.

He shows how class terms and statements turn into equations. From those equations, valid conclusions follow by fixed steps. The pamphlet's claims were bold for a self taught Irish mathematician. Later thinkers built Boolean algebra on this start. That algebra now runs inside every computer on Earth. The seed text is short enough to read in one sitting.
boucher-de-perthes-antiquites-1847:
Jacques Boucher de Perthes presents flint tools in his Celtic and Antediluvian Antiquities, in French from 1847. The tools lay in gravel beds beside bones of extinct beasts. Humans, he argues, lived long before the Flood's supposed date in the old biblical reckoning of the world's age.

Learned men mocked him at first, then slowly came to see the pits themselves. His finds near Abbeville forced a new, vast age for mankind. The book gave humanity its deep past in hard stone proof. It stands as a founding document of archaeology, the work of a customs officer whose hobby rewrote human history.
boucher-de-perthes-antiquites-celtiques-:
Jacques Boucher de Perthes, a French customs man at Abbeville, brought out the first part of this work in 1847. Its title means Celtic and pre flood finds, in French. For years he had dug worked flints from deep gravel beds by the Somme.

The flints lay with the bones of beasts long dead, such as mammoths and rhinos of the ice age. Boucher de Perthes held that men made those tools in a time far past the flood of the Bible. Mocked at first, he was proved right in 1859, and a new view of man's age was born.
bronte-agnes-grey-1847:
Anne Brontë published Agnes Grey in 1847, under the name Acton Bell at first. The slim novel was her debut, a quiet account of a governess's working life in England. She drew it from her own years in service, which she had found hard and lonely.

Agnes, a parson's daughter, takes posts to help her poor family after her father's losses. Spoiled children and vain parents make her days a test of patience and self-respect in silence. She keeps her faith and her diary, and finds a friend in the curate Weston. A modest inheritance and a small school end her service on her own terms in peace. The book's plain honesty rebukes the glamor that hid governesses' real plight from readers.
bronte-jane-eyre-1847:
Charlotte Brontë published Jane Eyre in 1847, under the name Currer Bell at first. The novel became the defining first-person tale of female independence in Victorian fiction and beyond. Later governess novels and feminist coming-of-age tales all answer to its strong, plain voice here.

Jane, an orphan schooled at harsh Lowood, takes a governess post at Thornfield Hall in Yorkshire. She loves her master Rochester, whose wife, mad and hidden, lives in the attic above. Fire, a torn veil, and a voice on the wind drive the Gothic plot to crisis. Jane flees, inherits money, and returns to wed Rochester on her own free terms at last. Her insistence on equality of soul still gives the love story its sting.
bronte-wuthering-heights-1847:
Emily Brontë published Wuthering Heights in 1847, under the name Ellis Bell at first. Many call it the most radical novel of the Victorian era in form and feeling. Its storm-driven metaphysical romance broke every convention of the realist novel of its day completely.

Heathcliff, a foundling from Liverpool, is raised at Wuthering Heights on the Yorkshire moors there. His fierce bond with Catherine Earnshaw survives her marriage to Edgar Linton of the Grange. Her death drives his revenge on both houses across a whole second generation of Earnshaws. Nelly Dean and the baffled Lockwood tell the tale in frames within frames of voice. The moor wind blows through prose unlike any other English novel of its time.
cia-0000010447:
Conditions and trends in Latin America affecting American security fill a November 1952 CIA survey. The paper sweeps the hemisphere country by country in the early Cold War. Communist parties, military rulers, and weak economies all figure in its accounting.

Regional surveys let Washington rank worries and watch for the next Guatemala or Cuba. In 1952 the hemisphere seemed quiet next to Europe and Korea, which made trend-watching the whole task. The file shows analysts hunting early signs: labor unrest, arms deals, party growth. Its judgments fed the policies that shaped the hemisphere's Cold War decade.
cia-0000012247:
Raids across Borneo marked the undeclared war between Indonesia and Malaysia, and in August 1964 the CIA weighed the conflict's short-term prospects. Sukarno's Confrontation had run for over a year, pitting Indonesian forces against Malaysian and Commonwealth troops along a jungle border. The fighting stayed small in scale, but the rhetoric from Jakarta stayed loud.

The paper judges whether the raids and threats would grow, fade, or settle into a long stalemate. It weighs the cost to both sides and the growing pressure for a settlement. The study captures an odd war's late phase, when peace seemed possible yet still needed watching.
cia-0000013247:
American prisoners and missing men lost in Southeast Asia are the subject of a CIA report from November 1970. The catalog note marks the report as drawn from the Laos accounting. The Laotian missing were the war's most painful loose end. Men shot down over the trails vanished into a secret war their own government barely admitted, and their files stayed thin for decades.

The report gathers the raw material of that accounting in one place. Names, dates, last sightings, and rumors all entered the ledger. For readers, the page is the missing men's paper trail, kept by the side that owed them answers.
cia-0000013847: Captured US Pilots is the plain title of a CIA note dated May 6, 1967. More than one airman is covered, though the title gives no names or places. Reports in this plain style were filed again and again as the air war grew. Each one marked a crew lost over Vietnam and a new set of prisoners in enemy hands.
cia-0000015347: Unidentified Flying Objects is the plain title of a CIA file dated November 3, 1952. By late 1952 the phrase had become the official term of art. Files under it fed the studies that peaked the next winter. This one sits in the stack that built toward the famous 1953 panel. The November file on flying objects sits in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000015447: Swedish witnesses both saw and photographed UFOs, and an unidentified satellite was also seen, in a CIA record dated February 4, 1960. Photographs raised the value of a report, since film could be checked in a lab. A stray satellite added a space age twist. The entry joins two kinds of sky reports that officials had to sort out in those years.
cia-0000036847:
General Creighton Abrams consulted with Washington and received his orders without going in person, a CIA record dated January 6, 1970 notes. Abrams commanded American forces in Vietnam from headquarters in Saigon. The record concerns the channel between the field commander and the capital.

What survives is the fact of that remote command link, filed as a short item. Modern war let a general report and receive direction across the world in hours. The file is a small window on how the Vietnam War was directed from two ends of the earth. Abrams ran the war day to day, but his orders still came from the president and his advisers.
cia-0000038947:
Eugene H. de Bruin is the subject of a CIA record dated February 1, 1964. The title notes that his men were captured by Pathet Lao forces in Laos. De Bruin was an American working in Laos during its secret war years.

Inside, the file concerns de Bruin and the capture of the men with him. Americans in Laos served in a gray zone, often without public acknowledgment. Their work supported a kingdom fighting a quiet civil war of its own. The record preserves an early case from that hidden war. A named American and his team passed into Pathet Lao hands. The file became their trace in Washington.
cia-0000042347: Farmers were burning straw to make up for delays, in a CIA record dated July 4, 1989. The item is a small agricultural note, the kind that monitoring services clipped from foreign broadcasts and local press. Straw burning after a harvest can clear a field fast when time has been lost to weather or slow work. The record preserves one such practice note, a reminder that the daily file held farm news beside the politics of the day.
cia-0000044447:
Commentary on Killing of Priests is a CIA record dated October 1, 1989 in the catalog. It stands a day before its companion commentary file in the catalog. Two days of opinion, filed separately, show the story's pace.

Inside, more editorial voices weigh the murders and their meaning. Instant judgment is the habit of the opinion pages in a crisis. Writers reached for blame, lessons, and warnings within days of the news. Their haste is part of the record the file keeps for later readers. The file preserves that first rush of verdicts, useful now because it shows what informed readers believed before the slower work of investigation began.
cia-0000045247:
No breakthrough was seen in the Duarte kidnapping, in a CIA record on the 1985 crisis. The catalog dates the item to 1975, which the title and subject correct to 1985. Breakthroughs were promised often in that case and delivered late. Each new promise raised hopes that the next flat report then quietly took away again.

Inside, the absence of progress is the record's whole content. Negative reports are still reports, and this one fixed a low point. Officials reading it abroad learned the talks were going nowhere. The file preserves that flat stretch of the crisis, when the honest summary of weeks of effort was that nothing had yet been won.
cia-0000049147: A partly blacked-out report on the American embassy's task force for the Jesuit killings survives in a CIA item from 1989. The embassy in San Salvador set up the task force to follow the case Washington cared about most. Its work, pressure, questions, and presence, fills this report, minus the names still hidden.
cia-0000096947: Overview statements on CIA involvement in Chile in 1970 are declassified CIA document 0000096947, dated January 2, 1973. The heading dates the involvement to a single year, 1970. The brief file gathers overview statements on that role, companion to the ITT Chile testimony records filed the same week in this catalog cluster. Readers meet the record through its catalog heading and date.
cia-0000102947: Living conditions for Western technicians in the Kuzbass coal basin, plus a second cut-short topic, are declassified CIA document 0000102947, dated November 2, 1983. The heading concerns foreign workers' housing, not prisoners. Readers get a short living-conditions record that widens the cluster's Soviet subject from forced labor to the treatment of outside specialists.
cia-0000103347:
Aircraft: The Achilles' Heel of the Bolivian Cocaine Industry is declassified CIA document 0000103347, dated April 2, 1990. The sample text is broken into columns and hard to read, but its argument is clear. Aircraft were the primary means of trafficker transport, within Bolivia and to neighboring countries.

Disrupting air routes or seizing aircraft would seriously impede, or even shut down, some trafficker groups, the text argues. Yet proper training, equipment, and experience were lacking, so air interception might not work for the Bolivian Air Force. Stronger enforcement of existing antinarcotics law could still bring confiscation of many trafficker aircraft.
cia-0000107447: Soviet Officials in the Levant is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000107447, dated April 1, 1948. The heading names Soviet officials working in the Levant, the eastern Mediterranean lands. No official is named in the title itself. The brief record dates from the spring of 1948, in the first years of the agency's reporting from that region.
cia-0000108047: Use of Prison Labor in Arkhangelsk Oblast is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000108047, dated June 2, 1986. The heading names one region, Arkhangelsk Oblast, and one practice, prison labor. No camp or project is named in the title itself. The brief record is a regional labor item from the summer of 1986 in the northern Russia files.
cia-0000112347: Tale 1 Pf 2--LEGAL Official on Defense, Security Issues is the heading, with take and of mistyped, on declassified CIA document 0000112347, dated April 4, 1992. The title marks the first of two parts, carrying a legal official on defense and security issues. The official is not named in the heading itself. The brief record preserves both mistyped words as released.
cia-0000117847: Current Intelligence Bulletin -- is the whole heading, ending with dashes, on declassified CIA document 0000117847, dated March 6, 1960. The title names a regular bulletin of current intelligence, with nothing added after its name. No single topic is stated in the heading itself at all. The brief record is one dated bulletin issue from the spring of 1960.
cia-0000119747: Current as of midnight on November 4, 1956, this CIA report covers Hungary on the day Soviet forces stormed Budapest. The midnight timestamp belongs to the darkest hours of the crackdown, and the report records the assault as it unfolded. November 4 was the morning the second intervention began in force, and a midnight report catches the crisis at the hinge between hope and defeat.
cia-0000124247: A February 1960 CIA scientific intelligence report, Monograph Four of the series, covers Soviet space vehicles. The set took Moscow's space program apart topic by topic, and this volume handles the rockets and craft themselves. It preserves the technical picture as the agency drew it then. Vehicle studies fed estimates of payload and range, the figures that decided how seriously Washington took Soviet claims about rockets and later about missiles.
cia-0000132247: Situation report 564, from January 1991, covers political developments, including Saddam responding to something the heading does not finish naming. His public responses were staged for several audiences at once. The object of this one is lost, but the report records the response. Responses without named objects are the series' recurring puzzle: the heading assumes a reader who already knows the day's news that the summary was written against.
cia-0000132647: Communists set to run a Latin American youth meeting in Havana fill a CIA paper dated May 2, 1960. Its headline says the meeting was to Havana, wording kept from the original. Youth groups were a prime target for party organizers across the region. The short paper looks ahead to the meeting and the groups expected to control it.
cia-0000132747:
Bloc aid, both economic and military, to the Castro regime fills a CIA paper dated January 4, 1961. Its headline breaks off before the closing words of its title. Months before the Bay of Pigs, the agency was counting what its foe could draw on from abroad.

The paper surveys the aid in goods, loans, weapons, and trained men. Such counts fed straight into the invasion plans then being drawn up in Washington and Florida. For readers, it gives the balance sheet of one side of the coming fight. The totals help explain the confidence, and the errors, of the planners that winter. Both would be tested within four months.
cia-0000134247: A basis for joint action against Cuba, put forward by an Argentine official, fills a CIA paper dated June 5, 1960. The charter of the regional body would become the legal weapon of the anti-Castro camp. Buenos Aires was hunting for legal cover before moving against Havana in the open. The short paper reports the plan and its grounds.
cia-0000135747: Another Spanish document dated 1 March 1961 is held in the declassified 2506 Brigade collection; the date recurs across this stretch of the file. The brigade, Cuban exiles trained by the CIA, was in its final preparation for Cuba. No subject is recorded for this item in the catalog. It survives in the original Spanish as a primary source, one more dated unit in the brigade's crowded March archive.
cia-0000136247: Dated 5 May 1954, a declassified CIA cable deals with harmless smoke grenade and flare bomb drops, ordnance for show rather than for killing. As the Lincoln station file, it forms part of PBSUCCESS, the CIA plan that ended with President Arbenz driven out in June 1954. Its worth is in the detail it pins down, one dated piece of a covert war fought largely on paper.
cia-0000136947: Keep the Voice of Liberty unspecific, headquarters warns LINCOLN in June 1954. Frank Wisner signed the cable. A Salvador broadcast had noted Guatemala's false claim. Guatemala said it had found and captured the station. The broadcast also cited the station's line on the Caracas declaration. That line is excellent so far. But the station must not get more specific about American programs. Its black character must be maintained. Its programs must keep an indigenous feel.
cia-0000141147:
JMWAVE, the CIA station in Miami, cabled headquarters in April 1961 to clear up the flight records of two B-26 bombers, numbers 933 and 927. Phone calls between stations had caused mix-ups, the cable says, because callers had to guard their words for security. It then sets out the corrected times: 933 left for the base called Tide, and 927 left as well.

One note ties the paperwork to a loss. The crew in question came from a B-26 that force-landed on 17 April at Boca Chica. That date was the first day of the Bay of Pigs landing, when exile-crewed bombers flew the air war over Cuba.
cia-03153747:
East Germany opens the Central Intelligence Bulletin dated 22 February 1958. Moscow appears worried by party reaction to Ulbricht's recent purge. If opposition threatens party unity, the Kremlin may reassess the whole East German position. Fritz Selbmann, a leading purge victim now in Moscow, may be questioned about the party's mood. Premier Grotewohl is also in the Soviet Union, officially on a health cure.

Rebel sources claim the Indonesian air force bombed two Central Sumatran towns on 21 February. Djakarta, the brief judges, cannot mount a ground attack soon. Egypt and Syria vote on their union without serious incident. Nasir backs down in the Sudan border dispute and postpones negotiations. Bourguiba's closure of French consulates in Tunisia blocks any French conciliatory gesture. Reinforcing Algeria will strain France's defence plans.
cia-03156047:
Laos opens the Central Intelligence Bulletin dated 7 August 1959. The military lull of the past three days continues. Hanoi calls Laos' letter to the UN secretary general, and talk of recourse to SEATO, provocative and dangerous. The Communist bloc section of the summary page is left blank in this copy.

Kerala follows: tension eases as federal officials take over from the dismissed Communist government. President's Rule machinery is being set up, with elections likely within six months. Communist leaders attack Nehru in parliament but keep street protests nonviolent. In Indonesia, Nasution posts army officers into government ministries. Trinidad's premier campaigns hard against the American naval base at Chaguaramas, weakening London's defence of the 1941 bases agreement. Guatemala's president and the left trade recriminations, ending his bridge-building.
cia-03185147:
Libya opens the Central Intelligence Bulletin dated 6 August 1960. A Soviet delegation in Tripoli negotiates building two gift hospitals. Earlier talks since 1958 stalled on Moscow's demand to staff them. The new proposal trains Libyan medical staff instead, though Soviet trainers would stay long. The USSR also fired an unusual missile from Kapustin Yar on 3 August, possibly to extended range.

Khrushchev's latest letter to Macmillan shows a tougher Soviet line. In the Congo, Hammarskjold seeks an urgent Security Council meeting to pressure Tshombe into admitting UN troops to Katanga peaceably. African nationalists plan disorders around Salisbury in Southern Rhodesia on 8 August, and police prepare for spread. South Vietnamese Communist guerrillas keep up widespread attacks. Morocco rejects Spain's offer to withdraw troops by December 1961. Trujillo may stage a fake coup in the Dominican Republic on 7 August.
cia-06626647:
Unclassified USINFO cable of September 1979, in two sections, forwards a New York Times article on Argentina. The article opens by stating that for the second time in little more than a year, the Argentine Supreme Court had ruled Jacobo Timerman should be set free. He had been detained without charges since April 1977.

The article calls the new ruling a unanimous decision by the court's five justices, telling the ruling military junta to release the former publisher of La Opinion. A previous ruling in July 1978 had also found no judicial grounds to hold him. A court-martial had cleared him of involvement with subversive groups, the article states. He stayed under house arrest, it reports, at the insistence of hard-line army officers led by General Carlos Suarez Mason.
cia-06754247:
Cable distributed 2 May 1984, classed Secret and NOFORN, reports campaign tactics in San Vicente, El Salvador. Its subject line accuses the Nationalist Republican Alliance Party, ARENA, of using bribes and intimidation. Source and office details are redacted under (b)(1) and (b)(3) in the header.

The cable reports that in late April 1984 ARENA ran a vigorous presidential campaign in San Vicente ahead of the 6 May run-off election. Party leaders allegedly offered cash payments to members of the National Conciliation Party and the Salvadoran Authentic Institutional Party for public endorsements. Other party representatives are reported gathering to denounce unauthorized acts by their own members. They also criticized candidate Roberto D'Aubuisson for publicizing militant members' work. Army Fifth Brigade officers loyal to ARENA allegedly aided by intimidating rival party members.
cia-06763947:
Affidavit by Stansfield Turner in the case Donald Ray Woolbright v. Federal Bureau of Investigation and Central Intelligence Agency anchors this court filing. The case number is CV 76-2448-LEW in the United States District Court for the Central District of California. Government attorneys listed include United States Attorney William D. Keller and Assistant United States Attorney Stephen D. Petersen.

Turner swears that he is Director of Central Intelligence and executive head of the CIA, in post since 9 March 1977. He sets out the Agency's duties under the National Security Act of 1947, including advising and making recommendations to the National Security Council. Later paragraphs submit, as Attachment B, a certified copy of a Vance affidavit from earlier litigation. They state that action responsibility for the HGE Project sat with the CIA under its authority to run certain activities free from public disclosure.
coverdale-bible-1535-bagster-1847:
Miles Coverdale gave England its first complete printed Bible in 1535, working from Latin and German versions where his Hebrew and Greek ran short. Samuel Bagster's 1847 reprint, the second modern edition, keeps the original text and spelling. The Apocrypha stands in its old place within the set.

Coverdale's phrasing of the Psalms proved so fine that the Church of England kept it in its prayer book for centuries. Lines like his rendering of the twenty-third Psalm still echo in English worship. The 1535 book was printed abroad and smuggled home at real risk. Bagster's reprint let Victorian readers hold the Tudor Bible as its first readers saw it.
davis-principles-nature-1847:
Andrew Jackson Davis speaks in trance in The Principles of Nature, his vast book of 1847. Davis was a youth from Poughkeepsie with scant school. In trance, he is said to have spoke for hours on God, stars, life, death, and the fate of man. A scribe took down each word. The book is the fruit of those long trance talks.

It came a year ere the Fox raps made his name as a seer of rank. Fans call him the John the Baptist of the new faith. The book is its first great text in his land.
demorgan-formal-logic-1847:
Augustus De Morgan, a London professor of math, published Formal Logic in 1847. Logic at the time still followed rules set by Aristotle two thousand years before. De Morgan set out to give the subject a sharper, more exact form.

He treats reasoning as a kind of calculus, where statements can be combined by clear rules. The book widens logic to cover relations and quantities, not just simple class terms. The pair of rules now called De Morgan's laws appears here in print. Later thinkers built modern symbolic logic on ground he cleared. It also picks sharp fights with the logic teaching of his day.
des-hn-bernhardi-grafen-von-der-marck-un:
