Chemical writings on the blessed stone of the wise fill this German book of 1747, issued at Vienna. The author named is Bernhardi, Count of Mark and Treviso, the famed Bernard of Trevisan. His Latin work is here turned into German, with notes by Joachim Tancke and other learned men.

A dedication to Prince August of Anhalt opens the book. It holds hermetic philosophy to be an old, true, and most useful art, whose first end is a universal medicine. Metallic bodies are to be cured and raised by it, as sick men are. Geber, the Arabian philosopher of near a thousand years before, is cited as a witness. Male and female seed in the work get close treatment. The book is a classic of the art in German dress.
doe-osti-2572823-nuclear-data-sheets-for:
Brookhaven report BNL-228418-2025-INRE, by S. Ota and E. A. McCutchan of the National Nuclear Data Center, issued in July 2025, is a Nuclear Data Sheets evaluation for mass number 47. Evaluators combed every published measurement on the A=47 nuclei and rebuilt their level schemes from radioactive decay and reaction studies. The volume runs to hundreds of pages of adopted levels, gamma rays, and decay data.

Highlights include the first gamma-ray transitions seen in argon-47 and the first excited levels and gamma transitions in manganese-47. A new high-precision measurement of potassium-47 beta decay also enters the record. All data received by April 1, 2025 were evaluated, drawn mainly from the NSR database. The evaluation supersedes the earlier full A=47 review by T. W. Burrows from 2007. Compilations of this kind are the reference layer that reactor, medical, and basic nuclear physics work builds on.
dumas-forty-five-guardsmen-1847:
Alexandre Dumas published The Forty-Five Guardsmen in 1847, the conclusion of his Valois trilogy in French. The romance sets Henri III's forty-five Gascon guards against the Guise faction in Paris and Anjou. Critics often call it Dumas at his most cinematic, with duels staged like film scenes.

Chicot returns, older and graver, as the king's realm frays under League and Spanish plots. The forty-five young Gascons, swaggering and loyal, guard a king who trusts almost no one near him. Diana's revenge for Bussy's murder threads through court war and the Salcede trial in Paris. Henri of Navarre waits in the wings as the Valois line nears its bloody end. The trilogy closes with the crown in peril and France on revolution's brink.
emerson-poems-1847:
Ralph Waldo Emerson published Poems in 1847, his collected verse of that early period of work. The volume holds Concord Hymn and The Rhodora, the verse counterpart to the famed essays in prose. Emerson's poems favor thought over music, yet several entered the marrow of American memory for good.

Concord Hymn, sung at the battle monument in 1837, gave us the shot heard round the world. The Rhodora finds God and beauty self-sufficing in a wild flower blooming alone in the woods. Hamatreya broods on earth owning men who thought they owned her fields and farms in Massachusetts. Brahma and Days compress his philosophy into quatrains still quoted in schools and speeches across America today. The verse shows the sage in a second, starker dress than the flowing essays.
eminent-victorians-pg2447:
Lytton Strachey announced a new kind of biography in Eminent Victorians and then wrote four lives to prove it. His preface rejects the two fat volumes of funeral praise and promises instead a searchlight lowered into obscure corners. The subjects are Cardinal Manning, Florence Nightingale, Thomas Arnold of Rugby, and General Gordon. The preface sorts them as an ecclesiastic, a woman of action, an educational authority, and a man of adventure.

Strachey retells each career with irony, compression, and a novelist's eye for the telling detail. Victorian saints come out complicated, ambitious, and sometimes absurd. Published at the end of the First World War, the book changed English biography by making detachment and style into weapons. Almost every modern life-writer works in its shadow.
europmc-pmc10005347:
Dakanalis and a large team review the clinical evidence on emotional eating in a 2023 paper. Emotional eating means eating in response to feelings rather than hunger. Clinicians see it as a risk factor for gaining weight back after loss, and for harm to both body and mind.

The review gathers what studies show about links with excess weight, depression, anxiety, and daily food choices. It weighs how strong each link is and where the proof is thin. The paper helps readers sort solid findings from claims that still need better tests.
europmc-pmc10465647:
Rowson and colleagues measured head motion in football hits in 2012 to build a concussion risk curve. Concussion is a brain injury from a blow that shakes the brain. The team fixed motion sensors inside the helmets of 335 players. The gear logged each hit through games and drills.

In all, the logs held 300,977 mild hits and 57 hits that caused concussion. Rowson reports that a mild hit spun the head at 1,230 units of rotational acceleration on average. Concussion hits averaged 5,022 units, four times as hard. At 6,383 units with a matching spin speed, the risk of concussion hit 50%. The curve gives helmet makers and leagues a firm target for safer gear.
europmc-pmc10474147:
Park and co-authors traced the history of cell death research in 2023. Death was once seen as a plain end for worn-out cells, with swelling as a sure side effect. Decades of work have shown that many deaths run on gene programs. Those programs clear cells that are surplus or too damaged to keep.

Some forms are calm, such as apoptosis, the tidy self-dismantling of a cell. Others stir swelling, such as pyroptosis and necroptosis. Park lists fresh forms found in recent years, from ferroptosis to cuproptosis and erebosis. Each has its own switches and triggers. The review ties each form to health and disease, and to drug ideas that may follow.
europmc-pmc10960047:
Katsoulakis and a large team survey digital twins in health care in this 2024 review. A digital twin is a computer copy of a real thing that updates as the real thing changes. In health, such twins could model a patient, a ward, or a whole care system. Growth in big data and AI has sped this work, yet the health field is still at an early stage.

The review catalogues current uses across care management, treatment, prevention, and daily health upkeep. It examines shared research centres and notes their limits. Industry, government, and military groups all run twin projects, the authors find. The paper closes by mapping fresh research openings. The authors call for a joint global effort among all parties to turn the concept into routine care.
europmc-pmc1188247:
Dondorp and colleagues tackled a hidden problem in severe malaria in 2005. In falciparum malaria, infected red cells stick inside small vessels of vital organs. Blood counts miss those hidden parasites entirely. Yet their total load drives how sick a patient becomes.

A protein the parasite releases, called PfHRP2, offered a new measure. The team measured it in blood from 337 adults in Thailand. A model then turned protein levels into total parasite load estimates. Dondorp gives doctors a way to gauge hidden burden and judge risk. It appeared in PLoS Medicine in 2005.
europmc-pmc1193547:
Lindequist, Niedermeyer, and Jülich reviewed healing compounds in mushrooms in 2005. Mushrooms have a long record in Asian medicine. Western interest grew only in recent decades. Many species hold active compounds worth study.

Compounds covered can fight germs, viruses, and tumors in lab work. Others calm swelling, lower blood sugar, or guard the liver. Some affect the brain and immune system as well. Lindequist also touches on how such compounds get produced. The review maps a wide field for drug hunters and growers alike. Mushroom output and compound production get brief coverage too.
europmc-pmc1810547:
Solovyev and co-authors reported in 2006 how their Softberry software performed in a blind test of gene finding. The EGASP workshop asked programs to reproduce expert annotation of the human genome. Their pipeline targeted three features: genes, pseudogenes, and promoters, the start signals before genes.

The Fgenesh++ pipeline found 91 percent of coding DNA letters with 90 percent specificity on 44 test regions covering about 30 million letters. Their pseudogene finder caught 90 percent of hand-marked pseudogenes, which are dead gene copies, and found some new ones. The promoter program located 80 percent of one promoter class with one false hit per 2,000 letters. For the harder class without that signal, it found half, with one false hit per 650 letters.
europmc-pmc1904447:
Rosa, Vieta and co-authors validated in 2007 a short test of daily functioning for people with bipolar disorder. Many patients struggle at work, in relationships, and in self-care even when mood symptoms remit. Most existing tools give one global score instead of showing which life domains fail.

Their test, named FAST, has 24 items across six areas: autonomy, work, thinking, finances, relationships, and leisure. They gave it to 101 patients in a Barcelona bipolar program and 61 healthy controls. Internal consistency came out very high in the results reported. The study also checked agreement with other measures. It tested whether scores separate patients in an acute episode from those in remission. Factor structure and the stability of repeat scores were also examined. The aim was a brief, domain-level tool for clinic and research.
europmc-pmc2072847:
Apelberg and colleagues studied in 2007 whether two fluorinated chemicals in newborn cord blood relate to birth size. Animal studies had shown developmental harm from PFOS and PFOA. The team analysed cord serum from 293 single births in Baltimore, Maryland. Cord blood reflects exposure in the womb. Mothers' details and babies' measurements came from medical charts.

After adjusting for other factors, both chemicals linked to lower birth weight and smaller head size. Each rise in PFOS corresponded to about 69 grams lower weight, and each rise in PFOA to about 104 grams lower, though the intervals included zero. A body proportion measure, the ponderal index, fell significantly for both. Neither chemical linked to newborn length or pregnancy duration. The authors urge replication in other populations.
europmc-pmc2124647:
Frederick C. Herrick asked in 1907 why portal pressure rises in portal cirrhosis of the liver, and he answered with flow experiments. His summary is direct. In the cirrhotic liver, blood from the artery and blood from the portal vein mix far more freely than normal. Dilated capillaries pass arterial pressure straight into the portal vessels.

Other supposed causes fall away. The artery also carries a larger share of flow, compared with the portal stream, than it does in a healthy liver. From a portal inflow, return runs only through the hepatic vein, a fact he ties to valve-like arrangements in the arterial network. Each pressure also drives the other, more strongly in cirrhosis. Readers get a mechanical account of a clinical problem, tested by plumbing rather than by guesswork.
europmc-pmc2125147:
Simon Flexner, Paul F. Clark, and Harold L. Amoss of the Rockefeller Institute mapped the pathology of epidemic poliomyelitis in 1914. The virus, they show, is nerve-loving in the broadest sense. By inoculation tests it can be found living, and probably multiplying, in the nerve ganglia outside the cord and brain.

All the ganglia carry lesions like those of the cord. The intervertebral ganglia suffer worst, the Gasserian ganglia next, and the abdominal sympathetic ganglia least. The disease is therefore general across the nervous system, though its fame rests on the motor injury. The virus itself is hardy: it survives glycerin for over two years and weak phenol for over one, though months of freezing kill it. Phenol, they warn, is unsafe for weakening it into a vaccine.
europmc-pmc2125547:
Montrose T. Burrows and Clarence A. Neymann fed pure amino-acids to embryonic chicken cells in culture in 1917, opening a series on cell metabolism in vitro. All ten alpha-amino-acids tried inhibited the cells' growth and finally killed the cultures. A short burst of activity precedes the inhibition; then the cells round off and begin to dissolve, as the plates show against the spindle-shaped controls.

The amino-acid toxicity is a matter of concentration and exposure time, as with any cell poison. The finding reaches beyond the dish: it likely explains why animals die when hydrolyzed protein mixtures are injected too fast. Slow injection of large amino-acid amounts leaves kidney and gut functions largely undisturbed. Readers get digestion's smallest building blocks caught poisoning the cells they were assumed merely to nourish.
europmc-pmc2125947:
I. J. Kligler tested how well aniline, some of its chemical kin, and the triphenylmethane dyes hold back bacteria, publishing alone in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1918. He compared the compounds across growth media of differing richness and acidity, looking for the features of a molecule that give an antiseptic its power.

Kligler found the medium itself steers the result: richer protein content lowered the dye dose needed, and acidity shifted the action, likely by changing the bacterial cell. The killing power rested on the benzene ring at each compound's core, on the added chemical groups, and on how many of them there were. Ethyl groups boosted power more than methyl groups, though methyl green broke the pattern and lost almost all effect. His closing conclusions stay cautious, framed as tentative rules for judging such antiseptics.
europmc-pmc2128147:
Elizabeth Pauline Wolf opened a series on inflammation by testing which chemicals draw white blood cells toward them. Her paper appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1921. She used Wright's method, slightly changed, counting exactly how many leucocytes leave a blood clot and stick to surfaces holding the test substance. That count graded each substance's pull.

The calcium ion proved the only inorganic ion with a positive pull of its own. It attracted cells strongly at all strengths and in nearly all combinations. The citrate pairing was the exception, since citrate's negative pull canceled calcium's and left a neutral result. Sodium and magnesium ions were themselves neutral. Their salts pulled or repelled only as their partner ion dictated. All sodium phosphates attracted strongly, and they could lend their pull to mixtures with neutral or repelling partners.
europmc-pmc2128247:
Wade H. Brown and Louise Pearce described the scrotal lesions of primary syphilis in rabbits and the course the reaction runs. This paper is part two of the second in their series, in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1920. It rests on scrotal inoculations with Treponema pallidum in a large series of rabbits, followed closely from the first swelling onward.

The reaction generally appeared within seven to fourteen days, though timing varied considerably. Early signs were watery swelling and congestion with new vessel growth, or a gathering of fixed tissue cells. The reaction might stay in one small bounded area or spread widely. As infection advanced, cell gathering and growth dominated, with shedding, tissue death, and ulceration on top. The course moved in waves: active advance, quiet or retreat, then renewed activity. In all this the scrotum mirrored the testicle's known reaction.
europmc-pmc2128347:
G. O. Broun examined whether exercise works the bone marrow harder, in the third paper of his blood destruction series. It appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1923, from the Rockefeller Institute. Earlier papers had shown that exercise destroys blood. This one follows the young red cells that signal fresh production in the marrow.

After exercise, animals kept sedentary before showed a clear rise in young red cells. Shifts in hemoglobin, cell ratios, and red counts agreed with the author's earlier proof of increased blood destruction. Replacing the destroyed blood by transfusion prevented the young-cell reaction entirely. Animals made overfull of blood and then exercised showed no rise while the excess lasted. Exercise, Broun stresses, must be a key factor in keeping blood-forming tissue fit. A quiet body lets its marrow idle; work keeps it producing.
europmc-pmc2128447:
Carl A. L. Binger measured lung volumes in patients with chronic heart disease, using a method that works even on patients short of breath. His paper appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1923. Several patients were measured repeatedly, in both the failing state and the recovered, compensated state, and all values were compared with normal subjects.

In heart disease the vital capacity forms a smaller share of the total lung volume than in healthy people. The mid-capacity and the leftover air form larger shares instead. As a patient slips from the compensated state into failure, these shifts grow more pronounced, and absolute volumes move with the clinical state as well. Lung volume thus becomes a measurable shadow of the heart's condition. Binger's three-way comparison, shares, size-matched absolutes, and one patient's own course, gives clinicians a breathing measure of cardiac failure.
europmc-pmc2131247:
Fred Stewart opened his 1927 series on local treatment of pneumococcal meningitis with experiments in rabbits, at The Rockefeller Institute. He placed Type I pneumococci into the cisternal space and followed the disease that resulted. The aim was to learn how the infection behaves in the membranes around the brain before trying to cure it.

With highly virulent germs, rabbits did not hold the infection in the meninges. Blood poisoning set in early, and death came from that rather than from the meningitis, with little cell reaction in the membranes. Prior immunization partly checked the blood infection and slowed the membrane disease. Serum placed in the spinal space clumped the germs and sped their uptake by white cells, yet treatment after infection only lengthened life a little in most cases.
europmc-pmc2140447:
Harper Zoller and Mansfield Clark studied the volatile fatty acids made by dysentery bacteria in a 1921 paper. These germs ferment their food and give off formic, acetic, and other acids that escape as gas-forming products. The pair grew Shiga and non-Shiga strains with and without sugar, and with air present or pumped out, comparing the acid output.

In air with glucose present, all the organisms agreed closely in total acid and in the formic-to-acetic ratio. On peptone alone in air, they made propionic acid instead of formic, while the medium turned more alkaline. Without air, formic acid returned, with some butyric acid too, in both strain groups. The huge output of formic acid, they suggest, may share in the digestive upsets of dysentery.
europmc-pmc2220047:
Hämäläinen and co-workers screened 36 plant flavonoids in 2007 for anti-inflammatory effects in macrophages. These immune cells, when triggered by bacterial products, make large amounts of nitric oxide via an enzyme called iNOS. Blocking that output is a marker of anti-inflammatory action. The team exposed macrophages to a bacterial stimulus and measured nitric oxide, iNOS levels and two transcription factors that switch iNOS on.

Eight compounds blocked iNOS and nitric oxide production in a dose-dependent way. They included flavone, genistein, quercetin and naringenin. All eight inhibited activation of NF-kappaB, one switch for iNOS. Four of them, genistein, kaempferol, quercetin and daidzein, also blocked the second switch, STAT-1. The others inhibited only NF-kappaB. The split mechanisms partly explain how dietary flavonoids calm inflammation.
europmc-pmc2243147:
van Vliet, Heijenbrok-Kal, Hunink, Kuipers and Siersema pooled studies in 2008 comparing three scans for staging oesophageal cancer. Staging tells whether cancer has spread, guiding curative or palliative choices. The methods were endoscopic ultrasound, computed tomography and FDG-PET, a metabolic scan. The team searched PubMed for studies before January 2006 reporting full test accuracy data for lymph node and distant spread, then pooled sensitivity and specificity statistically.

For regional lymph nodes, endoscopic ultrasound was the most sensitive method at 0.80, while CT and PET were more specific, so they proved better at ruling spread in when a result came back positive. This pooled analysis covered the published staging studies. For distant metastases, PET beat CT clearly on sensitivity, at 0.71 against 0.52, and it was also the more specific of the two. The authors suggest each test plays a distinctive role in staging.
europmc-pmc2361347:
Weisberg and co-authors reviewed AMN107, later named nilotinib, a new drug for leukaemia. The target diseases, chronic myelogenous leukaemia and one form of acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, are driven by a faulty gene called BCR-ABL. The standard drug imatinib blocks that gene's protein, but many advanced patients relapse when the gene mutates.

AMN107 was designed to grip the protein's binding pocket more tightly than imatinib. It proved stronger against the normal protein, working at doses under 30 nanomolar, and it stayed active against 32 of 33 imatinib-resistant mutants tested. In lab and animal studies it attacked both normal and resistant cells. Early patient trials then produced blood and chromosome responses in people who had failed imatinib or never responded to it.
europmc-pmc2430947:
Eisenmann reviewed a continuous risk score for metabolic syndrome in children in 2008. Metabolic syndrome is a cluster of problems: belly fat, high blood pressure, high blood sugar and fats, and low protective cholesterol. With childhood obesity rising, the syndrome now appears in youth, but no agreed definition exists for them.

Estimates put the condition in about 2% to 10% of young people, depending on the cut-offs used. Because yes-or-no labels miss borderline children and rates are low, researchers built a continuous score instead. The score adds up each child's graded risk factors into one composite index. Eisenmann explains how such scores are derived from the underlying measurements and standardised against reference groups. He argues the score tracks risk more sensitively in population studies, and suits tracking change over time better than a fixed diagnosis.
europmc-pmc2528947:
Wirth and colleagues reconstructed the deep history of the tuberculosis bacteria in this 2008 study. This group, the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex, is among the most successful human pathogens, yet when and where it arose was disputed. The team used repeating DNA sequences as genetic markers across many strains from humans and animals.

Their tree split into two branches: one holding only human tuberculosis lineages, and one mixing animal and human strains, itself likely descended from a human lineage. That pattern supports an original human host rather than a jump from cattle. Dating the tree put the group's age near 40,000 years, matching the modern human expansion out of Africa. Most lineages then swelled recently, in step with the human population explosion of the last two centuries.
europmc-pmc2667647:
Gibson and co-authors found in 2009 that the antibody-making cell mix of some very old people collapses into a narrow set of clones. B cells produce antibodies, and variety in their ranks is what lets the body meet new germs. The team read B-cell patterns in blood from people aged 86 to 94, and compared them with adults under 55.

A share of the elders showed a dramatic loss of variety. Reading the DNA showed the cause: a few B-cell families had multiplied hugely, crowding out the rest. The loss tracked health closely. People with narrowed ranks were more often frail, and the pattern linked with shorter survival and low vitamin B12 levels as well. A blood test of this kind, the authors say, could flag immune frailty and general frailty together.
europmc-pmc2684747:
Hahne and co-authors released in 2009 flowCore, a software package for handling flow cytometry data at modern scale. Flow cytometry reads single cells as they stream past lasers, a workhorse method in immunology and drug trials. Automation had swollen experiments to thousands of samples, but analysis tools still assumed small, hand-run studies.

Built for the R language inside the Bioconductor project, flowCore gives researchers shared data structures that hold whole cohorts at once. The same steps can then run across every sample in a study, instead of one file at a time. That shared frame lets statisticians, programmers, and clinicians build on each other's work rather than start over. Several later packages already stand on it. The authors argue that common plumbing, unglamorous as it sounds, is what lets a field model rich trial data properly.
europmc-pmc2744247:
Howard and co-authors studied in 2009 azole resistance in Aspergillus fumigatus. This mold causes severe lung and invasive disease in people with weak immunity. They also tracked how resistance evolves during treatment failure. Azoles are the only licensed oral drug class for this disease, so cross-resistance would remove that option. Resistance usually comes from changes in the drug target gene, cyp51A.

Screening a large referral laboratory collection gathered from 1992 to 2007, they found resistant isolates linked to patients whose treatment had failed. Resistant strains carried cyp51A mutations at known hotspots and often resisted several azoles at once. Typing showed distinct strains rather than one outbreak clone, which suggests resistance emerges within patients under drug pressure.
europmc-pmc2753847:
Nielsen and Lund presented NN-align in 2009. The neural network method predicts which peptides bind MHC class II molecules. Those molecules show fragments from outside the cell to helper T cells. Predicting binding helps explain host-pathogen interactions and guides vaccine work. Class II binding is harder than class I because peptides vary more in length and binding core position.

NN-align finds the binding core and the binding affinity at the same time, and corrects bias from redundant cores in training data. Adding information about residues flanking the core significantly improved accuracy. On a large benchmark of six data sets covering fourteen human class II variants, it outperformed other state-of-the-art methods and was released as a public web service.
europmc-pmc2760147:
Selmecki, Dulmage, Cowen, Anderson, and Berman tracked in 2009 how extra chromosomes evolve during drug resistance in Candida albicans, a common human fungal pathogen. Resistance to fluconazole, the most used drug for it, is often linked to aneuploidy, an abnormal chromosome count. Its dynamics over time were unclear. They ran a controlled lab evolution study with and without the drug.

No extra chromosomes appeared in drug-free populations. In every drug-treated population, an extra chromosome arm appeared soon after exposure. It raised fitness in the drug and became fixed over time. Further gains coincided with the highest resistance levels. Some carriers were fitter even without the drug, which helps explain why resistance persists in patients.
europmc-pmc2763347:
Urban and co-authors showed in 2009 that neutrophil extracellular traps carry calprotectin. The traps are web-like structures neutrophils release to catch microbes. Calprotectin is their main antifungal weapon against Candida albicans. The traps were known to ensnare and kill microbes, but their full protein makeup and killing mechanism were unclear. The team mapped trap proteins with proteomics and high-resolution electron microscopy.

They identified twenty-four trap-associated proteins, largely modified nucleosomes plus a strict selection of others, several of them from the cell's interior. Calprotectin, a two-protein complex, proved to be the major antifungal part: traps lacking it lost all antifungal activity in the dish. In three mouse infection models, calprotectin was crucial for clearing the fungus, confirming its role in living hosts. Careful counting of the trap contents made that case hard to dispute.
europmc-pmc2770847:
Fredholm and co-authors asked in 2009 why breast cancer in young women carries a worse outlook despite intensive treatment. Breast cancer is uncommon under forty yet still the most frequent cancer in that group. Using a registry cohort of over twenty-two thousand women diagnosed from 1992 to 2005, they compared survival across age bands and stages.

Five-year relative survival was lowest in women aged twenty to thirty-four. Their excess death risk, nearly triple that of women in their fifties and sixties, appeared only in stages I and II. It peaked in tiny tumors of one centimeter or less, where it rose almost sevenfold. The youngest women generally got more aggressive treatment than older patients. After adjusting for stage, tumor traits, and treatment, age under thirty-five stayed an independent risk factor for death.
europmc-pmc2788247:
Joppa and Pfaff showed in 2009 that the world's protected areas sit in biased locations, high and far from the land conversion they are meant to stop. About an eighth of Earth's land is protected, most of it during the twentieth century. They tested the networks of one hundred forty-seven nations for bias in elevation, slope, distance to roads and cities, and farm suitability.

The significant majority of national networks leaned toward higher elevations and steeper slopes. They also sat farther from roads and cities than chance would give. Within countries, the most strictly protected areas were the most biased of all. Protection, in short, clusters where conversion pressure is weakest, even if every reserve worked perfectly. Siting rules applied country by country, and carbon payments that reward avoided deforestation, could redirect protection toward threatened land.
europmc-pmc2829047:
Wooley, Godzik, and Friedberg wrote a primer in 2010 on metagenomics, the study of whole microbial communities through their DNA without growing them in a lab. Cheaper, faster sequencing now lets researchers sample microbes straight from soil, sea, or gut. A sample can hold over ten thousand species, and its sequence data arrive noisy and in fragments.

The primer walks through each computing step, from sampling and piecing fragments together to spotting genes and guessing their jobs. It notes which software tools exist for each step and how well they serve. Sample studies close the piece, showing finds the approach has already produced. The authors stress that sorting signal from millions of mixed sequences remains the field's core challenge.
europmc-pmc2872647:
Heinrich and co-authors showed in 2010 that support cells from the brain's cortex can be converted into working nerve cells of chosen types. The support cells, called astroglia, share a birthplace with neurons but normally never fire signals. Forcing single master genes for early brain development into cultured astroglia had turned some into neurons before, yet the kinds made were poorly controlled.

By picking the master gene to match a target, the team steered cells toward either excitatory neurons, which pass signals on, or inhibitory ones, which damp signals down. The converted cells formed synapses, the contact points neurons use to talk, and fired in the patterns of their chosen kind. Stable conversion of local support cells hints at a repair route that uses the brain's own spare cells.
europmc-pmc2901947:
Meyer and the IberoAmerican Cryptococcal Study Group typed in 2003 three hundred forty isolates of Cryptococcus neoformans. The yeast causes life-threatening lung and brain infection. The isolates came from nine Latin American countries and Spain. Two DNA fingerprint methods sorted the isolates into the eight known molecular types, building the region's first baseline map of this pathogen.

One type, VNI, accounted for over two thirds of all isolates, matching its global dominance in human disease. The remaining types appeared in smaller shares, including four types belonging to the sibling species variety that carries different surface markers. A few hybrid isolates showed a gene pattern never reported before. Regional typing lets future outbreaks be matched against this baseline to trace sources.
europmc-pmc2916847:
Saccone and a vast consortium meta-analyzed in 2010 the chromosome 15 region that genetics had tied to smoking, lung cancer, and lung disease. The region holds the genes for nicotine receptor parts, and one variant had been linked to how much people smoke. With extensive genotyping across many cohorts, the team asked whether one signal or several independent ones drive the associations.

They resolved multiple independent loci in the region, each affecting smoking quantity on its own. The famous receptor variant was joined by at least two statistically separate signals tagged by other markers. Patterns for lung cancer and chronic lung disease lined up with the smoking effects, consistent with genes acting through cigarette consumption rather than directly on the lung. Untangling the loci matters for judging whether the region also harms the lung outright.
europmc-pmc3053347:
Bouyer and colleagues showed in 2011 that a gene silencing system controls the moment a plant seedling must stop living like an embryo. The system, called PRC2 in short, places a repressive mark on DNA packaging proteins and keeps whole gene sets off. By working around its role in seed food tissue, the team grew plants fully lacking one of its core parts.

Without the system, the repressive mark vanished across the genome, yet the basic body plan still formed normally. Seeds instead stayed dormant too long and germinated poorly, as if stuck in the embryo phase. Seedlings that did sprout soon stalled and grew tumor like lumps instead of proper shoots. Only some target genes switched on, and master control genes were among them. The authors call the system a robust guard of life phase changes in plants.
europmc-pmc3056147:
Nuytemans, Theuns, Cruts, and Van Broeckhoven updated in 2010 the catalog of inherited changes behind familial Parkinson disease. Five genes are firmly tied to the disease, and more than five hundred distinct changes in them had been reported. Most are simple letter changes in the gene code, while roughly a fifth are missing or extra copies of whole sections.

The team organized every published change into a free online database so doctors and researchers can check a new finding against all known ones. They warn that some change types are likely undercounted, because few studies checked all five genes for both kinds of change. The same genes also turn up in related brain conditions with similar protein clumps. The authors urge full screening of patients, followed by lab work to prove which changes truly cause disease.
europmc-pmc3084247:
Hörnberg and colleagues reported in 2011 that shortened versions of the androgen receptor in prostate cancer that has spread to bone mark the most stubborn and deadly cases. Normal prostate growth is driven by male hormones acting on this receptor. Cancers that keep growing after hormone blocking treatment sometimes make receptor variants that lack the hormone sensing end and stay permanently on.

The team measured these variants in bone metastases, the most important spread site, comparing cancers never treated with hormone blockade against resistant ones. Variant levels were clearly higher in resistant tumors, and one variant appeared only there. Tumors with the highest variant levels, about a third of resistant cases, showed disturbed cell cycle control and the patients died sooner. The authors propose testing whether such patients gain more from drugs that attack the receptor's working end directly.
europmc-pmc3164647:
Rebecca Corrigan and colleagues discovered a new signalling molecule in a major hospital pathogen in a 2011 paper in PLoS Pathogens. The bacterium's wall polymer is vital for growth, yet rare mutants survive without it. Sequencing those survivors revealed changes in one gene, pointing to a cyclic molecule the gene's enzyme destroys.

The team showed the molecule is genuinely made in this species by a dedicated builder enzyme, and that blocking its destruction sends its levels soaring. High levels thickened the wall's cross-linking, perhaps compensating for the missing polymer, and shrank cell size noticeably. The messenger thus helps control cell size and helps the bacterium endure wall stress, a fresh angle on a pathogen famous for drug resistance.
europmc-pmc3179347:
Ulrike Mödder and colleagues measured a bone-formation brake in the blood of nearly seven hundred adults in a 2011 paper in the Journal of Bone and Mineral Research. The protein, made by bone-embedded cells, blocks a key growth signal. Nothing was known about how its blood level varies with age, sex, or bone mass in people, so the team sampled a whole community age range.

Men carried clearly higher levels than women. Levels climbed steeply across life, more than doubling in women and rising several-fold in men. At any given amount of bone, older people carried more of the brake than younger people. The age rise may help explain why bone formation falters late in life, and the study gives the reference patterns needed before the protein can serve as a clinical marker.
europmc-pmc3179447:
Shlomo Rotshenker reviewed how injured peripheral nerves clear the way for their own regrowth in a 2011 paper in the Journal of Neuroinflammation. When a nerve is cut or crushed, the segment beyond the injury must be remodelled before new fibres can grow through it to their targets. That remodelling, a process named over a century ago, is run largely by the innate immune system.

Support cells, fibroblasts, scavenger immune cells, and vessel cells act in concert, stripping away growth-blocking insulation debris and switching on nourishing properties. Speed matters: a response that starts fast and ends cleanly prepares a growth-friendly path, while a sluggish or lingering one leaves poor recovery. The review frames nerve repair as an immune performance that succeeds or fails on timing and coordination.
europmc-pmc3186747:
Philipp Schuetz, Werner Albrich, and Beat Mueller reviewed a blood marker that guides antibiotic use in a 2011 paper in BMC Medicine. Standard infection tests are slow or vague, so antibiotics are often started blindly and run too long, breeding resistance. The marker, procalcitonin, rises far more specifically in bacterial infection, and trials had tested algorithms built on it.

For chest infections, post-surgery infections, and severe sepsis in intensive care, randomised trials showed marker-guided decisions safely cut antibiotic starts and durations. For other infections, early observational results look promising but trials are still needed. The review weighs the marker's reliability inside validated algorithms and charts where evidence is firm, where it is thin, and what studies come next.
europmc-pmc3206047:
Tuomas Kilpeläinen, Ruth Loos, and a very large group of collaborators pooled data from many studies in this 2011 meta-analysis of the FTO gene and obesity. FTO variants raise the risk of obesity, and the team asked whether being physically active softens that genetic effect. Their combined sample covered more than two hundred thousand adults and about nineteen thousand children.

Across the adult studies, physical activity substantially weakened the link between the FTO risk variant and obesity. In other words, the gene's effect was not fixed: active adults carrying the risk version fared noticeably better than inactive carriers. The work supports a gene-and-lifestyle view of obesity, where daily activity can partly offset an inherited tendency to gain weight.
europmc-pmc3257747:
Krista Crider, Lynn Bailey, and Robert Berry reviewed folic acid food fortification in this 2011 article in Nutrients. Taking folic acid around conception is known to cut a woman's risk of a baby with a neural tube defect, a serious malformation of the brain or spine. Many countries therefore require folic acid to be added to staple foods, and defect rates have fallen worldwide.

At the same time, worries persist about unintended consequences of higher population-wide intake. The authors trace the history of fortification programs, measure their effects, and air the concerns. Their message is that uncertainty makes continued monitoring essential, so programs can prove their benefits with accurate measures and respond as questions arise. The review ends by looking at where fortification policy may go next.
europmc-pmc3291347:
Wang and co-authors reviewed what was known about bats and the SARS virus in 2006. SARS had swept through many countries in 2002 and 2003 before being stopped, and its cause was a coronavirus new to science. The authors gathered evidence on where the virus came from and whether similar viruses still circulate in animals.

Work in animal markets found viruses nearly identical to the human one, and traders showed higher rates of past infection than other people. Most striking, researchers had found a varied set of SARS like coronaviruses living in horseshoe bats. The review argues that bats are a likely source pool, so fresh outbreaks from animal viruses remain a real risk.
europmc-pmc3298247:
Kilpatrick and colleagues built a better way to judge which mosquitoes spread West Nile virus to people, in a 2005 study. Control programs in the northeastern United States lacked clear targets because the roles of different species were poorly known. Their measure combined how many mosquitoes of each kind are present, how often they carry the virus, how well they pass it on, and how often they bite people.

Two Culex species that officials had largely overlooked came out on top. Together they may account for most human infections in the region, up to roughly four fifths. Focusing control on those two species could cut human cases while sparing wetland wildlife, and the authors say the same scoring method can be adapted to other places and diseases.
europmc-pmc3323247:
Morris and a large group of colleagues reviewed the changing pattern of a lung infection that preys on weakened immune systems, in a 2004 article. The infection, called PCP, is caused by a fungus like organism and was once the illness that first revealed AIDS in most patients. Strong HIV drug combinations had cut its numbers sharply by the time of the review.

Even so, PCP remained the most common serious opportunistic illness in people with HIV, especially where treatment is unavailable. The authors describe who stays at risk in rich and poor countries alike, including transplant patients and others on immune suppressing drugs. A growing worry is whether the organism is mutating toward resistance against the standard preventive antibiotic. The article introduces a series on that question and urges standardized data collection.
europmc-pmc3340347:
Monasta and colleagues produced the first global estimates of the burden of middle ear disease, in a 2012 review. Middle ear infections, called otitis media, are a leading reason children see doctors and receive antibiotics. Their complications are a major cause of preventable hearing loss, especially in poorer countries, yet no worldwide tally existed within the global burden of disease project.

Drawing on more than one hundred studies, the team estimated hundreds of millions of acute ear infections each year. Over half of them strike children under five. The chronic draining form adds tens of millions of cases, and roughly twenty one thousand people die yearly from complications such as meningitis. Hearing loss tied to the disease affects tens of millions. The authors urge ear focused action inside child health programs.
europmc-pmc3399847:
Krakauer and Krakauer proposed a new body measure in 2012, arguing that the standard body mass index misses the risk carried in body shape. Waist size hints at belly fat, but it rises and falls with body mass index itself, so its extra signal is hard to isolate. Their index, called ABSI, adjusts waist size for height and weight directly.

Built from a national survey of more than fourteen thousand American adults followed for about five years, the index barely correlated with height, weight, or body mass index. Death rates climbed steadily as it rose above average, and the link survived adjustment for smoking, diabetes, blood pressure, and cholesterol. Shape, they conclude, forecasts early death in its own right.
europmc-pmc3510747:
Errol Ozdalga, Ark Ozdalga, and Neera Ahuja review what smartphones were doing in medicine in 2012, when the devices were still new to wards and classrooms. They survey published uses relevant to physicians and students, setting surgical applications aside.

Sixty studies turn up uses spanning patient monitoring, point-of-care information, medical education, and communication. Dedicated apps, such as iWander for people with dementia, hint at future roles. Yet very few high-quality evaluations exist, so enthusiasm outruns evidence. The review maps where smartphones already help, where they might, and what proof is still missing before hospitals lean on them in routine care.
europmc-pmc3565747:
Matjaž Perc and colleagues reviewed group games on structured populations in the Journal of the Royal Society Interface in 2013. Their subject is how cooperation evolves when players sit on lattices or networks instead of mixing freely, using tools borrowed from statistical physics and evolutionary game theory. The model case is the public goods game, where each player may chip into a shared pot that benefits the whole group.

Compared with well-mixed groups, structure changes the fate of cooperation: neighbors who meet again and again can cluster, shield each other, and let sharing survive where free mixing kills it. The review also covers models where the network itself changes as play proceeds. Findings from bacteria colonies to human societies are drawn into one account. Readers gain a tour of when place and partners decide whether cooperation wins.
europmc-pmc3580047:
Graham Campbell and colleagues examined nerve cell power failure in multiple sclerosis in Annals of Neurology in 2011. Brain shrinkage tracks how this disease advances, and mitochondria, the cell's energy makers, are part of the story. Mitochondria carry their own small DNA, and damage to it can cripple the energy chain. The group hunted for such damage inside single neurons from people who had died with the secondary progressive form.

Ninety-eight brain blocks from thirteen cases supplied the tissue. Neurons unable to run one key energy step were far more common than in aged comparison brains, clustered deep in the cortex and nearby white matter. Single-cell tests showed most of these failing neurons carried heavy loads of deleted mitochondrial DNA, enough to explain the defect. The deletions spread across gray matter, and the authors propose that inflammation drives them, slowly starving neurons of energy.
europmc-pmc3586947:
Lin Song, Peter Langfelder, and Steve Horvath compared ways of measuring gene co-expression in BMC Bioinformatics in 2012. Networks of genes that rise and fall together help biologists find functional modules. Labs must choose a similarity measure first: plain correlation, hardier versions of it, or mutual information, a flexible measure borrowed from information theory that fans claimed catches links correlation misses. Which choice actually serves network building was unsettled.

Across eight real data sets and simulations, mutual information tracked correlation closely, because most gene pairs relate in straight or steadily rising ways. The two disagreed only in rare cases. For carving networks into modules, a robust correlation reshaped by a topological overlap step beat both mutual information and a newer maximal information score. The win was judged by how well modules matched known gene functions. A formula linking the two measures lets users estimate one from the other.
europmc-pmc3597547:
Gary Mirams and colleagues introduced a simulation library called Chaste in PLoS Computational Biology in 2013. Chaste, short for Cancer, Heart and Soft Tissue Environment, is open-source software for modeling living systems on a computer. It grew from two founding problems: the electrical waves that drive the heartbeat, and the growth of tumors. Both demand heavy mathematics that each new project otherwise rebuilds from scratch.

Shared modules handle meshes, the grids laid over virtual tissue, and solvers for the equations of cell and tissue behavior. Worked examples in the paper run on an ordinary desktop. Studies enabled so far include defibrillation shocks computed on realistic human heart shapes and cell-level models showing how stem cells behave in the gut lining, where colorectal cancers start. Industrial habits, especially test-driven development, guard the code's quality as new fields adopt it.
europmc-pmc3622347:
K. N. Venugopala, V. Rashmi, and B. Odhav reviewed natural coumarins as drug leads in BioMed Research International in 2013. Coumarins are a large family of plant chemicals built from fused benzene and pyrone rings; over thirteen hundred are known from plants, bacteria, and fungi, richest in fruits and seeds. People eat them daily in vegetables, fruit, coffee, tea, and wine, and herbal medicine has used them for centuries. Their safety record and low cost make them attractive starting points for drug design.

Reported activities fan out widely: calming inflammation, thinning blood, fighting bacteria, fungi, and viruses, slowing cancers, lowering blood pressure and blood sugar, easing seizures, and protecting nerve cells. The review explains the chemistry and naming of the family, then walks its pharmacology, toxicology, and body handling compound by compound. Separation and checking methods close the survey. The authors urge deeper evaluation of this dietary chemistry set.
europmc-pmc3632747:
Katrin Kierdorf and Marco Prinz reviewed what keeps the brain's immune cells quiet, and what wakes them, in Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience in 2013. Microglia survey the healthy brain in a resting state, but resting is an actively held position, vital in a tissue where neurons tolerate almost no disturbance. Small slips in the holding system can unravel into severe brain disease, so the controls matter.

Internal governors include the transcription factors Runx1, Irf8, and Pu.1, which set microglial identity. External brakes arrive as signals from healthy neurons and surroundings, through receptors such as CD200's partner, the fractalkine receptor CX3CR1, and TREM2. The review gathers recent work on each factor and on how they interact across development and adult life. The picture is of layered restraint: many small checks, each cheap to lose and costly to lose together.
europmc-pmc3634447:
Chiara Corrado and colleagues reviewed exosomes as cell-to-cell couriers in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences in 2013. Cells communicate by secreted signals and direct contact, and, as evidence had lately shown, by exosomes. These are nano-sized membrane sacs brewed inside compartments called multivesicular bodies. They are released when those compartments fuse with the cell surface. Their cargo is rich and varied, enzymes, signaling proteins, nucleic acids, and other active compounds.

A receiving cell can be reprogrammed by the delivery: new receptors installed, signals triggered, even genetic material transferred and used. The review follows exosomes through healthy physiology and through disease, where tumors and infected cells exploit the same postal system. Medical uses get a full hearing, from reading exosomes in blood as diagnostics to loading them as drug carriers. The authors present the vesicles as a genuine organelle-level signaling system, not debris.
europmc-pmc3637647:
Movement may start as a guess, not an order, in a 2013 theory article in Brain Structure and Function by Adams, Shipp and Friston. Motor cortex, the brain area that drives movement, sends signals down to muscles in a pattern much like the backward signals of the seeing cortex. That likeness is odd if the signals were simple commands, and the authors set out to explain it.

On their account, higher brain levels send down forecasts of body sense data, and movement acts to make those forecasts come true. Reflexes then read as ways to cut the gap between forecast and fact. The layered wiring of the motor system matches this scheme closely. The view may also explain why motor cortex lacks the grainy layer found in sense areas.
europmc-pmc3653747:
Mental illness labels built on symptoms alone miss the brain facts, Cuthbert and Insel argue in a 2013 BMC Medicine article. Current manuals sort disorders by the signs a patient shows, which can lump unlike causes under one name and slow new treatments. In 2009 the United States National Institute of Mental Health launched a new research scheme, called RDoC in the text, to sort mental illness by brain and behaviour measures instead.

The article sums up why the scheme was built, where it stands and where it aims to go. Seven sharp contrasts with current manuals are set out, the seven pillars of the title. Hard parts are faced plainly, among them proving the new groupings are real. The long goal is a body of work sorted by brain measures, ready to inform future manuals.
europmc-pmc3694547:
Chen and colleagues review matrix metalloproteinases, a family of zinc-dependent enzymes that cut proteins, as inflammatory regulators of blood vessel growth and remodeling. These enzymes break down the scaffold around cells. They also process signalling molecules. Several family members switch on in vessel walls under inflammatory stimuli.

Once active, they help recruit stem and progenitor cells. They open paths for endothelial and smooth muscle cells to migrate and invade. They also influence vessel cell growth and death. The review gathers this evidence to show how one enzyme family links inflammation to the building and reshaping of vessels, in healthy development and in disease.
europmc-pmc3712247:
Wei Xu, Peixue Ling, and Tianmin Zhang wrote a review in the Journal of Drug Delivery in 2013 on tiny drug carriers called polymeric micelles. Many new drugs do not dissolve well in water, so the body absorbs too little of them when they are swallowed. Micelles are small balls of chain-like molecules that can carry such drugs inside them.

The review explains four ways micelles can raise the share of a drug that reaches the blood. They shield the drug from the harsh gut, release it slowly at the right place, cling to the gut wall so it stays longer, and block pumps that push drugs back out. The authors present micelles as a strong option for hard-to-dissolve drugs given by mouth.
europmc-pmc3713347:
Ming Yang and William Brackenbury wrote a review in Frontiers in Physiology in 2013 on the voltage across the cell surface and its role in cancer. That voltage, set by channels and pumps that move charged atoms in and out of the cell, guides growth and change in many cell types. Cancer cells often show a less negative voltage than healthy cells.

The review covers the main channel types that set this voltage and how they affect cancer cell growth, movement, and change into other cell forms. A less negative voltage may help cancer stem cells stay in place and keep a tumor growing. The authors suggest the voltage could one day serve as a marker for finding tumors and judging outlook, and perhaps as a target to slow spread.
europmc-pmc3742447:
Amitabh Suthar and a large group of co-authors published a systematic review and meta-analysis in PLoS Medicine in 2013 on community-based HIV testing and counselling. Testing inside health centers misses many people at risk, and only about 15 percent of adults in recent surveys across 29 sub-Saharan African countries had test results from the past year. The team gathered the evidence on services offered outside health facilities.

The review gathered studies of these community approaches and compared how they performed on uptake of testing and on reaching people who had never tested before. Reaching people where they live and work matters because late diagnosis drives avoidable illness, death, and onward spread of HIV.
europmc-pmc3744747:
Peter Hillmen and a large group of co-authors reported long-term results in the British Journal of Haematology in 2013 on eculizumab for paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria, or PNH. In PNH, runaway complement activity destroys red blood cells inside vessels, causing fatigue, breathlessness, clots, and kidney damage. Eculizumab is an antibody that blocks the final stage of complement activation.

The study followed 195 patients for up to 66 months. Four deaths occurred, none blamed on the drug, giving a three-year survival estimate of about 98 percent. A marker of blood cell destruction fell by a median of about 87 percent and stayed down. Clot events fell by about 82 percent, kidney scores improved or held steady in about 93 percent of patients at 36 months, and transfusion needs dropped sharply.
europmc-pmc3810747:
Chowdhary and co-authors wrote in Emerging Infectious Diseases in 2013 about a new clonal strain of the yeast Candida auris behind bloodstream infections in Delhi, India. Twelve patients at two hospitals were infected during 2009 to 2011. The species had been named only in 2009, from a Japanese ear infection.

The isolates resisted fluconazole, a front-line antifungal drug, and routine lab machines misread them as the related species Candida haemulonii. DNA typing by two methods, M13 fingerprinting and amplified fragment length polymorphism analysis, showed the Indian isolates formed their own clone, distinct from earlier ones found in South Korea and Japan. The authors warn that because labs seldom name yeasts by reading their DNA, such cases are likely missed far more often than they are caught.
europmc-pmc3820047:
A review of non-celiac gluten sensitivity in Nutrients in 2013 carries Carlo Catassi as first author, with a large group of co-authors. Some people feel ill after eating gluten foods yet test clear of both celiac disease and wheat allergy. The review asks what this newer label means and how it can be told apart.

Symptoms span the gut and the whole body, and they overlap a lot with irritable bowel syndrome, which makes diagnosis hard. No blood or tissue test yet marks the condition, a key gap the review stresses. Other wheat parts, not just gluten, may drive some symptoms. First reports in children have also appeared. The authors call for strict rules so the label is used with care.
europmc-pmc3843747:
Ali Afshar-Oromieh and a team of co-authors compare two scans for prostate cancer in the European Journal of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging, with the record dated 2014. Both scans use PET imaging with a tracer that lights up tumor sites. One tracer rides on choline, the other on a protein found on most prostate cancer cells.

Patients whose cancer signs rose again after treatment got both scans within a short window. The scans were read side by side for spots judged to be cancer, and uptake strength was measured at each spot. The protein-based tracer gave stronger contrast in most cases, the authors report. A sharper scan helps doctors find small returns of disease early, when salvage treatment works best. The study was a look back at past cases, not a fresh trial.
europmc-pmc3922847:
Patrick Royston and Mahesh K. B. Parmar propose a different way to measure treatment benefit in trials where the outcome is time until an event, in BMC Medical Research Methodology in 2013. Such trials usually report a hazard ratio, which quietly assumes that the relative risk between treatment groups stays constant over time. Recent trials show that assumption cannot be trusted.

Their alternative is the restricted mean survival time: the average time lived up to a chosen horizon, read as the area under the survival curve. The paper shows how to design trials and size samples around this measure, using flexible survival curves that allow the treatment effect to grow or fade. Worked examples show the approach stays readable for clinicians while avoiding the constant-risk assumption.
europmc-pmc3938547:
Robert Carroll, Chris Metcalfe, and David Gunnell measure what happens after a hospital visit for self-harm, in PLoS ONE in 2014. Non-fatal self-harm is among the most common reasons for emergency admission, and it is the strongest known risk factor for later suicide. The team searched the international literature for studies following people who presented to services after deliberate self-harm, finding 177 relevant papers.

The pooled risk of suicide was 1.6 percent within twelve months of the hospital episode and 3.9 percent after five years. About one patient in six, 16.3 percent, repeated self-harm without dying within a year. The authors also examined what made estimates differ between studies and how rates shifted over thirty years, giving services benchmark figures for judging their own follow-up care.
europmc-pmc3942647:
Vladimir Riabov and five colleagues review how tumor-associated macrophages help cancers grow new blood and lymph vessels, in Frontiers in Physiology in 2014. A growing tumor needs oxygen and nutrients, and flipping an angiogenic switch gives it a blood supply and a route to spread. Macrophages, immune cells recruited and reprogrammed by the tumor, are a major source of the factors that flip that switch.

The review traces the partnership step by step. Tumor vessels release signals that draw in a special monocyte type, and macrophages sensing low oxygen in tumor cores release VEGFA and other growth factors that pull in vessel cells. In some tumors these macrophages are the main source of MMP9, an enzyme that frees stored VEGFA from tissue. The same machinery builds lymph vessels, opening another escape route.
europmc-pmc3960247:
Camilo Guzmán and four colleagues present ColonyArea in PLoS ONE in 2014. ColonyArea is a free plugin for ImageJ, an image analysis program. Its task is the colony formation assay. That assay is a cancer lab staple. Cells get radiation or a drug dose. The colonies that survive show how well the dose worked. Counting colonies by hand is slow. Counts also vary between labs.

ColonyArea works from photos of whole plates. It splits the image well by well. It cleans and crops each well on its own. Then it measures how much of the well the colonies cover. Stain strength counts too, as a sign of cell density. The authors show these measures track hand counts well. They work across plates with 6 to 24 wells. Labs gain a fast, shared way to score survival assays.
europmc-pmc3964947:
Donna Karolchik and the UCSC team describe the Genome Browser's 2014 state. Their update appeared in Nucleic Acids Research. The browser gives free public access to genome data. As of September 2013, it held about ninety organisms. Human and mouse genomes get the most use. Web tools let users view and compare data tracks. Users can share their own data sets in the same view.

New content leads the update. A sixty-species alignment now maps conservation on the mouse genome. The UCSC Genes tracks for human and mouse were refreshed. New variation sets and ENCODE data sets arrived too. One new tool predicts what uploaded variants do. Gene pages now show the letter variants people carry. Data hubs grew as well. They display data hosted on remote servers. The paper is the citation of record for the resource.
europmc-pmc3969247:
Jim McCambridge, John Witton, and Diana R. Elbourne review the Hawthorne effect in 2014. Their paper appeared in the Journal of Clinical Epidemiology. The label names a simple idea. People change behavior when they know they are being studied. The term is used loosely for many such effects. So the team set a broad definition. They gathered studies built on purpose to measure these effects. Extra interventions were kept out, to avoid muddy water.

Nineteen studies qualified for the review. Eight were randomized trials. Five were quasi-experiments, and six were observational. Nearly all sat in health research. Most found some sign of an effect. Being questioned or watched did shift the behavior under study. But designs and settings varied a lot. Bias risks were tangled as well. No firm size for the effect emerged. The authors call for sharper concepts in this field.
europmc-pmc4053947:
Kaie Lokk and ten colleagues profile DNA methylation across seventeen human tissues, in Genome Biology in 2014. Methylation patterns help set each tissue's identity. A shared reference map of those patterns was missing.

Samples from four autopsied donors were run on an array covering close to half a million methylation sites. Only a small share of sites stayed methylated in every tissue; those sat mostly inside gene bodies. A larger share stayed unmethylated everywhere, clustered near gene starts. Between those poles lay many tissue-specific regions, and their unmethylated forms sat beside genes doing that tissue's known work. Promoter methylation and gene activity moved in opposite directions, as expected. The team offers the atlas as a baseline for spotting where differentiation goes wrong in disease.
europmc-pmc4230647:
Carlijn R. Hooijmans, Miranda W. Langendam, and four co-authors built a bias checklist for animal studies in BMC Medical Research Methodology in 2014. Reviews that pool animal experiments help judge whether a treatment deserves human trials. Yet reviewers lacked a shared tool for spotting bias in those experiments, unlike the Cochrane tool used for clinical trials.

Their tool, from the SYRCLE centre, adapts the Cochrane version with ten entries tuned to animal work. It covers selection, performance, detection, attrition, and reporting bias, plus other threats, and each entry comes with signalling questions to guide the judge. Half the entries mirror the clinical tool; the rest adjust for how animal studies are designed and reported. The authors argue wide adoption would make animal evidence easier to trust and compare.
europmc-pmc4321847:
Abolghassem Emamverdian, Yulong Ding, Farzad Mokhberdoran, and Yinfeng Xie review how heavy metals poison plants and how plants fight back. Their review appeared in The Scientific World Journal in 2015. Metals build up in soils from industry and farming, enter plant cells, and stir up reactive oxygen that damages DNA, proteins, and membranes.

Damage shows as yellowed shoots, stunted growth, and burnt fat layers in cells. Plants answer by binding metals with special peptides and proteins, locking the complexes away in storage vacuoles, and pumping ions out of sensitive sites. The review organizes these defenses and the antioxidant systems behind them. It is aimed at readers working on cleanup planting and safer crops for polluted land.
europmc-pmc4404347:
Damaris Bausch-Fluck and a team of co-authors built an atlas of proteins on cell surfaces, in PLoS ONE in 2015. Surface proteins are prime drug targets and cell markers because drugs can reach them from outside. Yet the surface set of most cell types was only sparsely known. Using a capture method that fishes out sugar-tagged surface proteins, the team profiled 41 human and 31 mouse cell types by mass spectrometry, at high resolution.

The combined atlas holds 1,492 human and 1,296 mouse surface proteins with direct evidence, including 136 G-protein coupled receptors and 75 kinase receptors, both rich drug target classes. Comparing cell types showed their surface differences are mainly in amounts, not in which proteins appear. The atlas is published as an interactive database with a downloadable matrix, for drug target checks and cell classification.
europmc-pmc4419847:
Charles Dudley Mills gave a personal account in Frontiers in Immunology in 2015 of how macrophages came to be classed as M1 and M2 types. Macrophages are immune cells that can attack invaders or help repair tissue. Mills traces the experiments and disputes that led him and others to name these two opposed programs.

M1 responses kill microbes and can drive T cells toward attack, while M2 responses repair tissue and favor a different T cell path. Mills argues this flipped an old view: innate immunity, led by macrophages, directs adaptive immunity rather than simply obeying it. The same split, he notes, helps explain outcomes in infection, cancer, autoimmunity, and artery disease.
europmc-pmc4426947:
Anna Shvartsur and Benjamin Bonavida reviewed a cell surface protein called Trop2 in Genes and Cancer in 2015. Trop2, made from the Tacstd2 gene, passes calcium signals inside cells and is present in many normal tissues. In many cancers, though, cells make far too much of it, and high levels track with worse outcomes for patients.

Excess Trop2 helps cancer cells renew themselves, grow, invade nearby tissue, and survive, and it has also been tied to drug resistance. The review covers the signals Trop2 sends, the gene switches that control it, and the partners proposed to bind it. It then surveys attacks on Trop2, from antibodies and drug-linked antibodies to small blockers and tiny particles, which slowed tumors in lab and mouse studies.
europmc-pmc4448847:
David Colquhoun, writing alone in Royal Society Open Science in 2014, showed how often the standard p-value rule misleads researchers. Many scientists treat a result with p below 0.05 as a discovery. Colquhoun calculates the false discovery rate behind that habit: the share of claimed discoveries that are in fact nothing, given how often the tested effect is truly absent.

Tree diagrams, borrowed from medical screening logic, and repeated computer runs of common tests make the point concrete. At the usual threshold, a claim is wrong at least roughly a third of the time, and in weak, underpowered experiments wrong most of the time. Effect sizes also come out inflated. To keep false claims low, he urges a far stricter threshold, or a three-sigma rule, and dropping the word significant. A script lets readers rerun the numbers for their own field.
europmc-pmc4550147:
Christina A. Nelson and six co-authors recount how many Lyme disease cases the United States really sees, in Emerging Infectious Diseases in 2015. Lyme disease spreads by tick bite and can cause rash, arthritis, nerve pain, and heart rhythm faults. Health departments counted about 36,000 reported cases in 2013, but underreporting was suspected to hide most of the burden.

Extending from a large medical claims database, the team estimated about 329,000 cases a year for 2005 to 2010. Cases cluster in the Northeast and upper Midwest. The paper explains why routine reporting misses so much, through gaps in lab and provider reporting and uneven local practice. The estimate resets expectations for prevention and doctor awareness in high-risk regions.
europmc-pmc4557747:
Sanjay G. Manohar leads an eight-author team showing that reward breaks a classic law of movement, in Current Biology in 2015. The speed-accuracy trade-off says faster actions are sloppier, across nearly all tasks and species. Yet reward seemed to make people both faster and more precise, a paradox the team set out to explain.

Their model adds a missing term: reducing the brain's own noise costs effort. If reward pays that cost, control can rise, buying speed and accuracy together. In an eye-movement distraction task, higher rewards did produce faster, smaller-error responses, and the costly-control model fit best. The paper extends the same logic to thinking tasks and to Parkinson's disease, where the reward messenger dopamine runs low.
europmc-pmc4598847:
Viram S. Vyas, together with colleagues, released a 2015 chemistry study on layered frameworks that use sunlight to make hydrogen from water. Covalent organic frameworks are porous crystals built from light organic parts, and their properties can be tuned by design. The team varied the nitrogen content of the building blocks. The work appeared in Nature Communications.

They built a family of stable azine-linked frameworks from hydrazine and aldehyde building blocks. As nitrogen content in the frameworks rose, light-driven hydrogen production improved step by step. The change came from the altered electronic and shape features passed from the building blocks into the crystals. The study shows that careful molecular design can dial up the performance of these light-active materials.
europmc-pmc4629747:
Working with colleagues, Dan L. Crouse published a 2015 study linking long-term air pollution exposure to death rates in Canada. Most earlier studies tracked only one pollutant at a time. Their cohort held about 2.5 million Canadians followed for sixteen years. Yearly tax records let them track where each person lived. The work appeared in Environmental Health Perspectives.

Fine particles, ozone, and nitrogen dioxide each tied to higher death rates, even after adjusting for the others. Looking at particles alone understated the harm of the full air mix. Moving house during follow-up changed the estimates only slightly. Adding the three pollutants' effects together gave about a 7.5 percent higher non-accidental death risk across the exposure range studied. The findings support regulating the pollutant mix, not single gases in isolation.
europmc-pmc4654747:
David Castel and colleagues brought out a 2015 study splitting diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma, a deadly childhood brain tumour, into two mutation-defined subgroups. No real treatment progress had been made in fifty years. Ninety-one young patients received systematic biopsies, with gene testing and detailed scans. The work appeared in Acta Neuropathologica.

Nearly every tumour carried a K27M change in a histone gene or lost the related chemical mark. Tumours with the change in the H3.3 gene responded worse to radiotherapy, relapsed earlier, and spread more often. Tumours with the H3.1 version showed a different cell character and more vessel-growth signals. The split gives doctors a prognostic tool and suggests the two groups may need different treatment strategies in future trials.
europmc-pmc4700047:
Sheena McCormack, David T. Dunn, Monica Desai, and a large trial team reported the PROUD study of HIV prevention in The Lancet in 2016. Daily pills combining two anti-HIV drugs had already cut infection risk in blinded trials. The open question was real-world behavior: would men who knew they were protected take more risks and cancel the benefit? PROUD enrolled HIV-negative men at English sexual health clinics who reported recent condomless sex.

Half started the pills at once; half waited a year. Infections diverged fast: three in the immediate group against twenty in the deferred group, an eighty-six percent reduction. The gap was so clear that the waiting group was offered the pills early. Rates of other sexually transmitted infections did not differ between groups, undercutting the risk-compensation worry. No serious drug reactions appeared. The pilot proved PrEP works in routine clinics, not just in trials.
europmc-pmc4737147:
Kim A. Lennox and Mark A. Behlke tested how a long non-coding RNA's address inside the cell affects attempts to silence it, in Nucleic Acids Research in 2016. Thousands of these RNAs are known, most with unknown jobs, and the standard probe is to destroy them and watch what changes. Two destruction toolkits exist, antisense oligonucleotides and RNA interference, working in different cell compartments. The pair compared both against seven non-coding RNAs chosen for known locations.

Nuclear residents fell best to antisense treatment, cytoplasmic ones to RNA interference, and those living in both compartments answered to either. Mixing both toolkits improved knockdown, especially for the dual residents. The moral is to match the weapon to the address, or bring both. For labs now interrogating non-coding RNAs, the study prevents a common false negative: a gene that looks functionless only because the silencer never reached it.
europmc-pmc4740747:
Dubin and twelve co-workers follow melanoma patients who start the drug ipilimumab. The drug frees the immune system to attack the tumour. In some patients it also sparks colitis, a bad gut inflammation. The team test stool samples taken before treatment starts. They ask if gut germs can warn who is at risk.

Patients rich in Bacteroidetes germs before treatment prove safe from colitis. Those whose germs lack genes for two tasks face more risk. One task moves polyamines. The other builds B vitamins. Such tests, done before the first dose, could one day guide steps to shield the gut.
europmc-pmc4866047:
Bernard Pereira and a large team profiled mutations in 2,433 primary breast cancers in Nature Communications in 2016. They sequenced 173 genes and joined the results to copy number data, gene activity reads, and long-term patient outcomes. Breast cancer varies hugely between and within tumors, and that spread drives treatment trouble.

The scan found 40 driver genes whose faults push cancer growth. Mutation patterns tied to copy number profiles, tumor traits, and survival in telling ways, such as PIK3CA faults and worse outcome in some groups. Mutant cell shares also gauged how mixed each tumor was. The refined map helps sort breast cancers into truer groups for care.
europmc-pmc4952147:
Jens Hoeppner and ten co-authors set out the ESOPEC trial, a head to head test of two treatment plans for esophageal cancer. Their trial protocol appeared in BMC Cancer in 2016. Both plans combine treatment around surgery for localized adenocarcinoma of the esophagus. One uses chemoradiation before surgery, the CROSS protocol. The other uses chemotherapy before and after surgery, the FLOT protocol. Each had beaten surgery alone, but they had never been compared directly.

ESOPEC is a multicenter randomized phase III trial run across German centers. Patients are assigned to one of the two arms, then followed for survival. The authors predict the chemotherapy arm will win on overall survival. They expect equal local control but better control of tiny distant spread. The paper lays out eligibility, treatment doses, and outcome measures so the trial can be judged and repeated.
europmc-pmc4968547:
Camilla Urbaniak and five co-authors compare bacteria in breast tissue from women with and without breast cancer. Their study appeared in Applied and Environmental Microbiology in 2016. The team had earlier shown breast tissue is not sterile. Here they sequenced bacterial DNA in tissue from cancer patients and healthy controls. They asked whether the local microbiome differs with disease, since tissue bacteria might sway cancer risk.

Cancer patients carried higher shares of Bacillus, Enterobacteriaceae, and Staphylococcus in tissue beside the tumor. Tissue from the tumor itself looked much like the adjacent tissue. Two species common in patients, Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus epidermidis, caused double strand DNA breaks in lab cells. That damage can scar chromosomes. The authors stress the open question: do the bacteria help cause the disease, or does the disease favor the bacteria?
europmc-pmc4999647:
Emma Deas leads a team showing how clumped alpha-synuclein protein generates free radicals that kill neurons in Parkinson's disease. Their study appeared in Antioxidants and Redox Signaling.
