Qian, Zhang, and Jiang mine U.S. drug harm reports for the cancer drug selpercatinib. The drug blocks RET changes found in some cancers. Trial data leave gaps on rare harms seen in wide use. The team pulled reports from the FDA adverse event system. Four math methods flagged harms tied to the drug.

They found 464 reports covering 1,007 harms. Three new harms stood out: trouble swallowing, fluid around the heart, and weakness on one body side. Abnormal liver tests were more common in Asian reports, mostly at doses above 160 mg. Allergy reports also ran high in Asian patients and in those under 50 kg. Dose, weight, and sex each shaped the harm pattern.
pmc-11625247:
Mona-Lisa Coutinho, Ricardo Portela e Silva, André Postiga, and Valentina Almeida report, published in 2024, a bronchoscopy that turned into an emergency in a woman of sixty-one. She carried an undiagnosed case of granulomatosis with polyangiitis, a rare disease where inflamed blood vessels attack organs, airways included. During the camera exam of her airways, her voice-box area swelled badly. Her vocal cords barely moved. Air stopped flowing well, her oxygen crashed, and her heart arrested.

The team presents the case as a warning about hidden airway disease. The illness had given no signs beforehand, only unexplained breathing symptoms. A scope that is safe in most patients can trigger disaster in a swollen, stiff airway. The authors urge doctors to keep this disease on the list when breathing trouble has no clear cause. Airway checks before procedures, and a skilled airway team on hand, are their practical lessons.
pmc-11625947:
Farid Haghdadi and colleagues save a snapped front tooth without surgery, in this case report from twenty twenty-four. Horizontal root fractures usually spare the tip segment, which stays alive. Their patient's upper central incisor broke that rule: the apical segment had died, an unusual necrosis that normally invites root-tip surgery.

Age and the tooth's stability argued against the knife. Instead, the team sealed both segments, tip and crown side, with mineral trioxide aggregate, a bioactive dental cement. The conservative route worked across a two-year follow-up, preserving the natural tooth. The authors offer the case as evidence that MTA sealing can substitute for apical surgery in this rare fracture-plus-necrosis combination. It keeps intervention proportionate for a tooth with life left to live.
pmc-11630847:
DeBord and a large team ran tests in twenty twenty-four on shade and capped feed for young beef cows in heat stress. Heat can cut growth, raise thirst, and strain the herd. They split near nine hundred cows into high-fuel capped feed or free rough feed, with or without shade.

Capped cows ate less but gained more per feed unit than free-feed cows. Shade cows also gained more per feed and drank less than no-shade cows. Pant scores were lower with shade and with capped feed both. In gut tests capped feed raised food break-down, and shade kept gut sour lower.
pmc-11636247:
Lina Wang leads a team on COVID outcomes in blood cancer patients. Their study from twenty twenty-four is set in the late phase of the pandemic. Blood cancer folks face high risk from this virus.

Data came from one hospital in Shanxi over one month. The group held just over two hundred inpatients. Life span was the main outcome the team tracked. Stats tests sought traits that raised death risk. Cases spanned leukemia, myeloma, and like blood diseases. Late stage virus still shaped outlook for these folks. Risk traits are listed for care teams.
pmc-11638247:
Felix P Lützenkirchen and colleagues report a two thousand twenty-four study of a protein called neurobeachin at inhibitory brain synapses. These synapses use the signal chemical GABA to calm nerve cell activity. Their strength changes when receptors move into or out of the synapse surface.

The team found neurobeachin sitting at these synapses and binding their anchor protein, gephyrin. Its arrival depended on activity, and it drove receptor removal through a protein kinase A pathway. Neurons missing one copy of the gene failed at this removal unless normal neurobeachin was restored. The work names a player in how inhibitory synapses scale down.
pmc-11640747:
Kamil Candan and colleagues published a 2024 study of a small Anatolian lizard. The species had never had its life history measured. Samples came from Iğdır Province in Türkiye. Bone growth rings revealed each lizard's age. Males and females were compared directly.

Males averaged larger and older than females. Body size rose with age in both sexes. Survival rates also favored males. Females matured into shorter expected adult lives. The growth curves differed clearly by sex. Such baseline data supports future conservation work. It also feeds comparisons across related lizard species.
pmc-11642047:
Wanzhen Chen and six co-authors identify a wheat protein that holds back the making of the waxy coat on leaves. Their study was published in twenty twenty-four. That wax seals the plant surface and guards against dry air and other stresses, so breeders want to know how it is controlled.

Quieting the gene for the protein, called TaCFL1, raised leaf wax by about fifteen in each hundred parts and made the leaf skin less leaky. Two partner switch proteins pushed wax the other way: quieting either cut wax, and quieting both cut it by nearly a third. A third protein was shown to be a core part of the wax-making chain. The results sketch a control circuit that wheat breeders could tune for tougher crops.
pmc-11644347:
Hongying Li and co-authors report nine years of conservation farming trials. The trials sat on the sloped farmland of China's Three Gorges Reservoir area. Soil quality there is in decline. Orchard plots set standard citrus planting against three other ways. Those ways were citrus with white clover, straw mulch, or daylily hedgerows on contour lines. Crop fields set a standard wheat-peanut rotation against hedgerow intercrops and a ryegrass-sesame rotation. The team took soil samples at upper, middle, and lower slope spots.

The green practices raised soil traits at all three slope spots. The effect of the practice beat the effect of slope spot itself. A soil quality index summed up the gains. The authors read the long trial as proof of a clear point. The right planting system, more than terrain work alone, rebuilds soil on sloped farms.
pmc-11645247:
Kai Wang and four co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-four on a joint care for severe sepsis, the body's runaway response to infection. The care pairs hybrid blood filtering with a drug, ulinastatin, drawn from urine protein. One hundred fifty patients form the look back, split by which care they got. Scores of illness depth, two small RNA marks, and inflammation factors are tracked.

After care, all marks fell in both groups. The joint group fell more on each count. Their pain eased sooner, gut enzymes settled faster, and hospital stays ran shorter. The team says the pair lifts short term odds in severe sepsis.
pmc-11650347:
Zhang and six colleagues track a complement protein in kidney cancer tissue and during immunotherapy in twenty twenty-four. The protein, C3a, showed in most tumor samples from over one hundred cases. Bigger tumors and higher stage carried more of it. Blood levels were then watched in thirty advanced patients on immune drugs.

After four cycles, levels fell in patients whose disease shrank or held. Levels rose in those whose disease grew. Patients with falling levels stayed progression free longer. Other traits like age and grade showed no link. The marker may mirror treatment effect to some degree, they conclude.
pmc-11654347:
McDonald Nyalapa and three co-authors study what helps or hinders nurses learning about diabetes in Malawi in this two thousand twenty-four paper. Studies across sub-Saharan Africa report low diabetes knowledge among nurses. Yet little work asks why. These nurses staff tertiary hospitals in the center and south of the country. They both treat patients and teach them how to manage the disease.

The team ran focus group talks with twenty-six nurses from two hospitals. They sorted the answers into themes using a standard qualitative method. The themes cover barriers, such as time and training gaps, and supports, such as motivated peers. Knowing these factors is a first step toward better training. The findings can guide hospital leaders and educators who plan nurse education in low-resource settings.
pmc-11657747:
Otonicar leads a large team presenting a method to profile DNA and RNA in the same single cells, in work from twenty twenty-four. Single cell DNA sequencing decodes cancer variation cell by cell. Existing methods are low throughput or cannot be paired with transcriptome data from the same cell.

Their assay, HIPSD and R seq, profiles low coverage DNA and RNA in thousands of cells in parallel. It builds on a modification of a standard protocol, keeping it simple and accessible. Joint profiles let researchers link a mutation to its expression effect in the very same cell, a key step in understanding tumor evolution.
pmc-11658247:
Yingting Jiang and six colleagues published a survey study in two thousand twenty-four on phone addiction among nursing students in China. Heavy phone use harms students' health and training. Social anxiety and loneliness were suspected drivers, with sleep possibly in the mix.

Four hundred thirty-seven students in a career resilience programme were surveyed in late two thousand twenty-three. Students sorted into low, middle, and high social anxiety profiles. Loneliness carried a clear share of the path from social anxiety to phone addiction. Sleep length did not significantly change those links. The authors say anxious students differ in kind, not just degree. They suggest loneliness-focused support to curb compulsive phone use.
pmc-11658747:
Albert Anastasio and a large team published a surgical outcomes study in twenty twenty-four on Haglund syndrome, the painful heel bump that frays the Achilles tendon. Operations split and clean the tendon, remove the bump, and reattach it. Some surgeons also transfer a toe tendon to add strength, but whether that adds complications was unstudied.

The review covered three hundred ninety patients operated between twenty fifteen and twenty twenty-three, fifty-two of whom had the tendon transfer. Over about ten months of follow-up, persistent pain affected ten percent and wound breakdown eight percent, with infections rare. Complication rates did not differ notably between the groups. The transfer appears safe to add when surgeons judge it useful.
pmc-11662447:
Agnieszka K. Banaś and co-authors watched seedlings wake up their photosynthesis in 2024, weighing red light against blue. Seeds germinating underground build pale precursor chloroplasts that cannot photosynthesize. Once light hits, these etioplasts transform into working chloroplasts during de-etiolation. The team illuminated etiolated Arabidopsis seedlings with monochromatic red or blue light at equal photon levels for twenty-four hours.

Both colors made working young chloroplasts, hence the title's joke that the process is almost color blind. But the steps did not proceed evenly: single stages of the transformation were tuned by one color or the other. Blue light sped the disassembly of the internal storage form, the prolamellar body, according to ultrastructure study. Fluorescence readings tracked the assembly of photosynthetic complexes. The fine print matters for controlled-setting farming, where light recipes are a design choice.
pmc-11665147:
Laureen Raelly-Muze, Rafael Vega, and Leslie Hutchins report a rare case combining penetrating brain injury with electrical injury. Their illustrative case from twenty twenty-four involves a man hurt by a welding spike. The spike entered through the orbit above the eyeball. Current passed through his body and exited at his toe.

Scans showed air inside the skull and a bleeding track through deep brain tissue. Remarkably, the eye itself escaped injury. The spike path also missed major organs and key brain structures. That lucky path let the patient recover with minimal deficits. The authors draw lessons for teams facing several injury types at once.
pmc-11666947:
Huo and co-authors give a step-by-step protocol for coating glass with a clear, conductive tin oxide film. The film is doped with tantalum to carry charge well. It shows low surface roughness, low resistance, and high carrier counts, making it a strong stand-in for standard clear conductors.

The method uses hollow cathode gas flow sputtering to lay the film down. Steps cover preparing and cleaning fresh float glass before coating. Later steps detail how to measure the film's light and electric traits. Full use notes point back to the team's earlier paper on this film.
pmc-11667147:
Nehal Shata and three co-authors tell of a young boy whose stiff neck was an early sign of skull base sink. Their case study appeared in twenty twenty-four. The boy had slow growth, lost motor gains, and stiff low limbs, with a right head tilt that grew worse. Gene tests found a variant that did not full tell his state.

Scans at last showed the skull base bone pushed in, with cord squeeze and swell at the top joint. A skull hole cut eased the press, and team care ran the rest. The boy got back motor skills and rose to the mid weight line. Late finds came from the plague years.
pmc-11669747:
Kristy Lau and a team of co-authors compared drugs for COVID-19 in the Omicron wave. Their review, from twenty twenty-four, set antiviral drugs against lab made antibodies. Antivirals were thought to still work on this variant. The antibody drugs had lost much of their power to block the virus. The team pooled trials that set each drug class against no drug or other drugs.

They searched many databases in mid twenty twenty-two, with updates later that year. They rated bias risk with standard tools. Readers who treat this disease get a ranked view of which drugs helped most in acute care. The work guides drug choice when a variant dulls one class.
pmc-11672547:
Ylenia Mazzocato and ten co-authors reported in twenty twenty-four a way to design ring-shaped peptide drugs with the help of machine learning. Such design tools tend to need large sets of test data, which are hard to build in the lab. The team worked with a small data set on blockers of a protease linked to tumors.

They chained three tools in turn: a random forest model, a method that reads how pairs of sites in a chain change together, and a sim-based search. The ring peptides shaped this way were then made and tested in glassware. They blocked the target more strongly than the best past blockers. A crystal view of one peptide bound to the protease showed a wide contact face and a stiff ring shape. The work shows that smart pairings of methods can stretch small data sets a long way.
pmc-11673347:
Leonardo and four co-authors graded AI-made research ideas in twenty twenty-four for a teen spine curve ill. Doctors face tight clinic days, so fast idea tools could aid the field. Four chat models got the same prompt and gave ten to fourteen ideas each.

Each idea was checked in a paper bank and scored for how new it was. Mean newness scores sat close across the four models. A few ideas from three models had no past papers at all. One model gave no fully new idea in its set. AI can spark fresh study paths, they find.
pmc-11673747:
Shrivastava and coauthors test a fat-like compound in mice bred to mimic Alzheimer disease. In that illness, brain swelling fails to clear and nerve cells die. The compound helps the brain calm swelling and heal. The team gave it to the mice for a long time and then checked their brains.

Treated mice had less of the sticky protein that builds up in the illness. Fewer nerve cells died, and fewer showed signs of cell death. Brain immune cells also shifted to a calmer state. The results back more tests of calm-down compounds for this brain illness.
pmc-11674347:
Raluca Vlad and colleagues reported a fabricated illness case in 2024. A caregiver invented symptoms for a child. Tests were also altered by the caregiver. Doctors now call it factitious disorder. It counts as serious child abuse.

The child had prolonged reported fever. Hospital checks never confirmed the symptoms. Stories and test results never matched. Frequent visits raised early alarm signs. The mother stopped returning after attitudes changed. Staff distance replaced earlier empathy then. The authors stress careful communication skills. Unexplained stories deserve gentle questioning. Prolonged fever was the central puzzle.
pmc-11677147:
Dhinu Jayaseelan and co-authors map how the ways of past studies of pain in tendon ills range, to bare the lack of one way. Their scope review is from two thousand twenty-four.

Tendon pain curbs use of the limb. Proofs hint the pain paths work awry, in arm and leg ills alike, but in unlike ways. Five stores and gray works were searched to a spring cut. Near three thousand works came up; a small set was kept. They split near even twixt arm and leg themes. The team reads the tests, tools, and groups each used. The aim is to show the spread, so a shared way can be built.
pmc-11677347:
Shan Gao and colleagues studied a traditional Chinese herb for depression in two thousand twenty-four. The herb is a daylily species used historically for mood. Its active ingredients and mechanisms stayed unclear. Chemical profiling found dozens of compounds in the plant. Stressed mice modeled human depression for testing. Computer network analysis predicted likely targets.

Gene activity studies in brain tissue added more clues. Protein tests then verified key pathway changes. Several plant compounds emerged as likely active ones. Dozens of depression-related targets were implicated. The herb seems to act through many routes at once. Such multi-target action fits traditional medicine patterns. Modern checks now support further study.
pmc-11678147:
Rebecca Rossetti, Vittoria Strinati, and Alessandra Caputi lead a team piloting a ketogenic diet for women whose polycystic ovary syndrome has thinned their periods. Their study appeared in two thousand twenty-four. The syndrome is a common hormone disorder of fertile-age women. Diet is one of its few non-drug levers.

Eighteen women ate ketogenic for forty-five days, then reintroduced carbohydrates gradually. Twelve finished the six-month course. Periods became more frequent, and ovarian volume shrank. Key hormones shifted in favorable directions. Those gains did not depend on how much weight was lost. Testosterone and excess hair, by contrast, improved only with weight loss. Even normal-weight women benefited on cycles. The authors read this as evidence for a direct metabolic effect. A controlled trial is the clear next step.
pmc-11679247:
Anna Voziki, Olga Deda, Melania Kachrimanidou, and Victor Gault wrote this review paper, published in 2024. It gathers mouse studies on fecal transplants as a treatment for a stubborn gut infection, judging success by the chemistry of the gut rather than symptoms alone.

The infection, caused by the Clostridioides difficile bacterium, often returns after antibiotics. The reviewers screened 460 papers and kept five that profiled metabolism in treated mice. In all five, transplanting gut microbes from healthy donors restored the gut community and shifted its chemistry. Levels of short fatty acids and processed bile acids rose, and both are known to hold the germ back. The transplant beat antibiotics and probiotics at rebuilding a healthy gut. Results still varied with donor and method, so the authors urge careful reporting over rushed standardization.
pmc-11679847:
Laia Miralles-Llumà and ten colleagues published a clinical trial report in two thousand twenty-four on weight loss in people with severe sleep apnea and obesity. Sleep apnea stops breathing briefly during sleep and is closely tied to body weight. The trial tested whether a year-long intensive programme changed body makeup, not just weight.

Thirty-four patients were split into a programme group and a standard care group. The programme used a low-calorie Mediterranean diet with close support. After a year, the programme group had lost over eight percent of body weight, while the control group lost almost none. Scans showed the loss came mostly from body fat, including deep belly fat. Breathing during sleep also improved, along with blood measures linked to heart risk.
pmc-11680147:
Di Bao and colleagues studied a pig diarrhoea virus in gut cells in 2024. The virus causes enteritis in piglets. It can kill young pigs quickly. Mitochondrial DNA can fuel inflammation responses. Inflammasome involvement was unclear before this work. Cultured pig intestinal cells were infected.

Infection damaged mitochondria inside the cells. Mitochondrial DNA escaped as a result. That escape switched on the NLRP3 inflammasome. A second signal boosted a key inflammatory protein. Reactive oxygen from mitochondria helped that signal. The protein interleukin was then secreted. The authors claim a first full mechanism. Pig virus inflammation is now clearer.
pmc-11682847:
Emanuella Brito and seven colleagues published an evaluation in two thousand twenty-four of ChatGPT as a patient education source on breast reduction surgery. The operation is common and relieves real burdens, but patients arrive with many questions. Whether chatbot answers are trustworthy was the concern.

Fifteen typical patient questions were put to ChatGPT. Five board-certified plastic surgeons graded each answer as appropriate, too thin, or inaccurate. Of seventy-five gradings, ninety-two percent called the answers accurate. Six responses worried the experts: four lacked needed detail and two were wrong. The authors say the tool is broadly reliable for basic education but not flawless. They advise professional oversight of AI patient materials.
pmc-11687947:
Guo leads a large team improving variant calling in exome data, in work from twenty twenty-four. Whole exome sequencing reads the protein coding parts of the genome for cancer diagnosis and association studies. Results depend on mapping reads to a reference genome.

A single standard reference may fit some populations poorly, causing missed or false variants. Using a population matched reference can sharpen mapping and calls, the team argues. Their work tests that gain directly. Better calls matter most for patients whose ancestry differs from the reference builders, a known source of genomic medicine inequality.
pmc-11698547:
Senapati, Kattamuri, and Deoker describe a carotid body tumor found by chance in a 75-year-old woman. These rare tumors grow near the split of the carotid artery and often cause no symptoms. Scans, not biopsy, are used for diagnosis, since biopsy can cause bleeding.

She came to the emergency room with nausea, vomiting, and a severe headache. Her blood pressure was very high and her heart rhythm was irregular. Neck imaging showed a stable mass of 38 by 53 by 15 millimeters. Given her age and other illness, radiation was planned instead of surgery.
pmc-11710047:
Pedro JDMR Pinho and five colleagues use a national Brazilian aging study, published in 2025, to test how memory complaints match real memory loss. Many older people say their memory is poor. Such complaints may warn of later dementia, but they do not always match test results. The link is poorly studied in mixed populations like Brazil's.

The team used data from over nine thousand Brazilians older than fifty. People rated their own memory, and all took a word list test. Among those with complaints and full data, about a quarter had true memory loss on testing. More schooling, more trouble with daily tasks, and more signs of depression went with true loss. Higher household income went with less loss. The authors note that most people with complaints test normal, so complaints alone should not drive care.
pmc-11710347:
Monika McAtarsney-Kovacs, Shahina Pardhan, Raju Sapkota, and Ian van der Linde test a memory skill, published in 2025, that may flag early decline. The skill is binding: holding together the traits of an item, such as its shape, color, and place, for a few seconds. Earlier work hints that binding fails early in mild cognitive impairment. If so, quick binding tests might catch decline sooner.

Three groups took computer tests: young adults, healthy older adults, and older adults with mild impairment. Tasks paired items with places, names with places, and colors with places or words. Healthy older adults scored below the young on some tasks. The impaired group scored below healthy older adults on three more. Binding scores also matched standard thinking tests well. The authors argue that the weakest tasks may serve as early markers of decline.
pmc-11710647:
Sarah Marzi studies how gene risk for Alzheimer disease shows up in the brain's immune cells, in work published in 2025. Those cells, called microglia, help defend the brain. Genetic risk for the disease clusters in the switch regions that control microglia genes. Marzi asked how risk burden changes those switches, using both a mouse model and human brain tissue.

Human microglia grown from stem cells were placed into mice bred for the disease. The cells carried different forms of APOE, the strongest common risk gene. As risk rose from the safer form to the riskiest, the cells turned up inflammation signals. Helpful cell states linked to defense were turned down. In donated human brains, microglia showed wide changes in the same switch regions. Some changes could be tied straight to gene variants. The work links inherited risk to the cell changes seen in disease.
pmc-11727347:
Gregor and a team including Mirolo and Brandes reported in twenty twenty-four the first known case of a cat leukemia virus gut ill in a wild Eurasian lynx in Germany. The lynx is at grave risk in that land, so new germs matter for its care. The young female fell ill with gut signs and died in a week.

Her gut showed bleed and tissue death, with worn lymph parts and thin bone marrow. Tests proved the virus, a first for this lynx kind. Two gut germs had also moved in as second ills. The case warns that pet cat germs can reach rare wild cats.
pmc-11727747:
Merve Berika Kadioglu, Mirac Sezer, and Bulent Elbasan compared hands-on manual therapy with a home exercise program for young adults who grind their teeth. Bruxism can bring jaw pain, poor sleep, and stress. Writing in twenty twenty-four, they ran a small randomized trial over eight weeks. Patients filled in standard scales for sleep quality, stress, jaw function, and quality of life before and after treatment. The team counted sore trigger points and rated pain during activity, at night, and at rest.

Both treatments improved nearly every measure, including sleep, stress, and quality of life. The home group alone failed to improve rest pain. Manual therapy did better than home exercise on sleep quality, jaw function scores, and trigger point counts, while pain, stress, and quality of life gains were similar between groups. The authors present both options as useful care.
pmc-11788847:
Gary Hodge and colleagues gathered the views of patients, families, and professionals on what blocks good palliative and end of life care in South-West England. Care at the end of life is widely reported as patchy in Britain, and the region adds rural and coastal distance, an older population, and little prior research. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team ran focus groups across the region with health and care staff, people nearing the end of life, family caregivers, and the bereaved. The groups were asked what gets in the way of good care.

Five barriers stood out: too few specialist staff, especially out of hours; poor communication and coordination between services. The rest were unequal access, lingering strain from the pandemic, and reluctance to talk about death and dying. The authors say hearing all three viewpoints together shows where fixes must aim.
pmc-11805047:
Ankita Kondhalkar and four co-authors measure iodine in the food of mothers in India's Vidarbha region. Their study, from twenty twenty-four, sits inside a newborn screening program. A baby in the womb depends wholly on the mother for iodine. Too little iodine can stunt brain and body growth for life.

Salt, water, and staple foods from mothers in rural and town areas are tested. The work runs with several departments at a medical college in Wardha. Even mild lack in the mother can dull a child's school path later. The data can show where diets fall short. Local fixes, like salt checks, can then be aimed well.
pmc-11867947:
Wenpeng Cao and colleagues test a plant flavonoid against stroke damage in mice, tracing its target, in this study from twenty twenty-four. The compound is cynaroside, known for calming inflammation and oxidation. The injury modeled is the harm done when blood flow returns to a blocked brain artery.

Treated mice woke from the model stroke with milder deficits, smaller dead zones, and less swelling, and their brain immune cells stayed calmer. Computer docking and binding tests pointed to one target: Alox15, an enzyme the compound appears to grip directly. With it suppressed, the inflammatory alarm chain quieted and the markers of ferroptosis, an iron-driven cell death, fell. Toxin signals such as interleukin-1 beta dropped in both mouse brains and dish-grown immune cells. The authors propose cynaroside as a stroke candidate working through this enzyme.
pmc-12698547:
Hou studies how vocational college students accept an online English course in twenty twenty-five. The course is a MOOC, a large open online class. The study uses a model that links ease of use, usefulness, attitude, and intent to use. A survey of four hundred thirty-four students provides the data.

Ease of use raised how useful students found the course. Usefulness in turn improved attitude and raised intent to use the course. Stronger intent linked to a better learning experience for students. In a surprise result, a positive attitude alone linked to a worse experience. The author argues that course content and teaching design shape the experience more than first impressions. The findings offer tips for building MOOCs for vocational learners.
pmc-12699847:
Valji, Valji, and Lam survey fairness, diversity, and inclusion in Canadian anesthesiology training in twenty twenty-five. No prior study had charted who trains in the field there or what programs do on inclusion. An anonymous online survey went to residents in all seventeen programs. One hundred twenty-three replies came from fifteen programs.

Near parity held for gender among respondents. Some ethnic groups fell well below their share of the national population. Most residents called inclusion important, yet over half knew of no program efforts. Two in five had no training on the topic at all. The authors urge programs to name, run, and track their efforts. Barriers to action need study next, they add.
pmc-12700947:
Yan Hu and Chuntao Liu studied regulatory T cell control in asthma in 2025. Asthma harms many people worldwide. Regulatory T cells balance immune reactions. Boosting them may calm airway swelling. Gene network analysis flagged sugar-tagging steps. Fat burning pathways also stood out strongly.

One protein tag ran the pathway. Animal tests backed how it works in living animals. More of these cells slowed asthma growth. Both major asthma types were blocked. Sugar tagging of proteins was carried out. Fatty acid burning supplied the route. Aimed treatments gain a base in theory. Boosting these cells is the plan.
pmc-12708747:
Zhentao Lao and colleagues used single-cell data in 2025 to find a cell group that marks where head and neck cancer spreads in lymph nodes. This cancer type is common and often deadly because it reaches the nodes, yet the spread mechanism is poorly understood. Gene activity was read cell by cell to map interactions inside metastatic nodes.

A macrophage group carrying a distinctive marker clustered close to blood vessel lining cells in spread nodes. Vessel density was also higher there, confirmed by tissue staining and spatial imaging. The authors suggest signalling between these macrophages and vessel cells helps build a niche for metastasis, offering leads for prognosis and precise treatment.
pmc-12712847:
Hesti Lina Wiraswati and colleagues test a lab-made compound against a stubborn breast cancer type, in this study from twenty twenty-five. The cancer is luminal B, nearly forty percent of breast cancers, and hard to treat well. The compound, pyrazoline B, had already hurt several cancer cell lines. Here it faced BT-474 cells, a standard model of this subtype.

The compound hit from several sides at once. It froze the cell cycle by cutting a key growth protein, lowered two growth signal receivers, and killed cells through oxidative stress by a route that skips the usual executioner enzymes. Paired with the standard drug paclitaxel, it strengthened the drug's brake on growth and movement. Computer forecasts of how the body would handle it looked better than for paclitaxel. The authors name it a multi-target lead, with animal tests the clear next step.
pmc-12717847:
Green and coauthors ask how elephant seals change their dives when food is rich. Past studies gave mixed views on that link. Sex, sea habitat, and study scale all seemed to shift the result. A core snag is that food gain at sea is hard to gauge as dives unfold.

The team built a large set of dive records from 609 seals over many years. Shifts in body fat gave a proxy for food gain on each trip. They tracked dive time, rest time, and swim speed. Seals changed dives in the same way when food gain rose. Sex and habitat did not change that core pattern.
pmc-12723847:
Fareeda Abo-Rass and Jesse Bump argue that academic publishing quietly polices which truths global health may speak, in this comment from twenty twenty-five. Peer review is meant to guard rigor. For scholars from marginalized and colonized communities, the authors say, it also guards the vocabulary, and with it the reality, that journals will print.

Their case is concrete: an article recommended for publication was then pressed by editors to swap politically accurate terms about Palestinians for state-approved labels. They read this language policing as control over knowledge itself. The cost is an evidence base that edits out occupation, violence, and segregation, the very forces shaping health, and wears the edit as neutrality. The authors demand structural change: protect scholars' right to name their own communities' experience, and treat political conditions as data, not as bias.
pmc-12732647:
Shouxia Xiao, Yuelin Hu, Xin Wang, and Hongsong Yu published a review in twenty twenty-five on epigenetic mechanisms in autoimmune thyroid diseases. The group covers Hashimoto's thyroiditis, which lowers thyroid function, and Graves' disease, which raises it. Genes alone do not explain these diseases; environment matters too.

Epigenetic changes sit between genes and environment, reshaping how genes are read without changing the DNA itself. The review covers DNA methylation, histone modifications, and non-coding RNAs, and how each steers disease course. Because these marks can be measured and sometimes reversed, the authors present them as tools for earlier diagnosis and more personal treatment.
pmc-12738547:
Junrui Liu and others put out a 2025 chemistry study showing a molecular attraction missed before. Alkynes are triple-bonded carbon units used widely. Their sideways pulls were largely unmapped. Two cage-shaped metal mixes provided the test bed. Crystal builds showed a surprise stacking pattern.

Shake signals shifted just as foretold. Computer work showed a real interaction. A data bank search found it in hundreds of crystals. The force is weaker than classic ring stacking, yet it shapes traits. Its shake signature could flag useful builds. Imaging probes might exploit the signal too. A missing piece of how molecules are built is now named.
pmc-12738647:
Bowman compares the mouthpart dentition of seventeen free-living mite species from bird nests, in a study from twenty twenty-five. These astigmatan mites share one commensal community. Explaining their coexistence requires knowing how each one feeds. Bowman decomposed the chewing digit patterns into functional groups.

Two morphotypes emerged: hook-like tearing digits and nibbling digits. The default chewing surface design is described in fine detail, likened to fine grinding grades. Angles of the surface features suggest adaptation to aggregate material. Various species show gripping, bladed, scooping, or scraping specializations. One species is classed a crusher, another a chewer, and some approach saw designs. Miniaturization, Bowman notes, limits how far feeding designs can diverge. The atlas explains how seventeen species partition one small habitat.
pmc-12743847:
Yue Yu and four co-authors test a biologic drug, ustekinumab, in Crohn's disease, with a focus on cases limited to the small intestine, in a study published in twenty twenty-five. Crohn's disease inflames the gut, and disease in the small bowel alone often needs stronger drugs and more surgery. Few studies had checked how well this drug works by disease site.

The team followed patients for a year, using scopes, scans, ultrasound, and lab tests to judge healing. They compared patients whose disease sat in the small bowel with those whose disease reached the large bowel. Outcomes included full remission, healing of the gut lining, and healing through the whole bowel wall. The study gives site-by-site evidence for planning care.
pmc-12745647:
Wenjing Liu, Ning Jiao, and six co-authors tune feed energy for a new green-shell laying hen. Their study, from twenty twenty-five, works with Wenshui hens at peak lay. No feeding standard exists yet for this breed. Six hundred hens, aged thirty-three weeks, split into five groups for a six-week trial.

Each group ate feed with a set energy level, from low to high. Output rose then fell as energy climbed, a curved pattern. The second-highest level gave the best laying output and nutrient use. Blood fats rose steadily with energy, while one mid-level group led on antioxidant strength. The results name a target energy for peak-lay diets of this breed.
pmc-12748547:
Siqing Xiang and colleagues improved ghost imaging under noise in 2025. Ghost imaging builds pictures from light patterns. Compressed sensing cuts the needed measurements. Noise usually degrades the final image. A Bayesian method was proposed here. Sparse coding used a learned dictionary.

A three-level graph structured the estimation. Messages passed between levels during solving. Simulations and bench tests both succeeded. Complex objects imaged accurately despite noise. Sampling stayed very low throughout. Solving ran faster than rival methods. Precision stayed high at the same time. Biomedical imaging is one suggested use.
pmc-12750747:
Mohd Hazim Ahmad Fuad, Ely Zarina Samsudin, Nik Nairan Abdullah, and Ahmad Nazim Aimran set out a study protocol in twenty twenty-five on how hospital staff in Malaysia cope with workplace violence. Violence against health workers is a known hazard that harms mental health and care quality. The protocol centers on psychosocial safety climate, the degree to which a workplace guards mental well-being, and asks how it shapes coping.

The plan runs in two phases. First, a survey of at least four hundred forty workers in public hospitals will gauge safety climate, violence exposure, and coping styles with standard scales. Then, six to twelve workers with recent violence experience, drawn from high-climate wards, will be interviewed in depth. The two strands will be merged to guide climate-based steps that help staff cope and soften the impact of violence.
pmc-12751847:
Shabnam Shahabi Nejad and seven co-authors test whether the blood fluid of obese mice speeds aging in lean mice, in this twenty twenty-five study. Obesity brings long-term swelling in the body and early aging of cells. The team asked if factors carried in blood alone can pass that aging on.

Lean mice got weekly shots of pooled blood fluid from fat or lean donors for four weeks. The team then weighed fat pads and immune organs and read aging marks in fat tissue and blood cells. Genes tied to cell aging and swelling were also measured. The design tests blood as a carrier of obesity's aging effect.
pmc-12753747:
Ziwen Lv and four co-authors built a chart to predict sudden breathing failure in lung cancer patients, in a study from twenty twenty-five. Breathing failure is common after surgery and in cancer care, yet few tools forecast it for this group. They mined a large intensive care database for risk factors.

About a third of the patients in the data developed breathing failure. Ten factors fed the final chart, including clotting time, blood sugar, kidney markers, breathing and heart rates, lung disease, shock, and race. The chart sorted patients with fair accuracy, and repeat checks showed its risk estimates lined up well with real outcomes. The authors offer it for bedside use in judging individual risk.
pmc-12755747:
Divya Nair Narayanan and Samsiah Awang published a study protocol in two thousand twenty-five on measuring foot self-care in Malaysians with diabetes. Foot ulcers cost patients money and quality of life, and painless damaged feet mean problems get missed. Clinics lack a standard local tool to score how well patients care for their feet.

The protocol runs in two phases. First, the team drafts questions from the literature, checks them with experts, translates them, and pre-tests them with patients and clinic staff. Second, a pilot and a larger field test across urban and rural clinics will validate the tool. Scoring bands and their meanings will be set. The aim is a simple instrument for daily use.
pmc-12757247:
Sumin Kim, Jaehak Jeong, and Sojung Kim build a growth model for greenhouse cherry tomatoes under long heat stress. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Heat in glass houses cuts yields as the world warms, a key fear for this top Korean crop. Two breeds were grown in heat and their shape traits taped to feed a yield model, with cast warm paths laid in.

One breed put more growth in leaf and stem and bore less fruit share; the other bore more. In warm casts, the leaf-heavy breed gained yield while the fruit-heavy one lost. Its leaf mass kept food make high in heat. The team offer the model for yield casts.
pmc-12766847:
Yona Lunsky and a large Canadian team set out the plan for testing a national brain health course for people with intellectual disabilities, in this protocol from twenty twenty-five. The course was built with this group, not just for it. Adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities face higher dementia risk than others, yet brain health programs usually leave them out.

The course, Brain Health-IDD, is a virtual class co-designed and co-taught by clinicians and people with lived experience. Three groups from across Canada will take it: adults with disabilities aged forty and up, family caregivers, and health and social care providers. Surveys and focus groups at the start, at course end, and three months later will track attendance, satisfaction, knowledge, and confidence. Health habits, wellbeing, and whether memory screening gets started are also on the list. Findings will be shared with advocacy and policy groups.
pmc-12789547:
Wanglong Wan and five colleagues fuse several machine learning models to diagnose faults on electrical distribution lines. Single-model classifiers lean on one feature type and need lots of simulated training data, while real fault records are scarce and noisy. The team extracted time-frequency features across multiple dimensions from real-world data.

A Dempster-Shafer evidence theory method then combines the models' judgments, weighing conflicting evidence formally. Experiments on collected field data reached an average accuracy of 74.6 percent across four grounding fault types, including tricky intermittent arcing. The authors present the fusion framework as a practical step toward faster, more reliable fault handling that keeps power supply stable.
pmc-12815747:
Li and co-authors rank traditional Chinese exercises for knee osteoarthritis using a network of trial results. Knee arthritis burdens many middle-aged and older adults. Four exercise forms entered the comparison: Tai Chi, Baduanjin, Wuqinxi, and Yijinjing. The team gathered 20 randomized trials with 1,457 patients from six databases. Outcomes covered pain, function, walking distance, and life quality. A Bayesian network method let forms be ranked even without head-to-head trials.

For pain relief, Yijinjing ranked at the top of the network. Rankings for stiffness and function differed by outcome. The layered result helps clinics pick an exercise by the patient's main complaint.
pmc-12816647:
Fengchai Wang and Kun Wang present FL-TEAR, a routing frame for fog cloud Internet of Things networks that learns trust by federation and weighs energy in path choice. Safe, sound, low energy links are hard across mixed, weak nodes. The study came out in twenty twenty-five.

Static trust scores give way to shared learning: nodes train one global trust and energy model without baring raw data. Trust scores update from behavior, link soundness, and leftover energy. Paths are picked by a score that blends trust, energy, delay, and link steadiness. The layered design spans things, fog, and cloud, cuts chatter, and guards privacy. Tests beat strong baselines.
pmc-12820047:
Atefeh Zeinali and Leila Moradi published a catalysis study in twenty twenty-five on a three-part nanocomposite built to make complex drug-like molecules quickly and cleanly. The composite marries a carbon nitride sheet, chitosan, and a zinc-based porous framework. A battery of imaging and spectroscopy checks confirmed the hybrid's structure.

It then catalyzed a one-pot, four-component reaction assembling phenazine-fused products in a water-ethanol mix. Yields ran from seventy-seven to ninety-six percent within two hours at most. The catalyst survived six reuse cycles without appreciable loss of activity. Green credentials, speed, and recyclability are the selling points. The authors present the design as a template for rationally assembled catalysts rather than lucky finds.
pmc-12831047:
A large team of trainers from ELIXIR, the European life-science data network, surveys online teaching across its member groups in this white paper from twenty twenty-five. Bioinformatics skills are in demand far beyond any one campus, so the network has leaned on e-learning to reach more people. The paper maps what exists now and what good online training needs.

It profiles shared platforms such as the Training e-Support System and a Slovenian e-learning platform, and notes how course files in a shared format can move between sites for reuse. It also covers blended courses that mix online work with live sessions, and set learning paths that guide a student step by step. The closing part looks ahead: better trainer skills, more open materials, and training records that follow open data rules. The aim is steady, shared growth of skills across Europe.
pmc-12831247:
Catalina Medina and six co-authors mapped street food stalls near public schools in Mexico City, in a study from twenty twenty-five. Food sold around schools shapes what children eat, yet street stalls had been little studied compared with shops. The team surveyed stalls within a short walk of dozens of public schools.

Well over a thousand stalls were found, and more than four in ten sold only unhealthy fare by their scoring tool. Stalls in the poorest areas were not always the worst scorers, and distance from school mattered too. Unhealthy stalls cluster near schools in at-risk areas. The authors note new rules now aim to cut this exposure, and their effects need study.
pmc-12846247:
Lin and co-authors test a weakened live vaccine against a gut disease of pigs. The bacterium Lawsonia intracellularis causes a thickening of the pig gut that harms growth. Few vaccines against the disease are on the market. The team weakened a strain by growing it through 90 rounds in lab cells. The tamed strain, JS-G90, was then given to pigs by mouth.

Vaccinated pigs shed fewer bacteria and showed no gut tissue damage, which signaled safety. The team then exposed pigs to the wild bacterium. They checked shedding, tissue harm, and both antibody and cell-based immune responses. The work weighs whether JS-G90 can anchor a new vaccine for pig farms.
pmc-12846347:
Qiqi Zhang and a team of co-authors mapped HIV types and drug resistance in Wuhan, China. Their study, from twenty twenty-five, used blood samples kept from twenty twenty-two. HIV types vary by region and shift over time. China now has many types in play at once. The team took one hundred forty-nine samples from a Wuhan hospital. They drew out cells, pulled the virus code, and read three key gene regions.

The reads showed the local mix of virus types and where drug resistance marks sit. Such maps guide which drug mixes to use first. Readers who plan HIV care in central China get a local view of type spread and resistance. The work backs care choices with lab proof from the city itself.
pmc-12847847:
Xiaoyue Ma and colleagues published a 2025 study on ultra-fast wireless links using light. Radio spectrum is crowded and limited. Laser beams offer a huge alternative bandwidth. Steering light beams without moving parts is the challenge. The team used a chip of thin-film lithium niobate.

Their phased array steered beams electronically. Multiple targets could connect in real time. One channel reached extremely high data rates. That pace exceeds current mobile network peaks. Uncompressed high-definition video streamed stably in tests. Chip-scale light links could serve dense data centers. Vehicle and indoor networks may follow.
pmc-12853847:
Jinyan Chen and five colleagues map a three-way RNA rivalry in the blood cells of new diabetics, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Long noncoding RNAs can sponge up microRNAs in the cell. That frees the genes those microRNAs hold down in their work. Such networks may yield blood tests for type 2 diabetes.

Blood cells from newly diagnosed patients and healthy controls went through microarray and sequencing screens. RNAs that split in their levels were built into a competing network. Its named axis links the noncoding RNA PRNCR1, a microRNA, and the gene SSTR3. Laboratory assays validated the levels of the molecules in the axis. Accuracy analysis tested how well it could sort cases, set against clinical parameters. A leukocyte-based signature would be an accessible window into diabetes biology. It can be drawn from an ordinary blood draw.
pmc-12864547:
Eline Hooijman and colleagues check whether labs worldwide can spot decay in a radioactive prostate cancer drug, and what that decay does in the body, in this study from twenty twenty-five. The drug carries lutetium-177 to PSMA on tumor cells. Its own radiation slowly chews it up, a process called radiolysis, and broken drug may wander off target.

Hospitals compared their liquid chromatography methods and could each measure the damage consistently, with only small spread between labs. One official method separated peaks better but lost more sample, with no gain in the purity verdict. In mice bearing prostate tumors, batches made at three purity levels behaved as feared: the more degraded the drug, the less it favored tumor over kidney. The authors say quality control for radiolysis is trustworthy across sites, and worth keeping tight.
pmc-12892847:
Rusinova and six colleagues strip rat sciatic nerves of cells to make graft scaffolds for wide nerve gaps in twenty twenty-five. A day long wash of enzymes and detergents clears the cells while sparing the nerve's frame. Rats then got the scaffold or their own nerve graft across a long defect. Recovery was scored at ninety days.

DNA fell to a fifth of native levels, and no nuclei stayed. Skin tests showed no macrophage attack on the scaffold. Fiber counts in scaffold grafts trailed the own graft gold standard. Small myelinated and motor fibers regrew, though. The team calls the scaffold a promising graft stand in.
pmc-12905847:
Xinjie Li and thirteen co-authors test blood sugar chain profiles as a no cut way to spot major liver harm in chronic hepatitis B. Early spotting of harm guides when to start virus drugs. The study came out in twenty twenty-five.

Standard no cut tests miss hidden harm, most of all when liver enzyme levels look normal. The team studied over six hundred patients who had never had virus care and whose harm was proven by liver biopsy. Sugar chain profiles came from an automated read method. About two thirds had major swelling and over half had major scarring. Set peaks rose or fell in a clear pattern with harm, the authors report.
pmc-12926447:
Kexin Cheng, Weihong Li, and five co-authors review plant scents sniffed as a cure for depression. Their review, from twenty twenty-six, covers essential oils given through the nose. Depression is common and disabling, yet standard drugs act slowly and often cause side effects. The nose offers a direct path to the brain that skips a key barrier.

The team pools forty studies from twenty fifteen to twenty twenty-five. Plant oils hold many small fat-loving compounds that act on several targets at once. The review sums up dose plans and timing used in the studies. It also lays out how the oils may lift mood. Gaps that block clinic use are flagged for future work.
pmc-13084047:
Rehab Salah Eldeen and three co-authors tuned a power filter controller with a hybrid search. Their paper, from twenty twenty-six, deals with hybrid active power filters, which clean harmonic junk from power lines. Their control rests on a fractional order PID, a five knob scheme with tight links between knobs. Plain tuning goes shaky on such a set. The team joined two nature drawn searches: a pelican method and a grey wolf method.

The pelican side adapts the hunt; the wolf side adds pack smarts. Joint, they tune all five knobs with more balance than each alone. Aim marks are firm dynamic acts and deep harmonic cuts. Readers in power electronics get a steadier way to set a hard controller.
pmc-13096947:
Gabriela Galarza-Arévalo, Myriam González, and Maria Romero published a review in twenty twenty-six on metallic nanoparticles already at work in clinics, as diagnostics, therapies, and both at once. Iron, gold, hafnium, gadolinium, silver, copper, titanium, and zinc particles are surveyed across cancer, infection control, coatings, and imaging.

Clinical numbers anchor the survey. Iron oxide particles heated glioblastoma tumors during magnetic therapy. Gold shells ablated most treated prostate lesions. A gold particle ferried a potent cytokine safely through the body. Silver fluoride cut children's dentin caries progression notably. The authors argue the field has crossed from promise to practice in specific niches, while integration of diagnosis and therapy in one particle remains the frontier.
pmc-13142147:
Pulkit Mehrotra and colleagues reported an adult Wolfram syndrome case in 2026. Wolfram syndrome usually starts in childhood. Diabetes and optic nerve wasting define it. Brain degeneration progresses alongside both. Adult cases are easily missed clinically. A thirty-eight-year-old woman presented late here.

Her diabetes needed insulin from early on. Antibodies were absent in her tests. Vision loss advanced from optic atrophy. Brain scans showed cerebellar shrinkage too. Genetic testing found a novel variant. Both gene copies carried the fault. Suspicion and imaging guided the diagnosis. Trial eligibility may now follow.
pmc-13156547:
Grant M. Pham and Roger N. Pham published a 2026 case series on an unusual shingles pattern. Shingles usually strikes one skin strip on one side. Two young healthy men broke that pattern. Their lesions crossed several skin regions. Neither man had immune problems.

Ages were thirty-five and twenty. Psychological stress preceded both cases. A skin microscope tool aided early recognition. Antiviral treatment started promptly for both. Supportive care included stress reduction advice. Both men recovered fully. Stress may help reactivate the dormant chickenpox virus. Doctors should not rule out shingles in young, healthy patients.
pmc-13164147:
Wiset and six co-authors optimize infrared roasting for immature rice, in work from twenty twenty-six. Immature rice is eaten across Asia for its green color, soft texture, distinct flavor, and nutrition. Its fragile grains and sensitive pigments make processing tricky.

Roasting temperature and time in a rotary infrared roaster were varied across wide ranges. Effects on physicochemical traits, nutrition, and cooked rice quality were measured. Infrared heat is fast and even, but too much destroys color and texture. Optimized settings give small processors a recipe that keeps the qualities consumers pay for while making the product shelf ready.
pmc-13183747:
Yohei Iimura and Seiichiro Kuroda map treatments for skin harm from cancer drugs. Their review, from twenty twenty-six, covers three known side effects. One is the rash tied to a class of targeted drugs. The others are sore hand and foot syndromes from two drug families. These harms cut life quality and can make patients quit treatment.

Fifty-one clinical studies enter the map. For the rash, antibiotic plus steroid cream plans cut severe cases. For one hand-foot form, blocking an inflammation enzyme helps by mouth or skin. Barrier care and strong steroid creams serve the other form. Each harm has its own mechanism, so care must match the drug.
pmc-13186147:
Aditi Sharma, Rajesh Kaushal, Naveen Chitkara, and Ekkarat Boonchieng design a blockchain-based system for remote patient care. Body sensors can track vital signs at home, but the flood of data raises safety and privacy worries. Medical images, in particular, had not been tied into such record systems. The team's model stores images off the chain and the rest on a shared ledger with set access rules.

In tests with twelve hundred transactions, the system kept pace with the send rate up to a high load and lost no transactions. Delays stayed short, and reads were near instant. The paper shows the design can be both safe and fast enough for live care.
pmc-13190447:
Thomas Aston, Georgios Machtsiras, and Filipe Teixeira-Dias benchmark deep learning models for head pose estimation in sports impacts in a 2026 study. Measuring head movement from video, called videogrammetry, can quantify collisions, but standard training data lack the big rotations, speed, and blocking views of real play. Ten participants performed controlled football headers.

Fast infrared cameras gave true head orientations while two video cameras filmed front and side views. All three models estimated pose with mean errors in single digits of degrees. A full-body mesh recovery model scored lowest and coped best with blocked views, beating dedicated head-only models. Errors grew for side views, rotational headers, and low face visibility.
pmc-13198447: Heather L Gelhorn and colleagues are authors of a study corrected in a 2026 note in Quality of Life Research. The study used mixed methods to define meaningful change for patients with tenosynovial giant cell tumor, drawing on exit interviews and trial data. During publication, spacing, capitalization, and table and figure header and footer errors crept in. The note states that the original article has been corrected.
pmc-13198547:
Manon Giraudier and colleagues tested nerve stimulation to aid recall of emotional memories in a 2026 study. The vagus nerve links the gut and brain and helps set arousal. It shapes how emotional memories form, but its role at recall was less clear, so the team applied gentle ear stimulation during a memory test.

Volunteers had viewed unpleasant and neutral scenes a week before, with no task attached. During recall, real stimulation was compared with a sham version. Real stimulation selectively boosted vivid recall of the unpleasant images. The effect was modest in size. The authors offer first human proof that this nerve helps retrieve emotional memories, a lead for future therapy work.
pmc-13200547:
Yuhua Fan and three colleagues regularize deep neural networks for genomic prediction, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Genomic datasets hold far more markers than they hold samples to learn from. Residual networks can catch nonlinear gene effects in that data. But they overfit with zeal when the data is set up in that way.

Proximal regularization is their cure for that flaw. It is folded head-on into the optimization algorithm at the heart of the work. The team extends a stochastic adaptive proximal gradient method for residual networks of this kind. Both convex and non-convex penalty shapes have support in the frame. Convergence gets a fresh analysis in the paper as well. Breeding and genetics applications drive the work. To predict traits from DNA is just where samples are precious and features are legion. A network that holds up there earns its complexity.
pmc-13202547:
Anna Dornisch and co-authors put out the protocol in 2026 for RadTARGET, a multicenter phase two trial rethinking how prostate cancer is irradiated. Modern radiation cures many intermediate and high-risk cases, but escalating dose to the whole gland injures the bladder and bowel in the process. The trial's wager is geographic: most recurrences after radiation start in the dominant visible tumor, so dose should be concentrated there and on purpose lowered everywhere else in the prostate.

Patients are randomized between that image-guided plan, boosting the dominant lesion while de-intensifying dose to non-suspicious tissue, and standard radiation. The immediate question is toxicity, whether the reshaped dose reduces acute urinary and gastrointestinal side effects, with imaging by advanced magnetic resonance methods and molecular scans guiding the targeting. The results are clearly built as the base for a larger phase three trial of efficacy and safety.
pmc-13202747:
A questionnaire about how people trust information gets a skeptical audit in a 2026 psychometric study authored by Nicola-Hans Schwarzer. The research article evaluates the German version of the Epistemic Trust, Mistrust, and Credulity Questionnaire in 567 university students, comparing its original structure with published shortened models.

Confirmatory factor analyses found that neither the fifteen-item nor the twelve-item version fit the data acceptably. Reliability and variance measures fell below accepted thresholds for all three subscales in every model tested. Links with related traits behaved as theory expects for mistrust and credulity but diverged for trust, leading the authors to recommend thorough item revision before wider use.
pmc-13208347:
Ten researchers led by Adiyadolgor Turbat review how fungi that live inside plants make a key plant hormone, indole-3-acetic acid. The hormone steers plant growth, root shape, and branching. Many inner fungi make it too, shaping how plant and fungus get along, yet the fungal routes are less mapped than plant or bacterial ones.

The review gathers work from twenty twenty to twenty twenty-five on which fungi make the hormone and by what paths. It weighs how to prove the fungus, not the plant, is the maker. It then covers gains such as growth boosts and stress tolerance, noting effects hinge on dose and setting.
pmc-13210047:
Nabeel Israr and colleagues used first-principles computation to vet a new family of lead-free double perovskite crystals for solar and heat-to-electric uses. Perovskites are tunable light absorbers, but the best contain toxic lead. The candidates swap in rubidium, indium, and copper with one of three halogens. Writing in twenty twenty-six, the team ran density functional calculations, including spin-orbit effects, to check stability, electronic bands, light absorption, and thermoelectric behavior across a wide photon energy range.

The crystals passed stability checks and showed direct band gaps in or near the useful solar range, shrinking as the halogen grows heavier. Absorption was strongest in the ultraviolet. Heat-to-electric performance was promising for the fluoride member, whose efficiency figure neared values of practical interest. The authors present all three as candidates for sustainable optoelectronics.
pmc-13210947:
Mingju Chen and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how image generators can be controlled by many kinds of input at once. Diffusion models once worked mainly from text. Newer systems take sound, three-dimensional data, and body signals as well, and the review organises how those mixed signals are mapped and injected into generation.

Coverage follows the shift from older U-Net designs to newer transformer-based generators, and from single inputs to combined multi-source control. The authors sort evaluation measures and describe trade-offs between image quality and control. They close by pointing to hardware testing, physics-based limits, and causal reasoning as routes toward faster, more reliable controllable generation.
pmc-13212847:
Abdirasak Sharif Ali and Augustus Osborne chart in 2026 how stunting among Somali children under five changed over nearly twenty-five years. Stunting, meaning a child is far too short for their age, reflects long-running malnutrition and carries lifelong effects.

Using World Health Organization modelled estimates, the pair found national prevalence fell from about a third of children in 2000 to under a quarter by 2024. Boys stayed consistently more affected than girls throughout, and the relative gap barely narrowed. The authors call the remaining level a serious public concern. They urge sex-sensitive nutrition action plus wider measures on mothers' schooling, household wealth, and climate resilience.
pmc-13213047:
Zhaoran Su and a large team investigate in 2026 why some colorectal cancer cells resist a therapy that uses alternating electric fields to wreck cell division. The treatment, already used for a brain cancer, had never been tested systematically across many bowel cancer cell lines.

Across a broad panel of patient-derived lines, the fields damaged cells through several routes, from scrambled division machinery to DNA damage and cell death. One gene stood out as switched on in resistant lines. Silencing it made cells sensitive again, and computer screening nominated two existing drugs that might block its product and boost the therapy. The gene could become a target for combination treatment.
pmc-13214447:
Ayodhia Pitaloka Pasaribu leads a very large group reporting in 2026 on an Indonesian stakeholder meeting about curing relapsing vivax malaria. A multi-country trial had tested a single-dose drug and a shorter high-dose course against the standard two-week regimen.

Officials, clinicians, and programme staff met in May 2025 to weigh the Indonesia-specific findings for national policy. Gaps remain around pairing the single-dose drug with the malaria combinations used locally, they agreed. The high-dose week-long course looked ready to adopt sooner, provided testing for an enzyme deficiency that makes these drugs risky is strengthened. Attendees stressed tailoring plans to Indonesia's varied regions and keeping political commitment to elimination.
pmc-13215047:
Kelnner Portela Luz and Danilo Lopes Ferreira Lima report in 2026 a first field test of a digital platform for endometriosis care inside Brazilian public primary care. Diagnosis there often takes seven to ten years, hitting poor, rural, Black, and Indigenous women hardest.

Sixty women and health professionals used the platform for eight weeks across ten clinics. Usability and acceptance scored high, and users finished most educational modules. Pain and anxiety eased while knowledge, treatment adherence, and referrals rose, though with no comparison group those shifts count as exploratory signals only. Subgroup patterns hinted at equity-relevant differences. The authors frame the tool as feasible for low-resource settings.
pmc-13215747:
Jarzabek and Denny reviewed tests for cutaneous leishmaniasis in twenty twenty-five, a skin disease caused by a parasite spread by sand flies. The World Health Organization has set target goals for a better test: more accurate and cheaper than current tools. Knowing the exact species matters more now as drug resistance grows.

Blood tests cannot identify the species, while gene tests need costly machines. Heat-based gene tests called LAMP are promising, but few are species-specific so far, and Ethiopia is neglected in this work. Cheap devices built during the COVID-19 pandemic await testing for this disease. Image analysis by AI offers another route. The authors map both the chances and the hurdles ahead.
pmc-13216147:
Víctor López-López and co-authors present a 2026 multicentre study of bile leakage after robotic liver surgery in expert Spanish centres. Bile leaks are among the most troublesome complications of liver resection, and robotic series with solid numbers have been scarce.

The database covered 492 consecutive patients in three high-volume centres, most operated on for cancer. Bile leakage occurred in just nine patients, a rate of 1.8 percent, and none of the leaks reached the most severe grade. All were handled without reoperation. Overall complications within ninety days affected 29.3 percent of patients, mortality was 1.6 percent, and the typical hospital stay was three days. The authors credit centralization in expert hands.
pmc-13216547:
Mostafa A. Gouda and co-authors present a 2026 food science study comparing Grison, the air-dried cured meat of Swiss tradition, made from three different animals: cattle, buffalo, and camel. Rising cattle prices and interest in alternative proteins motivated the head-to-head test.

Topside from each species was dry-cured under controlled conditions and tracked through processing and in the finished product. Camel meat and its Grison ran moister, with higher pH, residual nitrite, and redness, but less protein, fat, and lipid oxidation than the others. Tasters gave camel the best colour and flavour scores. Cattle Grison was fattiest and lightest in colour. Buffalo Grison was toughest and least juicy. The authors judge camel a genuine rival to the traditional product.
pmc-13216647:
Wessam M. Salama and co-authors present a 2026 wireless engineering study on estimating the radio channel in MIMO systems. Many antennas talk at once there, and the channel must be measured before data can flow. Deep learning estimators usually need retraining whenever conditions change, which limits their use.

Their hybrid framework combines a Transformer network, zero-shot learning that maps channels into a shared attribute space, and the Muon optimizer. In simulations it beat classical least-squares and MMSE estimators and several deep learning baselines, especially in channel conditions never seen during training. Growing the array from 2 to 128 antennas at high signal quality cut estimation error by about 94 percent. The authors present the design as ready for next-generation networks.
pmc-13217447:
Ahmed Omar Siyad and co-authors present a 2026 case report of severe lung failure after measles in a two-year-old unvaccinated girl treated in a resource-limited setting. Measles pneumonia can escalate into acute respiratory distress syndrome, a complication seldom documented where intensive care is scarce.

The child arrived after a week of fever and worsening breathlessness following a measles-like illness, critically ill with oxygen saturation far below safe levels and depressed consciousness. Chest imaging showed diffuse infiltrates, and heart ultrasound excluded a cardiac cause. She spent fourteen days on a ventilator with antibiotics, vitamin A, transfusion for severe anaemia, and careful fluid management. She left intensive care on day eighteen and went home well after twenty-seven days. The authors stress vaccination and early referral.
pmc-13218147:
Yi Chen and colleagues describe a 2026 protocol for a randomized trial of a symptom-monitoring system for pemphigus vulgaris. The disease is a rare autoimmune blistering condition with recurring sores on skin and mucous membranes, heavy symptom burden, and relapses that are hard to predict. Care still leans on medication plus hospital follow-up, leaving home monitoring thin.

The multicentre trial will randomize 160 adults with confirmed disease and active lesions to the Intelligent Multimodal Symptom Assessment and Response System or to standard care. The system combines patient-reported outcomes, wearable body-signal data, and photographs of lesions on one platform over twelve weeks. The main goal is better symptom alerting and management. Secondary goals cover self-management, sticking with treatment, and quality of life. The team will ask patients how usable the system feels, since people with a rare disease must keep using a tool for it to help.
pmc-13221747: Jacob P Thönes and colleagues publish a 2026 correction in BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders that fixes the title of their earlier article. The notice is a correction only: part of the original title was missing, dropping the words covering knee extension strength. The full title concerns estimating knee joint angle and extensor strength from electrical impedance during concentric knee extension. No data, methods, or conclusions change; the journal record and the article itself have been updated to carry the complete title.
pmc-13222347:
Izadora de Souza and colleagues review the double-edged role of the NRF2 pathway in ferroptosis, an iron-driven form of cell death, in a 2026 article. NRF2 coordinates genes that shield cells from oxidative stress. In cancers, constant NRF2 activity helps tumors resist chemotherapy by boosting detoxification and antioxidant defenses.

Many NRF2 target genes also control ferroptosis through glutathione production, fat metabolism, and iron handling. Depending on cell type and metabolic state, the pathway can guard against ferroptotic death or set it up. The review traces how this network was discovered and flags the pivotal target genes. Tuning NRF2 deliberately might push resistant tumors into ferroptotic death.
pmc-13222947:
Andarva leads a large team studying an immune enzyme and fat droplets in prostate cancer cells, in work from twenty twenty-six. Secreted phospholipase A2 group IIA is an innate immune mediator, an enzyme that cuts fat molecules. Lipid droplets inside cells store fat and support tumor growth.

The enzyme modulated lipid droplet formation in prostate cancer cells, the title reports. How an immune related enzyme reshapes fat storage in cancer cells links inflammation with tumor metabolism. That link could suggest new drug angles, since starving cancer cells of stored fat is one route to slowing their growth and spread.
pmc-13223647:
Jessica M Jarvis and co-authors ask caregivers how confidently they could report rehabilitation use after a child's traumatic brain injury, in a 2026 qualitative study meant to shape a new measure. Fourteen caregivers of hospitalized children up to age eighteen joined remote semi-structured interviews. Sampling sought variety in factors tied to service use, and sessions ran until no new themes appeared.

They felt confident reporting services and satisfaction by setting, with rough dosage, though confidence varied between care settings. They endorsed a full reporting form with built-in meanings and guided prompts, ideally electronic, to fill in from home. A caregiver-report tool spanning the whole care path looks acceptable and feasible on this evidence.
pmc-13224347:
Stephanie Denise M. Sison and colleagues analyse a 2026 Medicare study of how frailty and dementia, alone and together, shape costs and time spent at home. Home time loss counts days spent in hospitals or facilities rather than at home, serving as a rough quality-of-life measure. The team used fee-for-service claims for older beneficiaries and grouped people by both conditions.

Both spending and lost home time climbed as frailty grew more severe. Dementia behaved differently depending on physical state: it came with higher costs among robust beneficiaries, yet lower costs among the frail. Those contrasting patterns suggest the two conditions drive distinct kinds of care, and the authors call for better recognition of frailty in planning services.
pmc-13224747:
Dawn M. Holman and colleagues analyse a 2026 national survey report on sunburn among United States high school students, using 2023 Youth Risk Behavior Survey data. Sunburn raises skin cancer risk, and teenage rates have stayed stubbornly high for years. The team estimated how many students burned at least once, and how many burned five or more times, in the previous year.

Just over half of students reported at least one sunburn. Among those who burned, about twenty-three percent burned frequently. After statistical adjustment, rates differed by sex, race and ethnicity, body weight, substance use, diet, activity, and social media use. The authors argue that persistently high figures justify continued prevention work in schools, clinics, and communities.
pmc-13226047:
Murray Baron and colleagues test a 2026 workaround that lets artificial intelligence analyse older lung scans saved as sparse slices. AI tools for interstitial lung disease need continuous high-resolution CT stacks, but many archived scans survive only as about thirty separated slices. The team rebuilt full stacks from fourteen systemic sclerosis patients by inserting copied slices between the real ones.

Both original and rebuilt scans went through the same commercial AI program, which scored honeycombing, reticular pattern, ground-glass change, and total disease. Agreement between versions was excellent on nearly every measure, judged by several statistical checks. One pattern score showed a weaker result on a single test. The trick could unlock large archives of legacy scans for modern analysis.
pmc-13226247:
Yifan Chen and colleagues review a 2026 synthesis of how skull and facial bones develop under two kinds of control at once: molecular signals and physical forces. Unlike trunk bones, craniofacial bones arise from neural crest tissue and form through distinctive patterns, so lessons from limb bones transfer imperfectly. Chewing, growth stresses, and other mechanical loads feed back into the signalling that shapes them.

Recent work maps where force-sensing and classic developmental pathways meet, and how imbalance between them produces congenital and acquired disorders of the face and skull. The authors argue that treating the mechanical and genetic sides as one system opens new preventive and therapeutic angles for craniofacial disease.
pmc-13227947:
David J Irwin and a large team localise a 2026 brain-pathology signature in globular glial tauopathy, a rare protein-clumping disease that can present as progressive aphasia, the slow loss of language. Earlier work had spotted iron-rich inflammation in mid-to-deep cortical layers without mapping it against symptoms. Brains from five confirmed patients and one control were imaged whole at ultra-high resolution after death and examined digitally.
