The iron-rich inflammation sat in different places matching each patient's language syndrome. Those with non-fluent speech showed it across frontal and motor regions, while the semantic-variant patient's damage concentrated in the front temporal lobe. One patient's lifetime scan showed the same frontal signal seen after death, raising hope that this inflammation could be detected and used diagnostically in life.
pmc-13233447:
Minyue Cao and colleagues published a 2026 multi-omics study of uterine corpus endometrial carcinoma, a womb cancer that often resists immunotherapy because few T cells enter its tumors. The team combined genetic association data with splicing and expression data to nominate driver genes. One splicing factor, SNRPE, emerged and was linked to poor survival in patient cohorts.

Silencing SNRPE in laboratory models and in a mouse xenograft sharply slowed tumor growth. The factor keeps the splicing of several dual-function genes accurate, including PAK1, SOS1, and PIK3CB, and disrupting it derails those messages. Single-cell data and immune cell co-culture experiments also tied SNRPE to immune evasion. The authors propose it as both a prognostic marker and a drug target.
pmc-13233647:
Marina Koutsi, Fotios Mpekris, and Triantafyllos Stylianopoulos published a 2026 computer study of ultrasound-triggered drug delivery to solid tumors. Fat bubbles called thermosensitive liposomes carry chemotherapy and spill their cargo when warmed. The team built a three-dimensional model coupling ultrasound spread, tissue heating, and heat-triggered drug release, then checked its predictions against published experiments.

The model matched real tumor growth and drug concentration data well. Longer ultrasound exposure beat higher frequency for shrinking tumors, and treating fast-growing tumors early mattered a great deal. Faster drug release raised drug levels inside cells. Medium liposomes worked best in typical vessels, while larger ones suited leakier tumor vessels. The framework is offered as a design aid for future thermally triggered treatments.
pmc-13233847:
Martje G Pauly and colleagues published a 2026 neurology study testing a brain ultrasound marker for X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism, an inherited movement disorder with damage centered on the striatum. Transcranial sonography can reveal an unusually bright lentiform nucleus, a deep brain structure. The team scanned 138 people: 61 patients, 19 carriers without symptoms, and 58 healthy controls, and compared results with MRI volumes and genetic repeat counts.

The bright-nucleus sign appeared in eighty-one percent of patients and nearly half of symptom-free carriers, against twenty percent of controls. Carriers and patients showing the sign tended toward younger onset and carried more genetic repeats. The third ventricle was wider in patients, while another deep structure showed no size difference. The authors propose ultrasound as a cheap way to flag carriers nearing symptom onset.
pmc-13234347: Shiqi Zhou and colleagues published a correction in 2026 to their earlier study judging how well video language models assess dry eye science videos. The notice is a correction only, removing one affiliation that had been listed in error for an author. That Singapore university address no longer appears, and the remaining author affiliations have been renumbered to match. No findings, methods, or conclusions of the original article are changed by the notice.
pmc-13234947:
Chengcheng Zhang and co-authors asked in 2026 whether growing Medicaid raised health coverage for Americans living in poor-quality housing. Homes lacking basic needs often come with greater health needs and money strain. National survey data from 2010 to 2019 weighed states that expanded Medicaid against states that did not. The analysis focused on low-income people whose homes missed at least one basic need.

Expansion raised Medicaid coverage by more than twelve points for that worse-off housing group. Being without coverage fell by roughly six to seven points relative to non-expansion states. Gains were slightly smaller, though, than for people whose homes met all basic needs. Disparities between the two housing groups therefore narrowed without disappearing. The authors suggest wider eligibility alone cannot remove barriers beyond cost, so outreach and sign-up support remain key.
pmc-13235447:
Fátima Cañas Tornero and colleagues evaluated in 2026, in Spanish, a reorganized care team model across three health centres near Jerez in Spain. The model joins family medicine, nursing, and a citizen attention unit into one functional team that sorts incoming demand. Thirty doctors with continuous service were followed for two months before and after the change. The main measure was average days waited for a scheduled medical appointment.

Median waiting time fell from nearly nine days before the model to under five days afterward. That change represents a median relative reduction near forty percent in the analysis. Improvement appeared in twenty-eight of the thirty doctors tracked across the period. Statistical checks tied the gain to team redesign rather than to individual doctor traits or workload. The authors present the model as a clinically meaningful boost to primary care access in their setting.
pmc-13236947:
Xiaoqin Luo and Xian He built a prognostic index in 2026 for head and neck squamous cell carcinoma. The index rests on genes tied to regulated cell death and cellular senescence, the aging-like shutdown of cells. They first grouped tumors into two subtypes using ten kinds of molecular data and ten clustering methods. One subtype resisted nearly every treatment type.

From that resistant subtype's marker genes, the team tested 270 machine-learning combinations and kept the best, a six-gene index called CDCSI. Patients with low scores responded more often to radiation, chemotherapy, targeted drugs, and immunotherapy. The index also mapped how tumors interact with the immune system. The authors offer it as a guide for matching patients to treatment, pending further checks.
pmc-13238247:
Pambis and colleagues review stem cell and cell-free strategies for osteoarthritis, the world's most common joint disease. Worn cartilage brings pain and disability to hundreds of millions. Current care eases symptoms but does not stop the joint from worsening, so a therapy that truly repaired cartilage would change the field.

Mesenchymal stem cells are the most advanced candidate, tested for both their repair signals and their calming effect on joint inflammation. Cell-free options, using only the healing cargo cells release, promise fewer risks and easier storage. The review weighs the evidence for both, and what durable regeneration, rather than brief relief, would require.
pmc-13238647:
Yuheng Jiang, Yuhao Nie, and Zhiqiang Ge sequenced the complete mitochondrial genome of the pitviper Ovophis makazayazaya in 2026 and placed the species on the family tree of Asian pitvipers. The circular genome runs 17,230 bases and holds the standard animal set: thirteen protein-coding genes, two ribosomal RNA genes, twenty-two transfer RNA genes, and one control region. Its base mix leans toward adenine and thymine.

Every protein-coding gene showed signs of purifying selection, meaning harmful changes are weeded out. Family trees built from the thirteen genes placed the species firmly among the crotaline pitvipers, near the genus Protobothrops. Because only one Ovophis species was sampled, the study cannot test whether that genus forms a single branch. The authors offer the genome as a reference for snake systematics and mitochondrial evolution.
pmc-13239147:
Md Shahriar Rahman and colleagues tested fecal samples from eighty captive wild animals at two Bangladeshi facilities in 2026, the national zoo and an eco park, for gut helminth worms. Captive wildlife near dense cities carries a double concern: the animals' own welfare and spillover to people. Samples covered mammals, birds, and reptiles, and parasites were identified by their shapes under the microscope.

Just over half the animals carried at least one helminth, and five worm groups turned up, including families with known human relevance. Every reptile sampled was infected, while carnivorous and omnivorous mammals showed the lowest rates, and over a quarter of infected animals carried mixed infections. None of the animals looked sick. The authors call for routine monitoring, better husbandry, and targeted deworming under a One Health frame.
pmc-13240947:
Jihad Al Hassan and co-authors present a 2026 review built around three cases of non-immune hydrops fetalis. In this condition, fluid builds up in two or more parts of the unborn baby. It is a warning sign rather than a disease itself, and outcomes are often poor.

The cases span common causes such as infection and chromosome problems, plus rarer ones involving the mother. Current diagnosis rests mainly on ultrasound and blood-flow studies that locate the fluid and hint at its cause. The authors expect genetic testing to enter the process earlier as it grows faster and cheaper. Early, accurate answers help doctors plan care and support parents facing hard choices.
pmc-13241247:
Zhao and co-authors at Ningxia Medical reviewed 3D-printed bone scaffolds built on triply periodic minimal surfaces. These lattices promise strength, cell-friendly curves, and open channels in one print. It pulls in work from many labs. The review stresses versions that also fight infection. Mixed materials and germ-fighting plans receive detailed treatment.

Pairings like polylactic acid with magnesium titanate show the mixed path. The authors explain how scaffold surfaces and released agents suppress germs. Bone growth and infection control, they argue, can reinforce rather than trade off. The survey aims to guide next-generation repair materials.
pmc-13241647:
Mineko Tomomura leads a team on a plant alcohol and bone balance. Their study from twenty twenty-six deals with geranylgeraniol. Bone is shaped by builder cells and breaker cells together.

The compound sits in the mevalonate path in cells. It blocked formation of the bone breaker cells. A key switch gene for those cells was turned down. One stress kinase path was also damped by it. In builder cells it raised enzyme activity and mineral build. Builder mark genes rose under its action. Two signal routes are named in the title.
pmc-13242447:
Akemu Xiamusiya and colleagues surveyed Singapore households to update national benchmarks for the EQ-5D-5L health questionnaire. Their paper appeared in Quality of Life Research in 2026, using responses gathered from May to July 2024. Just over two thousand citizens and permanent residents aged fifteen and older described their mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain, and mood. Earlier Singapore norms dated from before the COVID-19 pandemic.

Just over half of respondents reported no health problems at all, while pain or discomfort and anxiety or depression were the most common complaints. Average scores remained high overall. Older age tracked most strongly with lower quality of life, and higher income and better housing tracked with higher scores, while gender showed no clear link. The new norms give health economists a post-pandemic yardstick for judging treatments.
pmc-13242847:
Yan Zhang and co-authors offer a 2026 review of histone methylation in the shift from fatty liver disease to liver cancer. Fat-related liver disease and its inflamed form are major precursors of this cancer. Chemical tags on the proteins that package DNA can lock in abnormal gene programs, and the review asks how they drive the change.

These tags are placed, removed, and read by dedicated protein teams, making them reversible in principle. Abnormal patterns appear early and may dominate the move from simple fat buildup to malignancy. The authors summarize the molecular machinery and findings tying specific changes to tumor development. They propose the marks as early warning biomarkers and as targets for intervention before cancer forms.
pmc-13243247:
Yumo Liu and co-authors present a 2026 case of lupus in a child whose first signs were growth problems. Lupus is an immune disease that can attack many organs, yet slow growth and late puberty rarely lead the picture. Their patient was a 12-year-old Chinese girl seen at a hormone clinic for stalled growth.

Tests found protein in her urine, low blood protein, swollen glands, and immune changes that confirmed lupus. Drugs that calm the immune system improved her general health and her lab results over time. Her growth and puberty still lagged behind despite the better disease control. The case warns doctors to think of lupus when short stature comes with urine or immune findings.
pmc-13244247:
Xiaorui Zhao, Xiaoqing Fu, and Wenqiang Li report a lung clot that dressed itself as a heart attack on the ECG. Their case report appeared in Case Reports in Cardiology in 2026. A seventy-four-year-old man arrived with chest tightness and breathlessness, and his tracing showed ST-segment elevation across both front and lower leads, the signature of a blocked heart artery. Yet he described no crushing ischemic pain.

Other clues pointed elsewhere. His D-dimer was raised, a clot sat in a calf vein, and ultrasound showed lung pressure strain without the wall damage a heart attack leaves. Emergency CT angiography settled it, showing clots in both pulmonary arteries. He received intravenous heparin, moved to oral blood thinners, and went home after nine days. The authors urge teams to keep pulmonary embolism on the list whenever ST elevation appears. The mimic is rare but deadly if missed.
pmc-13244547:
Juhwan Lim and co-authors watch a chemical treatment improve a one-atom-thick semiconductor in real time in 2026. Sheets of molybdenum disulfide glow weakly because surface flaws trap energy before it leaves as light. A lithium salt treatment can heal those flaws, but its spread over time and space was unseen.

The team filmed the glow of a treated flake as it brightened over about five minutes. Brightening was slow, which points to a reaction-limited process rather than fast flooding. Some spots responded far more than others, so differences across the flake grew even as the whole improved. The method gives makers a live view of uneven surface chemistry in thin materials.
pmc-13244847:
Kristin Byström and colleagues translated a questionnaire on fear of movement in injured athletes into Swedish and tested whether it measures well. Their psychometric study appeared in BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation in 2026. Ninety-five amateur soccer players injured within the past year completed the Athletic Fear Avoidance Questionnaire alongside the Tampa kinesiophobia scale. A subset retook it later so scores could be checked for stability.

The Swedish version held up. Its scores tracked the Tampa scale strongly, matching the team's preset hypothesis. Individual items proved good to substantially stable on retest, and the total score's reliability rated excellent, with internal consistency judged satisfactory. Players and clinicians gain a short, user-friendly tool in their language for spotting fear that can stall rehabilitation. One gap remains: whether high scores predict unsafe or delayed return to sport is untested, and the authors flag that as the next study.
pmc-13244947:
Yiyi Shan and colleagues show that a pig virus borrows the cell's own gene-silencing machinery to copy itself faster. Their study appeared in Veterinary Research in 2026. Porcine circovirus type 2 attacks the pig immune system and costs the swine industry heavily. The host protein EZH2, which switches genes off by tagging their packaging, was the suspect. The team raised and lowered EZH2 in infected cells and measured both the virus and the genes EZH2 controls.

More EZH2 meant more virus; blocking its enzyme activity or silencing it meant less. Gene sequencing fingered two matrix-chewing enzymes, MMP1 and MMP12, as the mediators: EZH2 sits on their promoters and keeps them quiet, and those enzymes normally suppress the virus. Release the brake, by disabling EZH2's tagging domain, and the enzymes rise and replication falls. The finding hands drug designers a host-side target against a stubborn farm virus.
pmc-13245547:
Connell and co-authors ran a pilot health program for Bangladeshi-American adults in Atlanta in this 2026 JMIR Formative Research study. South Asian Americans face high rates of prediabetes and type 2 diabetes. The program's twist was to enroll each patient's social partners, trusted household members who joined five long health-education sessions in English and Bengali.

Fifty-four patients and over one hundred partners took part. After six months the patients' average blood-sugar marker had fallen clearly, systolic blood pressure had improved, and partners reported healthier eating and activity habits of their own. The authors say the family-based approach is feasible, though larger controlled trials must prove the partners are what made the difference.
pmc-13246247:
Burbelo and co-authors asked whether low blood pressure during hip replacement surgery harms patients afterward, in this 2026 Bone and Joint Open study. Drops in pressure are common under anesthesia and have been linked to complications in other operations. The team reviewed nearly four hundred primary hip replacements at one academic hospital, tracking pressure in two ways: against a fixed floor, and as a fall from each patient's own baseline.

Crossing the fixed floor showed no link to readmission or longer stays, however it was measured. A relative drop from baseline, though, came with clearly more repeat operations within ninety days, and heavier blood loss predicted longer stays. The authors argue for watching pressure relative to the individual patient.
pmc-13246547:
Andelieri and co-authors studied feeding economics on a robotic-milking dairy farm in southern Brazil, in this 2026 Tropical Animal Health and Production paper. Their measure was revenue minus feed cost: what each cow earns in milk minus what her feed costs. The farm's seventy-six Holstein cows were managed as one group in 2022, then split into high- and low-production groups with targeted rations in 2023.

The high-production group earned the best margin and used feed most efficiently despite eating the most expensive ration. Low producers lagged, especially late in lactation. The authors conclude that grouping cows by output, and feeding each group to its needs, pays under commercial robotic-milking conditions, while single-group results need cautious reading.
pmc-13247847:
Vaughan and colleagues test a team model of diabetes care for low-income Hispanic adults. Community health workers, local staff trained to support patients, visit and coach people at home. Phone and video links tie the workers to clinic doctors in a set feedback loop.

In the trial, more than two hundred fifty adults were split between the new model and usual care. After one year, the new model cut average blood sugar by about one full point. That drop is twice the level doctors count as a real gain. Care steps in national guides were also done more often. The team reports yearly net savings from the model as well.
pmc-13249547:
Hatem Ahmed and nine co-authors review what is known about vaping and outcomes in adults with inflammatory bowel disease. Their systematic review was published in twenty twenty-six. Many patients vape while quitting cigarettes, yet the clinical effects in this group were unclear.

The team searched four databases and grey sources through late twenty twenty-five, then rechecked in twenty twenty-six. Two reviewers screened and extracted data on their own, with bias checks suited to each design. Only four observational studies, with under two thousand people and fewer than two hundred vapers, qualified. In non-surgical settings, one matched study found no link between current vaping and a combined bad outcome. The authors stress how thin the evidence still is.
pmc-13250247:
Sun and colleagues review tiny engineered carriers that could deliver drugs straight into the jaw joint. Their 2026 International Journal of Nanomedicine paper covers temporomandibular joint osteoarthritis, where cartilage breaks down and the joint lining stays inflamed. Standard treatments reach the joint poorly and wash out quickly, limiting their benefit.

The review surveys liposomes, polymer particles, micelles, metal-organic frameworks, and hydrogels designed to stay longer and release drugs slowly or on cue. Newer materials such as nanozymes may also calm inflammation and help cartilage repair. The authors caution that most evidence comes from other joints, not the jaw itself. They call for jaw-specific testing, smarter responsive systems, and standard ways to judge results.
pmc-13250447:
Calarco argues in this 2026 PNAS editorial that open data rules built for numbers can endanger interview-based research. Journal policy requires authors to share all data, materials, and code with reviewers and, after publication, in public repositories. Exceptions exist in theory, but the grounds for granting them are left unclear.

Calarco explains the exemption won by a study based on deep interviews with ninety-nine young Black and Hispanic men in a Chicago violence prevention program. Even with false names, full transcripts could expose histories of violence, victimization, and incarceration, with legal and ethical risks. Sharing such data could also chill future participation. The piece asks editors to protect sensitive qualitative work rather than force it into quantitative norms.
pmc-13250547:
Jeffrey M. Hord and colleagues report 2026 mouse research on dystroglycan, a protein that anchors muscle fibers to their surroundings. The team focused on the part of the protein that sits inside the cell, at the junction where motor nerves meet muscle. They asked whether that inner section is required for the junction to mature and work.

Mice engineered to lack only the inner portion of beta-dystroglycan developed severe neuromuscular disease. Their nerve-muscle junctions failed to mature properly, and muscle function suffered as a result. The outer part of the protein, which binds the material around cells, was not enough on its own. The authors argue that the inside segment carries signals the synapse needs to stay stable. The finding helps explain how damage to this protein complex produces muscle disease.
pmc-13252747:
Georgina Mathlin and colleagues explore a resettlement support service in open prisons in this 2026 qualitative study from England. People with a likely personality disorder diagnosis face a risky stretch when leaving prison, and the service studied supports those at high risk of being sent back.

The team interviewed ten staff and nine service users across male open prisons. Three themes emerged. Arriving in open conditions felt like a shock, a halfway world between locked prison and community. Users prized support built around their own needs, which grew trusting relationships. Staff then used that trust to help men face inner barriers and move through their sentences. Personal plans, not one-size rules, drove the progress.
pmc-13252847:
Mengistie Tariku and a large team pool hookworm data for pregnant women in Ethiopia in this 2026 review. Hookworm, a gut parasite picked up from soil, is a chief cause of anaemia in pregnancy, yet a national summary for Ethiopia was missing.

Following standard review methods, the team combined 33 studies with 13,367 pregnant women published between 2010 and 2024. About twelve percent carried hookworm, and among women with any gut worm, hookworm made up 44 percent of infections. Rates peaked in the Amhara region at about 13 percent and bottomed out in Gambella near four percent. Test method also shifted the numbers, a caution for comparing regions.
pmc-13253047:
Tomáš Figura and colleagues ask why two Asian orchids spread so well abroad in this 2026 study. The bamboo orchid and the Philippine ground orchid have expanded into the Americas, the Pacific, and Africa, and the team tested whether seed traits and fungus partnerships explain the success.

Both orchids carry unusually large seeds stocked with fats and proteins, yet seedlings still need a fungus partner or a sugar supply to start. In the lab, both sprouted with fungus strains from several continents, one species pairing with a wider range. That flexibility, plus self-pollination in one species and larger seed reserves in the other, likely fuels their spread into disturbed ground.
pmc-13253847:
Julian Schumann and co-authors model how drivers dodge crashes in a 2026 paper. Avoiding a collision needs fast threat spotting and a quick, apt move, yet past models covered only parts of that skill. Their model uses active inference, a theory that the brain acts to cut surprise and uncertainty.

The model was tested on three crash setups: a lead car braking, an oncoming car drifting in, and a car failing to yield. It matched broad findings from past reviews and fine details from two simulator studies, covering timing, choice of move, and execution. The authors offer it as a general frame for driver behavior.
pmc-13254847:
Elavarasan Subramani and a large team follow a failed trial endpoint to a new treatment idea for aggressive prostate cancer in a 2026 report. Aggressive-variant prostate cancers ignore hormone therapy but partly answer to taxane-platinum chemotherapy. Their phase two trial tested induction chemotherapy followed by a maintenance drug, olaparib, against observation, hoping to extend the time before progression.

The primary endpoint was not met. The trial was weakened because 38.5 percent of patients progressed during the opening chemotherapy, before randomization even happened. No DNA alteration predicted that early failure, but gene activity analysis found metabolic pathways, prominently arginine metabolism, enriched in the fast-progressing tumors. Starving the models of arginine with an enzyme drug called ADI-PEG20 then made the same chemotherapy work better, in dishes and in animals. The authors say the detour exposes real biological variety inside this cancer class.
pmc-13255047:
Tamara Kozytska and co-authors wrote a 2026 review of Listeria ivanovii, a bacterium often missed in animal health. Its better-known relative, Listeria monocytogenes, draws most attention as a foodborne threat to people. Listeria ivanovii instead mainly infects ruminants such as sheep, goats, and cattle.

The review covers the germ's biology, virulence tools, spread, testing, drug response, and control on farms. Cases appear scattered, sometimes causing abortion storms in small ruminant flocks, yet big outbreaks have not been seen. Human cases stay rare and mostly hit people with weak immune defenses. The authors note that routine labs often fail to tell Listeria species apart, so the true burden is likely missed, and they urge better species-level testing.
pmc-13255947:
Sriphuthorn, Dabseepai, and Senasri tested whether dry feed mixes can replace fresh algae for farming the fairy shrimp Streptocephalus sirindhornae. Seven diets were compared over twenty days: fresh Chlorella as control, and six blends of spirulina powder, commercial shrimp feed, fish meal, and rice bran. Growth and survival were checked across three early life stages.

A half-spirulina, half-shrimp-feed blend matched the fresh algae control at every stage and beat the other dry diets, with late-stage survival just above sixty percent in both groups. Shrimp raised on that blend also carried more protein, lipid, carotenoids, and amino acids than algae-fed shrimp. The authors recommend it as a practical hatchery diet.
pmc-13256747:
Chi-Cheng Li and co-authors show in a 2026 zebrafish study that titanium dioxide nanoparticles disturb the gut microbial mix so strongly that gut and gill bacteria begin to resemble each other. The particles are mass-made for products from paint to sunscreen and persist in aquatic ecosystems, yet their effects on host microbes are rarely studied.

Fish exposed to 5 mg/L for six days lost helpful gut bacteria, including a 333-fold drop in Cetobacterium, while pathogenic Mycobacterium rose sharply. pmc-13257647:

pmc-13258047:

pmc-13258947:

pmc-13259247:

pmc-13259447:

pmc-13260647:

pmc-13261347:

pmc-13262547:

pmc-13262847:
Gebremedhin B Gebretekle and co-authors weigh infant protection plans against respiratory syncytial virus in Canada in a 2026 journal article. pmc-13263347:

pmc-13263647:
Marwa Mady and a multinational team gather what is known about test anxiety among medical students. Exam dread can derail performance and wellbeing in a famously pressured degree. Their 2026 systematic review screens six databases for studies from twenty nineteen to mid twenty twenty-five.

Thirteen cross-sectional studies from Asia, Africa, and Europe qualified, with samples up to seven hundred thirty-five students. pmc-13263747:

Corruption cases leaned on it least among the top five categories. Judges and prosecutors, they argue, undervalue what forensics can prove because the law leaves it ambiguous. Naming it an independent evidence category is their central recommendation.
pmc-13263847:
Jun-Wei Pan and colleagues described in 2026, step by step, how to clear pelvic lymph nodes during a kidney and ureter removal done entirely from behind the abdominal cavity. Their patients lay on their side, an approach that spares the peritoneum but cramps the working space. pmc-13263947:
Pamela R Matías-García and a large team reported in 2026 on DNA methylation, a chemical mark on DNA, after mild SARS-CoV-2 infection. Using data from four large population cohorts, they asked whether marks in blood stay changed for months. The study sits inside the wider ORCHESTRA project.

pmc-13264347:
Charles Z Jiang and colleagues audit a cost-conscious single-incision repair for torn distal biceps tendons in a 2026 chart review. The technique reattaches the tendon at its natural site to restore twisting strength while limiting surgical harm. Eighty-four arms treated by two surgeons at one center between 2016 and 2024 met follow-up rules. Complete tears formed the majority, and records were checked for re-tearing, other complications, reoperation and operating times over the study period.

No re-ruptures were documented, a notable result for the primary endpoint. Overall complications affected about one quarter of arms, mostly minor nerve or skin issues typical of elbow surgery. Operating times averaged a little over an hour. Long-term data support the method durability while keeping its complication profile in view.
pmc-13264447:
Daniil Lisik and co-authors wrote a 2026 paper proposing a way to judge whether machine learning clusters are truly useful in care. Such clusters sort patients into subgroups from data, but many never help doctors in practice. No shared guide existed for checking their real value.

The authors set out three tests. First, a cluster must be relevant to care and tied to outcomes that matter. Second, it must stay stable and hold up in new groups of patients. Third, doctors must be able to spot it with ease in daily work. They argue these checks would help readers sort strong cluster papers from weak ones and guide future work toward patient benefit.
pmc-13264747:
Bingbin Dong and colleagues examine heavy node spread in otherwise small breast cancers in a 2026 population study. Among more than sixty thousand patients with small tumors recorded in a national registry from 2010 to 2012, under three percent had extensive node involvement. The comparison group held patients with limited or no node spread, assembled for the analysis.

pmc-13264847:
Zufar Mulyukov and colleagues published a 2026 modeling study on dosing of brolucizumab, an eye drug for wet age-related macular degeneration, a sight-stealing disease of older adults. pmc-13264947:

pmc-13265647:

Results held in sensitivity checks without volume weighting. The authors argue system-wide safety culture shapes even specialised surgical results.
pmc-13266047:
Seongbeom Park and a large team published a 2026 study predicting which patients with mild cognitive impairment will progress to dementia, using CT scans instead of costly MRI or spinal fluid tests. pmc-13266147:
Hyungil Lee and colleagues test a homeopathic supplement in nursery pigs under vaccination and regrouping stress, published in 2026. Modern pig production repeatedly stresses young animals. pmc-13266847:

pmc-13267247:

pmc-13267447:

pmc-13267547:

pmc-13268047:

pmc-13268147:

pmc-13268947:

pmc-13269647:

pmc-13270147:

pmc-13270747:

pmc-13270847:

pmc-13271147:

pmc-13271547:

pmc-13271947:

pmc-13272147:

pmc-13272347:

pmc-13272447:

pmc-13272847:

pmc-13273447:

pmc-13274147:

pmc-13274247:

pmc-13274847:

pmc-13275147:

pmc-13275447:

pmc-13275647:

pmc-13276147:

Past music studies also leaned on what patients said they felt, rather than measurable body signals. The authors recommend pairing patient reports with brain and body assays in ongoing trials. They also propose using artificial intelligence to pick the right music for each symptom in a systematic way. Clearer definitions, they argue, would make results repeatable and easier to scale.
pmc-13276247:
Suchitra Biswal and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on whether eye scan measurements can predict vision in an inflammatory eye disease. Intermediate uveitis inflames the middle of the eye and threatens sight over time. The team tracked the choroid, a blood-rich layer under the retina, using light-based scans.

Ninety-one eyes from fifty-two patients had at least one follow-up visit. Eyes were classed as worsened, stable, or improved by clinical signs. Choroid thickness barely changed over time and did not differ between those groups. Still, thickness at the first visit predicted later sharpness of vision, after accounting for age and sex. Average thickness also predicted later central retina thickness. The authors propose baseline choroid measures as an early warning marker for this disease.
pmc-13276347:
David McWilliams and co-authors report a 2026 feasibility trial on pairing exercise therapy with optimized feeding after intensive care. Survivors of critical illness often leave the ICU weak from muscle wasting and poor nutrition. Support after ICU discharge is patchy, and whether a combined program can even be delivered was unknown.

The PHOENIX trial ran at two British university hospitals. Sixty eligible survivors were assigned by chance to enhanced physiotherapy plus tube-feeding optimization, or to usual care. Every recruited patient stayed in the trial for thirty days. Therapists delivered the exercise program on about four fifths of available days, beating the preset target. Calorie and protein targets were also met often enough to pass preset thresholds. The authors say a full trial of clinical and cost benefits is now warranted.
pmc-13276547:
Jianhua Liang and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on how the paths of breathing muscle weakness forecast chronic disease in older Chinese adults. Respiratory sarcopenia means loss of both general muscle and breathing strength. Single measurements miss how people change over time, so the team modeled trajectories instead.

Nearly forty-eight hundred middle-aged and older adults from a national aging study were followed. Breathing flow and arm-and-leg muscle mass defined the condition. Modeling sorted people into three paths: both measures high, one impaired, or both persistently low. About a fifth fell in the dual-low group. Versus the healthiest path, they faced much higher risks of new arthritis, asthma, chronic lung disease, and hypertension. The two declines amplified each other. The authors propose these paths as markers for sorting older adults by disease risk.
pmc-13276747:
Rifat Edizkan and co-authors release a 2026 image dataset for detecting a damaging tomato virus before symptoms appear. Tomato brown rugose fruit virus spreads fast and lingers in the environment, with few controls after infection. Early, pre-symptom detection is the main defence for greenhouse crops.

Two tomato and two pepper varieties were grown in controlled greenhouses in Adana, Türkiye, some infected and some healthy. Cameras recorded colour and near-infrared images over twenty-nine days from several angles. Infection status was confirmed with genetic testing at multiple points. The openly licensed dataset is organised into four labelled subsets for training detection models in precision farming.
pmc-13276847:
Yuanjia Zhang and colleagues investigate whether plastic particles from PET bottles worsen ischaemic stroke, in a 2026 study. PET microplastics are widespread pollutants now detected in human tissues, including brain. Their role in blood-vessel disease of the brain has stayed unclear.

Computer work first linked particle exposure to fifteen core genes tied to inflammation and oxidative stress. Mouse stroke models and stressed brain immune cells then tested the prediction directly. Exposed animals developed larger infarcts and worse nerve scores than unexposed animals. Brain immune cells drove stronger inflammation and oxidative damage under exposure. The authors present PET microplastics as an outside factor that can deepen stroke injury.
pmc-13277247:
Nayera S Khatab leads a 2026 rat study of two treatments against chemically induced liver cancer. A plant compound called quercetin and low-dose gamma radiation were tested alone and together in ninety male rats. The cancer-causing chemical raised liver enzymes and oxidative stress, meaning cell damage from reactive molecules, while weakening natural defenses.

Each treatment alone eased liver injury, lowered inflammation, and pushed damaged cells toward death. The combined treatment worked strongest, bringing most measures closest to normal and beating either single treatment. Tissue exams and cell tests matched the blood findings. Work in rats cannot prove benefit in people, but the pairing is the clear lead the study offers.
pmc-13277347:
Joyce Assunção Barros leads a 2026 study of training for nursing staff on palliative care, care that eases suffering in life-threatening illness. The work ran in a teaching hospital with nurses who care for adults and older people. Staff took a knowledge and confidence test, received teaching on the topic, and retook the test four weeks later.

A total of 179 nursing professionals took part, with an average age of about forty. Knowledge scores rose clearly after the teaching. Confidence scores also rose, though the authors' summary reports the gain in mixed terms. Both changes passed standard statistical checks. The team says such training can support wider use of good palliative care in health services.
pmc-13277447:
Zahidul Hasan Tushar and co-authors review two emerging chicken breast defects in a 2026 article. Fast industry growth for cheap protein has brought muscle disorders linked to rapid growth. Spaghetti meat frays the main breast muscle into a stringy texture, while gaping splits the smaller tender muscle.

Reported spaghetti meat rates range widely, from a tenth to over a third of birds in some flocks. Under the microscope both defects show fibre degeneration, scarring, and fat infiltration. Genetics, feed, housing, and processing steps such as delayed chilling all play a part. Detection still relies on visual scoring, though electrical and imaging methods are under study. The authors urge combined fixes across breeding, nutrition, and processing.
pmc-13277747:
Yupei Liu leads a 2026 computer-based study of whether artificial sweeteners may contribute to autoimmune diseases, illnesses where the immune system attacks the body. Sweeteners are widely used, but their immune effects are poorly understood. The team combined toxicity prediction, genetic analysis, gene mapping, molecule modeling, and gut microbe data.

Toxicity tools flagged high immune harm potential. Genetic analysis tied artificially sweetened cereal intake to a modestly higher risk of autoimmune disease. The work named 209 related genes and six core target proteins, with pathways tied to immune signaling. Sweeteners may also suppress a helpful gut bacterium. All results are computational leads, not proof of harm in people, a limit built into the design.
pmc-13278447:
Agness Thawani leads a 2026 study of rapid HIV tests run by lay providers in Malawi. Finding advanced HIV disease needs a CD4 cell count test plus screening for two dangerous infections, but lab access is limited. The study compared finger-prick lateral flow tests run by HIV diagnostic assistants against nurse-run reference testing in 308 participants.

Lay providers identified low CD4 counts with about ninety-five percent sensitivity and about ninety-two percent specificity, beating laboratory technicians on both measures in this study. Their other two tests agreed with nurse results in about ninety-eight percent of cases. Costs per CD4 test ran lower with the lay-run test than with the nurse-run device. Task-sharing could widen screening, the authors argue.
pmc-13278847:
Andrea Fuller wrote a 2026 editorial on two years as editor-in-chief of the journal Conservation Physiology. Fuller calls the term hard but enjoyable. She worked to hold high standards while building a diverse, supportive community, with strong backing for early-career researchers. Staff at the journal, its publisher, and the Society for Experimental Biology are credited for its strong position.

Board renewal is a theme. New members widen skills and the range of countries covered. Editors now serve four-year terms, renewable once, and plant science coverage is growing. Manuscripts increasingly arrive from beyond the journal's old base in North America and Australia. They now span Latin America, Asia, Europe, and Africa. A call for papers on modeling in conservation continues the push for breadth.
pmc-13278947:
B. Langley and co-authors report a 2026 study of carbon stored in sea floor mud in the far north. They ask where organic carbon, meaning carbon from living things, builds up most in Arctic and sub-Arctic seas. Those seas warm at least three times faster than the world mean rate.

The team used more than thirteen thousand mud samples and a computer model to map the stores. They found the Baltic, Barents and Chukchi Seas hold the largest shares for their size. Stores grew fastest near coasts, on shallow shelves and close to large Arctic rivers. Just about ten percent of the surface store lies in protected areas, so most of it faces risk from human harm.
pmc-13279447:
Tingyu Li and colleagues report a 2026 case of a newborn with a rare hormone and ammonia disorder. The syndrome joins too much insulin, which drops blood sugar, with high blood ammonia. It stems from faults in the GLUD1 gene, which codes a key enzyme in insulin cells. Their patient fell ill just forty three hours after birth.

The baby had severe low blood sugar and seizures, a classic start for the syndrome. Blood tests showed the paired pattern of excess insulin and raised ammonia without symptoms from the ammonia itself. The child responded well to diazoxide, a drug that curbs insulin release. Gene tests found a new missense change, a single letter swap, in the gene form and proved the diagnosis. New gene finds widen the map for fast newborn diagnosis.
pmc-13279747:
Marijn C T Tacken and colleagues published a 2026 prospective study measuring how many practice scans nurses need before they can reliably judge stomach contents with bedside ultrasound. Eight bachelor-level nurses with no ultrasound experience entered a structured training program. They scanned healthy volunteers whose recent eating status was randomized and hidden from them, with expert examiners as the reference standard.

Across 512 assessments, every nurse reached the competence bar, set at a 90 percent success rate over ten consecutive scans, after a median of 23 attempts. Learning-curve modeling put the requirement near 30 scans for a 95 percent success rate. The authors conclude that structured training reliably brings nurses to competence on healthy subjects. They note the volunteers had normal anatomy and no diabetes, so performance on complex postoperative patients still needs its own study.
pmc-13280747:
Zhenyu Yang and colleagues wrote a 2026 review on better ways to deliver melatonin, the sleep hormone. Melatonin can fight cell damage and swelling and may help many diseases. But it dissolves poorly in water and the liver breaks it down fast. Little of a swallowed dose reaches where it is needed. Walls in the brain, skin, and gut block it as well.

The review covers tiny carriers built to slip past those walls. It explains how carrier design fits each route, such as by mouth, skin, or nose. It sums up lab tests in models of brain disease, heart attack, eye disease, low mood, and cancer. The authors close with blocks to clinic use, such as making the carriers at scale and proving long-term safety.
pmc-13280847:
Pitchapa Pittayavinai and colleagues published a 2026 study converting zinc battery casings into a catalyst that turns carbon dioxide into ethylene, a chemical feedstock. Spent zinc-carbon batteries are a poorly recycled waste stream. The team oxidized recovered casings into zinc oxide nanorods and decorated them with copper oxide particles. They then ran carbon dioxide electrolysis across a range of voltages.

The catalyst produced ethylene at one voltage setting, with a Faradaic efficiency of 5.62 percent, meaning that share of the charge ended up in ethylene. Minor methane, carbon monoxide, and hydrogen formed alongside. After reuse, the catalyst still made the simpler gases but no ethylene. Images showed the copper particles had clumped and detached, killing the active sites. The efficiency is modest, and the authors present the work as a proof of route: battery waste can become a catalyst. Keeping its structure intact through reuse is the next problem.
pmc-13281547:
Angela Luzia Herscheid and colleagues published a 2026 case report on a young woman who froze into stillness. She was nineteen and carried a rare gene flaw, missing the tip of one chromosome in some cells. After a COVID infection she fell into catatonia, a state of mute stillness and stiff limbs. She held odd poses, refused input, and withdrew. Brain, infection, and immune checks all came back clear. A brain wave test showed brief odd bursts on one side.

A calming drug called a benzodiazepine brought her speech back within a day. All the frozen signs cleared within four days. Later brain wave tests were normal, and the state did not return. To the authors' knowledge, this gene flaw has never been tied to catatonia before. They warn that stress, like a virus, may trigger the state in such patients. Early drug care, they stress, can cut it short.
pmc-13281947:
Margarethe Woeckel and colleagues linked traffic fumes to brain change in a 2026 study. Long exposure to road fumes is a known health risk. Germs of the idea hold that fumes may reach the brain along the smell nerve. The team used head scans from a population study in Augsburg, Germany. Four hundred adults, averaging fifty-six years, were scanned. Models estimated each home's long-term fume load. Scans read white matter scars, tiny bleeds, brain sizes, and the smell bulb's glow.

Higher fume loads went with higher odds of white matter scars. The link held for soot-dark particles and showed in most brain zones. Rear zones also tied to nitrogen gas and coarse dust. The team then tested whether the smell bulb carried the fume effect to the wider brain. The bulb is treated as a suspect bridge. The authors say fumes mark the aging brain.
pmc-13282247:
Dotun Ojo and co-authors propose a 2026 treatment algorithm for pilonidal disease, based on thirty years of outcomes at two British hospitals. Pilonidal disease is a chronic infected condition near the tailbone, mostly in young people. It disrupts work and social life, and no single treatment cures everyone. Their proposal matches the operation to disease severity, instead of using one approach for all.

The cohort covered one thousand three hundred eight operated patients treated between 1991 and 2021 under one clinician. Four methods were used, from pit-picking and a small trephine tool to cleft closure and laying the tract open. Disease was sorted into four types by its spread and past surgery. Mild disease can be handled with non-cutting methods, while wider disease needs removal with closure away from the midline. The authors argue that selection by type should cut failures and spare mild cases needless big operations.
pmc-13282347:
Juliane Silberschmidt Freitas and Renan Nunes Costa report a 2026 study on how warming changes the harm of metals to tropical tadpoles. Amphibians are highly exposed to pollutants as larvae in shallow ponds. The team tested five metals on tadpoles of two frog species at twenty-eight and thirty-four degrees Celsius. They measured the dose lethal to half the animals over ninety-six hours, then built sensitivity curves with data from other species.

Copper was most toxic in both species, and nickel least or near least. In almost all cases, higher temperature made the metals more deadly at a given dose. One species could not be fully tested for lead, for lack of tadpoles. Lead-exposed tadpoles developed body swelling. Both study species ranked among the most sensitive overall. The authors argue that safe water limits should account for heat, especially in warm regions facing climate change.
pmc-13282547:
Mingchen Sun and co-authors present a 2026 study on a simple blood ratio as a marker of heart failure risk in people with high blood pressure. The ratio, shortened to NPAR, combines neutrophil percentage, a measure of inflammation-linked white cells, with albumin, a blood protein that falls in poor health. The team analysed three thousand forty-five adults with hypertension from a United States national survey in 2017 to 2020.

Heart failure affected about six percent of this group, and those with it had higher ratio values. After full adjustment for age, lifestyle, and other diseases, higher values still meant greater odds of heart failure, rising in a roughly linear way. The ratio sorted cases with acceptable accuracy, and a best cut-off value was identified. Drinking habits and past stroke changed the strength of the link in subgroups.
pmc-13282847:
M Alibone and co-authors present a 2026 study checking whether a large German health insurance research database fairly represents the population for epidemiology studies. The InGef database holds anonymised claims from about ten million people with statutory health insurance. The team compared it with national statistics and registries over 2015 to 2023, using lung cancer and asthma as test cases, with age and sex adjustments.

Age and sex matched the general population closely, deviating by under one percentage point. Overall mortality ran slightly below national figures. Standardised asthma prevalence rose then fell across the period, and asthma antibody prescribing matched insurance benchmarks almost exactly. Lung cancer incidence averaged about forty-two cases per hundred thousand people, closely matching registry data. The authors conclude the database is a valid, reliable source for population research, provided analysts apply suitable methodological adjustments.
pmc-13283147:
Sloppy training labels, more than model size, may cap self-driving vision in bad weather, Dalal Z Zreiqat's 2026 experiments suggest. Car vision works well in clear daylight but fails more in rain, fog, snow, and night. The team asks how much faulty training labels hold back small detectors.

Tests used road images from the MUSES dataset across five weather types. Lightweight YOLO models were trained on raw labels and then on cleaned labels. A strong teacher model drafted new labels, and a human checked and fixed them. Clean labels lifted detection scores sharply under the same training setup. The authors argue that data quality, not model size alone, limits all-weather driving vision.
pmc-13283347:
Aishwarya Kamble and co-authors pooled trial evidence in 2026 on timing of invasive care after a type of heart attack called NSTEMI, where an artery is partly blocked. The question is whether opening the artery within a day beats waiting longer. The team searched three databases and followed standard review methods, combining results from ten studies.

Five studies favoured early action, four found no clear gain, and one saw more harm. The combined figures showed lower overall death rates and fewer heart failure readmissions with early care. No clear gain appeared for repeat heart attack or heart death at five years. Most studies came from wealthy countries, so the authors warn the findings may not transfer to places with few catheter labs.
pmc-13283447:
Mohamed Ali Ben Halima and co-authors traced in 2026 which French private-sector workers move from sick leave to a disability pension. France counted 843,000 pension recipients in 2022, so the path matters for cost and prevention. The team followed 228,514 insured employees from 2018 to 2023, covering nearly 365,000 sick leave spells.

About two in every hundred spells ended in a disability pension. Risk ran higher for workers aged fifty and over, those on the lowest pay, staff in large firms, and some higher-status groups. Sick leave past 180 days raised risk sharply, while part-time therapeutic work lowered risk only for short spells. Most risk factors faded after twelve months. The authors flag that first year as the window where support counts most.
pmc-13283947:
Whether CT scans judge vessel invasion in pancreas cancer as well as surgery and tissue checks is tested by Gala Nacul Mora and colleagues in 2026. Correct staging shapes whether removal surgery should proceed at all. Three radiologists read scans independently for fair comparison.

Records covered 103 untreated patients who had successful primary removal surgery. Median age was 68 years, and most patients were male. Reader agreement was strong for vein invasion and moderate for artery invasion. Surgeons found vein involvement in about a third of patients during operations. Tissue checks found vein invasion in a smaller share than scans suggested.
pmc-13284147:
Cristian Osgnach and co-authors proposed a fresh way in 2026 to measure mechanical load in rugby. Knowing how much work players do guides training, fatigue care, and injury prevention. Standard GPS measures treat speed and acceleration separately, which can misread hard efforts that start at high speed. Their approach builds each player's acceleration-speed profile and turns it into external power, one combined figure for running work.

Data came from 51 professional matches across two seasons. Backs recorded more high-power actions and more total external work than forwards. Fixed acceleration thresholds misclassified some demanding efforts, mainly those beginning at pace. The authors present external power as a companion to current GPS measures and call for work linking it to body responses and contact demands.
pmc-13284447:
Ponticorvo and colleagues piloted an unusual brain scanning method in 2026 that reads both neural activity and spinal fluid movement at once. Ultrashort echo time imaging catches fresh blood flowing into the scan slice, giving a signal tied to flow rather than the usual oxygen marker. Thirteen volunteers performed a visual task in a very strong 7-tesla scanner while the team recorded breathing and heart signals for comparison with standard imaging.

The method found solid, repeatable activation in visual cortex across participants. Its contrast was weaker than the standard method's, but group maps and statistical power came out similar. The spinal fluid signal in the fourth ventricle, a fluid cavity in the brain, moved against the signals in cortex and neck arteries and was driven mainly by the task itself. The authors say the approach can probe how blood and fluid dynamics interact to keep the brain in balance.
pmc-13284547:
Elena Gloria Torres García and co-authors describe a 2026 case of a rare fungal prostate infection in a man with type 2 diabetes. The 72-year-old had poor diabetes control and an enlarged prostate, but lacked the usual hospital-linked risks for invasive Candida infection. He arrived with fever, urinary symptoms, and a sharply raised prostate marker.

Urine and blood cultures both grew Candida glabrata, pointing to prostate infection that spread to the blood. No other source was found despite a full workup. The authors note his dapagliflozin treatment, which raises urine sugar, may have added risk alongside blockage and diabetes. They urge alert care when several such risks meet.
pmc-13285747:
Binjin Zhao and co-authors probe blood markers that may link metabolic syndrome with thinking decline in older adults, in a cross-sectional study from 2026. The syndrome bundles belly fat, high blood pressure, and poor sugar and fat control. The team asked which small molecules in blood carry its effect on memory and attention.

Banks of blood from 42 patients with the syndrome and 42 healthy peers were read with magnetic resonance profiling. Thirteen molecules stood out between the groups, among them amino acids, lactate, and a marker of inflammation. Several of these molecules carried part of the link between the syndrome and weaker delayed recall. Lactate alone carried the whole link with attention, a clue the authors say needs tests over time.
pmc-13285847: Zhaolai Guo and co-authors issued a correction in 2026 for their 2024 study of how maize roots make flavonoid compounds under lead stress. The notice is a correction only. The authors state that the extra files for the study were left out of the first published version. They have now sent those files again so the record can be fixed. They state that the study's findings stand as they were. An editor at the journal approved the change, and the first version has been updated.
pmc-13286147:
Wanjun Ma and co-authors build a deep learning model that predicts whether a drug will bind a target protein in a 2026 methods study. Labs can test such pairs directly, but the cost and time make wide screening impractical. Their model reads a drug as a graph of atoms and a protein as a chain of letters, then uses shared attention to fuse the two views before judging the pair.

Trials on three public benchmark sets put the model ahead of rival methods on the standard scoring measures. Cutting out the shared attention step hurt accuracy, which confirmed that the fusion does real work. High-confidence calls from the model also lined up with pairs that make biological sense on inspection. Code is posted in public, and the authors pitch the tool as a way to rank pairs for costly wet-lab checks.
pmc-13286247:
Xiyuan Li and colleagues test farm-belt dust against human immune cells in a 2026 laboratory study. Airborne particles from California's Imperial Valley and San Joaquin Valley rank among the nation's dirtiest, and their size and recipe shift with field work. Human macrophage cells met three size grades of dust from both valleys while the team read inflammation genes, cell survival, and a chemical-sensing receptor.

Gene responses shifted with dust source, size grade, and exposure length all at once. Imperial Valley dust generally stirred stronger gene activity than Parlier dust of matching size. The smallest and largest grades hit hardest in twelve-hour runs, while the tiny and fine grades switched on the chemical-sensing pathway most. Coarse dust instead drove a separate inflammation route, evidence the authors tie to distinct particle mixtures calling on distinct cell machinery.
pmc-13286347:
Ashley N Peterson and Matthew J McHenry model how small fish dodge a slow stalker in a 2026 simulation study. Lionfish hunt damselfish not by speed but by dogged pursuit and a sudden sucking strike, so classic flee-fast math misses the contest. Their agent-based model pairs a lionfish that steers straight at its target with a damselfish that darts in bursts, biased away from danger.

Simulated chases lasted about as long as real ones recorded in tanks. Probing which traits mattered most flipped the expected answer: prey lasted longest by swimming toward the predator, not away. A lionfish turns sluggishly, so a bold dash past its nose buys escape room that flight cannot. The work shows how coupled models can surface survival tricks that distance-based theories overlook.
pmc-13286447:
Viola Bianca Serio and co-authors introduce a 2026 journal collection on sharpening precision medicine by joining artificial intelligence with multi-omics data. Care is shifting from one-size-fits-all treatment toward plans built for each patient. Combining genome, protein, and metabolite data creates maps too complex for ordinary statistics to read.

Studies in the collection use deep learning to sort patients into groups and graph-based models to chart how molecules interact. Themes include fresh biomarkers for chronic disease, reusing existing drugs for new purposes, and predictions that respect each person's genetic makeup. The editors also flag hard problems: messy data standards, models that clinicians cannot inspect, and privacy during shared learning across hospitals.
pmc-13286747:
Barbara Pala and co-authors examine whether a common cholesterol drug protected cancer patients' hearts during chemotherapy with doxorubicin, a drug known to damage the heart. Their 2026 study reviews 80 patients treated with anthracycline regimens. Heart checks included tracings, blood tests, and pumping-strength measurements before and after treatment.

Only seven patients developed a weak heart by the formal definition, yet many more showed early electrical changes. Those changes clustered in patients not taking simvastatin. Most patients whose tracings stayed stable were taking the drug. Treated patients also lost far less pumping strength on average. Adjusted analyses kept the association, and the authors suggest that fat-soluble statins may blunt early heart injury, while noting the study was not randomized.
pmc-13286847:
Fuchao Qu and co-authors report a 45-year-old man whose coronary arteries kept clamping shut after a stent, despite standard anti-spasm medicine. The 2026 case report describes attacks at night and early morning. He could not tolerate the main drug because his resting heart rate was already low, and provocation testing in the lab reproduced severe spasm and his chest pain.

His pattern suggested overactive vagal nerve influence. Guided by a three-dimensional heart map, doctors ablated clusters of autonomic nerve cells on the heart. Repeat provocation then caused only mild spasm that faded on its own. Two months later his angina had vanished. The authors propose nerve ablation as an option for drug-resistant spasm with high vagal tone.
pmc-13287147:
Ana Beatriz de Almeida Duarte and colleagues ran a 2026 laboratory feeding study on whether adding the enzyme xylanase to tropical grass haylage could cut methane output in rumen fluid. Four grass cultivars, Andropogon, Mombaça, Massai, and Marandu, were each tested with and without the enzyme.

Forty baled lots were opened after ninety days and mixed into complete rations for bench incubations. Cultivars differed in protein level and in the mix of fermentation acids produced. Xylanase left breakdown of organic matter and total gas unchanged, though methane showed a downward tendency. The authors say other enzyme doses still need testing before firm claims can be made.
pmc-13288447:
Ting and co-authors test a theory about how people reason through close and distant relationships. Their 2026 study uses strong-ties and weak-ties rationality scales, which measure logic centred on family and close friends versus logic centred on wider contacts. They asked whether these outlooks predicted stigma, help-seeking, and health behaviour during COVID-19 in four societies.

The team surveyed 918 people drawn from Han-Chinese, Chinese-Malaysian, Malay-Malaysian, and White-Australian groups. Strong-ties reasoning was linked more strongly to public stigma, to seeking help from close ties, and to personal care habits. Weak-ties reasoning was linked more strongly to public health behaviours such as following population-level guidance. The strength of these links also differed between the Han-Chinese and White-Australian samples.
pmc-13288547:
Peng Liu and co-authors mine intensive care databases in a 2026 retrospective study of a lipid ratio called the atherogenic index of plasma. They analyzed 5,872 critically ill patients with cardiovascular disease in the MIMIC-IV database, checked findings again in the eICU database, and focused on the most severe stage of acute kidney injury.

Severe kidney injury struck 20.7 percent of patients overall and climbed steadily across index quarters, as did the need for dialysis treatment. Higher index values stayed tied to severe injury and dialysis after adjustment, to longer hospital and unit stays, and, partly through kidney injury, to dying in hospital. Prediction models performed especially well for dialysis need, supporting the index as a cheap early warning marker.
pmc-13288947:
Liangshan Mu and colleagues describe a 2026 trial plan for a malaria drug in PCOS. Polycystic ovary syndrome disrupts periods and hormones. A past small trial gave hopeful signs for dihydroartemisinin. That drug is known by the short name DHA. No fair test against placebo exists yet.

The new trial will enroll 150 people with PCOS. Half will get DHA pills for 90 days. Half will get placebo pills instead. Neither group will know which they take. The main goal is return of regular periods. Staff will also track ovary counts and metabolism. Results should show if the drug truly helps.
pmc-13289347:
Joseph V Sakran and coauthors propose a 2026 framework for hospitals facing immigration enforcement inside care spaces. Emergency rooms, wards, and restricted areas have seen enforcement activity that can scare patients and disrupt urgent care. Trauma bays and operating areas face the highest risk of delay and lost trust during such encounters.

The nonpartisan plan rests on duties to keep patient information private, follow emergency care law, and guard clinical areas. Three phases guide action: prepare ahead, respond step by step during an encounter, and support patients and staff after. Concrete steps include a written policy, a round-the-clock legal contact, staff training, and keeping immigration status out of records unless truly needed.
pmc-13289447:
Asmaa Wafeeq Abdelaziz led a 2026 comparison study on a fat-related blood protein, FABP4, as a possible marker for autism spectrum disorder in children. Fat metabolism and its hormone-like signals draw growing interest in autism research. The team tested whether blood levels separate autism from intellectual disability and from typical development in young children.

Ninety children aged 3 to 12 were split evenly into autism, intellectual disability, and healthy control groups of 30 each. Blood levels ran much lower in both autism and disability groups than in controls. Levels separated either group from controls almost perfectly in this small sample. They separated autism from intellectual disability poorly, however, and did not track with age, body mass, or autism severity.
pmc-13289947:
Sai Veena Sunkara and coauthors assess a 2026 grid study on how hydropower loss affects resource adequacy in the western United States grid. Hydropower supplied about a quarter of nameplate capacity in 2020, yet drought, operating limits, aging dams, and water needs squeeze output. The team simulated 16,384 loss scenarios mixing fourteen major water regions to find which regions matter most for keeping the lights on.

Full regional loss is unlikely, but stress tests expose outsized roles clearly. Even after accounting for installed size, Pacific Northwest hydropower contributed most to system-wide adequacy in the results. Northern California and the Desert Southwest added moderate support on top. Tree models also revealed compounding when regions fail together.
pmc-13290447:
Sixty-one cases of thyroid lymphoma, a rare cancer that is hard to recognize, are reviewed by Shuchang Li and colleagues in a 2026 cohort study. The cases come from the First Affiliated Hospital of Zhengzhou University, diagnosed between 2014 and 2025, and were analyzed for presentation and treatment.

Two-thirds of patients also had Hashimoto's thyroiditis, and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma was the most common subtype, at 60.7% of cases in the series. Survival stood at 85.0% after one year, 78.4% after three years, and 75.6% after five years. Within the B-cell group, chemotherapy was independently tied to longer survival, while age of 60 or more and high C-myc expression predicted earlier progression. Li and colleagues argue that staging should guide management when disease extends beyond the thyroid.
pmc-13290947:
A rare blue plant oil can be made sweeter-smelling without losing its punch, Ting Fang and colleagues show in a process study from 2026. Artemisia umbrosa yields a chamazulene-rich blue essential oil, but extraction is inefficient and the raw odor is pungent, blocking industrial use.

The team tuned ultrasound-assisted distillation to a 1:13 material-to-liquid ratio, 3 hours 20 minutes, and 2% salt. Then they polished the oil with silica gel to strip harsh notes while keeping the blue color and chamazulene steady. The finished oil held 36 volatile constituents with chamazulene at 50.68%. It beat a related yellow oil on antioxidant tests and killed Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli at low doses, before and after deodorizing. Fang and colleagues warn the blue pigment frays under heat, light, and oxygen, but offer the route as scalable for natural preservation and cosmetics.
pmc-13291047:
Consent that people can change over time, built for a lung screening program in Taoyuan, Taiwan, is designed in a 2026 framework paper led by Jui-Chu Lin. Low-dose CT screening creates imaging and biobank data that may be reused for years, and one-time paper consent fits that long life poorly under privacy law.

A Web 3.0 platform lets participants in the Taoyuan screening program view and update their choices digitally at any point. Blockchain hashes lock each consent record for tracing, de-identified data sit in certified secure storage, and artificial intelligence helps with risk checks and governance. The system is being piloted toward an enrollment target of 15,000 people, offering a model other screening and biobank programs could copy.
pmc-13291247:
A rare kidney tumor of childhood still defies strong treatment. Zhigang Yao leads a 2026 mini review of care for this cancer. It strikes mostly in infancy and spreads early. Survival stays poor despite surgery and strong drug mixes.

Most tumors share loss of one gene, SMARCB1. That loss shapes the cell control system in tumors. It also gives doctors a firm test for the disease. New drugs aim at weak points the loss creates. Two drug classes show early proof of concept. Immune drugs are also being tried. Clear markers to pick patients are still lacking. Kidney-specific trial data remain very thin.
pmc-13291547:
Drug-proof gut bacteria need a fresh kind of blocker. Soumyadip Ghosh and Sudha Ramaiah hunt one by computer in a 2026 study. Shigella flexneri causes severe diarrheal disease worldwide. Young children in poor lands bear the highest burden.

Standard drugs fail as the germ mutates its targets. Two enzyme targets change shape and shrug drugs off. The team trained learning models on known drug strength data. A library of drug cousins was screened in silico. Top picks faced toxicity and quantum checks. One molecule aims to block both targets at once. Mutant forms are included in that aim. Lab proof must come before any clinic hope.
pmc-13291747:
Bonnie Fraser and a large consortium present a reference genome for the eastern mosquitofish in 2026. Gambusia holbrooki is a small freshwater fish spread worldwide to eat mosquito larvae. It now ranks among the most damaging invasive fish, harming native species on several continents. The team assembled its genome into two parental copies and chose the primary copy as the reference. Chromosome-level scaffolding organized the sequence for annotation.

The assembly spans about 0.67 billion letters across twenty-four chromosome-scale pieces plus the mitochondrial genome. It rests on 421 contigs joined into 318 scaffolds, with strong continuity scores. Because the fish also anchors research on life history evolution, a solid reference serves two fields at once. Invasion biologists can trace which genes travel with successful colonizers. Comparative genomicists gain another member of a fast-growing fish family model. The resource comes from the ERGA-BGE genome program and is openly shared.
pmc-13292447:
Türkan Akyol Güner surveys a 2026 digital health tangle among older adults in Zonguldak, Türkiye, at a family health center. Three hundred three internet-using adults aged 65 and over, seen between March and December 2025, completed scales for online health literacy, cyberchondria, and perceived stress. Cyberchondria means health anxiety fed by repeated online searching.

All three measures sat at moderate levels on average. Literacy ran higher in women, the younger-old, and richer, better-educated, heavier internet users. Oddly, stronger eHealth literacy came with stronger cyberchondria, a firm positive link in the regression models. Cyberchondria in turn showed a small negative tie to perceived stress, while stress mostly followed health variables. Güner says teaching older adults to judge online health content may matter as much as teaching them to find it.
pmc-13292547:
Danny Tagle-Freire and colleagues test a 2026 processing puzzle: how the way oat protein is separated, and later heated, changes how well people could digest it. Three ingredients went head to head: a dry-fractionated concentrate, an alkali-extracted isolate, and a water-only extracted isolate, plus plain oat flour. Lab digestion followed the INFOGEST protocol, and hydrated samples were heated at two temperatures.

Protein digestibility spread widely, from 26.3 percent for the water-only isolate to 66.2 percent for the flour, with the concentrate at 61.4 percent in between. Starch digestion barely varied. Mild heating at 70 degrees changed nothing for protein, but 110 degrees cut flour digestibility by roughly 30 percent and concentrate by about 21 percent in their runs. Composition alone could not explain the gaps; particle shape and prior processing did.
pmc-13292647:
Sylvain Marcel Lybrecht Llinares sets out a 2026 scoping review protocol on a neglected intensive care question: how nurses adapt humanized care for migrant patients. The protocol, registered on the Open Science Framework before screening began, promises the first map joining three separate literatures on migration, ICU humanization models, and care across cultures in critical care. Searches in English, Spanish, and French will cover seven databases.

The review follows JBI methods and PRISMA-ScR reporting, with screening in Rayyan and thematic grouping across five objectives. The stakes are concrete: missing professional interpretation in ICUs is independently tied to higher mortality and readmission odds in the cited background. The protocol also answers 2024 critical care guidelines urging units to hunt down equity barriers in family-centered care. No results exist yet; the value lies in the map to come.
pmc-13292847:
Zijun Yan and co-authors test a Chinese version of a daily-life flexibility scale in a 2026 study with people who have obsessive-compulsive disorder. Rigidity in thought and routine is central to the disorder, yet standard lab tasks may miss how it feels day to day.

The 37-item scale was translated and given to 157 people, split between patients and healthy controls, with some patients repeating it after one month. The original five-part layout fit poorly in this group. Analysis instead supported 25 items in three parts, covering adapting to context, rigid thinking and behavior, and routine and control. Scores held steady over time, supporting careful use in clinics.
pmc-13293447:
Suraj Sapkota and co-authors hunt, in a 2026 study, for oat genes that resist crown rust, a leaf disease caused by a fungus that keeps evolving new strains. Lasting, broad resistance would help breeders build tougher oat varieties for farmers.

A breeding population from a cross of northern and southern parent lines was scored in four field settings over two years and mapped with 956 DNA markers. Six regions on five chromosomes shaped resistance, and two held up in a separate oat set. One major region on chromosome 7C worked across all settings. Linked markers could guide selection of resistant plants in breeding programs.
pmc-13293747:
Laura Grégoire and co-authors measure how sorghum and pearl millet release water through their leaves, in field-style experiments published in 2026. Both crops feed people in hot, dry regions, and how a plant paces its water loss under strong evaporative demand can decide survival in drought. The team tested 467 inbred lines across three outdoor platforms, from simple low-tech setups to precision weighing systems, comparing two ways of expressing the air's drying power.

Reference evapotranspiration, a weather-based index, explained plant water loss better than vapor pressure deficit in every experiment. Water loss rose in a straight line with demand rather than leveling off, and the slope of that line differed by genotype. In pearl millet the trait was strongly heritable across platforms. A low-cost platform worked well for screening large collections, which helps breeders select water-saving lines.
pmc-13293847:
Rudong Li and colleagues use large gene datasets in a 2026 study to hunt for fibroblast-linked genes that matter in colorectal cancer. Fibroblasts sit around tumors and can help them grow. The team combined single-cell sequencing, cell communication tools, network analysis, and five bulk datasets, then tested one lead gene in lab and animal work.

Single-cell data revealed 17 clusters across 10 cell lineages, with fibroblasts central in signaling. Network work produced 123 candidate genes, narrowed to five core genes. One gene, DRAM1, was higher in tumor tissue and chosen for validation tests covering growth, movement, and tumor formation.
pmc-13294147:
Mario Pescatori reviews surgery for anismus in a 2026 article. In anismus, the puborectalis muscle fails to relax during straining, blocking bowel emptying. The problem affects 44% of constipated patients with obstructed defecation in the cited figure and often travels with anxiety and depression, which lower cure chances. First-line care stays conservative, with biofeedback training and botulinum toxin shots.

Cutting the tense muscle can free emptying, but full division at St Mark's Hospital was abandoned after frequent incontinence. A gentler bilateral partial cut gave better function, though a Wexner group review found disordered continence in 12% of cases. Cure at 1 year was about 70%, so patient selection matters greatly.
pmc-13294347:
Ali Can Albaz and co-authors follow quality of life after laser surgery for urinary stones, in a prospective study published in 2026.
