Rapid blood tests measured oxidative stress and total antioxidant capacity in equal-sized groups. High stress alone did not split patients from controls, but it was far commoner once cancer had spread. Low antioxidant capacity appeared much more often in patients, most of all in metastatic ones. The combined pattern flagged advanced disease most strongly.
pmc-13608247:
Yueheng Ouyang leads a seven-author team testing a Chinese botanical formula against precancerous change in the food pipe. Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma develops through a long precancer stage, opening a window for gentler intervention. The team first charted the formula, Zishui Qinggan Yin, chemically: a panel of 40 compounds was monitored in extracts of the batch fed to mice, and 38 were confirmed.

In mice given a cancer-causing chemical, treatment was linked to lower-grade lesions. A battery of methods, from network analysis and docking to blotting and tissue staining, pointed at the PI3K/AKT/mTOR growth pathway. Activation marks fell across it, with fewer dividing cells and more dying cells. One exploratory test suggested the formula protects the AKT1 protein in tissue extracts. The authors are explicit: nothing here proves direct binding or that the pathway causes the benefit. The claim stays at association.
pmc-13612847:
Cerda, Suarez-Pellicioni, Wicha, and Booth study math in two languages in the brain, in work from twenty twenty-six. Bilingual people usually learn multiplication in their first language. They tend to solve problems faster and more exactly in that language.

Adult learners with limited second language skill checked small and large multiplication problems in both languages during brain scans. Small problems lean more on verbal memory, while large ones need more calculation. People were faster and more exact in their first language. Scan data showed how brain areas for language and number overlap or split by language. Proficiency shaped the gap, the study design suggests.
pmc-13613347:
Billal Tedbirt led a 2026 study of a rare blistering illness that attacks the moist linings of the mouth, eyes, throat, and other organs. Scarring in this illness can threaten sight and breathing. The work asked whether blood signals point to a drug target, and whether blocking one signal helps people whose disease stays active after standard care fails. Blood from patients was set against blood from healthy donors and from people with a related blistering illness.

The blood maps showed higher levels of several immune signals, most notably interleukin-6, than in either comparison group. Nine people with severe disease that had resisted prior care then received tocilizumab, a drug that blocks the interleukin-6 receptor. Their disease scores fell sharply on average. Seven reached partial remission and one reached full remission at the last check, with only mild side effects noted.
pmc-13614147:
Xingfeng Lei and colleagues report a 2026 study of aromatic polyimide plastics that glow, a pairing that has long been hard to achieve. Polyimides are tough, heat-resistant plastics wanted for future screens and lights, yet their strong internal charge shifts usually kill their glow. The team built the chains around tetraphenylethylene, a unit known for shining brightly even when crowded, making versions with two shapes of that unit and two partner building blocks.

Surprisingly, those main-chain plastics barely glowed at all, failing the hope placed in them. The paper follows that setback and the search for designs that keep the glow alive. Negative results like this one save other labs from repeating a dead end, and they point to where the charge problem bites hardest. The enhanced glow promised in the work comes from the design route the study tests next.
pmc-13614747:
Kaile Zhai and colleagues gather the case reports on infections by rare wild molds, in this review from twenty twenty-six. As more people live with weak immune systems, these little-known fungi invade more often. They are often misread, or treated the wrong way. The review covers cases from twenty twenty to early twenty twenty-six.

Most rare mold infections, the review finds, still yield to standard antifungal drugs. The deaths cluster in three spots. The mold is barely known, no drug is advised for it, or the mold is resistant by nature and no one suspected it. So naming the mold fast, and testing which drugs work on it, matter as much as the drugs. The authors also survey natural products active against these molds. They fold all of it into a plan, from fast naming to targeted treatment, meant to seed standard protocols.
pmc-13614947:
Sabirin and eight colleagues test whether washing surface starch off sago analog rice speeds its cooking, in a study from twenty twenty-six. The analog rice blends sago starch and fiber with rice flours. Partially pregelatinized starch binds the grains. Extrusion formed the rice under controlled heat and moisture.

A post-extrusion wash separated soluble amylose from the grain surfaces. Washed rice showed greater porosity and lower crystallinity. Its cooking time fell from roughly a quarter hour to under ten minutes. Antioxidants survived the washing step intact. Higher gelatinization onset also tracked with faster cooking. The authors target the quick-cooking rice at emergency relief and busy urban kitchens. It offers sago-based nutrition without the wait.
pmc-13616247:
Kangtai Xu leads a team showing in mice how switching on a cannabis-related receptor on pain-sensing nerves can ease pain after surgery without touching the brain. Painkillers that act only outside the brain are badly needed, since central side effects limit current options. Using mice with a surgical cut in the paw, plus mice whose pain nerves lack the CB1 receptor, the team pinned the effect to those nerves.

The receptor sits beside an acid-sensing channel called ASIC3 on the same pain fibres and physically links with it. Switching the receptor on damped the channel's currents and the calcium surges that follow, quieting the nerve and its pain signals. A peripheral switch that mutes a pain channel directly offers a route to after-surgery relief without sedation or addiction risk.
pmc-13616747:
Michael B. Pritz traces how the wiring between the thalamus and the forebrain first grows in the American alligator. This reptile's brain development can test whether rules drawn from mammals hold across backboned animals. A tracer dye that travels both ways along nerve fibres was placed in the relay region or in the forebrain bundles themselves. Four circuits appeared in the alligator embryos.

Three circuits rose from the dorsal thalamus toward the front brain. One bundle ran on the same side through the lateral path. Two ran through the medial path, and one of those crossed to the other side. The fourth circuit ran the other way, down from the basal nuclei to the thalamus, and it was the first to develop. Reptile wiring following a staged order much like that of mammals hints at an ancient shared blueprint for the forebrain.
pmc-13616847:
Khushal Gupta and four colleagues compare hypothalamic obesity in children and adults who survive craniopharyngioma, a rare tumor near the hormone control center of the brain. Damage to the hypothalamus during treatment can drive severe weight gain. Their scoping review draws on studies published between 2000 and 2025 and separates childhood-onset from adult-onset cases.

Obesity rises far more sharply after treatment in children than in adults, and severity tracks the extent of hypothalamic damage. The review links the condition to broken melanocortin signaling, leptin and insulin resistance, and inflammation in brain tissue. Weight-loss drugs and bariatric surgery help some patients, though trial results are mixed and direct age comparisons are lacking. Both groups face higher risks of diabetes, fatty liver disease, and early death, so care must be tailored by age.
pmc-13616947:
Mengyao Wang and five colleagues ask whether body composition measured on chest scans can flag people whose lungs show a high share of damaged, low-density tissue. They studied two hundred sixty adults aged forty and older who had chest and quantitative CT scans during health checks at Kaifeng Central Hospital between January 2023 and January 2025. Participants were graded by the percentage of low-attenuation lung area, a marker tied to emphysema-like change.

People in the highest grade had the smallest and least dense chest muscles, the least under-skin fat, and the lowest spine bone density, while fat infiltration of the chest muscle was highest. Several scan measures separated the highest grade with moderate-to-good accuracy, and the results held after checks for chance error. The authors suggest that one scan visit could usefully report lung damage and body composition together.
pmc-13617247:
Abdullahi Ali Roble and twelve colleagues present a neonatal case report from Somalia of a baby born with no eyes at all, a rare defect called bilateral anophthalmia. The three-day-old full-term boy was born in a rural, resource-limited setting, and examination confirmed the complete absence of both eyeballs. Brain imaging showed no further abnormalities inside the skull.

During his hospital stay the infant developed fast breathing while feeding, poor feeding, tiredness, and sweating, signs of significant shunting of blood inside the heart. Ultrasound of the heart revealed three defects together: holes between both the lower and upper heart chambers and a persistent ductus arteriosus vessel. With no advanced children's heart surgery available locally, doctors stabilized him and referred him abroad. The authors stress full body checks and fast referral whenever a newborn shows a major birth defect.
pmc-13617347:
Whitfield Jones and co-authors survey a fast-moving field in this 2026 narrative review of sepsis care. They read papers from January 2025 to June 2026 with care. The topics span screening, diagnosis, prognosis, and custom treatment. Sepsis is the body's self-harming response to infection. It is still grouped by bedside syndromes. Those predict results and treatment responses poorly.

The team sees three technologies converging. Rapid diagnostics name pathogens and resistance in hours. Multi-omics profiling sorts patients into biological subtypes. Artificial intelligence integrates both into dynamic calls. As a set, the tools could shift sepsis treatment away from one-size-fits-all playbooks. Care could move toward immunotherapies matched to the individual patient's state. Oncology made cancer care custom in a similar way, the authors note. Their caveats are about practice. New trial designs must validate the tools. Clinics also need the infrastructure to use them. Doctor engagement matters too.
pmc-13618947:
Timothy R. Entwistle and five colleagues audit how often therapies that work in small animals for acute injury become approved human treatments. Their systematic review gathered studies in rats, mice, and like models from 1990 to 2010. The review tested interventions not yet in routine care, then traced each therapy through trials, regulatory decisions, and post-market safety records.

Over twelve hundred studies yielded one hundred distinct therapies. Twenty percent reached human trials, matching the commonly quoted figure, but that number flatters reality. Of eighty-three drug therapies, only three, under four percent, won first-in-class approval for the tested indication, while fifteen failed trials outright. Eighty-six percent of drugs counted as successes by any definition later showed major safety concerns. The single drug still in routine caveat-free use was not a new translation. The authors say animal results predict approval far more weakly than headline rates suggest.
pmc-13619247:
Yaxian Yang, Chunyu Wang, Ruiyuan Xu, Wang Xuan, and Xiaoai Chen review and meta-analyze blood biomarkers of sarcopenia and sarcopenic obesity. These geriatric syndromes combine reduced muscle mass and strength, with obesity in the second. Their set biomarkers and paths remain unclear.

The authors searched major databases for fifteen years of work linking serum biomarkers to either condition. Eligible designs ranged from studies at one point in time to cohorts that track ahead and case series from past records. There were no bars on who was studied or on group size. Screening followed criteria set ahead. Data were drawn out, and study quality was graded. Pooled effects were worked out as mean differences, with confidence intervals. Forty-three papers entered the sum-up.
pmc-13619347:
Keng-Yin Lai and nine colleagues built a wireless needle probe that delivers DNA or RNA into tissue using a single electric pulse. Gene electrotransfer can move large therapeutic molecules into cells without a viral carrier, yet deep tissue targets are hard to reach. Their disposable probe pairs a laser-etched electrode array with tiny fluid channels and a low-conductivity carrier that focuses the field where it is needed.

Lab tests with human kidney cells carrying a glowing reporter gene showed the clamping approach widened the treated zone up to threefold. In mice, the probe produced lasting reporter expression in a leg muscle, standing in for deep tissue delivery. The device runs from its own capacitor and needs only one insertion point. The authors pitch it as a compact, low-cost route toward more precise gene therapies.
pmc-13619447:
Aya Nusir and four colleagues mapped how microglia, the brain's resident immune cells, are arranged in the hippocampus across a monkey's life. They used tissue from fifteen female rhesus macaques ranging from late pregnancy to over thirty years old. Spatial statistics measured cell density, spacing between neighbors, and clustering within the hippocampus and its subfields.

Cell density followed a U shape, falling after birth and then rising through adulthood and old age, with one subfield changing most. Cells sat farthest apart in the early postnatal period, and aged animals showed a wider empty zone around each cluster. In the oldest animal, clustered microglia sat near amyloid and tau deposits, the proteins linked to Alzheimer's disease. The authors offer their measurements as a baseline for studying immune change in the aging primate brain.
pmc-13619647:
Varisa Assapattarapun and thirteen colleagues report imaging findings for a rare, aggressive mouth cancer in a 2026 case report. Their patient, a seventy-eight-year-old man, had redness, swelling, and pain at the front of his lower jaw, with exposed bone and a growth poking through the skin. Doctors first suspected dead bone after earlier cancer treatment, though returning disease could not be ruled out.

Scans told a fuller story across several methods. X-ray showed a fuzzy pale area, CT measured a large mass destroying bone and reaching the skin, and MRI mapped damage through the jaw's outer plates. A PET scan showed intense uptake in the tumor with no spread to nodes or distant sites. Tissue from surgery confirmed basaloid squamous cell carcinoma. The authors stress that layered imaging guides decisions, while tissue testing still gives the final answer.
pmc-13620847:
Quyige Gao and twelve colleagues mapped how stress, anxiety, and poor sleep connect in Shanghai's public health nurses across two phases of emergency work. They surveyed every community health center in the city twice. The first round came during the acute crisis of late 2022, with over fifteen hundred nurses answering; the second a year later, during the grinding chronic phase, with even more respondents. Network models then charted which symptoms sat at the center of the web each time.

Overall distress eased in the chronic phase, yet the web itself rewired. During the crisis, unclear roles and heavy effort demands anchored the network alongside jumpy anxiety. During chronic strain, relentless workload and trouble relaxing took the center. Work stressors sat upstream in every model, feeding the rest. Younger nurses showed tighter symptom webs during the crisis. The authors say support must change with the phase, clarity first and recovery later.
pmc-13621347:
Rabbia Shoukat and seven colleagues created a two-job material built from a neodymium iron oxide perovskite spread over carbon nanotubes. Perovskites are crystal structures prized for catalytic tricks, and this one was aimed at both sides of clean technology: helping split water for hydrogen fuel and breaking down dye pollution under light. A long list of lab techniques confirmed the composite's structure and makeup.

Against a stubborn blue dye, the material removed nearly all color from a strong solution within five minutes under tuned conditions. On the electrical side, it drove the oxygen half of water splitting at a modest extra voltage with quick kinetics. Its large active surface beat the sluggish behavior that usually plagues that reaction. The authors argue the cheap nanotubes plus perovskite pairing rivals noble metal electrodes closely enough to merit scale-up work.
pmc-13621547:
Xiaowei Ma and ten colleagues tested gentle electrical stimulation of the scalp as a treatment for mild Alzheimer's disease, in a 2026 prospective trial. Alzheimer's brains show weakened gamma rhythms, the fast brain waves tied to memory. Patients at one Chinese hospital were randomized to real or sham stimulation at forty cycles per second over both parietal lobes, thirty minutes daily for fifteen straight days.

The stimulated group improved on global cognition, memory, language, attention, and executive function, and their behavioral symptom scores fell. The sham group barely moved. Gains held up reasonably at a ten-week check. Brain recordings showed information flowing more strongly from temporal and rear regions toward the front after treatment. Imaging found tighter links inside the default mode network and between it and a control network. The authors call the approach safe and feasible, with effects plausibly running through these network changes.
pmc-13621747:
Nikolai Ramadanov and colleagues tested whether ChatGPT can redo complex layered meta-reviews from hip studies. Language models now aid medical research, yet their grasp of stats-heavy layered models was unknown. Their rerun study collected seven earlier layered meta-reviews with data tables allowing solo reworking, spanning 40-plus pooled results.

ChatGPT's pooled results matched human-derived results closely, with small median gaps for number-based and binary results and minimal overall bias. Spread results also agreed, with larger gaps limited to extreme-spread or messy-input results. Ramadanov and colleagues back language models as adjunct rerun aids, with expert watch still needed.
pmc-13623147:
S Sakthivel leads a materials study on barium molybdate, a compound tested as an electrode for supercapacitors, devices that charge and release energy very fast. The team made the material in hot pressurised water and varied the cooking time from five to twenty hours to see how growth time shapes the particles and their performance.

Microscope work showed the particles growing from early nuclei into even, round, well-formed crystals, with the fifteen-hour batch the purest and most regular. That batch stored the most charge in tests and kept ninety percent of its capacity after ten thousand charge cycles. A full device pairing it with activated carbon delivered strong energy and power figures and kept most of its capacity after five thousand cycles. The authors explain the results through the stable crystal frame and the active molybdenum sites, and they propose the material for next-generation storage.
pmc-13624047:
See Yoon Kim, Zhengchao Xu, and Zsolt J Balogh systematically review whether researchers actually use the two agreed definitions of polytrauma, the condition of severe injuries in several body regions at once. The Newcastle and Berlin definitions were created over a decade ago to give the field one language. Without shared definitions, studies cannot be compared cleanly.

Following standard review methods, the team screened studies of polytrauma patients published from 2015 to the end of 2025. Of more than two thousand three hundred initial hits, only eighty-eight stated any explicit definition at all. Within that small set, ten used the Berlin definition and six used Newcastle, together under a fifth. Use peaked in 2024 but remained rare. The authors conclude that both consensus definitions are still under-used, and they call on journals and researchers to state and apply them.
pmc-13624547:
Dewan Imtiaz Rahman and a large surveillance team examine what predicts death in acute encephalitis syndrome, a sudden brain inflammation seen across Bangladesh. Their records came from the national Nipah watch system at eleven hospitals, covering January 2021 through December 2023. Staff screened patients in person and logged each case with a standard form.

Among 12,603 patients, about one in five died. Death rates differed sharply by region, with Rangpur the highest, and the odds rose for older patients, for women, and for people who reached hospital late. Patients aged sixty or more stood out as a high-risk group. The findings press for faster referral and closer early care where risk clusters.
pmc-13625947:
Jun Ma and co-authors design a tiny self-propelled carrier meant to swim deep into glioblastoma, the most aggressive brain tumor. Drug particles usually stall at a tumor's rim, so the team paired a ferritin cage, a natural protein shell that crosses the blood-brain barrier, with a cerium oxide engine. The engine splits hydrogen peroxide, common in tumor tissue, into oxygen, and the bubbles push the carrier up the peroxide gradient toward cancer cells.

In large tumor spheroids, the motors spread through the core while unpowered cages clung to the edge. Loaded with the chemotherapy drug doxorubicin, the motors killed tumor cells at a third of the dose unpowered cages needed, and a fifth of free drug. Animal tests are the stated next step.
pmc-13626147:
Asal M Abdulraheem, Khouloud A Alkhamis, Suhair S Al-Nimry, and Anjali Chauhan blend two blood pressure drugs into a single disordered solid to help them dissolve. Hydrochlorothiazide and valsartan each dissolve poorly alone, so the team made co-amorphous mixtures at three ratios by evaporating a shared solution, then probed the powders with X-ray, heat, and light-based tools. The mixtures proved truly glassy, one unified phase rather than two powders side by side.

The blends stayed stable in dry air for at least eight months and shrugged off heat to one hundred degrees. In buffer fluid both drugs dissolved far faster from the blends than from raw powders or loose mixtures. A validated liquid chromatography method let the team track both drugs at once, a practical step toward a combined pill.
pmc-13626547:
Kara Mizokami-Stout leads a team scoping a young research method that pairs momentary mood diaries with continuous glucose sensors in diabetes. Phone prompts can catch stress, sleep, and feelings as they happen, while sensors stream sugar readings, and together they might reveal how daily life moves glucose. Searching three databases from 2009 to late 2025, the reviewers screened 782 papers and kept nineteen that truly collected and analyzed both streams together.

Most kept studies enrolled adults, and three-quarters focused on type 1 diabetes. Diary runs lasted a median of two weeks with a handful of prompts a day, though designs swung wildly, from one prompt to twenty-eight. The review catalogs those choices and the gaps between them, giving the next wave of studies a firmer common playbook.
pmc-13627247:
Stefano Palomba and nine colleagues, publishing in 2026, ask whether breastfeeding shields women with polycystic ovary syndrome from lasting heart and metabolic trouble. The analysis drew on two prospective cohorts of 241 women whose pregnancies were complicated by high blood pressure or pregnancy diabetes: 101 with the syndrome and 140 without. Eighteen months after delivery, each woman was examined, monitored for blood pressure, and given a glucose tolerance test, with feeding history sorted into exclusive, partial, or formula.

Women with the syndrome breastfed for fewer months and exclusively far less often. Their rate of lasting blood pressure or sugar problems was nearly five times the controls' rate. Exclusive breastfeeding, though, stood out in adjusted models as a strong independent link to lower risk, which makes lactation support a cheap, drug-free lever for this high-risk group.
pmc-13627347:
Pieter Spee leads a large team testing a new antibody drug against cancer, in this twenty twenty-six paper. The drug targets a surface protein that helps tumors switch on a growth signal that also calms immune attack. Blocking that signal while drawing immune cells to kill tumor cells could hit cancer twice at once.

The antibody was built in human form with a sugar change that boosts cell killing. Lab tests checked its killing power, its block on the growth signal, and its safety around platelets. It was also compared with rival antibodies already tested in clinics. The results support moving the drug toward patient trials.
pmc-13629947:
Gowrie Balasubramaniam and fourteen colleagues ran ASGARD, a British feasibility trial comparing two treatments for gout flares in people whose kidneys are too weak for standard anti-inflammatory drugs. The double-blind study randomised twenty-one patients across four centres to five days of anakinra injections or a single steroid injection, with dummy treatments keeping everyone masked.

Recruitment fell short of target, the trial's main failure, though eligible patients joined at good rates, crossovers stayed rare, and pain diaries were well completed. Pain fell substantially over a week in both arms, with anakinra hinting at faster relief. Participants grumbled about questionnaire burden and treatment delays. The authors conclude a full trial is feasible with better community case-finding.
pmc-13630347:
Alex Skolnick and two colleagues interviewed ten teens and young adults about one therapy technique. All were aged fifteen to twenty-one and recovering from anorexia nervosa. The technique treats the illness as apart from the person, an outside controller. It anchors family therapy for the condition. Yet young people's own views of it are rarely gathered. The study appeared in 2026.

Three themes organised the accounts. Many first felt the illness as fused with who they were. They resisted the split as a threat. Later they found the framing freeing. It cut blame and guilt. It united families against the disorder. Holding that stance over time was its own struggle. The authors draw lessons for clinicians. They cover how to introduce the approach and how to sustain it.
pmc-13630847:
Masato Takii and six colleagues built the first questionnaire aimed at why patients with eating disorders steal, a behaviour clinicians see often yet researchers have barely measured. Published in 2026, the pilot study gave the new scale to forty-six women with anorexia nervosa held at a Japanese medical prison, all imprisoned for theft and none with stimulant abuse histories.

Statistical analysis sorted the items into three independent drivers: elation or pleasure around the act, material or monetary desire, and plain impulsivity. Answers were stable on retesting, and two factors lined up with the official diagnostic criteria for kleptomania while the desire factor pointedly did not. The authors offer the scale as a foundation for research into a neglected corner of eating disorder care.
pmc-13632847:
Juan Carlos Rivillas led a 2026 study of how childhood hardship in Colombia echoes into heart and metabolic health and faster biological aging in older adults. Adverse childhood experiences are known to harm later health, but their link to biological aging in Latin America was poorly understood. The team used a nationally representative survey of 3,385 adults aged sixty and older. They scored five hardships before age fifteen: emotional abuse, domestic violence, food scarcity, poor childhood health, and forced migration from armed conflict.

Among women, emotional abuse, domestic violence, food scarcity, and poor childhood health each raised the odds of cardiovascular disease. Among men, forced childhood migration raised risks of diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and hypertension. Forced migration also tracked with faster biological aging, more strongly in women, and cumulative hardship showed dose-response patterns.
pmc-13633147:
Luca Guerra and eight colleagues published this 2026 expert consensus on using PET scans to find lymphoma patients who should get cell therapy early. The lymphoma type, diffuse large B-cell, often returns after first treatment or never fully responds. CAR-T therapy, which retools a patient's own immune cells, can cure some of these patients, yet referral often comes late. The panel of imaging specialists and blood cancer doctors reviewed evidence on scan timing and measures.

Scans at diagnosis give tumor volume measures that sharpen risk estimates beyond standard scores. Scans during treatment can flag high-risk patients early through standard rating scales and changes in tumor uptake. A final scan after treatment remains essential for judging response. The panel calls the scan a central marker for this disease. They also demand shared standards for scanning and reporting so results match between hospitals.
pmc-13635047:
Marcus Varanis and three colleagues published this 2026 modeling study refining a classic math description of the circulation. Simple lumped models treat the heart and vessels as an electrical-style circuit, which keeps them fast and readable. Most versions assume artery stretchiness stays fixed, yet real arteries stiffen as pressure climbs. The team made aortic stretchiness vary with pressure in their closed-loop model of the heart, body, and lung circuits.

Under normal settings, the new model matched the classic one almost exactly, producing sensible pressures and flows. Away from that point, the rule changed mainly the pulse near the heart, while average pressure, stroke volume, and output stayed steady. Adjusting single parts reproduced the waveform fingerprints of a leaking aortic valve and stiffened arteries. The authors offer the compact model as a test bench for scenarios that would be impractical or unethical to stage in people.
pmc-13638047:
Lijuan Zheng and nineteen colleagues build a non-invasive test for alveolar echinococcosis, a dangerous parasitic disease caused by a tapeworm's larval stage in animal hosts. Diagnosis usually leans on blood antibody tests, which miss some patients and cannot separate active infection from old exposure. The team targeted a protein the parasite secretes abundantly. They raised monoclonal antibodies and pinpointed two short stretches of the protein that sit exposed on its surface.

Those two target stretches are strictly conserved across the parasite genus yet differ sharply from the matching host protein, promising clean recognition. Two test formats followed. The standout was a sandwich test that detects the protein directly in feces, catching most infections in mouse samples at an early stage with precise, repeatable readings. The authors present the proof of concept as a path toward screening animal hosts without blood draws.
pmc-13639047:
Zexuan Wu and eleven colleagues published a 2026 mouse study identifying the protein SORBS2 as a guardian of the heart's relaxation phase. Failure of the heart to relax properly underlies a common form of heart failure, yet the cell-level causes remain unclear.

Mice lacking SORBS2 in heart muscle cells developed worsening relaxation problems while pumping strength stayed normal, and many died early. Restoring the protein reversed the relaxation defects and extended life. The protein links cell adhesion, the internal skeleton, and calcium handling; without it, fibers scar and stiffen. A drug blocking one part of that chain partly rescued relaxation.
pmc-13639647:
Naoyuki Iwahashi and one colleague present a 2026 perspective arguing that mutant p53, the protein altered in nearly half of human cancers, can behave like an amyloid disease protein. Many cancer-linked mutants lose their shape, expose sticky segments, and clump into fibers that may seed further misfolding.

Such clumps have been found in ovarian, breast, and lung tumors and track with aggressive disease and poor outcomes. The authors propose treatments that block clumping, restore folding, clear misfolded protein, or stop spread between cells. Their framing borrows from brain disease research to open a new front in precision oncology.
pmc-13642247:
Leihong Wu and two colleagues present GANomics, a 2026 tool that turns gene data from old lab chips into the form made by modern gene reading, and back again. Labs hold decades of chip data that cannot be mixed with new data as they stand.

The system learns from a few samples run on both kinds of gear. It can then swap data either way. In one cancer group of 498 samples and about ten thousand genes, swapped data matched real data well with as few as ten shared samples. Five more data sets gave the same result. Old data can thus join new studies.
pmc-13642947:
Junyuan Wang and twelve colleagues present a 2026 study of RDP3, a food-derived peptide that speeds healing of oral ulcers. Mouth ulcers are common and painful, and current products mostly soothe symptoms rather than repair tissue in several ways at once.

At very low concentration the peptide accelerated mucosal repair in animals and cells and steadied the mouth's microbe balance. It works by blocking part of the interleukin-2 receptor, which quiets a harmful signaling route and stops an inflammatory cell-death process called pyroptosis. Less tissue burned away, inflammation eased, and the lining regrew. The authors position RDP3 as a multifunction ulcer therapy candidate.
pmc-13646147:
Rawan Abdul Mahdi Neyef Al-Saliti and five colleagues test a stress inoculation program for performance anxiety among physical education students at Ajloun National University in Jordan. Thirty students took part in a quasi-experimental study with a comparison group and a later follow-up check. The program taught coping in three stages: learning about stress, practicing mental and behavioral skills, and applying those skills to real performance situations. A purpose-built scale measured anxiety before and after.

Students who received the training reported clearly lower performance anxiety than the comparison group after the program. The gain was still present at follow-up, with no meaningful drift back. The authors conclude that stress inoculation works for this group and may help students face exams, demonstrations, and teaching practice with steadier nerves. They offer the staged program as a model other university courses could adapt.
pmc-13647347:
Hui Zhang and nine colleagues read the complete chloroplast genome of Rosa willmottiae, a wild rose valued as an ornamental plant with some medicinal use. Chloroplasts carry their own small genome, and its sequence helps untangle rose family history. High-throughput sequencing assembled the full circular molecule. The team catalogued its genes and compared it with relatives to place the species on the rose tree.

The genome runs just over one hundred fifty-seven thousand letters, split into two single-copy stretches and a repeated pair. It holds one hundred thirty genes, most of them protein-coding, plus the usual transfer and ribosomal RNA genes. The closest relative proved to be the Kushui rose, a cultivated hybrid. The analysis strongly supports this wild rose as that hybrid's mother-side ancestor. The authors offer the sequence as a reference for rose breeding and evolution studies.
pmc-13648147:
Chang Ho Jae and six colleagues, publishing in 2026, examine whether bisphenols measured in urine relate to metabolic syndrome in Korean adults. Bisphenols are hormone-disrupting chemicals found in plastics, and newer substitutes are replacing the best-known one, BPA, so the team also studied two alternatives, BPF and BPS.

Their sample held 2,639 adults from a national environmental health survey carried out in 2018 and 2019. Higher urinary BPF was linked with greater odds of metabolic syndrome, and the highest BPS group showed a similar link, while BPA showed no significant association. The authors present the findings as a baseline and call for long-term prospective studies.
pmc-13648747:
Yi Fang and eleven colleagues follow how sleep relates to cognitive decline at different ages, pooling three long-running cohorts of adults from midlife into very old age. Earlier findings conflicted, and poor sleep might either cause decline or signal its earliest stages, depending on life stage.

The combined sample held 16,884 participants with harmonised sleep and memory measures. Trouble falling asleep predicted faster memory decline around age fifty, but the link weakened and even reversed at advanced ages, and similar gradients appeared in all three cohorts. Short sleep showed a weaker version of the same pattern. The authors read midlife insomnia as a modifiable risk factor and late-life reversal as a possible early dementia sign.
pmc-13649447:
Nana Wang and six colleagues gathered the best current proof on drug-free ways to lift thinking in people with Alzheimer's disease. Drugs help only so much in this illness, so carers need clear guidance on other options. The team searched sources up to late January 2026 and graded what they found.

Fifteen works passed their screen, from one guideline to seven expert agreements, six reviews, and one trial. They distilled 18 key points in six groups: brain training and digital therapy, brain stimulation, exercise, daily life and memory-based care, music and sense-based care, and needle therapy and mixed plans. Staff should match the plan to each patient and watch quality in use, they advise.
pmc-13649647:
Mingwei Liao and eight colleagues present a vast open dataset of mouse brain neurons, built to train and test smart reconstruction tools, in a paper published in 2026. Tracing each neuron's full shape is key to mapping brain circuits, yet shared datasets with careful labels were scarce.

The team imaged whole mouse brains at fine detail, then joined machine tracing with proofreading by many human users. Their set draws on more than ten thousand neurons from 258 brains and holds about eight million graded data units, each tagged by how hard it is to trace. Users can pull data through an online interface or in bulk. The authors call it a benchmark for machine-driven neuron mapping.
pmc-13649747:
Hamad Alsawalqah and five colleagues asked what helps or blocks small and mid-sized firms in Jordan from taking up artificial intelligence tools. They spoke with 15 people: tool sellers, firms that had adopted the tools, and firms still weighing the choice. Answers were sorted with a frame that splits forces into tech, firm, and outer world.

Clear gains, good fit with old systems, boss support, funds, and past tech use all pushed firms toward adoption. Outer forces, such as rival pressure and rules, mattered too but unevenly. Sellers stressed skill and client readiness, while firms on the fence named cost, doubt, and staff pushback. The authors call the findings a local snapshot, not a rule for all poor lands.
pmc-13650047:
Alexander Muacevic and five colleagues report an older woman who developed dangerously low magnesium after about a year on a common acid-blocking drug. Such drugs, called proton pump inhibitors, are widely used for reflux and stomach acid problems and are usually well tolerated, which makes this rare complication easy to miss.

Her illness began with muscle cramps and tremors, then worsened to a seizure and confusion, with low calcium as the clearest blood abnormality and a classic hand spasm sign on examination. The team replaced the missing minerals and stopped the acid blocker, and she improved. A urine test that could have shown how magnesium was being lost could not be done, so the exact route of loss stayed unproven. The case warns clinicians to consider the drug link in long-term users with matching symptoms.
pmc-13650147:
Ethan T Cardwell and twelve colleagues, publishing in 2026, describe how they built the clinical pathway for Test it. That web-based service provides sexually transmitted infection testing aimed at Victorians aged 16 to 29. Moving a traditionally in-person service online risks losing quality, and little published guidance covers how such services should be designed.

The team worked through evidence review and repeated consultation with end users, clinical experts, and software developers alongside other stakeholders. Their paper lays out the ten steps of the online pathway, from ordering through results and treatment, and narrates the problem-solving used to settle each step. The goal was a service as safe and acceptable as clinic care. The authors offer the process as a model for other regions translating testing services to the web.
pmc-13650347:
Anne Sage and six colleagues, publishing in 2026, report early Australian experience with avacopan in teenagers who have ANCA-associated vasculitis, a rare disease where the immune system attacks small blood vessels. The drug blocks a complement receptor and helps adults reduce their steroid dose, yet almost no published experience covers children.

Eight adolescents nationwide received the drug as an add-on after standard induction treatment, starting at a median of two months after diagnosis. Five improved well and were able to taper steroids, while three still progressed to organ damage. No major side effects or serious infections appeared over a median of six months on the drug. The authors find the short-term safety reassuring and the benefit encouraging for most patients, and they call for larger studies in this rare childhood disease.
pmc-13650547:
Danfeng Zhang and five colleagues review molecular point-of-care testing, the shift of gene-based diagnosis from central laboratories to the bedside, the clinic, and low-resource settings. Conventional molecular tests are accurate but slow, costly, and chained to sophisticated buildings and cold chains.

New platforms copy DNA or RNA at constant temperature instead of cycling heat, use CRISPR systems to recognize targets with high specificity. Platforms also run everything on microfluidic chips linked to smartphones, giving sample-in, answer-out devices. Uses already span infection control, early cancer screening, heart emergency triage, and metabolic disease care. Obstacles remain: channels interfering when many targets run at once, enzymes that spoil without refrigeration, pricey core parts, and missing regulatory pathways. The authors look to synthetic biology, tighter integration, and artificial intelligence to carry the approach into routine care.
pmc-13651447:
Shane B Devine and five colleagues describe a 42-year-old woman whose skin eruption broke the usual rules of adult mastocytosis, a rare disorder of mast cell buildup. Children typically show varied, large lesions confined to skin, while adults usually show small uniform spots and carry disease in the bone marrow and beyond, so her case sat between the patterns.

Varied brown spots spread across her chest, abdomen, and arms, with flushing episodes, itching, and a positive skin-stroking sign. Biopsies of two lesions confirmed extra mast cells around vessels and between skin fibers. Bone marrow biopsy and blood testing found none of the markers of systemic disease: no dense clusters, no abnormal cell markers, no signature gene mutation, and a normal tryptase level. Antihistamine-style treatment settled symptoms. The authors urge clinicians to keep this polymorphic cutaneous form in mind for adults and to keep monitoring for systemic spread.
pmc-13656947:
Kelly Rea and colleagues interviewed teenagers and young adults who live at home with a durable heart pump, a ventricular assist device that supports a failing heart. More children are being sent home on such pumps, yet little was known about how adolescents experience daily life with one. Writing in twenty twenty-six, the team used a semi-structured interview guide spanning eight domains, developed with a learning network of centers and family input. Participants were current or recent home pump users at network sites, and two coders analyzed answers independently.

Emergency situations topped the list of worries, followed by infection and bleeding. Every participant reported some limits on life, most often time with friends and sports. Still, the title quote captures the balance many struck: life is not the old life, but the device still means freedom. The authors aim to improve discharge support.
pmc-13679147:
Rashid and co-authors pin gold-bismuth forms on a graphite base to make hydrogen. The forms sit on a pencil graphite prop in the build. Work ran in sour wet for the split of wet to gas. Gold parts bear a full 5d band, which caps their push. Bismuth parts grow skin rust fast, which caps theirs too. Each lone part thus shows thin push for the gas step.

Joined, the pair makes a base that boosts that push a lot. Gold lone needs 486 mV to hit the set flow mark. Bismuth lone needs 442 mV for that same flow mark. The joined base needs just 139 mV for the same mark. A Tafel slope of 141.4 marks the pace cap step there. That step is the first grab of a charge part in the run.
pmc-2763347:
Urban, Ermert, Schmid, and co-authors show that neutrophil extracellular traps carry calprotectin, a protein linked to defence against Candida albicans. Neutrophils are the first immune cells to reach an infection site. They kill microbes by swallowing them, by releasing stored proteins, or by casting out web-like traps.

Those traps were already known to ensnare microbes. The team found calprotectin, a protein complex from inside the cell, as part of the traps' killing cargo. The result ties a known antifungal protein to a newly found immune weapon, sharpening the picture of early defence.
pmc-3653747:
Cuthbert and Insel outline a new future for psychiatric diagnosis through the RDoC framework. Current diagnostic systems for mental disorders rely on presenting signs and symptoms. As a result, their definitions do not adequately reflect the underlying brain and behavioural systems involved.

That mismatch impedes research on causes and mechanisms, and slows development of better treatments. The authors present seven pillars for building diagnosis around dimensions of brain function instead of symptom checklists alone. RDoC reshaped how funding agencies frame mental health research, even as clinical diagnosis changes more slowly.
pmc-3969247:
McCambridge, Witton, and Elbourne published a systematic review in 2014 on the Hawthorne effect. The term names the idea that people change how they act when they know they are being studied. The review asked three things: does the effect exist, when does it appear, and how big is it.

The authors gathered and weighed all the evidence they could find under a broad definition. Their work shows the evidence is mixed and the concept is used in loose, conflicting ways. They argue that research needs clearer ideas about how taking part in a study shapes behavior, so future trials can be planned and read with more care.
pmc-4230647:
Hooijmans, Rovers, de Vries, and their colleagues built a risk of bias tool for animal studies in 2014. Systematic reviews of animal experiments were still uncommon, though their value was gaining notice. Animal studies differ from human trials in many ways, so trial tools do not fit them well.

Their tool, from the SYRCLE group, checks animal studies for the flaws most likely to bias results. Items cover how animals were assigned, housed, and assessed, and whether all outcomes were reported. Fair checks like these help reviewers judge whether animal findings are solid. Better appraisal can cut wasted follow-up work and improve translation to human medicine.
pmc-4700047:
McCormack, Dunn, Desai, and their team reported the PROUD study results in 2016. Earlier blinded trials showed that daily oral pre-exposure prophylaxis, or PrEP, lowers the risk of HIV infection. A worry remained that users might take more risks and cancel out the benefit.

PROUD was a pragmatic open-label trial, meaning participants knew they received the drug. Its pilot phase tested effectiveness under real-world conditions in clinics. The results addressed whether PrEP works when people know they are taking it. Evidence of this kind shaped national programs that offer PrEP to people at high risk of HIV.
pmc-4866047:
Pereira, Chin, Rueda, and their colleagues profiled mutations in breast cancers in 2016. Breast cancer genomes are highly varied, and that variety, within and between tumors, makes treatment hard to plan. The team sequenced a panel of genes in a very large set of primary breast tumors.

By combining mutations with copy number and gene expression data, plus long-term outcomes, they refined the genomic and transcriptomic landscapes of the disease. Patterns in the combined data separate tumors into groups with different behavior. Such maps help doctors predict which cancers will return and which drugs fit each type. The study is a reference cohort for breast cancer genomics.
pmc-5481147:
Wick, Judd, Gorrie, and their team made Unicycler in 2017, a tool that builds bacterial genomes from mixed read types. One major platform gives reads that are short but near-exact, so genomes built from them are sound but broken into chunks. Other platforms give long reads that can span a whole genome, but with more errors.

Unicycler blends the two. It uses short reads for exactness and long reads to bridge gaps and close the genome into its full circle. Whole, closed genomes let labs track outbreaks and resistance genes with no missing pieces. Work that once took days of hand fixing became a single automated run.
pmc-5809547:
Sacha Epskamp, Denny Borsboom, and Eiko Fried wrote this tutorial on psychological networks in 2017. Network models treat mental traits and symptoms as parts that affect each other directly. Interest in this view has grown fast across psychology.

The tutorial shows how to estimate such networks from data and how to judge whether the result can be trusted. It warns that busy-looking networks can rest on shaky numbers. Worked examples guide readers through checks for accuracy and stability. For researchers tempted by network plots, the paper sets a careful standard for what claims the data can support.
pmc-8282847:
Ruben Sanchez-Garcia and colleagues presented DeepEMhancer in 2021, a deep learning tool that cleans up three dimensional maps from cryo-electron microscopy. These maps are a prized source of information for building models of protein structures. They usually arrive blurred at fine detail, because contrast fades at high resolution, so they need post-processing before modelers can read them well.

Older fixes adjust the whole map with one global correction, which can leave local detail uneven. DeepEMhancer instead learns from examples how a sharpened map should look, and applies that judgment throughout the volume. The authors show it improving the readability of real maps, helping structural biologists place atoms with more confidence.
pmc-8310547:
Pranavi Koppula, Li Zhuang, and Boyi Gan reviewed in 2020 a protein that many cancers lean on, the cystine transporter known as SLC7A11 or xCT. This transporter pulls cystine into the cell, where it feeds production of glutathione, a key part of the cell's antioxidant defenses. It is switched on at high levels in multiple human cancers.

The authors explain how that extra supply helps tumors grow and, at the same time, creates a dependency doctors might exploit. Blocking the transporter can starve cancer cells of antioxidant protection and push them toward ferroptosis, an iron linked form of cell death. The review connects basic transport biology to a concrete strategy for therapy.
prescott-conquest-mexico-vol-2-1847:
William Hickling Prescott published Volume 2 of his History of the Conquest of Mexico in 1847, part of his classic four-volume history of the Spanish conquest. Prescott, a Boston historian who worked with failing eyesight, drew on Spanish archives and chronicles. Volume 2 carries the story forward from the first volume.

Hernán Cortés and his small force press deeper against the Aztec world, facing alliances, battles, and reverses. Prescott told the tale with a novelist's pace while grounding it in letters and reports of the time. His history set the English-language account of the conquest for generations. This volume keeps the drama of the march and the siege at the center.
prescott-conquest-mexico-vol-3-1847:
Volume 3 of Prescott's History of the Conquest of Mexico appeared in 1847, continuing his four-volume account of the Spanish conquest. Prescott built the work from Spanish documents, soldiers' letters, and Aztec accounts in translation. The story now moves toward its climax in the Aztec capital.

Readers follow Cortés through flight, regrouping, and the long siege of the great lake city. Prescott weighed the cruelty and courage on both sides and described a world being destroyed in detail. His narrative was praised for fairness as well as style. The volume brings the conquest nearly to its end and shows why his history stayed a standard work for so long.
prescott-conquest-mexico-vol-4-1847:
Volume 4 of Prescott's History of the Conquest of Mexico, published in 1847, completes his classic four-volume history of the Spanish conquest. Prescott closed the story he had built from archives in Spain and Mexico. The fall of the Aztec Empire and its aftermath fill these pages.

Cortés rules a conquered land, faces rivals and royal inquiries, and ends his career under a cloud. Prescott judged the conquest's violence honestly while admiring the daring of its leaders. He also traced the early years of Spanish rule that followed. With this volume the first great English history of the conquest reached its end, and it shaped views of Mexico for a century.
prescott-conquest-peru-1847:
William H. Prescott published History of the Conquest of Peru in 1847, a companion to his Mexico volume. Francisco Pizarro and a small band of Spaniards confront the Inca Empire. Atahualpa's capture at Cajamarca, after a massacre in the square, opens the conquest. Civil war among the conquerors follows the empire's fall.

Prescott describes Inca roads, temples, and rule with romantic admiration. Gold, greed, and daring drive his narrative as in the earlier work. He worked, as before, from Spanish chronicles with the help of readers. The two conquest histories made American historiography respected abroad. Peru remains a gripping, if dated, epic of empire's violent birth.
quicherat-proces-jeanne-darc-vol4-1847:
Further papers and the old chronicles fill Quicherat's fourth volume, printed in 1847. The rehabilitation record runs on here, past the witness testimony of the third volume. To it Quicherat adds chronicles written in Joan's own century.

The chronicles tell her campaigns and capture as news and memory of the time, not as court proof. Set beside the trial files, they show how her fame spread while she still lived. The volume rounds out the picture of Joan beyond the courtroom walls. It gives the whole edition its depth in the wider record of the age.
reynolds-wagner-the-wehr-wolf-1847:
George Reynolds sends a cursed man through old Italy in Wagner, the Wehr-Wolf, his serial of 1846 to 1847. Wagner is a sage who sells his soul for youth, wealth, and a dark gift: he turns wolf when the moon is full. Love, crime, and the stake crowd his path through courts, woods, and the grip of the church's sleuths in a rich, wild plot.

The tale ran in cheap parts that crowds bought by the stack. It made the wolf man a star of mass print. Its zest and gore set the tone for cheap horror. It still reads fast.
savage-gorilla-description-1847:
Thomas Savage, a missionary and naturalist on the Gabon coast, named the gorilla to science in 1847. His paper, Notice of the External Characters and Habits of Troglodytes gorilla, gave the beast its first full learned account. The wild man of the woods of sailor tale became, in his hands, an animal of record.

Savage tells the gorilla's size, build, and ways from skins, skulls, and the tales of hunters he trusted. He sets the new ape beside man and the chimpanzee and marks where it stands apart. The paper founded the science of the gorilla at a stroke. All later study of the great ape starts from Savage's page.
schoolcraft-notes-on-the-iroquois-1847:
Henry Rowe Schoolcraft worked as an Indian agent in the Great Lakes region and married into an Ojibwe family, giving him rare access to native knowledge. His 1847 book gathers what he learned about the Iroquois confederacy, the powerful league of nations in New York.

Schoolcraft covers Iroquois government, the council system, and the condolence council that mourned dead chiefs and raised new ones. He retells myths and traditions and prints Iroquois pictographs, the picture records used to hold memory. Though later scholars corrected some of his claims, the book shaped American views of the Iroquois for generations.
schwann-microscopical-researches-1847:
Theodor Schwann was a German scientist who studied living tissue under the microscope. His Microscopical Researches appeared in English in 1847, in a version by Henry Smith. The book set out a bold claim about how plants and animals are built.

Schwann argued that all living things are made of cells. He showed how cells form, grow, and work in both plant and animal bodies. That single idea gave biology a firm base and still shapes how life is taught today. Few books have changed a whole science so deeply. Doctors and students across Europe read the work with care.
schwann-microscopical-researches-smith-1:
Theodor Schwann announced the cell theory in his Microscopical Researches, Englished by Henry Smith in 1847. The Sydenham Society published Smith's translation of the German work. Schwann argued that all living things, plant and animal alike, are built of cells. Structure and growth follow the same plan in both kingdoms.

He compares tissues under the microscope and traces how cells form and change. Eggs, embryos, and adult parts all fall under his single scheme. The book founded cell biology as a shared field. Its claim unified two sciences that had grown apart. Readers still cite it as a founding document. The evidence is patient and close.
sisters-pg4947:
Kathleen Norris wrote this novel of two sisters, issued as volume ten of her works and inscribed to Frances Rose Benet. A verse dedication honors a mother's grace carried into a daughter's work. Chapter one brings Cherry Strickland home in a rush of joy on a May night in California.

Cherry is eighteen and has been engaged to Martin for twenty-one minutes. Lilac scent and wet woods fill the air as she shuts the door and leans on it, breathless. Sweet fear mixes with her joy: the wonder may prove a dream. Norris builds a family tale on that threshold of love.
slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of-slave: Slave Narratives gathers talks with former slaves. The typed records came from the Federal Writers' Project of 1936-1938. The Library of Congress project put the set together. The Washington issue of 1941 names Paul Edwards as administrator. B. A. Botkin served as chief editor of the writers' unit. The contents list state sets in order. Alabama, Arkansas, and Florida come first. Nine files on the running of the project follow the opening note.
snow-ether-inhalation-1847:
John Snow turned to surgical anesthesia in his 1847 pamphlet on inhaling ether vapour. Ether had just entered surgery, and doses were guesswork. Snow made the first scientific study of how much vapour a patient needs. He built an inhaler to give a measured, steady dose.

Case reports from operations show the method at work on real patients. Snow records pulse, breathing, and depth of sleep with care. His aim was to make painless surgery safe as well as possible. The pamphlet marks the birth of anesthesia as a measured craft. Snow later became the queen's own chloroform doctor. The first edition holds the founding study.
state-of-the-union-addresses-pg5047:
George H. W. Bush gives three yearly addresses in one set. Their dates are January 31, 1990, January 29, 1991, and January 28, 1992. Three stars part each address from the next. The first opens by saying what it is not. He comes not to speak of the state of the government. He will not detail each new plan for the year. He comes to speak of the Union itself, and of the world.

Lone moments in the past split time in two, Bush holds. Many in the chamber lived in a world set in 1945. That year fixed the shape of nations. It fixed the pace of progress for millions. The year just ended broke that frame. The great turn of 1989 set off a chain of changes. A new era in the world's affairs starts there, he holds.
thackeray-vanity-fair-1847:
William Makepeace Thackeray published Vanity Fair in 1847, a long novel of English society during the Napoleonic Wars. Becky Sharp is a poor, clever orphan set on rising in the world. Her friend Amelia Sedley is kind, gentle, and far less worldly. Their fortunes rise and fall through love, marriage, war, and money troubles.

Thackeray calls his setting a fair where vanity is bought and sold. The Battle of Waterloo changes several lives at the midpoint. No character is a pure hero, as the subtitle warns. Thackeray narrates with wit, pity, and sharp social insight. Vanity Fair stands among the great panoramic novels in English.
the-great-round-world-and-what-is-going-:
Dated September 30, 1897, No. 47 of The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It is a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. Its lead item concerns the Armenians. The Sultan of Turkey is said to have ordered a commission to visit the villages that suffered from the massacres. Two Mussulmans, three Armenians, and a single Greek make up the commission. It is to note the schools, churches, and monasteries destroyed. The Sultan means to rebuild every one, and to raise orphan asylums for the children left parentless.

The paper adds the peace news. England holds firm: the Turks must quit Thessaly. The other Powers seem ready to fall in with her. The Sultan has raised no fresh bar. Peace, it seems, will be settled within a very short while. A further item begins on the Cubans. They are rejoicing, the paper says, over a great victory for their cause.
the-half-hearted-pg17047: John Buchan wrote The Half-Hearted. A note states that the tale is set in the closing years of the 19th century. Part I chapters include Evening in Glenavelin and The Makers of Empire. Part II chapters include The Eastern Road and The Hill-Fort. Later titles include The Way to Nazri. Only the title page, note, and contents are present here. The chapters themselves do not appear. A second record in the library carries the same front matter.
the-lock-and-key-library-the-most-intere: Despite its record title, what is present is the front matter of Stories by Modern French Novels, number five in the Lock and Key series edited by Julian Hawthorne. Only the header and table of contents are present, so the stories themselves do not appear. The contents list Victor Cherbuliez's Count Kostia, Paul Bourget's Andre Cornelis, and two anonymous pieces, The Last of the Costellos and Lady Betty's Indiscretion. The electronic edition is dated January 2000. The mismatch between the record's title and the French contents shown should be noted.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
The Mirror's number for Saturday, May 16, 1829, No. 370, illustrates Laleham Park, temporary residence of the young Queen of Portugal. Laleham, a Middlesex village between Shepperton and Staines, is famed among anglers for its transparent shallows. The Earl of Lucan's villa there, set in forty acres of fine elm timber, houses the little queen, kept in England out of harm's way.

She is described as lively and interesting, within a month of the age of Princess Victoria and Prince George of Cumberland, all born in May 1819. Her hair is very fair, her complexion pale, her eyes a sparkling light blue. She arrived in London the previous October and stayed first at Grillon's Hotel before her health required country air. A flat joke about Laleham being very low is duly recorded. Readers meet a child sovereign treated as a village celebrity.

For Saturday, November 28, 1829, the Mirror's No. 401 illustrates the Siamese Twins, newly arrived to occupy the whole town's attention. The engraving is called an accurate sketch of this extraordinary sport of nature. Deviations from nature's usual forms usually offend, the editors argue, but these boys' appearance raises no unpleasant emotion.

The earliest account is Dr. J. C. Warren's of Boston, in Silliman's Journal of October. Captain Coffin and Mr. Hunter received the twins from their mother in a Siamese village, where Hunter saw them fishing. Their father was dead, and the family lived in poverty, confined within limits by the Siamese government. Exhibition abroad was proposed to better their condition, for liberal compensation and a promised return. Their mother accompanied them aboard ship. Readers meet Chang and Eng's exhibition career at its London launch, framed as science and spectacle together.

No. 565 of The Mirror, dated September 8, 1832, describes a Persian bath from Mr. Buckingham's travels. The extract comes from his Travels in Assyria, Media, and Persia, published in 1829. Bathing in the East, the editors note, was a known luxury among readers of travel books.

The bath stood at Kermanshah, an important frontier town of Persia. A clean, painted porch led to a square undressing hall lit from above. Raised recesses ran along three sides, carried on four marble pillars with spiral fluting. A large marble cistern of cold water filled the centre, with coloured glass jars of fresh flowers at each end. Walls painted white on blue, with trees, birds, and beasts, complete the scene.
theophilus-essay-upon-various-arts-1847:
Theophilus was a monk and metal hand of the 1100s in Germany. His work, De Diversis Artibus, tells how the arts were then done. Robert Hendrie gave it English dress in 1847 as An Essay Upon Various Arts. The book is the chief text on the craft shops of the mid ages.

Paint, glass, and metal form the three great heads of the work. The monk tells how to grind hues, blow glass, and cast bells and cups. Each step is set down as a hand at the bench would need it. Few books bring the mid age shop so close to life.
tob-10047:
Apuleius wrote The Golden Ass in Latin in the ancient Roman world, and William Adlington's 1566 version was its first English translation. No other complete Latin novel survives from Rome. Its hero, Lucius, is a curious young man whose dabbling in magic goes badly wrong.

Instead of power, Lucius gets the body of a donkey. Kicked, beaten, and sold from master to master, he watches human greed, lust, and folly at close range and cannot speak to stop it. Release comes only when the goddess Isis restores him. Bawdy comedy and genuine religious feeling sit side by side throughout his misadventures.
tob-10347:
Jacques Collin de Plancy published his Dictionnaire Infernal in France in the early nineteenth century and kept enlarging it. The dictionary covers demons, magic, omens, and the occult in short entries. Later editions added the demon portraits that made the book famous.

Entries give each demon's rank, form, and powers, drawn from older grimoires and folklore. The engravings show horned, winged, and beast-like figures that still define how demons are drawn in popular culture. De Plancy wrote first as a skeptic and later as a Catholic, and the shift shows in the text. Part reference work, part show, it remains a rich source on demon lore.
tob-10547:
Nikola Tesla told his own life story in My Inventions, a set of six articles printed in 1919. The Serbian-born inventor had changed electrical power with his work on alternating current. Late in life, famous and short of money, he looked back.

Tesla recalls boyhood in Croatia, the flash of insight that gave him the rotating magnetic field, and his huge tests at Colorado Springs. He describes his habit of building machines whole in his mind before touching metal. The articles blend hard fact with bold claims, in a voice as odd and bright as the man himself.
tob-13147: John C. Street published The Hidden Way Across the Threshold in 1887, a work of the spiritualist age. It deals with contact with the dead and with the soul's passage beyond death, questions that filled seances and lecture halls in that era. Street writes as a believer explaining a hidden path across the boundary between the living and the dead. The book survives as a period piece of the seance era, of interest to readers who study nineteenth-century occult and spiritualist belief.
tob-4047:
William Blake published Songs of Innocence and of Experience as paired poems showing two contrary states of the human soul. Innocence sings of the Lamb, laughing children, and a piper piping joyful songs. Experience answers with the Tyger's burning symmetry, poison trees, and chimney sweepers whose waking misery indicts the world that made them.

Blake etched and hand-illuminated the originals himself, wedding text and image as one visionary work. The same titles recur transformed across the divide, a child of joy becoming a voice of accusation. Deceptively simple in form, the Songs remain the most visionary children's poems for adults in English, short enough to memorize and deep enough to argue over for life.
tob-4147:
Vishnu speaks to the earth goddess in the Garuda Purana, a scripture named for his eagle mount. S. V. Subrahmanyam's 1911 translation carries its teaching on death and what follows. It traces the soul's road after the body fails, past the judges of the dead. It ends with the heavens and hells that reward and punish.

Funeral rites and gifts for the dead receive careful directions, since Hindus still read the Purana at mourning times. Medicine, gems, and conduct also find room in its wide frame. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry. Hindus know it as their book of the dead.
tob-4185-78147:
Volume two of Goodwin's Moralia carries on Plutarch's essays on the conduct of life. One famous piece weighs superstition and finds it worse than unbelief, since fear of the gods poisons every joy. Others praise brotherly love and ask why divine justice sometimes seems slow.

Plutarch also teaches the art of listening, a skill he thinks schools neglect. Stories from history enliven each lesson, and the counsel stays concrete. He writes as a wise friend rather than a stern judge. Goodwin's dignified nineteenth-century English suits the material well. Readers gain a full picture of Greek moral thought at its kindest.
transactions-of-the-american-society-of-:
Beverly S. Randolph studies how locomotive pulling power changes with the length of a grade in Paper No. 1172. Discussion by C. D. Purdon and John C. Trautwine Jr. follows the paper. Randolph argues that careful study of grade resistance can cut the cost of running a railway.

The usual rule credited a locomotive with 20 to 25 percent of its driver weight as pull, but practice varied widely. Randolph gathered operating records from many roads to find a working basis. His table shows the share of driver weight used in draft depends on grade length as well as steepness. Data come from Baldwin Locomotive Works catalogues and later records.
turgenev-jew-and-other-stories-1847:
Constance Garnett translated the early tales in The Jew and Other Stories from Ivan Turgenev's first years as a writer. The title story, written in the 1840s, is set amid the Napoleonic wars in Germany. A young Russian officer tells how an army spy, a Jewish sutler, was caught and hanged despite his pleas.

Other tales here try out themes Turgenev later mastered: first love, wasted lives, and kind hearts in hard places. The hand is younger and the plots lean on chance more than in his novels. Still, the clear prose and sympathy that mark his best work are present. The volume lets readers watch a major novelist learning his trade story by story.
twelfth-night-pg2247: Malvolio's downfall delights in this edition: the puritan steward, tricked by the forged letter, smiles himself into the dark room. Meanwhile Viola loves Orsino, who loves Olivia, who loves Cesario. The most musical of the comedies, melancholy and merry together.
twining-memo-1947:
The Air Force's chief of materiel gave the first high word on the flying discs in September 1947. General Nathan Twining's memo of September 23 holds that the thing reported is real and not a dream or fake. His Air Materiel Command had charge of the new reports that summer.

Twining tells of craft that climb and turn past any plane of the age, as pilots had sworn to him. He asks for a full study, and Project Sign was born of that ask. The memo stands at the head of the whole Air Force UFO file. No later paper in the line counts for more.
ueber-den-verfall-der-alchemie-und-die-h:
A German lecture on the decline of alchemy, delivered on January 31, 1845, opens by recalling an earlier talk. Two years before, the speaker had traced alchemy's origin and spread: the art of making gold and silver from matter that holds none. The philosopher's stone stood at the center of that account.

Now he turns to the fall, and to one late proof of alchemy's reach: the hermetic society active around 1800. Gold-making fever, he says, entered every rank of cultivated Europe as early as the thirteenth century. Learned men defended the art, courts and theologians backed it, and physicians dreamed of an alchemical cure-all. The lecture survives in widely spaced, hard-read print.
ueber-die-alchemie-ein-vortrag-im-wissen: A Berlin lecture on alchemy survives here through a damaged title page dated 1847. The page announces a talk given to a scientific society at Berlin on February 20, 1847. The speaker held a doctorate in medicine and philosophy and a chair of chemistry at the University of Halle. Eduard Anton published the pamphlet in 1847. The author's name is too garbled in the scan to read with confidence. Only this title page is present here, so the lecture itself does not appear.
un-ga-res-1747:
Southern Rhodesia, a British colony in southern Africa run by a white minority regime, came before the UN General Assembly in Resolution 1747, adopted on 28 June 1962. The Assembly had weighed the report of its decolonization team. It notes that most people in the colony had rejected the 1961 constitution forced on them.

The text deplores the denial of equal rights and votes to the African majority. It faults Britain for not yet handing all powers to the people of the land, as the 1960 call for an end to colonial rule requires. The fight over Rhodesia would run at the UN for two more decades.
un-ga-res-47:
Thanks close out the story of Resolution 47, passed by the General Assembly on 11 December 1946. A year before, the Assembly had formed a team to drum up support for UNRRA, the relief agency feeding a war-torn Europe, in its final stage. The team now reports back: member states had backed the agency's work to a large degree, and the aid had helped rebuild lands laid waste by war.

The Assembly warmly thanks the team's chair and members for their work. It notes that a small share of the pledged sums had still not come in. The chair is asked to press the states concerned to complete their gifts, so the agency can finish its task in full.
un-ga-res-a-69-47:
Standard arms, the guns and tanks of daily war, do their worst harm close to home. Resolution A/69/47, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session, argues that control of such arms must be sought first at the level of regions and sub-regions. Most threats to peace since the Cold War, it notes, flare up between states that share the same corner of the map.

The text recalls a long chain of yearly votes on the point, back to 1993. It holds that keeping a fair balance in the defense strength of states in a region serves calm. Arms control built on local trust, in this view, beats rules imposed from far away.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 1747 (XVI) was adopted on 28 June 1962. It took up the question of Southern Rhodesia. The Assembly backed the findings of its Special Committee on decolonization. It stated that the territory was a Non-Self-Governing Territory under the Charter. Its people had mostly rejected the constitution set in December 1961.

Britain, as the ruling power, was asked to call a conference of all political parties at once. The conference was to write a new constitution based on one person, one vote. The text also asked Britain to restore the rights of the non-European population. It asked Britain to end laws built on racial discrimination and free political prisoners. It asked Britain to work toward a free African state.

General Assembly Resolution 47 was adopted on 11 December 1946, at the fifty-fifth plenary meeting. It concerned the closing stage of UNRRA, the relief body for lands wrecked by war. The Assembly thanked its UNRRA committee for drumming up support. It noted that most pledged gifts had arrived, but a small share had not. It urged the member governments concerned to send in the balance. That way UNRRA could finish its task with the full sum its council had set.

General Assembly resolution 69/47 (2014) argues that conventional arms control belongs mainly at the regional and subregional level, because most post-Cold War threats arise between neighbors. The Assembly decides to give urgent consideration to regional conventional arms control. It asks the Conference on Disarmament to formulate principles that could frame regional agreements. It requests the Secretary-General to collect member states' views and report to the seventieth session. Keeping a balance of defence capabilities at the lowest possible level is treated as the goal.
un-sc-res-1347:
Judges for the Rwanda war crimes tribunal were the business of 30 March 2001. The Security Council had received nominations for the International Tribunal for Rwanda. Under the tribunal's statute, the Council forwards a shortlist to the General Assembly. The Assembly then elects the judges. The names sent forward came from five African states. They were Benin, Zambia, Lesotho, Malawi, and Madagascar.

The one-paragraph act is a standard step in building the court. The tribunal, based in Arusha, tried those accused of leading the 1994 genocide in Rwanda. Its bench needed judges from many legal systems. Forwarding the list kept the election timetable on track.
un-sc-res-1447:
Iraq's oil-for-food programme was extended by the Security Council on 4 December 2002. The programme, set by resolution 986 (1995), let Iraq sell oil to buy food and medicine under United Nations control. The Council said it remained a temporary measure for the civilian needs of the Iraqi people. It pointed to the Secretary-General's report of 12 November 2002 on the programme's working.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council kept the programme's provisions in force for a new 180-day period starting on 5 December 2002.
